papers.abstract:
Across developed nations, economic and political inequalities have crossed the threshold. In their historical trajectory, severity, and resistance to change, twenty-first century inequalities suggest more than an unfortunate confluence of circumstances in markets or geopolitics, more than an ill-fated policy consensus or coalition of political movements, and more, even, than a pernicious ideological or technological paradigm. Involving but transcending such factors, the inequality crisis engulfing the developed world suggests the emergence of oligarchy. 

This article offers a new procedural account of democracy that tracks and conceptualises the emergence of oligarchy. This new procedural account specifies developed nations' primary and secondary means of political production, which oligarchy captures through private financial control. The means of political production function as mechanisms for participation, representation, leadership, accountability and moderation of state power, but never in a neutral sense. Whether those mechanisms are equal or unequal, democratic or oligarchic, depends on a great body of fundamental law, the law that constitutes governments, governs law and policy making, and determines the relationship between private financial power and political power.

Part I analyzes the minimal procedural definition of democracy that spread around the world at the end of the twentieth century. Part II examines the extreme inequalities, democratic backsliding and unmitigated climate change produced in conjunction with this limited form of democracy. Part III analyzes a neglected body of evidence that exposes what the components and mechanisms of oligarchy that emerged within the limited procedural definition of democracy. Part IV arranges these components and mechanisms in a systematic fashion to provide revised procedural accounts of democracy and oligarchy.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: The Fundamental Law of Oligarchy: on the Transnational Constitutional Foundations of the Inequality Crisis

papers.abstract: Does capital or labor income drive overall relative income mobility? This article examines the dynamics of capital and labor intra-generational income mobility, utilizing individual-level income registers from Norway covering almost 300,000 individuals observed over 26 years. It introduces a novel methodological framework to decompose total income mobility into the contributions of its components across the life cycle. We present three key findings on the subject. First, different capital and labor income mobility measures along the respective uni-dimensional distributions do not convey clear income-factor mobility orderings. Second, upward total income mobility is mainly driven by upward labor income mobility and by the joint upward mobility of capital and labor. Third, downward total income mobility is mainly driven by downward capital income mobility and by the joint downward mobility of capital and labor.  These results are robust to considering only high upward or downward jumps and are discussed in light of recent theoretical and empirical findings on the dynamics of compositional inequality and homoploutia in capital and labor, both within countries and globally.
papers.subtheme: Income Mobility Over the Life Cycle
papers.title: Capital and Labor Income Mobility

papers.abstract:
Demographic ageing in Europe is expected to increase age-related public expenditures while placing pressure on future tax bases, raising concerns about the long-term sustainability of public finances. At the same time, the ageing of large wealth-holding cohorts will substantially increase the volume of intergenerational wealth transfers. Since 50–60 percent of wealth in Europe is inherited rather than self-accumulated, the design of inheritance taxation is central to debates on wealth concentration, intergenerational equity, and fiscal sustainability.

This paper applies the Inheritance Tax Simulation Model (INTAXMOD) to 13 EU Member States, combining HFCS microdata with a top-tail Pareto correction using rich-list information and harmonized demographic projections. It presents the first cross-national microsimulation of a harmonized inheritance tax framework in the EU. Three policy scenarios are analyzed: a French-style progressive schedule, a main-residence exemption scheme, and a top-1% inheritance tax. The results show that inheritances are highly concentrated, with roughly two thirds accruing to the top decile, and that all scenarios can generate substantial revenue—around 0.5% of GDP—despite high exemption thresholds. Projected inheritance volumes are expected to double by 2050, underscoring the growing relevance of inheritance taxation for addressing wealth inequality and ensuring fiscal sustainability.
papers.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
papers.title: The Distribution and Taxation of Inheritances: Microsimulation Evidence for a Common European Inheritance Tax

papers.abstract: Using an original survey of 12,000 respondents representative of eleven high-income countries (the United States, Japan, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and seven European countries), I examine public support for international redistribution and climate policies, as well as its sensitivity to key policy features such as the size of transfers and country coverage. Although global inequality is not a salient concern, it is perceived as a significant injustice. There is majority acceptance in every country for nearly all global policies tested, including those that would redistribute 5 percent of global income or entail personal costs for respondents. An information treatment shows that support for global policies causally increases among respondents who perceive them as likely; an effect opposite to warm glow. Support for international policies decreases only slightly as country coverage shrinks. Overall, the results reinforce previous findings and suggest that a broad coalition of countries could feasibly advance sustainable development.
papers.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
papers.title: Public Acceptance of International Redistribution in High-Income Countries

papers.abstract: Newly matched data on IVF treatments are used to estimate the long run impact of children on labor market earnings, also known as child penalties. We compare the earnings of first-time treated women and men up to 25 years after their first IVF treatment. For women, not  men, we find a large penalty shortly after the birth of the first child, but in the long run, the penalty fades out, vanishes after 10 years, and even turns into a positive but insignificant premium after 15 years. These findings challenge the notion that children are the primary drivers behind the persistent gender gap in earnings.
papers.subtheme: Gender Inequality - General
papers.title: Is There Really a Child Penalty in the  Long Run? New Evidence from IVF Treatments

papers.abstract:
Although economists widely advocate carbon pricing as an effective
solution to reduce carbon emissions, this mechanism has had so far limited
effects. This paper proposes a new type of tax to help finance (and accelerate)
the green transition. The A Carbon Wealth Tax (CWT) is proposed
to be levied on carbon-intensive (brown) wealth rather than primarily on
carbon-intensive goods. We consider tax implementation issues such as tax
base, incidence, and efficiency. Moreover, we analyze the impacts of such
a tax scheme by setting up a model of asset pricing and dynamic portfolio
decisions. Green and carbon-intensive returns used in the model are
calibrated with low-frequency returns on stock prices between 2010 and
2021. We find that such a tax and subsidy scheme is a feasible and effective
instrument in speeding up the transition to a greener economy, particularly
in protracted periods of economic contraction. Our approach also brings a
new perspective to the wealth inequality discussions.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: A Carbon Wealth Tax: Modelling, Empirics, and Policy

papers.abstract:
In India, elections decide both political power and access to economic resources. Agricultural credit, vital for rural livelihoods, is particularly vulnerable to partisan influence. This study investigates whether political alignment with the ruling coalition systematically affects the allocation of agricultural credit and uncovers the mechanisms through which alignment shapes credit delivery. In doing so, it connects the literature on distributive politics, agricultural institutions, and causal inference using close elections.
The study employs a fuzzy regression discontinuity design (RDD), exploiting quasi-random variation from closely contested state assembly elections in India from 2010 and 2024. Electoral data from the Election Commission of India are merged with district-level agricultural credit data from the Reserve Bank of India. Political alignment is defined as the share of constituencies in a district represented by members of the ruling coalition. In this two-stage least squares (2SLS) framework, the instrumental variable is the fraction of constituencies narrowly won (≤2% margin) by the ruling coalition, following established close-election approaches. Robustness checks, including alternative bandwidths, election-year fixed effects, and covariate continuity tests, confirm the validity of the design.
The analysis shows that political alignment exerts no significant impact on aggregate credit flows across all banks. However, disaggregated results highlight important institutional variation. Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) exhibit statistically significant increase of 6.02 percent in direct agricultural credit to aligned districts. Given their hybrid governance structure (jointly owned by the Centre, the State, and sponsoring banks) and deep rural penetration, RRBs emerge as the primary conduit of politically motivated credit allocation. Private and Small Finance Banks display positive but less robust responses, suggesting indirect sensitivity to political cycles through integration with public schemes. The effects are concentrated in direct agricultural lending (e.g., crop loans, input financing), which is electorally salient and immediately visible to rural voters, rather than in indirect credit for long-term investments.
This study contributes to political economy debates by showing that partisan alignment influences not only intergovernmental transfers, but also sector-specific credit delivery. It highlights the institutional channels, particularly RRBs, through which distributive politics operate in rural economies and demonstrates the utility of fuzzy RDD and electoral discontinuities for causal inference in complex political-financial contexts. The findings underscore that, while aggregate agricultural credit flows remain stable, political alignment systematically shapes their distribution through local institutions. This raises concerns about allocative efficiency, moral hazard, and regional inequality in rural credit markets, offering new insights into the intersection of politics, finance, and rural development.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Political Influence on Agricultural Credit Allocation: Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design in India

papers.abstract: This study uses Costa Rica to examine how income shocks and inequality affect declining voter turnout and the rise of multi-party systems. Since 1998, Costa Rica has experienced a significant decrease in electoral participation, providing a unique perspective to investigate socio-economic factors influencing voter behaviour. By combining electoral registries with social security employer-employee records at the individual level, this research delivers novel insights from a developing democracy with a robust electoral tradition. The findings indicate a positive relationship between income and voter turnout, significantly moderated by inequality. High inequality increases electoral mobilisation among voters at income extremes, while lower inequality enhances participation among middle-income groups. Individuals experiencing downward income mobility exhibit higher electoral engagement, suggesting economic hardship motivates voter turnout in the short term. These conclusions are validated through three identification strategies: random assignment of voters to polling stations within polling centres, income loss from unexpected mass layoffs, and income variations linked to changes in international agricultural prices. Income shocks have also notably reshaped electoral dynamics, especially affecting the historical PLN party, which shifted its support from middle-income voters to the poorest and wealthiest segments.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Income Shocks, Economic Inequality, and Political Realignment: Voter Turnout and the Shift to a Multi-Party System in Costa Rica

papers.abstract: We examine how intergenerational educational mobility has evolved in South Africa - one of the most unequal countries in the world, where inequality is historically rooted in a single key inherited circumstance: race. Using nationally representative panel data, we estimate both absolute and relative mobility trends across birth cohorts spanning five decades covering both the Apartheid and post-Apartheid periods, and formally decompose mobility into within- and between-race components. We show that mobility has risen dramatically, with South Africa now ranking among the most mobile countries in the world with respect to educational attainment. These gains are heterogeneous. Mothers exert stronger influence than fathers; daughters, who began with lower mobility, have converged to sons; and mobility has improved most for African Black and Coloured adults. Most importantly, we show that the structure of persistence has shifted fundamentally from being historically overwhelmingly explained by between-race differences to now being determined by within‐race variation. These findings indicate that race no longer primarily determines intergenerational mobility, reflecting real progress in dismantling the legacy of Apartheid in the country, but should not be interpreted as evidence that broader economic inequality has eased.
papers.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
papers.title: Progress and Persistence: Race and Intergenerational Educational Mobility in South Africa

papers.abstract:
This paper introduces a novel global database on estate, inheritance, and gift (EIG) taxation,
which covers more than 160 countries — some with data going back to the 18th century — and
represents over 90% of the world’s population and GDP. Using this comprehensive and harmonised dataset, we document long-term global trends in EIG taxation, which are marked by
declining numbers of countries levying such taxes, reductions in top marginal rates, and diminished progressivity since the 1980s. However, substantial cross-country heterogeneity persists in tax design, rates, and exemption thresholds. Leveraging both global and U.S. state-level data, we estimate the elasticity of EIG tax revenues with respect to top marginal rates, finding that a one percentage point increase in the top rate raises revenues by approximately 7%, with larger effects in recent decades.We also show that the erosion of EIG taxes is associated with long-term increases in wealth concentration: five years after a one percentage point decrease in the top rate, the Gini coefficient increases by 0.14, on average. Our conclusions offer new insights into the pivotal role of EIG tax policies in shaping fiscal resources and wealth distribution.
papers.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
papers.title: Inheritance Tax Around the Globe Over Two Centuries: Revenue and Distributional Implications

papers.abstract: This paper compares the "mental maps'' of redistribution among politicians and citizens across seven parliaments, using original in-person surveys of sitting MPs and nationally representative citizen samples. Fairness beliefs and ideology are the strongest correlates of support for redistribution in both groups, while misperceptions of wealth concentration matter for citizens but much less for politicians. A central finding is that politicians hold markedly more polarized views on redistribution than citizens, including within the same party families. We also find systematic elite-voter gaps: left MPs are more supportive than their voters (notably on inheritance taxation), whereas right/liberal MPs are less supportive than theirs. These patterns point to a representation concern and a bargaining space among elites that is narrower than in the electorate.
papers.subtheme: Preferences for redistribution
papers.title: Preferences for redistribution policies among politicians and citizens

papers.abstract: Since intra-household resource distribution is unobserved, it is difficult to compare how women and children fare across countries. To address this, we analyze 45 household expenditure surveys from predominantly low- and middle-income countries, i.e. an international sample of around 2.4 million individuals. Using harmonized estimations of intra-household resource sharing, we construct globally comparable measures of gender inequality and child poverty in consumption. Our findings reveal a widespread imbalance: women receive about one-fifth less than men, leading to a 60% higher poverty rate. Children appear to fare even worse, though this is partly explained by differences in needs and sibling economies of scale. Intra-household inequalities are more pronounced in poorer countries and among low-income households within countries. Cross-checks with nutritional proxies tend to validate our results, linking household poverty and intra-household disparities to child undernutrition. Finally, we decompose global individual consumption inequality and find that 13%-32% (across measures) stems from inequality within households.
papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: Global Evidence on Gender Gaps and Child Poverty in Consumption

papers.abstract: Evidence increasingly highlights large disparities in emissions both between and within countries. However, detailed individual-level data on emission-intensive activities remain scarce. In this paper, we analyze the asset and sectoral composition of the wealth of the top 501 billionaires and construct a dataset linking assets to emissions. Our estimates reveal extreme concentration of wealth and emissions even within this small sample, with publicly traded equity in Basic Materials, Industrials, and Utilities playing a disproportionate role as sources of emissions. We propose a carbon wealth tax that achieves a triple objective: effectively taxing billionaires to curb inequality, targeting the most polluting activities, and raising substantial resources to finance a sustainable and equitable transition.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Billionaires’ emissions and climate finance: the case for a carbon wealth tax

papers.abstract: This paper investigates how global governance structures shape the provision and distribution of global public goods (GPGs). We compile a novel historical database on the finances and governance of multilateral institutions since their inception after World War I, covering annual balance sheets and decision-making rules of the League of Nations, the Bretton Woods institutions (IBRD, IDA, IMF), the United Nations and its key agencies (ILO, WTO, UNESCO, WHO), as well as regional and multilateral development banks. We find that less democratic institutions—those governed by wealth-weighted voting systems such as the World Bank and the IMF—generate two systematic distortions: (a) unequal burden sharing and (b) geopolitical appropriation of resources. First, richer countries with greater voting power contribute less as a share of GDP, contradicting Olson’s (1965) hypothesis of the “exploitation of the great by the small” and revealing instead an “exploitation of the small by the great.” Second, around 90% of IBRD and 60% of IMF disbursements are directed toward G7 military and commercial allies. To address potential endogeneity, we exploit the network structure of partnerships to construct leave-own-out instrumental variables based on third parties military alliances and free trade agreements. Importantly, more democratic institutions such as the United Nations display progressive contribution schemes and show no evidence of GPG appropriation. Finally, we develop a simple theoretical model of GPG provision under weighted-voting systems that rationalizes these empirical patterns. The findings have implications for the design of a more democratic and equitable architecture of global governance.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: The Global Democratic Deficit: Institutional Asymetries and the Provision of Global Public Goods

papers.abstract: Inequality in the Global North has skyrocketed over the past few decades, and yet voters have not demanded redistribution at the ballot box. This curious phenomenon has recently revitalised the study of political cleavages and political inequality. Why are redistributive parties not electorally successful and why are poor voters not supporting them en masse? In this paper, I argue that the 2010s saw the emergence of a new type of redistributive party, that was both electorally successful and supported by working class voters. I call these parties anti-austerity parties, because they emerged in European countries that implemented severe austerity after the Global Financial Crisis. I assemble a dataset that includes the history of political cleavages in the so-called European periphery (Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Ireland, Portugal, Spain). To that end, I also include an original discussion of the history of political cleavages in Greece (1981-2023) and Cyprus (2001-2021), adding both countries to the World Political Cleavages and Inequality Database (WPID). This allows me to analyse the distinct demand-side characteristics that anti-austerity parties display. My main finding is that unlike other left-wing parties, anti-austerity parties continue to enjoy strong working-class support.
papers.subtheme: Voting, Participation and Electoral Cleavages
papers.title: The Anti-Austerity Party: A Neglected Party of the Working Class

papers.abstract:
The effects of regional mobility during childhood on educational attainment and its transmission across generations remain underexplored in Europe. Using micro-level data on three linked generations from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), we track moves across European regions linked to historical GDP per capita at the regional level. For the parents’ generation (G2), born between 1920–1950, moving to a better region before age 18 is associated with gains of up to 0.85 years of schooling. Conversely, for the children’s generation (G3), born between 1960–1980, it is associated with a reduction of roughly 0.6 years of education, except when parents have tertiary education, in which case moving becomes beneficial. To achieve causality, we also adopt a sibling comparison strategy exploiting variation
in the age of move and length of exposure which nets out all unobserved parental
characteristics. We find that an additional year in a better region raises educational
attainment by about 0.03 years. Overall we find evidence of a generational reversal
indicating growing stratification by family background.
papers.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
papers.title: Born Here, Raised There: Regional Mobility And Intergenerational Transmission of Education in Europe

papers.abstract: Wealth inequality is increasing around the world, sparking political and academic debate about whether and how to address it; hence, a wealth tax is back in the discussion. Evidence about the distribution of wealth in Latin America is relatively scarce but is growing, pointing at an extreme concentration of wealth. Could a wealth tax help reduce this inequality? How much revenue could it actually raise? We combine wealth surveys, lists of billionaires, and net wealth macro-aggregates to simulate the distributional effects of different designs for a wealth tax in Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Uruguay. We also account for administrative costs and behavioural responses, based on the literature, to assess the tax's capacity to raise revenue and illustrate some of the trade-offs to be considered. The estimates of the distributional effects of such taxation are modest in the short run, but a simple dynamic exercise shows that the cumulative effect is substantial. In addition, our benchmark revenue estimate, which takes into account behavioural responses, indicates that a 1% tax on the top 1% of the wealthiest households would raise on average 0.9% of the GDP in revenue. Different designs of this tax (both in terms of rates and tax base) and assumptions regarding behavioural responses change the projected revenue, but the orders of magnitude involved suggest that wealth taxes could indeed help raise much-needed revenue in the region.
papers.subtheme: Wealth Taxation and Capital Income Tax Design
papers.title: Taxing the Rich in Latin America: Effects of a Wealth Tax on Revenue and Distribution

papers.abstract:
Using a combination of individual-level, bioclimatic, ethnographic, and archaeological data, we investigate the ancient origins of cross-country differences in preferences for redistribution. Our hypothesis is that contemporary attitudes toward redistribution originate from ancestral levels of inequality, which are the result of adaptive responses of pre-Neolithic hunter-gatherer societies to seasonal food shortage determined by the seasonality of the wild progenitors of domesticated crops. 
Employing contemporary survey data and an epidemiological approach, we first show that migrants originating from countries with higher ancestral inequality exhibit lower support for redistribution, and we establish that this relationship is driven by the level of crop seasonality in the migrants' origin countries. 
Next, using data from premodern societies, we show that crop seasonality induces food storage practices, which in turn lead to inequality through population growth and social complexity. The positive effect of food storage on inequality is corroborated by data from archaeological sites. 
Finally, using data from preindustrial polities, we uncover that the mechanism linking food storage to redistributive preferences is represented by the positive influence of the former on tolerance for inequality.
papers.subtheme: Preferences for redistribution
papers.title: Ancestral Inequality and Preferences for Redistribution

papers.abstract: This paper examines how the use of formal childcare services affects parental allocation of paid and unpaid work time in Austria. Using microdata from the Austrian Time Use Survey 2021/22, we analyse a sample of 671 different-sex couple households with children who use some form of formal childcare. We distinguish between paid work, unpaid housework, and unpaid carework, and estimate the effects of increasing children’s hours spent in formal childcare on (1) parents’ combined working hours, (2) mothers’ and fathers’ individual work time, and (3) gender time gaps within households. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression models are employed to estimate the associations, controlling for relevant socio-demographic characteristics. The results show that increased use of formal childcare is associated with a significant increase in couples’ combined working hours on the labour market and an even bigger and significant reduction in unpaid working time, particularly in childcare duties, which results in an overall reduction in total working hours for parents. The results on parents’ individual work time patterns, however, reveal that these shifts are primarily driven by mothers, who reduce their unpaid care and housework hours while increasing their participation in the labour market. Fathers’ time allocation, in contrast, remains largely unaffected: their paid working hours show no significant change, and their unpaid work decreases only marginally. These findings demonstrate that the expansion of formal childcare services has substantial potential to alleviate mothers’ double burden of balancing paid and unpaid work, and to narrow gender time gaps within households. However, the persistence of traditional gender norms in Austria limits the extent of this progress. The observed convergence in parental working hours arises predominantly through mothers’ adaptation, rather than a corresponding increase in fathers’ engagement in unpaid work. From a policy perspective, the results imply that the provision of high-quality, affordable, and full-day childcare is a critical lever for promoting gender equality in both the labour market and the household and complementary social and family policies, such as non-transferable parental leave quotas for fathers, flexible working arrangements, and initiatives promoting men’s participation in carework are essential to foster more equitable work-family dynamics.
papers.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
papers.title: Closing the gender time gap: how formal childcare affects parental work and care dynamics

papers.abstract: This paper studies the distributional impacts of carbon pricing policies using a multi-sector general equilibrium (GE) model with input-output linkages, heterogeneous agents, and segmented labor markets. Households differ in their consumption patterns, labor types, and ownership of equity and capital. Pricing the carbon content of products affects households’ real income through an expenditure channel, according to the emissions intensity of their consumption baskets, and an earnings channel, as GE responses shift the relative demand for labor types and returns on profits and rents. Calibrating the model with matched microdata for the Brazilian economy, we find regressive effects stemming from both channels. Ignoring the production networks and the gross complementarity between fuels, inputs, and factors leads to a substantial underestimation of both aggregate and distributional effects. The incidence of the policy depends on how the revenue is recycled: expanding targeted social transfers fully offsets the regressive impact, whereas using the revenue to reduce preexisting consumption taxes improves efficiency but does not eliminate regressivity.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: The Network Origins of Carbon Pricing Regressivity

papers.abstract: Turnout gaps may arise from informal barriers that influence beliefs about voting rights, limiting the effective scope of universal suffrage. This study examines the role of gender norms and social pressure in shaping the gender gap in voter turnout in Switzerland. A triple-difference design exploits three sources of variation: results of the 1971 referendum on female suffrage to measure (male) local norms about whether women should vote, gender differences in turnout, and the staggered introduction of postal voting between 1978 and 2005, which reduced the observability of voting. Before postal voting, women in municipalities with more regressive norms voted significantly less, resulting in a wider gender turnout gap. This gap decreases by approximately 80% when voting becomes less observable, mainly due to higher turnout among women in regressive areas. These findings show that turnout gaps are not only due to preferences, but they are also influenced by social norms, and that reducing observability through institutional reforms can weaken social pressure, enhance representation, and strengthen universal suffrage.
papers.subtheme: Voting, Participation and Electoral Cleavages
papers.title: Gender Norms, Social Pressure, and the Gender Gap in Turnout: Evidence from Swiss Elections

papers.abstract: Western democracies seem to be approaching the tipping point of a long and profound transformation in the structures of their political conflict. This paper studies the Portuguese exception, a unique case where traditional left-right divides remain stable relative to other Western countries. Exploring newly assembled granular local-level data, I uncover a remarkable persistence of income, ownership, education, and professional political cleavages, even after the recent emergence of the nationalist right. Contrary to other countries, traditional left-wing parties continue to find strong support from the least educated and lower income working-class communities, while the traditional right attracts more educated and higher income voters. I argue that the Portuguese left's success in demonstrating effective predistributive education and labor policies has preserved its historic working-class voter base, while the traditional right has retained the support from upper middle-class voters with `meritocratic' preferences. The nationalist right was exceptionally successful in the richest but relatively less educated communities. Its rise could be seen as a backlash from historically privileged groups who have seen the catching-up of an increasingly educated upper middle class, and an increasingly well-off working-class, erode their previously unchallenged social status. Overall, these findings indicate that political parties' ability to carry out policies and reforms that effectively address long-term inequality can be a key factor in maintaining resilient voter bases.
papers.subtheme: Political Inequalities - General
papers.title: The Western Exception: Declining Inequality and Persistent Political Cleavages in Portugal

papers.abstract: Widely regarded as a barometer for equality of opportunity, intergenerational mobility has attracted renewed attention amid concerns that it has declined in the wake of rising economic inequality since the 1970s. Although earlier research documents stability, or even modest increases, in mobility among cohorts who entered the labor market before this period, evidence for more recent cohorts is limited and inconsistent. In this study, we analyze contemporary trends in class mobility using a new approach based on the "synthetic dynasties" represented in Markov chains. This approach yields several novel measures of movement and memory, which respectively capture how class positions differ from one generation to the next and how the influence of class origins dissipates across generations. Applying these methods to data from the U.S., we find that overall levels of movement and memory have remained largely stable across cohorts born between 1945 and 1990. This stability, however, masks offsetting class-specific trends. Among those from the upper and lower classes, movement has declined and memory has increased. In contrast, among the middle classes, movement has risen and memory has weakened.
papers.subtheme: Class mobility (U.S.)
papers.title: Class Mobility in the Era of Rising Inequality: A Synthetic Dynasty Analysis

papers.abstract: Transaction taxes on housing are widely used but often viewed as inefficient and poorly targeted. We study the United Kingdom's 2020-21 Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) holiday, which unexpectedly raised the tax-free threshold on residential purchases from £125,000 to £500,000 and temporarily eliminated tax liability for most transactions. Using universe-level administrative data on property transfers and SDLT receipts, combined with local-authority-level measures of exposure based on pre-reform price distributions, we implement a high-frequency continuous difference-in-differences event-study design. The holiday increased transactions by about 18 percent and raised prices by roughly 1 percent, with around 37 percent of the tax cut capitalized into higher prices. We estimate a fiscal cost of £1.6 billion - about one-quarter of residential SDLT revenue during the relief period - with no persistent stimulus once the policy expired. Distributional effects were markedly regressive: upper-middle-income households (income deciles 7-9) captured net gains of around 10 percent of annual income, while first-time and lower-income buyers benefited only marginally, and the Gini coefficient of transaction values increased slightly. Linking transactions to buyer wealth proxies, we show that SDLT operates as a de facto wealth tax that falls disproportionately on younger, middle-wealth cohorts rather than on the wealthiest households. The episode highlights a central policy trade-off: temporary cuts to transaction taxes can spur short-run market activity, but at the cost of eroding fiscal capacity and exacerbating wealth inequality.
papers.subtheme: Wealth Taxation and Capital Income Tax Design
papers.title: Transaction Taxes and Housing Inequality: Evidence from the UK Stamp Duty Holiday

papers.abstract: Recent G20 and UN discussions have considered an unprecedented globally coordinated annual minimum tax of 2% on the wealth of dollar billionaires. We present results from two original studies of 92,696 respondents across 40 countries, examining public and institutional support for the globally coordinated billionaire tax. The policy is supported by 72% of respondents and opposed by only 9%. It has majority support in every surveyed country and among voters in 167 of 168 represented political parties. Supporters often engage in pro-tax political activities (e.g., donations, petitions), while opponents to a lesser extent engage in anti-tax activities. Fairness is the value most strongly associated with support, while concerns about efficiency or national autonomy are limited. The billionaire tax is more popular than broad domestic redistribution in the West, driven by high support among high-income and right-leaning voters. Respondents in all countries underestimate the extent of global support and overwhelmingly doubt implementation. Correcting misperceptions about support substantially increases the share who believe the tax will be implemented, indicating that respondents see global support as influencing policymakers. At the same time, governments remain divided and often non-committal, leaving the policy’s future uncertain. Whichever direction global policy ultimately takes, our results show clear and widespread support for addressing rising top-end wealth inequality.
papers.subtheme: Perceptions of Fairness and Social Mobility
papers.title: Majority in 40 Countries Support Unprecedented Coordinated Billionaire Tax Discussed by G20

papers.abstract: This paper examines the long-run effects of a large-scale income shock on gender gaps in labor and education, leveraging agriculture productivity gains generated by the construction of India’s national irrigation canal network. Using a regression discontinuity design based on village elevation relative to canals, we identify the causal impact of canal access on labor force participation and educational attainment more than 30 years after construction. We find that canals raised agricultural productivity and household consumption but widened gender gaps: female labor force participation fell by 5\%, driven by women’s exit from paid agricultural work into unpaid domestic labor, while male participation declined only slightly, with some reallocation into services and education. Although education improved for both genders, men’s gains were nearly twice as large, further increasing the education gap. These effects are most pronounced among landowning households, who captured the largest income gains. To understand the role of cultural institutions in shaping these outcomes, we constructed a novel dataset linking over 140 million individuals to their caste group’s traditional gender practices.  Our findings suggest that localized development can generate persistent, unequal gains—highlighting a potential tension between income growth and gender equality.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Income shocks and gender gaps: long-run evidence from India

papers.abstract: Climate policies may impact inequalities through their effects on structural change via the source of income channel, and on household expenditures via the use of income channel. We compare the impact of carbon pricing on within-country inequalities when revenues are recycled through lump-sum transfers or labor tax cuts. We account for the impact of the labor share on inequalities, and compare results across regions with contrasted levels of economic development, using four macroeconmic models. We find that the progressivity of policies depends on the volume of tax revenues, and decreases as the carbon tax base depletes. We show that lump-sum transfers are progressive in all countries, while labor tax cuts are sometimes regressive in high-income countries and progressive in low-income countries. Overall, our results show that strong climate policy combined with carbon tax recycling over the coming decades is compatible with reducing inequality and increasing consumption among the poorest households in most regions, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Accounting for the impact of the source of income on inequalities reduces the performance gap between recycling schemes: it mitigates the regressivity of labor tax cuts, while reducing the progressivity of lump-sum transfers. These results highlight the central role of labor income in shaping the distributional consequences of climate policy beyond consumption-side price effects. They also suggest that sustaining the labor share in the economy can strengthen the progressivity of climate policies.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: The equity and efficiency of carbon taxation: a multi-model, multi-country analysis

papers.abstract: The welfare state is first and foremost discussed as a redistributive institution; however, as this paper illustrates, its policies also relate to patterns of inequality in political participation. This paper examines how welfare-state institutions are associated with political participation gaps between labour-market insiders and outsiders in Western Europe. Building on the resource model of political participation and policy-feedback theory, it shows that labour market dualization, both as a status-based divide between permanent and temporary contracts and as a risk-based continuum of exposure to unemployment and atypical work, is linked to systematic inequalities in political participation that vary across institutional contexts. The extent of dualization in income differs between countries and reflects distinct path-dependent responses of welfare states to heightened global competition and rising unemployment since the 1990s. Institutional configurations concerning Employment Protection Legislation and Social Investment Policies are not only relevant for labour-market structures, shaping income patterns, collective bargaining systems, and job security, but are also closely associated with the extent of political inequality between insiders and outsiders.  Using data from the European Social Survey (2012–2018), combined with OECD, ILO, and EU-SILC macro-indicators, the study estimates logistic regression models, linear models, and KHB decompositions to assess both conventional participation (voting) and unconventional participation (protest, petitions, boycotts, and organizational engagement). The findings show that outsiders participate less in elections than insiders across both measures of dualization. By contrast, temporary workers do not withdraw from non-electoral forms of civic engagement to the same extent, suggesting a form of silent protest through abstention from the ballot box rather than a wholesale retreat from political life. The welfare-state context appears closely connected to these patterns. Stricter Employment Protection Legislation is associated with larger insider advantages in electoral participation and with lower unconventional engagement among temporary workers. Welfare regimes also coincide with different participation gaps: Nordic welfare states show comparatively limited outsider demobilization, whereas continental and liberal regimes display markedly stronger withdrawal among groups facing higher labour-market risks. Overall, these results point to the political relevance of segmented labour markets and indicate that welfare-state design remains an important factor in sustaining democratic inclusiveness in post-industrial societies.
papers.subtheme: Voting, Participation and Electoral Cleavages
papers.title: The Democratic Welfare State: How does the Welfare State moderate Political Participation Gaps between Labor Market Insiders and Outsiders?

papers.abstract:
Introduction. Standard indicators such as the Gini coefficient summarize inequality but hide where inequality is most intense along the distribution. This limitation is especially visible for wealth, where negative asset positions inflate generalized Gini values and complicate cross-national comparisons. This paper introduces isogini measures, based on the isograph representation of medianized income and wealth over logit ranks, to distinguish inequality at the bottom, middle, and top of the distribution. This approach clarifies why countries with similar Ginis may have structurally different distributions.
Methods. Using aggregated data from the World Inequality Database (WID) for the years 2010 and 2020, the analysis considers income (tdiinc) and wealth (thweal) thresholds and their associated inequality indicators. Isoginis (iso10, iso50, iso90) are computed as percentile-specific Gini-equivalent measures derived from medianized distributions. Their behaviour is compared with traditional and generalized Gini coefficients, and their asymptotes are related to inverse Pareto coefficients to describe top-tail concentration.
Results. Income distributions across countries tend to be flatter and close to log-logit (Fisk) forms. Wealth distributions show steeper slopes, stronger deviations from Fisk regularity, and substantial concentration. The method identifies distinct shapes: countries such as the Netherlands display moderate wealth inequality at all levels; the United States and South Africa show extreme concentration both at the bottom and at the top; Sweden appears as a paradox in generalized Gini terms because it combines very low or negative median wealth with only moderately high top-tail concentration. Isogini asymptotes correlate strongly with inverse Pareto coefficients, while iso50 captures the structural weakness of middle-class wealth holdings.
Discussion. The results show that Gini coefficients alone can misrepresent inequality, especially for wealth. Isogini measures clarify whether high Gini values stem from top-end concentration, bottom-end deprivation, or both. This decomposition provides a clearer basis for cross-national comparisons and for interpreting the structural sources of income and wealth inequality.
JEL codes: D31, C16, C46. 
Keywords: inequality, income, wealth, distributions, isograph, logitrank
papers.subtheme: Distributional Decomposition and Counterfactual Methods
papers.title: Understanding distortions in Gini coefficient comparisons:   Isogini measures of income and wealth distributions with WID 2010-2020

papers.abstract:
Pricing greenhouse gas emissions is a crucial tool in environmental policy, following the Pigouvian principle. However, carbon pricing can have significant distributional consequences. To address these concerns, we examine household-level inequality in greenhouse gas emissions across the entire EU. We develop an improved cross-sectional dataset of household carbon footprints in all 27 EU countries by merging data from EXIOBASE, a multi-regional, environmentally extended supply-use dataset, with the European Household Budget Survey.
Our findings reveal substantial inequality in greenhouse gas emissions both between and within countries, with the major variation occurring within countries. Interestingly, net income is a weak predictor of households carbon footprints. A decomposition suggests that carbon emissions at the household level are due to the consumption-income relationship, the structure of the consumption baskets and differences in the emission intensity of different items of the consumption basket. To interpret these patterns and evaluate policy implications, we develop a heterogeneous-agent model with a non-homothetic CES aggregator that is able to replicate the empirical relationship between income, consumption, and emissions. After calibrating it to 26 EU countries, the model provides a framework for analysing the distributional and welfare consequences of carbon pricing.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Carbon Inequality in the EU

papers.abstract: This paper uses labor force surveys from 160 countries to build a new microdatabase on hours worked covering 97% of the world population in cross section. We also construct time series spanning over 20 years in 86 countries. Hours worked per adult are slightly bell-shaped with GDP per capita but weakly correlated with development overall. Hours worked by the young (aged 15-19) and elderly (aged 60+) decline with development, driven by growing school attendance and public pension coverage. Hours worked among prime-age adults (aged 20-59) are mildly bell-shaped with development for men while they are increasing for women. The fall in male hours in middle-to-higher income countries is driven by reduced hours per worker and is offset by increases in female labor force participation. These two forces have exactly compensated each other in many countries, leading to a remarkable long-run stability of prime-age hours worked. Labor taxes are strongly negatively correlated with prime-age hours worked both in international comparisons and overtime within countries. Controlling for government transfers only partly reduces the link between labor taxes and prime-age hours, ruling out substitution and income effects on labor supply as the only driver. Controlling for working hours regulations and the size of the formal sector eliminates this link, suggesting that regulations also play a large role in reducing intensive hours in higher-income countries.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Global Working Hours

papers.abstract: We analyze how the country of origin, alongside other uncontrollable factors like parental education and occupation, predicts income in adulthood in Europe. Using this definition of inequality of opportunity and employing advanced data-driven methods, we measure inequality of opportunity in household disposable incomes, treating Europe as a single entity. To ensure representativeness, we gather data from EUROSTAT and three different household surveys to construct a sample that exactly represents the population of Europe, accounting for country-of-birth population shares within countries. We estimate a level of overall inequality in Europe (2019) of 39 Gini points, with inequality predicted by ascriptive characteristics rising to 23 Gini points. The country of origin accounts for 64% of this inequality, emerging as the most significant predictor compared to other factors such as parental occupation (26%) and parental education (9%). Our findings demonstrate that, while European countries generally exhibit substantially lower levels of inequality of opportunity at the national level, accounting for country of origin as a circumstance and analyzing at the continental level reveal that equality of opportunity is still far from being realized. The level of inequality of opportunity observed is comparable to that in China and India and significantly higher than estimates for the United States.
papers.session_title: III/LSE Session: Inequality of opportunity around the world
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Playing the birth lottery in Europe

papers.abstract:
The super-rich contribute substantial sums to charity, with many publicly pledging
 to donate at least half of their wealth in the coming years. Western governments often
 offer favorable tax treatment for these charitable donations. Despite the considerable
 impact of such philanthropy, our understanding of its broader implications remains
 limited. This paper explores the implications of philanthropy for the politics of
 inequality through two studies conducted in the U.S. It argues that philanthropy
 can reduce individuals’ support for taxing the super-rich by enhancing perceptions
 of their benevolence and contributions to social welfare. The findings from Study 1
 indicate that respondents exposed to higher levels of philanthropy hold more positive
 views of these two aspects of the super-rich than those exposed to lower levels. The
 results from Study 2 replicate the association between levels of philanthropy and
 perceptions of the super-rich and, additionally, find that higher levels of philanthropy
 reduce individuals’ willingness to tax the super-rich. This reduction, however, is
 modest, suggesting that the charitable donations of the super-rich are seen only as
 partial substitutes for the taxes they must pay. Moreover, the results also show that
 supporting lower fiscal duties for the super-rich who make charitable donations does
 not imply reduced support for general public redistribution
papers.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
papers.title: Better Call Bill? Philanthropy and Preferences for  Taxing the Super-rich.

papers.abstract:
This paper presents the first systematic analysis of regional wealth inequality in Spain. We
do so by combining administrative fiscal data with household surveys and national
accounts between 2016 and 2022. We document substantial regional disparities in both
average household wealth and its concentration. Madrid stands out as the region with the
highest average wealth and top 1% wealth share. Our findings are relevant in the Spanish
institutional context, where autonomous communities exercise considerable control over
wealth taxation and public expenditure.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Regional wealth inequality in Spain: Evidence from the Spain wealth Atlas

papers.abstract:
This paper identifies a novel mechanism in the wealth-health causal relationship: wealth
 improves survival not through traditional health capital investment, but by enabling relocation
 to areas with superior health infrastructure. I leverage lottery and prize winnings as exogenous
 wealth shocks within a unique administrative dataset linking income and wealth tax records
 to population-wide health examinations, healthcare claims, and cause-specific mortality for a
 5% random sample of South Koreans aged 40–49 (2007–2018). Using a stacked difference-in
differences design, I find precisely estimated null effects of wealth on traditional health capital measures: all-cause mortality, non-external mortality, cardiovascular mortality, biomarkers
 (blood pressure, glucose, BMI, cholesterol), medication use, and most health behaviors are un
affected. However, mortality from external causes—accidents, homicides, drug overdoses, and
 natural disasters—declines by 35% within 1–2 years of winning. This reduction is driven by
 residential sorting: winners systematically relocate to cities with better health infrastructure.
 Critically, only substantial amount of windfalls that enable this migration produce these effects;
 smaller windfalls have no impact. These findings suggest that for prime-age adults, the “health
wealth gradient” operates primarily as a “health-location gradient,” with important implications
 for policies aimed at reducing health inequality.
papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: Wealthier and Healthier? Place-Based Mechanisms in the  Wealth-Health Relationship

papers.abstract: Inference about inequality indices based on conventional asymptotic and bootstrap methods is unreliable. We provide the first systematic application to real-world income data of three methods for improved inference – the semiparametric bootstrap and semiparametric asymptotic approaches proposed by Davidson and Flachaire (Journal of Econometrics, 2007) and Cowell and Flachaire (Journal of Econometrics, 2007), and the ‘Student-t’ approach of Ibragimov et al. (Econometric Reviews, 2025), while also modifying them to deal with survey weights and a large portfolio of inequality indices. The paper shows how these different approaches affect inference about inequality differences in comparison to the conventional asymptotic approach.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Assessing the statistical significance of inequality differences: the problem of heavy tails

papers.abstract: Achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement will require significant investment to replace the current capital stock with less carbon-intensive alternatives. The success of this transition depends largely on the actions of capital owners who control the production process and can direct investments towards cleaner technologies. However, such investments and the production process often require feasible third-party financing. In this context, we propose a new approach that distributes the responsibility for the environmental impacts of economic sectors between equity capital holders and creditors based on the sectors’ equity and financial debt ratios. The environmental accounting framework proposed prevents double-counting of emissions and can be used with any environmental responsibility allocation criteria (e.g. the production-based and the consumption-based accounting criteria). Additionally, by explicitly integrating the equity and financial debt ratios into an environmentally extended multi-regional input-output model, we can track the equity-financed and debt-financed environmental reasonability for emissions over the global value chains. Finally, we also assess the Spanish sectors’ exposure to climate-related transition risks using equity-financed/debt-financed emission intensities.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Capital- and finance-based environmental accounting framework

papers.abstract: We study the labour market impact of the “Veblen effect” by estimating the relation between inequality and average work hours in society, and how the effect varies between the poor and the non-poor households. Using data on actual hours worked by members of a household from India’s Periodic Labour Force Survey, we report three main findings. First, members belonging to absolutely and relatively poor households work for fewer hours than those in non-poor households. After controlling for a rich set of household-level characteristics and regional supply and demand side conditions, we observe that absolutely poor (relatively poor) households work, on average, 49 (25) minutes less per day than non-poor households. Second, we find that a one standard deviation increase in the regional 90/50 percentile ratio of the consumption expenditure distribution is associated with a 1.96 percent increase in the average work hours of non-poor and relatively poor households. However, the impact on the work hours of absolutely poor households is smaller at 0.81 percent. By isolating the impact of the rise in the 90th percentile’s consumption, we further demonstrate the cascading of the Veblen effect on the poor households. These findings are robust to alternate measures of inequality. We also demonstrate the robustness of these results to endogeneity concerns by instrumenting regional inequality with an indicator for conspicuous consumption, in addition to other approaches. Third, we find evidence that poor households are no less likely to be available to work for additional hours than non-poor households.
papers.subtheme: Experimental and Survey Evidence on Inequality Attitudes
papers.title: Poverty, Inequality, and Working Hours: Evidence on Veblen Effects from Labour Markets in India

papers.abstract:
This paper draws on the quantitative part of my book project to examine how does social hierarchy has shaped redistributive politics in Independent India. While mainstream theories of welfare are premised on the material interests of social classes, I argue that in societies like India with long histories of ascriptive discrimination, distributive politics in shaped by status inequality. High-status groups are more likely to oppose redistribution to maintain their ascriptive privilege, while low-status groups aim at reducing social hierarchy by prioritizing descriptive representation, which I refer as the politics of dignity. I test this theory by drawing on several sources of original data on major Indian states from 1960 to 2012. This includes data on the caste-identity of all legislators – high-status or upper-caste groups, and various low-status or lower-caste groups, including ex-untouchable castes called Scheduled Castes (SC), indigenous groups called Scheduled Tribes (ST), and intermediate castes called Other Backward Classes (OBCs). For the outcome variable – redistribution or proportion of developmental spending in social sectors, I digitized more than fifty years of public expenditures records from the Reserve Bank of India. I generate a new dataset on caste quotas from the colonial period. And finally, I develop an original measure of status inequality through data on endogamy.

Four main findings emerge. First, I find that states with higher status inequality, which reflects upper-caste dominance, are less likely to be redistributive. Status inequality is, in fact, a stronger predictor of redistribution than income inequality. Second, upper-caste political representation is consistently associated with negative redistributive spending, which aligns with our understanding of the economic elite (Acemoglu and Robinson 2006; Rueschemeyer, Huber, and Stephens 1992; Esping-Andersen 1990). These results hold after accounting for a range of relevant economic, political, and structural factors and remain robust to alternative measurement and estimation strategies. Third, unlike working-class coalitions, lower-caste political representation does not present a clear association with redistribution. I find that elites from politically mobilized groups have instead consistently prioritized representational policies – OBC representation in government is a strong predictor of OBC quotas. Finally, though such measures have traditionally been viewed as patronage or symbolic politics, this research demonstrates that places with higher OBC representation in both the legislature and bureaucracy (i.e., interaction effects) are associated with higher redistributive spending. To examine potential mechanisms, I rely on qualitative fieldwork in the state of Bihar that suggests that a representative bureaucracy can generate conditions for redistributive politics by reducing discrimination in policy design and implementation and weakening elite patronage networks. 

This research advances two agendas of the World Inequality Lab – Political inequalities, and Methodological advances in the measurement of inequalities. 

Political Inequality:

The findings of this study are closely aligned with the research on World Political Cleavages and Inequality Database. The India chapter of the book and related article (Gethin, Martínez-Toledano, and Piketty 2021b; Banerjee, Gethin, and Piketty 2019), in fact, drew on a previous version of this research (my job market paper) (Chakrabarti 2019). Banerjee, Gethin, and Piketty (2019) find strong evidence for political cleavages based on caste and religion in India, but show that these cleavages do not seem to shape redistributive spending. This seem to be in line with global trends wherein sectarian interests and cultural priorities have taken precedence over economic issues in recent years (Gethin, Martínez-Toledano, and Piketty 2021b; Norris and Inglehart 2019). In Western democracies, the rise of green and anti-immigration movements has resulted in a shift in the social base of the social democratic parties towards the educated elite while the right continued to attract the business elite, what the authors refers as the “Brahmin Left versus the Merchant Right” (Gethin, Martínez-Toledano, and Piketty 2021a). Banerjee, Gethin, and Piketty (2019) interpret their findings in India to suggest that the country’s poor record in social development stems from the salience of identity politics. However, they qualify their argument with an important caveat: “the big political fights seem to be about caste and religious identity in its many forms and the caste quotas in educational institutions and government jobs, the one place where the identity and economic dimensions intersect.” (Banerjee, Gethin, and Piketty 2019, 43 emphasis mine). This research speaks to this important gap in the literature. The question of quotas distinguishes India from its Western counterparts. Unlike other aspects of identity, caste quotas are not just symbolic or cultural. As the longest-standing identity-based affirmative action programs in the world (Jensenius 2017), the Indian case offers a unique opportunity to examine how status mediates the complex relationship between the identity of the political elite and the nature of distributional politics. The findings challenge influential works that have been pessimistic about the redistributive potential of caste politics (Jaffrelot 2003; Weiner 2001; Kohli 2012).

Normatively, the findings speak to the limitations of mainstream theories of social justice that is premised on equality of opportunity across social classes. The history of ascriptive discrimination in societies like India presents distinct challenges to social opportunity that mere investment in public goods cannot capture (Sen 1999). An identity-based idea of justice faces the additional burden of dismantling status biases – both psychological and institutional, thus involving concerns of recognition and systemic discrimination in addition to redistribution (Fraser 1995; Mills 2022). Lower-caste mobilization in India draws on a long tradition of anti-caste thinkers, including Phule, Periyar, Ambedkar, and Lohia, that is rooted in a broader notion of social justice that seeks equalization of status across social groups (Omvedt 2008; Teltumbde 2018; Ambedkar 2014; O’Hanlon 2002). It is hence not surprising that in contrast to the conventional left-right paradigm, ideological differences in Indian politics are based on the role of the state in regulating groups-rights and affirmative action (Chhibber and Verma 2018). The single most important finding in Piketty’s (2020, 7) thousand-page global history of inequality is that “inequality is neither economic nor technological; it is ideological and political.” From a policy perspective, it calls for the need to examine the role of discrimination in policy design and implementation. Further, by suggesting that the inclusion of low-status groups in the bureaucracy can influence development outcomes, this research pushes the boundaries of existing debates on affirmative action that have largely revolved around questions of meritocracy and efficiency (Bhavnani and Lee 2021; Deshpande and Weisskopf 2014).

Measurement of Inequalities:

Second, the research speaks to the research agenda on conceptualization and measurement of inequality (Piketty 2000). Most existing research, including the World Inequality Reports, have focused on income/wealth or socioeconomic inequality. This research focused on the undertheorized and understudied concept of status (Ridgeway 2019). This research contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded, contextually relevant, and generalizable measure of status inequality.

The idea of status goes back to Weber’s conceptualization of inequality, which he argued is based on three interrelated but distinct sources: resources, power, and status (Weber 1978). Status broadly refers to the ranking or position in a social hierarchy in terms of prestige, respect, and worth (Ridgeway 2019). The rise in right-wing populism in recent years has reignited interest in status politics (Parker 2021; Berman 2021; Norris and Inglehart 2019). Support for Trump, for example, was driven by status anxiety rather than economic hardship (Mutz 2018). Poor-high-status individuals, like the white-working-class in the United States and Europe (Baccini and Weymouth 2021; Gidron and Hall 2020) and poor-Brahmins in India (Suryanarayan 2019) have been shown to vote against their material interests to preserve their ascriptive privilege. At the same time, mobilizations for the “struggle for recognition” under the banners of nationality, ethnicity, and race have become the paradigmatic form of social movements since the end of the twentieth century (Fraser 1995). Concerns of status are at the heart of ethnic mobilizations across the ideological spectrum, but much like the literature on inequality, research on ethnic politics has also largely focused on economic inequality between groups (Baldwin and Huber 2010; Alesina, Michalopoulos, and Papaioannou 2016; Houle, Kenny, and Park 2019).

This research addresses this gap by drawing on theories of justice to distinguish between different forms of ethnic inequality – i) economic, ii) social, and iii) status. Consistent with the existing literature, I conceptualize economic inequality as disparity in economic outcomes, like income or wealth, while social inequality captures the idea in equality of opportunity, as reflected in disparity in access to public goods across groups (Sen 1999; Roemer 2009). In contrast to unequal access to material resources, status inequality, rooted in the idea of recognition, is manifested through segregationist norms in inter-group relations (Taylor 1994; Horowitz 1985). While difference in income and literacy between castes can be used to measure economic and social inequality respectively, this study develops an original measure of status inequality through data on endogamy. Endogamy captures the idea of segregation, which is the mechanism that has been shown to maintain and reproduce inequality between ethnic groups across different contexts.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Status Inequality and Ideology: How Social Hierarchy shaped Redistribution in India

papers.abstract:
This paper extends our earlier work with the World Inequality Lab on measuring inflation inequality in India. While the previous analysis focused on national patterns, this study turns to the state level to show how inflation is experienced very differently across regions and across income groups within those regions.  This paper is the first attempt to track the inflation rates of the distribution of households based on consumption weights of different fractiles of households from 2012 to 2024 at the state-level. This paper constructs the consumption basket of households in different consumption brackets based on the 68^{th} round of the NSS Household Consumption Expenditure Survey and also provides a comparison with the recent rounds of HCES survey in 2023--24. We compute the consumption expenditure shares  of different fractiles of households, from the poorest to the richest, and compute the inflation faced by them in all major states of India.


The data point to large fluctuations in state-level inflation, driven by varying levels of food dependence, storage capacity, market integration, and exposure to climate shocks. These differences translate into unequal welfare losses for households: in some states, the poorest groups face far sharper price volatility than the rich, affecting their nutrition, savings, and ability to plan for the future. Yet policy continues to rely on a single national inflation rate and a uniform monetary stance, even though inflation dynamics diverge widely across states and within the population strata for any given state.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Measuring Inflation Inequality in India: A State-level Analysis

papers.abstract:
Views on adult literacy programs are mixed. While there have been a few studies analyzing
maternal literacy and child health outcomes, there is scant literature examining the impact
of adult literacy on child educational outcomes showing null or at best modest impacts on
academic skills of children. In this paper, we explore the impact of such an adult literacy
program named ‘Saakshar Bharat’ implemented in 2009 in selected rural backward districts
in India for adults aged 15 or above, on a host of scholastic indicators such as private school
enrollment, probability of dropping out and reading scores of 5 to 16 year old children using
ASER data in a difference-in-difference framework. Results show that while private school par-
ticipation rises for some, dropout decisions and learning outcomes do not improve in general,
which point out towards a possible quality compromise with increased access in schooling, com-
monly referred to as the ‘quantity-quality tradeoff’ in educational context. There is significant
heterogeneity based on maternal literacy and child age-groups. Mechanisms reveal the role
of ‘aspiration-frustration-dynamic’ playing out in the form of reduced human capital invest-
ment and lesser parental involvement coupled with household labour substitution in these low
income-constrained households due to lack of time and resources.
papers.subtheme: Inequality Perceptions - General
papers.title: ‘Diminishing One Gap, Widening Another’: Unintended Consequences of Adult Literacy on Medium-Term Child Dropouts in India

papers.session_title: III/LSE Session: Inequality of opportunity around the world
papers.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
papers.title: Intergenerational Income Mobility around the World: A Meta-Analysis

papers.abstract: This paper revisits the longstanding question of how to decompose inequality indices into contributions of factor components, such as labor income and capital income. We start from the axiomatic framework of Shorrocks (1982) and discuss why one of his core axioms, two factor symmetry (Axiom 6), is not suitable for rank-dependent inequality indices such as the Gini coefficient and top income shares. We propose an alternative axiom, monotonicity, to replace two factor symmetry and show that the so-called natural decomposition is the unique source decomposition that satisfies the axioms for any rank-dependent inequality index. Furthermore, we show that the marginal decomposition by Lerman and Yitzhaki (1985) can be uniquely derived from a similar framework where two of the axioms are adjusted.
papers.subtheme: Distributional Decomposition and Counterfactual Methods
papers.title: Source Decomposition of Inequality Revisited

papers.abstract:
This proposal examines the link between global environmental inequality and the structural position of Latin America and the Caribbean within the world economic metabolism, in line with the objectives of the 3rd World Inequality Conference (WIC 2026). The analysis focuses on three dimensions that allow for the study of international environmental asymmetries: per capita CO₂ emissions, per capita domestic material consumption, and per capita material footprint. It draws on international databases and original calculations based on UNEP IRP (2025) and The World Bank (2025). Global per-capita Gini values show limited variation: in material consumption, the Gini declines from 0.50 in 1970 to 0.47 in 2024; in material footprint—calculated using the equation Material footprint = DE + RMEIM − RMEEX—it decreases from 0.53 in 1970 to 0.50 in 2024; in CO₂ emissions it drops from 0.76 in 1970 to 0.59 in 2023. These reductions express moderate convergence without significant structural changes in countries of the Global South that sustain the extraction and supply of resources to the rest of the world.
For Latin America and the Caribbean, these global values do not adequately reflect the region’s historical position or its material contribution to international trade. Regional per-capita material consumption (15.9 tons) is close to the world average (13 tons), with increases associated with GDP growth and population size. CO₂ emissions remain relatively low (2.7 tons compared to 9.9 tons in high-income economies in 2023), concentrated in industrial and urban sectors, which places the region far from the core group of countries responsible for global emissions concentration. A fundamental paradox emerges in the material footprint: countries with moderate domestic consumption contribute intensely to global material pressure through resource-based exports with high material burdens, revealing a structural inequality not captured by global coefficients and associated with ecological conflicts and socio-environmental costs that disproportionately fall on the region (Martínez Alier, 2023).
The analytical separation of emissions, material consumption, and material footprint allows for a more precise definition of the region’s position with respect to potential transitions toward dematerialization. Material consumption reflects the internal productive structure; emissions reflect the energy matrix and level of industrialization; the material footprint reveals the distributive effects of international trade and the externalization of impacts. The relationship between economic growth, material intensity, and export specialization determines whether countries in the region approach relative dematerialization—lower material use per unit of output—or remain far from absolute dematerialization, which would imply a real reduction in resource use. Economic growth may reduce material intensity without reducing total material use, making explicit the need to clarify the assumptions guiding the research.
The general objective is to interpret how global variations in the Gini coefficients of CO₂ emissions, material consumption, and material footprint between 1970 and 2024 help explain the position of Latin America and the Caribbean in transitions toward dematerialization. The specific objectives aim to interpret the trajectories of global Gini values and their translation for the region, to explain how productive structures and primary specialization define the absolute and relative use of materials and energy, and to determine whether the region, its subregions, and representative cases tend toward relative or absolute dematerialization, considering the role played by international trade in this interpretation.
The hypotheses suggest that the moderate reduction in global per-capita environmental Gini coefficients stems mainly from the rise in consumption in middle-income economies, without significant structural changes in countries of the Global South that sustain resource extraction. This pattern improves Latin America’s comparative position without altering its role as a supplier of materials to the world economy.
