The proposal further argues that the region exhibits weak relative dematerialization—with only small reductions in material intensity—while experiencing an absolute increase in extraction and total material use. Economic growth marked by strong extractive activities prevents advances toward absolute dematerialization and reproduces environmental inequalities both within and between countries.
The methodology consists of building global and regional historical series on material flows, emissions, and intensities based on UNEP IRP (2025) and The World Bank (2025), and interpreting the results within analytical frameworks from ecological economics and social metabolism. The expected contribution of the paper is to offer a rigorous interpretation of how the structural position of Latin America in the world economy conditions its dematerialization trajectories and reproduces environmental inequalities, in line with the thematic lines of the World Inequality Conference 2026 on environmental inequalities and methods for their comparative measurement.
References
Martínez-Alier, J. (2023). Land, water, air and freedom: The making of world movements for environmental justice. Edward Elgar Publishing.
The World Bank (2025). World Bank Open Data.
United Nations Environment Programme, International Resource Panel, Global Material Flows Database (2025). Global Material Flows Database.
papers.subtheme: Energy Transition, Fossil Lock-in and Decarbonization
papers.title: Transitions toward Dematerialization and Environmental Inequalities in Latin America: CO₂ Emissions, Material Consumption and Material Footprint in the Framework of the World Inequality Conference 2026 (1970–2024)

papers.subtheme: Firm Dynamics, Market Power and Productivity
papers.title: Global Labour Hours in Paid and Unpaid Work: Productivity and Structural Transformation, 1800-2100

papers.abstract: Corporate philanthropy has been increasing inWestern democracies in recent decades, a rise often explained by the development of tax policies offering substantial incentives to donate to charities. Yet, corporate philanthropy is also increasingly perceived as a means to influence politics. In this paper, we estimate the tax price elasticity of corporate donations, and investigate how it differs depending on the recipients’ purposes and the donors’ characteristics. To do so, we use an exhaustive administrative panel dataset on firms’ tax returns in France from 2013 to 2022, including the identity of the charities that benefit from the donations, from which we recover their purpose using state-of-the-art NLP methods. Exploiting two reforms that affect the price of donations for firms, we document significant bunching around major regulatory thresholds. We then show that the tax-price elasticityvaries significantly depending on the type of beneficiaries.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Tax Incentives or Political Motivations? Evidence from Corporate Contributions

papers.abstract: People’s ability to access essential services is key to their labour market and social inclusion. An important dimension of accessibility is physical accessibility, but little cross-country evidence exists on how close people live to the services facilities they need. This paper helps to address this gap, focusing on three types of essential services: Public Employment Services, primary schools and Early Childhood Education and Care. It collects and maps data on the location of these services for a selection of OECD countries and links them with data on population and transport infrastructure. This allows to compute travel times to the nearest service facility and to quantify disparities in accessibility at the regional level. The results highlight substantial inequalities in accessibility of essential services across and within countries. Although large parts of the population can easily reach these services in most countries, some people are relatively underserved. This is particularly the case in non-metropolitan and low-income regions. At the same time, accessibility seems to be associated with the potential demand for these services once accounting for other regional economic and demographic characteristics.
papers.subtheme: Spatial inequality, accessibility
papers.title: Geographic inequalities in accessibility of essential services

papers.abstract: This paper examines the effects of exposure to hard-security counterinsurgency operations during school-age years on human capital formation. We exploit the 1989 introduction of the Greyhounds—a specialized commando force created to combat Naxalite insurgents—in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, as a natural experiment. Among all states affected by Naxalite violence, only Andhra Pradesh established such a force during that period. Difference-in-differences estimates suggest that exposure to the policy during school-age years led to increased educational attainment. We provide suggestive evidence that a plausible mechanism underlying these effects is increased household investment in education due to reduced uncertainty stemming from improved security. Our findings highlight the economic returns to peace and stability in conflict-affected regions.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Guns and Gains: Human Capital Effects of Exposure to Counterinsurgency Operations

papers.session_title: III/LSE Session: Inequality of opportunity around the world
papers.subtheme: Income and Wealth Mobility - General
papers.title: Global estimates of opportunity and mobility: a database

papers.abstract:
Latin America remains one of the most unequal regions in the world, yet most empirical work still focuses on income distributions alone. This paper advances the emerging agenda on multidimensional inequality by applying the Foster and Lokshin (2024) methodology to harmonised household survey data from twelve Latin American countries, using the BADEHOG database compiled by ECLAC. We construct a household-level wellbeing index that combines three core dimensions – income, education and housing – with explicit normative weights and then measure inequality in this composite using a standard Gini index. The Foster–Lokshin framework allows us to decompose multidimensional inequality into a “specific” component, reflecting disparities within each dimension, and an “overlap” component that captures the extent to which disadvantages accumulate on the same households through the joint distribution of achievements. We also introduce a dynamic normalisation strategy that keeps normative weights constant while accommodating structural changes over time in each dimension. Together, these features provide a transparent and policy-relevant summary of multidimensional inequality that is comparable across countries and periods. The paper lays the conceptual, methodological and data foundations for a regional diagnostic of multidimensional inequality in Latin America. 

The results reveal substantial variation across the region and meaningful changes over the past two decades. Multidimensional inequality declines in most cases between 2003 and 2023, although several trajectories are non-linear, with increases during the 2000s followed by reductions in the subsequent decade. The structure of inequality also evolves unevenly: the overlap component varies widely and shifts in ways that indicate either increasing concentration of disadvantages within the same households or a more dispersed pattern of deprivations across dimensions. Under the dynamic normalisation, inequality falls more sharply—reflecting improvements in average education and housing—while the overlap component rises, suggesting a reconfiguration of deprivation patterns rather than simple convergence.

The paper lays the conceptual, methodological, and empirical foundations for a regional diagnostic of multidimensional inequality in Latin America.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Multidimensional Inequality in Latin America

papers.abstract:
Food consumption is a significant contributor to households’ carbon footprints. However, consumer heterogeneity in food-related carbon footprints remains underexplored, primarily due to limited data linking real-world consumption choices to environmental impacts. I address this gap by matching detailed purchase data with environmental impact estimates at the transaction level for a representative sample of 7,540 French households between 2017 and 2019. Using this unique dataset, I provide a comprehensive overview of the distribution of food carbon footprints and employ a structural demand
model to estimate how price and expenditure changes influence food basket composition and carbon emissions. The analysis reveals three key insights. 1) There is heterogeneity in the distribution of food carbon footprints, with 20% of households accounting for 40% of total food emissions. 2) Households with higher carbon footprints are more price-sensitive, particularly regarding high-emission products like red meat. 3) Simulations indicate that a 44.60€/tCO2e food carbon tax would reduce food-related emissions (8.5%), especially among high-emission households. While modest carbon tax levels appear effective at reducing emissions, they may also lead to a trade-off between lowering emissions and preserving diet quality.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Households' food carbon footprints

papers.abstract: How efficiently do societies convert collective time into the fulfillment of basic needs, and what are the implications for wellbeing and development? Traditional poverty and wellbeing metrics, such as the International Poverty Line and Multidimensional Poverty Index, largely ignore time as a critical resource. This article addresses this gap and proposes the “time conversion factor,” a metric that quantifies how effectively countries transform societal time inputs into outputs that satisfy essential needs. Empirical data from time-use surveys reveal stark cross-country differences in time spent on food provisioning, highlighting structural inequalities that limit discretionary time and economic growth. We demonstrate that time-inefficient provisioning systems trap societies in a cycle of deprivation and delay development. Prioritizing the measurement and improvement of time conversion in provisioning systems is therefore essential to advancing sustainable wellbeing and breaking persistent cycles of inequality.
papers.subtheme: Macroeconomic Drivers: Inflation, Growth and Cycles
papers.title: Time for Development

papers.abstract:
This paper examines causal mechanisms linking corruption awareness to inequal-
ity perceptions in post-socialist Europe. Using pre-registered vignette experiments
across Lithuania, Hungary, and Moldova (n=3,500), I demonstrate that factual cor-
ruption information increases inequality perceptions by approximately 5 percent-
age points yet produces no effect on redistribution preferences. This effect remains
consistent across countries despite substantial variation in institutional quality, EU
membership status, and corruption levels. Drawing on governance theory, system
justification theory, and social identity perspectives, I develop an integrated frame-
work identifying disruption of legitimizing narratives about economic fairness as
the primary mechanism. Effects prove particularly pronounced among right-wing
voters, older citizens, the economically insecure, and incumbent supporters, who
exhibit the largest perceptual shifts when confronted with corruption information.
These findings establish the first experimental evidence of causality between corrup-
tion information and inequality perceptions at the individual level, while revealing
a paradox: corruption information neutralizes partisan differences in inequality
perceptions but fails to generate policy demands.
papers.subtheme: Perceptions of Fairness and Social Mobility
papers.title: Corruption Information and Inequality Perceptions: Causal Evidence from Central and Eastern European Democracies

papers.abstract:
Income inequality across and within nations is trending in opposite directions: the former is declining, while the latter is increasing. This scissor-like trend of increasing GDP growth divergence within countries is also well documented in regional analyses across the OECD (OECD, 2024). Unlike cross-country comparisons, which can rely on robust purchasing power parity programmes for meaningful real-term assessments, harmonised data on spatial price variation are rarely accessible, constraining the ability to evaluate changes in wealth or disposable income in real terms and to draw fully informed conclusions about within-country disparities.
The lack of comparable subnational price data constrains and may significantly bias regional economic analysis. In the absence of subnational price indices, regional wealth/income indicators are often deflated using national-level indices, thereby not only masking the impact of regional price differences but also potentially inflating disposable income and wealth in many regions. National PPPs for OECD countries are primarily collected in the capital city-region, with some adjustments for the rest of the country done every six years. As a result, assessments of real wealth and living standards are less precise, limiting the effectiveness of policy design, targeting, and monitoring at the regional level.
To address this information gap, the OECD has launched an initiative to develop a harmonised framework for measuring subnational Purchasing Power Parities (sPPPs). The first phase of this initiative focuses on establishing a processing pipeline and an open-source R package, OECDsPPPs, that provides a fully documented framework for the methodological steps required to estimate subnational price indexes harmonised across and within countries.
OECDsPPPs builds on the existing methodological literature and follows the international standards of the International Comparison Programme (ICP) and the Eurostat-OECD PPP Programme. It leverages official data produced by national statistical offices (NSOs), often for consumer price index (CPI) programmes, as well as alternative data sources and regional household expenditure weights. The development of OECDsPPPs has been guided by expert input and extensive stakeholder consultations, including senior officials from national statistical offices in OECD member and accession countries. The platform has been co-developed with stakeholders to support ongoing methodological refinement and accommodate flexible extensions. It features robust data validation tools and options for non-linear estimation methods used in index construction. 
In the current phase of the project, microdata for Czechia, Germany, the Slovak Republic and the United Kingdom will be incorporated, with further European economies planned for inclusion in 2026. The present draft of the paper draws only on preliminary data and analysis for the United Kingdom and underscores the importance of adjusting regional wealth and income indicators for spatial variations in price levels. The emerging evidence suggests that price levels vary more widely for services than for goods, although even goods with relatively low variability display common patterns, most notably the capital city price premium. Price movements differ across categories and generally behave as expected, such as in food and communications, but some notable patterns also appear, including rising spatial variability in relatively homogeneous categories, particularly food. Consistent with cross-country meta analyses, variations in prices across regions, as well as the way these variations change over time, are strongly correlated with gross disposable household income in UK TL2 regions.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Mapping subnational price differences across countries: Evidence from OECD regions

papers.abstract: While the literature on technology and education is growing in India, specifically after the COVID-19 pandemic, yet there is a lack of evidence to date on understanding the inequalities in access to smartphones and internet and how it determines students learning outcomes. In this paper, using a recent nationwide rural household education survey, we examine socioeconomic inequalities in access to smartphones and internet and how they matter for children’s learning level in reading, math and language skills. We find significant socioeconomic variations in access to smartphones and internet among rural households in India - internet use is higher among rich and educated households than poor and less educated counterparts. We also find some evidence suggesting that access to smartphones and internet in the household produces learning gains in reading, math and language skills for children, with considerable variations across households’ socioeconomic positions. In a context where technology is increasingly integrated in educational transactions, our results have important policy implications for India and other developing countries. The study contributes novel insights to a nascent body of research in India on the impact of technology on student learning outcomes, as well as to a wider literature concerning technology and educational inequalities.
papers.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
papers.title: Does inequalities in access smartphone and internet lead to poor learning outcomes? Evidence from rural India

papers.abstract: What drives lifetime income inequality? We estimate a continuous-time lifecycle model incorporating human capital accumulation, innate ability, search frictions, job wage premia, and non-wage amenities. Workers make consumption-savings decisions, and their asset position affects job acceptance. We estimate the model on Danish matched employer-employee data for 2008–2023. Counterfactuals show that innate ability is the dominant source of lifetime earnings inequality, accounting for over 90 percent of the variance. Search frictions and amenities matter for welfare rather than earnings: removing frictions reduces lifetime utility inequality by nearly 80 percent while leaving earnings inequality unchanged. Finally, several mechanisms have opposite effects on cross-sectional versus lifetime inequality, showing that the two measures provide different information.
papers.subtheme: Lifetime cycles
papers.title: Drivers of Lifetime Earnings and Wealth: Skills, Frictions and Choices

papers.abstract:
Wealth distribution, and in particular the gap between the richest and the poorest, remains a highly relevant topic in the public discourse and an increasingly important concern for policymakers. While distributional results are available from micro-statistics, work in macro-statistics is relatively less developed. To address this gap, the Expert Group on Distributional Household Wealth (EG DHW) was launched in 2023 to help provide systematic, robust and comparable distributional information aligned to national accounts. The EG DHW is part of the G20 Data Gaps Initiative, with the main goal of producing annual wealth deciles by the end of 2026. 

The paper first presents the methodology that aligns micro data to the national accounts. This approach enables distributional information to be comparable with macroeconomic aggregates such as GDP, final household consumption, and net wealth. It also enhances the timeliness, international comparability, and coverage of such information. Second, the paper discusses inequality results from an experimental data collection conducted in 2025. Moreover, it examines the effects of employment-related pensions on the wealth distribution and the wealth share of the top 1% in the United States. The paper concludes with a discussion on the work’s future direction.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Distribution of household wealth in line with national accounts: Methodology and results from the 2025 experimental data collection

papers.abstract: Using historical income and wealth data, we show that war reduces inequality: the top-1% income share falls by 20\% and the top-1\% wealth share by 10%. We measure three key drivers of inequality---capital destruction, taxation, and inflation---in the data and quantify their role with a Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian (HANK) model. Destruction depresses profits and thus top incomes. Taxation primarily influences wealth dynamics, while inflation has little effect on top shares, but reduces indebtedness among poorer households. We validate our findings using new data on inequality across German towns in World War 2 and cross-country data on profits.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: The Great Leveler According to HANK

papers.session_title: The African Inequality Review: a Sneak Preview
papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: Introduction to AIR: Concept, Approach, and Research Questions

papers.abstract: How do wealthy individuals use offshore financial structures like shell companies to protect personal assets?  And how is such offshore wealth structuring itself variably organized? This article supplies the first systematic image of two key layers employed in offshore structures by analyzing expensive residential properties in the UK held via overseas entities. We use these data to make three contributions to debates around offshore. First, we identify a specific regional offshore circuit in flows and magnitude by isolating two key layers. These we term the entry layer, which is used to connect into the UK property market, and the action layer, which is used for the actual or projected appearance of managing the offshore structure. We next pinpoint three patterns of offshore formations between these layers, which we term global funnel, selective gateway, and self-stacker, and we discuss their implications. Finally, we offer indirect evidence of which jurisdictions people are more likely to choose for “brass plate” incorporation and which they employ for more complicated structuring, either in actuality or in appearance, which has implications for policymaking. Our findings supply a pioneering analysis of the scope, scale, and key formations of offshore structures for holding property that probes systematically beyond the first layer.
papers.subtheme: Asset Prices, Returns and Portfolio Dynamics
papers.title: Gateways, Funnels, and Stackers:  How People Hide Property Ownership through Offshore Structures

papers.abstract: This paper provides a new long-run database of group-specific rates of return to wealth for major advanced economies. We combine historical series on the asset composition of different wealth groups with asset-specific pre-tax returns and apply group-specific average tax rates to obtain post-tax returns to wealth. The resulting series cover more than a century and allow us to document how returns differed across the wealth distribution, how these differences evolved over time, and how they relate to changing portfolio structures and tax regimes. The database provides the first harmonised long-run evidence on heterogeneous returns across wealth groups and offers a new empirical foundation for analysing the long-run evolution of wealth inequality.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Returns to wealth for everyone: Long-run evolution of group-specific rates of return along the wealth distribution

papers.abstract:
We investigate long-term labour market risks and pension contribution dynamics among Italian workers enrolled in the Notional Defined Contribution (NDC) pension system, which applies to all individuals entering the labour market from 1996 onwards. Using a large administrative sample of individual contribution histories (covering about 15% of all workers, including the self-employed), we analyse career trajectories from labour market entry to 2021 for cohorts entering between 1996 and 2011.

We focus on two key dimensions of career fragility: (i) the share of weeks with actual or credited pension contributions—expressed also in full-time-equivalent terms—relative to potential weeks, and (ii) the accumulated pension wealth compared with that of a representative continuously employed worker earning either the median annual wage or the median full-time annual wage as benchmark. For each cohort, we document average trajectories, the incidence of “poor careers” (defined as contributing for less than 60% of potential time and/or accumulating less than 60% of the representative benchmark), and the degree of inequality in both labour supply and pension accumulation. Results are presented by gender, contractual status, and age at entry.

We complement the descriptive evidence with counterfactual simulations that vary GDP growth (the return on contributions), introduce wage floors, and reduce part-time and unemployment risks, thereby assessing the relative contribution of these factors to low pension accumulation.

Across the 1996–2011 entry cohorts, we find persistent and sizeable career instability, particularly among women. The share of individuals with low work intensity and insufficient contribution accumulation is high and increasing in more recent cohorts, even when observed at the same distance from entry. For example, in the 2001 cohort, after twenty years, around 30% of men and 40% of women have contributed for no more than 60% of potential time, and a similar share has accumulated less than 60% of the benchmark pension wealth—suggesting substantial risks of receiving very low pensions if career conditions do not improve.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: From fragile careers to inadequate pensions: a cohort comparison of career dynamics in Italy

papers.abstract:
This paper unveils a novel externality of product market regulation in the labour market. It
shows theoretically and empirically that higher barriers to entry in product markets translate into higher employers’ labour market power, measured by the wage markdown—–the ratio between the marginal product of labour and the wage. Using quasi-exogenous variation in investment restrictions across 389 manufacturing product markets in Indonesia, the analysis finds that wage markdowns would have been almost 10% lower without restrictions and workers would have earned a larger fraction of their marginal product. The analysis supports the model’s prediction that lower entry is the main driver of the positive relationship between investment restrictions and wage mark-downs, and that restrictions increase markdowns more in commuting zones where employers have already substantial labour market power. The restrictions do not affect employment, consistently with recent models based on search frictions and wage bargaining, but not with classical monopsony models.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Product Market Monopolies and Labor Market Monopsonies

papers.abstract:
This detailed draft presents an analysis of personal income and wealth distribution in Brazil for 2023 by innovatively combining data from the Individual Income Tax Return (DIRPF) and the Continuous Annual National Household Sample Survey (HS). This combined methodology, based on the work of Blanchet, Flores, and Morgan (2022), addresses the traditional limitations of household surveys in capturing high incomes and tax data’s lack of coverage at the bottom of the distribution. The integration of these sources allows for a more accurate evaluation of inequality, particularly across gender and race/color dimensions. Notably, the effective PIT rate exhibited regressivity at the very top, falling from a peak of 12.0% (93rd percentile) to 4.6% for the richest 0.01%.

Examining the full adult population, women are underrepresented in high-income strata and face a significantly lower average annual income compared to men. The largest income disparities were observed across the race/color dimension: white people constitute 78.6% of the richest 1%, while black women form the largest portion of the poorest 10%. These findings underscore that both gender and race/color are critical social conditioning factors that exacerbate income inequality in Brazil.
papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: Personal Distribution of Income and Wealth of the Brazilian Population

papers.abstract: In recent decades, the United States has experienced a notable rise in markups, a slowdown in productivity growth, and an increase in wealth inequality. We present a framework that unifies these trends into a common driving force. In particular, increased barriers to entry raises markups and boost corporate profits. Rising profits elevates firm valuations, fuels the demand for capital, and drives up asset returns. At the same time, the reduction in competition stifles overall economic growth. Wealth inequality is shaped by the return gap, r − g, which represents the difference between asset returns and the economy’s growth rate. The rise in capital demand together with a reduction in growth leads to a widening of the return gap, which amplifies inequality by affecting the saving patterns of households in different ways across the wealth distribution, deepening the divide between the rich and the poor. These trends result in substantial welfare losses for the majority of households, while only the top 1%, and especially the top 0.1%, experience gains.
papers.subtheme: Asset Prices, Returns and Portfolio Dynamics
papers.title: Market power, growth and wealth inequality

papers.session_title: The African Inequality Review: a Sneak Preview
papers.subtheme: Income Distribution Drivers
papers.title: The Latin American (LACIR) example: “here is one we made earlier…”

papers.abstract: This paper studies VAT avoidance in private jet ownership using administrative aircraft registry data from 41 European countries linked to high-frequency ADS-B flight tracking for 1,902 business jets. I document that 35% of European private jets are registered in tax havens, yet virtually none operate in their country of registration: only 7 of 664 tax-haven-registered jets are primarily grounded locally. Exploiting cross-country VAT differentials, I estimate that a 1-percentage-point increase in the VAT rate raises the probability of tax-haven registration by 3.8 percentage points, implying an avoidance elasticity of 0.22. Combining aircraft price data with statutory VAT rates, I estimate at least 1.05 billion in VAT avoidance over the past 15 years. The findings provide new evidence on the mobility of high-value assets and highlight structural weaknesses in VAT enforcement for cross-border luxury goods.
papers.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
papers.title: Turbulence in Taxation: A Study on Tax Avoidance with Private Jets

papers.abstract:
This paper leverages household-level data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID)
to investigate saving rate heterogeneity across the wealth distribution in the United States.
I estimate saving rates across wealth deciles using two complementary approaches: the
cross-sectional method and the aggregate method. Four empirical facts emerge. First, saving
rates out of labor income and new resources rise with wealth ranks (flow-based saving
rates), whereas saving rates out of wealth and composite resources are roughly stable
or only modestly increasing (stock-based saving rates). Second, wealth (rank) mobility
contributes substantially to saving rate heterogeneity. However, the direction of its effect
differs between cross-sectional and aggregate methods due to their distinct treatment
of wealth (rank) mobility. Third, the synthetic method (commonly used in the absence
of panel data) overestimates saving rates below the 80th percentile, and underestimates
them for the top 20%. Fourth, saving increasingly consists of saving out of capital gains
as households are richer: wealthier households save for the most part by holding appreciating
assets. The paper provides several empirical moments that are of interest to the
heterogeneous agent macro literature.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Saving Rate Heterogeneity across the Wealth (Rank) Distribution in the United States

papers.abstract: This paper examines the levels and dynamics of wealth inequality in Chile between 2007 and 2021, focusing on two major macroeconomic events: the sharp increase in housing prices following the introduction of a value-added tax (VAT) on new dwellings in 2016 and the large-scale liquidation of pension assets through early withdrawals during the COVID-19 pandemic. To do so, we construct a micro–macro consistent wealth distribution by extending existing methodologies to integrate administrative pension fund balances into household wealth surveys using machine learning techniques. Our results reveal pronounced wealth concentration: the top 1\% hold roughly one-third of total private wealth—levels comparable to those observed in the United States—driven by their disproportionate ownership of financial assets. In contrast, the bottom 50\% hold 7–9\%, primarily in housing and pension assets—shares that exceed those observed in most European countries. Nevertheless, we document a modest decline in wealth inequality over the period, particularly after 2016, reflecting the combined influence of two opposing forces: housing appreciation, which mostly benefited the bottom 90\% of households, and pension withdrawals, which broadly reduced wealth across the distribution while relatively increasing inequality. Our findings on levels, trends, and counterfactuals are robust across alternative specifications and methodological approaches.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: From Housing Gains to Pension Losses: Micro-Macro Integration to Reveal Wealth Inequality Dynamics in Chile

papers.abstract: This paper studies the role of changes in workforce composition in monopsony power, a significant driver of income inequality. We develop a monopsony model in which a firm’s wage markdown—the wedge between MRPL and wage—is a weighted average of markdowns for heterogeneous workers. We empirically test the theory using India’s National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA), which generates non-manufacturing jobs in rural villages. Consistent with the model predictions, at manufacturing firms, we find that the program increases average markdowns by crowding out mobile workers and effectively increasing the share of immobile workers with low labor supply elasticity.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Public Works Program, Labor Supply, and Monopsony

papers.abstract: We combine detailed administrative and survey data with national accounts to estimate the distribution of national income in Finland. In addition to being the first to construct distributional national accounts (DINA) for a Nordic welfare state, we make several methodological contributions. Most notably, we analyze how the treatment of retained earnings affects estimates of income inequality. We are currently working on allocating education and health care services using individual-level registry data, and on extending the DINA framework from annual income to income over the life cycle. On the distribution of income in Finland, the DINA series show higher levels of income inequality than the narrower fiscal income series, but trends are very similar across the two approaches.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Income Inequality in a Nordic Welfare State: Finnish Distributional National Accounts

papers.abstract: This paper examines the role of wealth inequality as a predictor of financial crises, analyzing data from 18 countries between 1870 and 2020. Unlike previous research focused on the effects of financial crises on inequality, we explore whether increases in wealth concentration—specifically in the top 1%—elevate crisis risk. Our findings indicate that, even after accounting for key crisis predictors, a one standard deviation rise in the growth of the top 1% wealth share is associated with a 3 to 8 percentage points increase in crisis probability, with results robust across various crisis lists and empirical approaches. Temporal dynamics reveal that while a credit boom can jeopardize the financial system as early as the following year, it takes several years for an increase in private wealth accumulation and wealth concentration at the top to significantly heighten the risk of a systemic bank run, serving as early signals of potential instability. Furthermore, we find evidence that asset price bubbles can serve as transmission channels, although these relationships vary by asset class and “bubble” definition. Our findings suggest that addressing wealth concentration could reduce inequality while acting as a stabilizing force for financial systems, highlighting the importance of incorporating broader inequality metrics in crisis prediction models and exploring policy mechanisms to mitigate systemic risks.
papers.subtheme: Asset Prices, Returns and Portfolio Dynamics
papers.title: Wealth Inequality, Asset Price Bubbles and Financial Crises

papers.session_title: The African Inequality Review: a Sneak Preview
papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: Fairer but Falling Behind: Africa's Inequality Paradox in a Shifting Global Order  -- Rodrigo Oliveira

papers.abstract: Using exhaustive microdata on the worldwide activity of multinational firms from Country-by-Country Reports linked to employer-employee data, we study how profit shifting affects workers' earnings. We overcome two challenges: we build a credible counterfactual profit allocation and relate profit-sharing to profit shifting using the mandatory profit-sharing policy in France. We estimate that large French multinationals shift 19% of their foreign profits annually to low-tax jurisdictions, resulting in €10.3 billion shifted out of France and €3.7 billion in lost tax revenues. We show that profit shifting then reduces annual employees' earnings by 2.6%. Low-income workers are disproportionately affected, the bottom 10% losing 3.2% of wages compared to 2.3% for top 10% earners. Changing the profit-sharing formula to account for global profitability, rather than subsidiary-level profitability, would increase wages by 4.1% for workers in profit-shifting subsidiaries.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Shift or Share? Profit Shifting and Implications for Workers Profit-Sharing

papers.abstract:
This paper constructs the first harmonized long-run series of Chinese national wealth from
1911 to 2020 by combining newly assembled archival data with historical national accounts.
The resulting evidence reveals a distinctive J-shaped trajectory of wealth-to-income ratios that
stands in sharp contrast to the U-shaped pattern documented forWestern economies. China’s
net national wealth-to-income ratio remained broadly stagnant around 300–400 percent for
most of the twentieth century—reflecting the combined legacies of political fragmentation,
wars, state intervention, and price distortions—and fell to a wartime nadir of around 200
percent amid the destruction of World War II, before rising steeply and persistently from
the mid-1980s to nearly 900 percent in 2020. This delayed yet dramatic surge suggests that
large-scale wealth accumulation in developing economies tends to emerge only when political
centralization coincides with institutional and market transformations, including property
rights reforms and the liberalization of asset prices. The long-run evolution of Chinese
national wealth also reveals profound compositional shifts driven by ideological change. The
public share of national wealth followed an inverted-U pattern—rising from negative shares
during the Republican era to nearly 90 percent under Maoist socialism, before falling back to
about 30 percent in the 2010s under a mixed-ownership regime—reflecting the century-long
redefinition of the boundary between state and private property. Within the private sector,
the asset composition shifted from farmland to residential housing and financial savings,
while public wealth became increasingly concentrated in corporate assets. Finally, we observe
a near-zero correlation between national saving and wealth growth, indicating that long-term
changes in Chinese national wealth were primarily driven by capital gains and losses shaped
by the interaction of market forces, state policies, and ideological transformations across
successive political regimes.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Ideological Shifts and Wealth Dynamics: Unraveling the Century-Long Accumulation of Chinese National Wealth, 1911-2020

papers.abstract: Although the nature of private wealth depends considerably on institutional contexts, studies have yet to elucidate how welfare states shape the patterns of wealth inequality. In this study we investigate wealth inequality and redistribution through pension systems by translating pension entitlements into wealth values. Using cross-nationally harmonized wealth surveys merged with remaining life expectancy data constructed from population projections, we estimate inequalities in ‘augmented wealth’ – a concept that counts pension entitlements as wealth – among older households across 17 high-income countries. Results show that augmented wealth inequality is considerably lower than marketable wealth inequality in all countries, with a substantial cross-national variation in the degree of redistribution through pension wealth. Moreover, the cross-national patterning of augmented wealth inequality resembles that of income inequality when pension entitlements are treated as a household wealth component. Our decomposition of inequality combined with regression analysis also shows that the relative size of pension wealth matters more than the system’s progressivity in achieving redistribution. Finally, it is the public-private mix rather than the sole capacity of public systems that limits the influence of marketable wealth. Overall, our study contributes to multiple bodies of the literature, including studies on wealth inequality, redistributive policies and institutions, and the public-private governance of the welfare state.
papers.subtheme: Global Wealth Dynamics - General
papers.title: Wealth Inequality and Welfare States: Pension systems, the Public-Private Mix, and Augmented Wealth in Old Age

papers.abstract: Do cooperative firms foster local economic development? This paper examines Mexico, assembling a new georeferenced panel dataset at the 10 × 10 km grid-cell level for 2015–2023. Across multiple research designs, we consistently find that cooperative presence boosts local development, measured by nightlight intensity. An event-study design shows persistent extensive margin gains of 6–8% within four years of entry. To address selection concerns, we implement a shift–share IV strategy based on endogenous lagged-cooperative presence and plausibly exogenous sectoral growth shocks; the results imply that one additional cooperative increases nightlight density by about 2.7%. Complementary census evidence links cooperatives to higher schooling, home asset ownership, and decrease migration pressures. We also document stronger effects in Indigenous communities, where cooperatives have longer survival spells. Aggregate patterns suggest that cooperatives increase agricultural specialization but with clear productivity gains, while redistributive effects raise local disposable income and decrease poverty. These findings provide novel causal evidence that cooperatives can function as engines of inclusive local development.
papers.subtheme: Firm Dynamics, Market Power and Productivity
papers.title: Lifting Each Other Up: How Cooperative Firms Foster Local Development

papers.abstract: The literature on inequality and top-income concentration in developing countries lacks studies covering longer time frames. This study introduces Ecuador’s first comprehensive Distributional National Account (DINA) series, covering the period from 1990 to 2022, and provides detailed pretax and posttax income indicators. An innovative integration method that merges extensive household and tax microdata allows for a nuanced analysis of income inequality across three decades characterized by economic booms and crises. The results indicate that Ecuador’s extreme income concentration at the top persists into the present. In 2022, the top 1% captured 25% of pretax income, and Ecuador stands out among Latin American countries for having the highest income share held by the top 0.1%. Although not designed for causal inference, this study offers insights into the political economy of inequality in a primary goods exporting country during exogenous economic shocks. Economic institutions in Ecuador have probably passed from an extractive equilibrium before the banking crisis and subsequent dollarization in 2000 to a weak inclusive equilibrium during the commodity price boom until 2014. This inclusive equilibrium has been endangered in recent years, as economic power concentration could not be further reduced and the redistributional capacity built up during the commodity price boom has been undermined after the COVID-pandemic.
papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: Extreme Income Inequality in Ecuador - Dollarization, Commodity Price Boom, and Citizen Revolution

papers.abstract:
Achieving global climate and biodiversity goals requires unprecedented levels of green investment, yet the financing conditions facing public and private actors remain deeply unequal. This paper develops a heuristic, dynamic framework to explain how financing conditions for green assets and actions emerge, evolve, and interact with macroeconomic structures. Combining insights from ecological macroeconomics, neo-Schumpeterian theory, and balance-sheet approaches, we conceptualise the green finance gap not as a static shortfall, but as a dynamic misalignment between needed actions, the agents capable of implementing them, and the funding sources they can effectively access. We demonstrate how heterogeneous costs, risks, expected returns, and context-specific constraints shape a path-dependent selection
of green investments, thereby influencing their distributive and economic effects.
Our approach clarifies how different green-finance mechanisms — including costreducing instruments, resource-enabling tools, and risk-mitigation schemes — can
reshape the investment environment and alter agents’ financing conditions to reach
ecological targets. These insights provide a foundation for more context-specific policy design and call for future empirical work linking project-level dynamics, institutional arrangements, and macro-financial vulnerabilities across diverse national settings.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Who Owns the Green Transition? Unequal Access to Finance in a Dynamic Framework

papers.abstract: Over the past decade, more than 100 jurisdictions have signed automatic exchange of financial information agreements (AEoI) in an effort to fight cross-border tax evasion. This paper studies the effectiveness and coverage of these agreements using account data leaked from an Isle of Man bank with a large customer base in countries participating to AEoI. We establish three sets of results. First, we find that the design of the governing AEoI agreement absolved the bank from reviewing and reporting a very large share (81%) of all the wealth owned by tax residents of AEoI participating countries, and instead the responsibility passed to smaller entities with weaker incentives to comply. Second, out of the wealth that fell under the bank's reporting responsibility, foreign tax authorities only received reports covering  50% of what their tax residents held at the bank. We estimate that a further 32% went unreported due to loopholes in rule design. The rest of the accounts did not appear to have been reported, although through the information available in the leak we classified them as reportable. Third, we find evidence that bank clients who were more at risk of being reported on preemptively closed their accounts, potentially circumventing the AEoI reporting process. This paper provides new evidence on the potential limits of these agreements and how sophisticated individuals can ultimately avoid the AEoI transparency shock.
papers.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
papers.title: When Bankers Become Informants: Behavioral Effects of Automatic Exchange of Information

papers.abstract: There has been a seismic shift in age-wealth profiles in the U.S. over years 1983 to 2022. The most notable is the sharp rise in the relative household wealth of age group 75 and over. Correspondingly, the relative wealth holdings of all other age groups dropped over these years. Using the Survey of Consumer Finances, the paper focuses on the youngest age group, 35 and under, and the oldest age group, 75 and over, and analyzes the factors behind these relative shifts in wealth. I find that the three principal factors are the homeownership rate, total stocks directly and indirectly owned, and home mortgage debt. The homeownership rate is the same in the two years for the youngest group but falls relative to the overall rate, whereas it shoots up for the oldest group both in actual level and relative to the overall average. The value of stock holdings rises for both age groups but vastly more for the oldest households compared to the youngest ones and accounts for a substantial portion of the elderly’s relative wealth gains. Mortgage debt rises in dollar terms for both groups but considerably more in relative terms for the youngest group.
papers.subtheme: Generational wealth dynamics
papers.title: The Extraordinary Rise in the Wealth of Older American Households

papers.abstract: Housing wealth plays a central but complex role as a factor shaping wealth inequality in advanced economies. Recent comparative research identifies housing equity as the central determinant of cross-national variation in wealth inequality, demonstrating that real estate is not only the largest component of household portfolios but also the most equally distributed relative to financial assets, nonhousing real assets, and consumer debts. Yet this literature treats real estate as a monolithic category, obscuring the dual nature of property as both a consumption good and an investment vehicle. We extend this framework by disaggregating housing wealth into Household Main Residence (HMR) and Other Real Estate (ORE) to examine how each contributes distinctly to national wealth inequality levels. Using harmonized microdata from the Household Finance and Consumption Survey (EU, 2021) and the Survey of Consumer Finances (US, 2022), we demonstrate that HMR and ORE operate as opposing forces: while primary residences equalize wealth distributions, secondary properties concentrate them. Using Gini decomposition methods, we show that ORE is the most unequally distributed wealth component in every country examined, exceeding even the concentration of financial assets. Thus, the equalizing role of housing, emphasized in prior work, holds only for primary residences while Other Real Estate, though largely overlooked, emerges as a potent driver of wealth concentration in advanced economies.
papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: The Wealth Inequality of Real Estate: Other Real Estate and Its Role in Wealth Concentration

papers.abstract: How do labor market institutions shape the propagation of inflation shocks? We address this question by studying Brazil’s annually indexed minimum wage in a highinflation context. Conventional wisdom suggests that inflation can “grease” labor market adjustments, but institutional wage-setting may alter this mechanism. Using administrative data, we show that indexation creates upward nominal wage rigidity: workers exposed to the policy experience fewer month-to-month wage increases before indexation events, and firms anticipate the policy by rigidifying wages of workers who will be newly bound. We evaluate the macroeconomic implications by introducing a cost-push shock to a New Keynesian model with heterogeneous labor and an indexed minimum wage. While staggered indexation amplifies the inflation as grease mechanism by introducing nominal rigidities, anticipation dampens it via intertemporal substitution. Overall, amplification matters more since cost-push shocks have a weaker effect compared to a setting where the minimum wage indexes every period. Our findings demonstrate that even in high-inflation environments, the institutional structure of wage-setting fundamentally shapes how shocks propagate through the economy.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Do Institutions Remove Inflation’s Grease? Evidence from Brazil’s Indexed Minimum Wage

papers.abstract:
We use population-wide administrative micro-data to provide new estimates of income
inequality and effective tax rates by income groups in Brazil, capturing all income and all tax
payments. Our data allow us to link businesses to their owners and thus to allocate business
income and associated taxes to the corresponding individual firm owners. We provide sharp
upward revisions to official inequality estimates: the top 1% earns 27.4% of total income in
2019, one of the highest level recorded in the world. The tax system, which relies heavily
on consumption taxes, is regressive: while the average tax rate in the economy is 42.5%, this
rate falls to 20.6% for million-dollar earners (roughly the top 0.01% of the distribution), due to
the non-taxation of dividends and provisions that reduce corporate tax liabilities. We provide
evidence suggesting that inequality in developing countries may be systematically underestimated, as even in Brazil—where dividends are untaxed, and hence incentives to retain income within companies are limited—attributing profits to business owners substantially raises in_x0002_come inequality.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Tax Progressivity and Inequality in Brazil: Evidence from Integrated Administrative Data

papers.abstract: This paper uses extended series on income and wealth inequality from the World Inequality Database (WID) covering all world regions over the 1800-2025 period, together with new series on hourly productivity and human capital expenditure, to revisit the relationship between equality and development, with a much broader comparative and historical perspective than previous studies. Over the long-run, we find a strong positive association between equality and productivity. Our proposed interpretation is that the rise of inclusive “social-democratic” institutions (including extended access to human capital, public services and democratic participation) led both to more equality and higher productivity, particularly in Western and Nordic Europe. We discuss the implications for future sustainable development strategies.
papers.primary_theme: Measurement of historical income and wealth inequality dynamics
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Equality and Development: A Comparative & Historical Perspective 1800-2025

papers.abstract: This study presents preliminary evidence that the European Emission Trading Scheme (EU ETS) is exploited by multinational companies to artificially shift profits between European countries.  Specifically, using the EU transaction log and Orbis ownership data, I highlight abnormally high levels of internal trade in emission allowances at year-end—despite the April surrender deadline – within firms under the same Global Ultimate Owner (GUO). This activity is especially marked in transactions involving firms without actual emission certificate needs. Towards the year-end, allowances are moved from subsidiaries in strict accounting jurisdictions to those in lenient ones, indicating regulatory arbitrage. These patterns hint to a potential misuse of the EU ETS for financial manipulation rather than emission reduction. I hope to add further analysis, in particular related to the market price of allowances, to contribute to ensuring the EU ETS remains an effective tool for environmental objectives without facilitating unintended financial exploitation.
papers.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
papers.title: Profit Shifting via Carbon Emission Trading: First Indications

papers.abstract: We show that high-income buyers earn higher financial returns to housing using detailed transaction data from Denmark. The gap in housing returns is explained by location, with little role for market timing, property type, buyer characteristics, or risk-taking. Higher-income households purchase in areas with persistently higher house price growth but comparable risk, liquidity, and downside exposure to those chosen by lower-income households. Credit constraints and consumption needs limit the feasible choice set of lower-income households, limiting access to high-return locations. Our results highlight how spatial sorting amplifies differences in wealth accumulation: returns on the largest household asset are shaped less by risk or investment skill than by consumption needs, housing supply, and financial constraints.
papers.subtheme: Macroeconomic Drivers: Inflation, Growth and Cycles
papers.title: Housing Returns across the Income Distribution

papers.abstract: We study whether higher taxes on housing relative to financial assets for wealthy households can improve housing affordability for the rest of the population. We exploit the 2017 French wealth tax reform, which transformed the comprehensive wealth tax into a real-estate tax and sharply deteriorated the after-tax return to housing relative to financial assets at the top. Using cadastral data, we construct a measure of local exposure to the reform and show that wealthy owners increased housing sales significantly more in highly exposed areas, while non-wealthy owners did not respond. We then examine local redistribution effects and find that, in the most exposed areas, post-reform transactions increasingly involve buyers who are less wealthy than the sellers, alongside a rise in first-time buyers. Finally, portfolio responses occur only for properties benefiting from capital gains tax rebates, suggesting an interaction with capital gains taxation. Our findings indicate that fiscal policies affecting portfolio incentives at the top can influence local housing market dynamics.
papers.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
papers.title: Portfolio Allocation and Housing Markets

papers.abstract: We provide new estimates of top fiscal income shares and top national income shares in Japan, using most recent tax statistics and other data in 2008-2023. We find that both top fiscal income shares and top national income shares increased only modestly during the period of economic recovery since 2012. When capital gains are included, however, the top 0.01% fiscal income share increased sharply in the recent decade, approaching the level reached at the peak of the bubble economy. When compared with major Western and East Asian countries, the degree of income concentration in Japan is at the lowest level in recent years. We also discuss data limitations and plan to address potential bias that may rise with those limitations.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Recent Trends in Income Concentration in Japan, 2008-2023:  New Estimates of Top Fiscal Income Shares and Top National Income Shares

papers.abstract:
Can the rise in the wealth-to-output ratio observed in advanced economies over recent decades be explained by an increase in top income inequality? Recent contributions that advance this interpretation struggle to account for the fact that the increase in wealth was driven by asset prices, rather than capital accumulation. This paper shows that these stylized facts can be reconciled in the presence of insatiable preference for wealth. Such preferences induce a cap on optimal consumption—which is more likely to become binding when income inequality is large. When it does, top-income agents accumulate diverging wealth over time while keeping their consumption bounded. This consumption-saving behavior then supports the existence of a  uniquely determined rational bubble, which grows at a rate that exceeds that of the economy.
The bubble crowds out investment, while its diverging price sustains a permanent rise in wealth
inequality. In this environment, wealth and capital income taxes are not equivalent, but both can shift the equilibrium from bubbly to non-bubbly—thus being potentially redistributive and growth-enhancing. A quantitative exercise suggests that a 1.5 percent wealth tax in the U.S. would raise capital by 4.5 percent over 30 years.
papers.subtheme: Savings, Capital Accumulation and Wealth Mobility
papers.title: A Scrooge McDuck Theory of Wealth Dynamics

papers.abstract: Because Marx is seen as a figure representing leftist politics, pro (anti) Marx camps argue that an increase (decrease) in income inequality over time – a trend, well established in the literature across several major economies – vindicates (invalidates) his predictions about capitalist development. Ironically, in his writing, Marx shows little interest in the distribution of income among individuals (as we generally measure today); instead, his focus remains predominantly on class struggle and the viability of the capitalist system. Thus, the laws of motion of capitalism remain largely disconnected with the data on income and wealth polarization today. Our paper intervenes at this point – we use Branko Milanovic’s recently proposed “inequality scenarios” that are consistent with Marx’s theory of capitalist development as well as measurable using modern data on national incomes and wealth concentration. We combine the World Inequality Database with Penn World Tables and a Hidden Markov Model to classify 129 countries into 7 “Inequality Scenarios” which are drawn as potential possibilities in Marx’s writings. In the most optimistic scenario, an economy can experience a secular increase in real wages, a decline in profit rates and a decline in wealth concentration. However, our computations show that over 1995-2019, most countries fall under a “Polarizing Regime” where wealth concentration occurs concurrently with rising real wages and falling rates of profit. We also document a high probability of regime transition in middle income countries. Our results have important implications for the political economy of income inequality in the 21st Century.
papers.subtheme: Global Wealth Dynamics - General
papers.title: Unequal Regimes, Profitability and its Consequences: Evidence from 129 countries

papers.abstract: This paper examines whether the 2006 Affirmative Action policy of higher education quotas for the Other Backward Classes (OBC) reduced or reinforced inequality within the beneficiary group. Using two waves of the nationally representative India Human Development Survey and a Difference in Differences design, I estimate the causal effect of the reform on educational attainment across sub-caste (jati) groups. The policy increased years of education for OBCs by 4.8 percent relative to Forward Castes. The effect, however, was highly uneven within the beneficiary group; dominant Elite sub-castes gained 16.4 percent, while Non-Elite sub-castes gained only 4.1 percent, a difference that is large and statistically significant. This fourfold difference indicates substantial elite capture. These results show that affirmative action can reduce between-group gaps, yet the decline is driven primarily by the Elite group, leading to a simultaneous rise in within-group inequality. The findings highlight the need to redesign quota policy to better reach the most disadvantaged sub-castes.
papers.subtheme: Discrimination (castes)
papers.title: Who Benefits from Affirmative Action? Sub-Caste Inequality in India

papers.abstract:
We propose three novel methods for the measurement of inequality with count variables. Traditional inequality indices assume continuous variables: they allow for transfers of real-valued quantities and the egalitarian distributions are degenerate at the mean. After redefining
transfers for exclusively natural numbers, we show that egalitarian distributions remain degenerate for count variables only when the mean is natural. Otherwise, egalitarian distributions feature pairwise differences between their values of at most one unit. We propose
an axiomatically characterised class of inequality indices for count variables which satisfies the traditional axioms, with a reworking of the transfer and equality principles incorporating modifications to the transfers and the egalitarian distributions, respectively. The indices in the proposed class are monotonic transformations of the difference between a symmetric Schur-convex function evaluated at the distribution of interest and the same function evaluated at any egalitarian distribution with equal mean. Our second proposal is using traditional relative inequality indices which enable the transformation of any inequality comparison into one involving only count-variable distributions with natural means. The third proposal is to measure inequality as the distance between a distribution and its corresponding egalitarian distribution using distance functions satisfying the transfer principle and other desirable properties. The indices in this proposed class are a symmetric Schur-convex function evaluated at the difference between a distribution and its egalitarian counterpart. We illustrate the usefulness of the new indices with an international comparison of inequality in household sizes.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Inequality measurement for count data: theory and application to inequality in household sizes across the world

papers.abstract: This paper provides the first estimates of top income shares in twentieth-century Mexico based on personal income tax tabulations. Using newly digitised schedular tax data for 1927, 1930, and 1943, together with global-income tabulations for 1970, I reconstruct gross taxable income at the top of the distribution and relate it to control income and population series consistent with national accounts. The benchmark estimates indicate very high concentration at the top of the distribution: the top 1% received about 15.5% of national income in 1927 and 18.4% in 1970, with no sign in the available tax data of the large mid-twentieth-century decline in top shares observed in many advanced economies. Evidence for the merchant elite-roughly the top 0.08\% of the population-shows that this group accounted for between 3% and 10% of total income across the four benchmark years. While the sparse nature of the historical tax record does not allow a full annual series, the new estimates close a major gap in the historical evidence on Mexican top incomes and, within the limits of the available benchmark years, are consistent with the view that Mexico did not experience the "Great Egalitarian Leveling" in top income shares that took place in many advanced economies during the mid-twentieth century.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Top Incomes in Twentieth-Century Mexico: New Evidence from Tax Records

papers.abstract:
Aguiar, Moll, and Scheuer (2024) show that whenever asset-price changes are driven by
changes in discount rates, the optimal tax base for capital gains taxes must target realized
trades. This result stands in contrast to recent proposals for the taxation of ultra-high-net-
worth individuals which generally feature accrual-based capital gains taxes (Zucman, 2024).
In this paper, I take the theoretical propositions in Aguiar et al. (2024) to an empirical
analysis focusing on U.S. billionaires and the publicly traded firms of which they are major
shareholders. Using data from Forbes, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and
Compustat, I show that (i) capital gains realizations of U.S. billionaires in 2024 amounted
to approximately 1.35% of their wealth and that (ii) between 1998 and today around 75%
of the increase in market valuation of the billionaire-owned publicly traded firms can be
attributed to the rise in their past and future expected profits while around 25% are due
to changes in discount rates. These results show that the theoretical propositions in Aguiar
et al. (2024) do not necessarily weaken the case for accrual-based capital gains taxes on
ultra-high-net-worth individuals.

NOTE to Conference Organizers: This work is a continuation of my master thesis at PSE and receives continuous guidance from my supervisor Gabriel Zucman. Part of the results in this work have been already leveraged and cited in "How Much Tax Do US Billionaires Pay? Evidence from Administrative Data" (Balkir et al., 2025). In my current position as Predoc in the Wealth Team at the EU Tax Observatory, I continue working on this project and plan to have a revised and extensively improved version to be presented at the World Inequality Conference. Among other extensions, we plan to retrospectively simulate the effects of different capital gains tax systems on the ownership shares of US Billionaires in the listed firms they own. The updated and improved version will hopefully be ready for circulation as a working paper around Summer 2026.
papers.subtheme: Historical Measurement - General
papers.title: Are US Billionaires' Unrealized Capital Gains "Paper Gains"?

papers.abstract: This article challenges the prevailing view that John Maynard Keynes ignored income distribution in his economic thinking. While scholars such as Branko Milanovic argue that Keynes lacked an “integrative vision” of inequality, a closer reading reveals that distributional concerns are woven throughout his work —from The Economic Consequences of the Peace to How to Pay for the War. Though Keynes never developed a full theory of distribution like Michał Kalecki, he embedded inequality into key parameters of his macroeconomic analysis, particularly in relation to effective demand, wage policy, full employment, and the burdens of war. We argue that Keynes’s evolving engagement with a “functional theory of distribution” —in which inequality is assessed mainly by its effects on the macroeconomy— offers essential insights for current policy challenges. Far from indifferent, Keynes provides a historically grounded and macroeconomically coherent framework for understanding inequality. Revisiting this overlooked dimension of his thought opens the way toward a Keynesian “economics of enough” for today’s ecologically constrained and unequal world.
papers.subtheme: Inequality Perceptions - General
papers.title: Keynes's Vision of Inequality (And Why it Matters)

papers.abstract: Despite the formal end of Apartheid in 1994, South Africa remains one of the most unequal countries in the world. This paper investigates the mechanisms behind this persistence of inequality by developing a spatial dynastic model with heterogeneous agents, incomplete markets, and endogenous choices over education, occupation, savings, and location. Drawing on newly assembled micro-geographic data, we document a shift in inequality from being primarily across races to increasingly within the Black population, with spatial segregation—especially the legacy of Townships—playing a key role. Our model, disciplined by detailed spatial and socioeconomic data, captures the slow intergenerational convergence in education and occupational outcomes observed in post-Apartheid South Africa. It shows how inherited spatial disadvantages—through high commuting costs, disparities in school quality, and limited access to credit—continue to shape households’ educational, occupational, and locational choices, reinforcing inequality long after formal legal barriers have been removed. Quantitatively, we find that removing persistent spatial distortions in Townships accelerates the transition to a race-blind equilibrium by 40% and reduces income inequality by 10%.
papers.subtheme: Racial segregation
papers.title: End of Apartheid, Not of Inequality: The Slow Transition in a Segregated Economy

papers.abstract: There is increasing interest globally in making extreme wealth more visible, governable, and accountable for the harms it generates. One contribution to that agenda would be the development of a social indicator of extreme wealth. This paper considers what lessons, if any, the last century of scholarship on poverty definition and measurement – which has led to a powerful suite of analytical and advocacy tools - holds for the development of extreme wealth as a social indicator. Analogies and disanalogies between poverty and extreme wealth are discussed, taking in turn each of the six steps required to define a social indicator – purpose, concept, evaluative space, metric, threshold and statistic. As social indicators, both poverty and extreme wealth have as their purpose to provide the means to monitor and evaluate social and economic arrangements. The underlying concept in both cases is harm, although the nature, mechanisms and incidence of harm are distinct. Poverty has been assessed uni- and multi-dimensionally using inputs, outputs, outcomes and capabilities. Extreme wealth could likewise, in principle, be captured in any of these ways, although the paper argues that inputs (wealth itself) and capabilities (potential harms) may be the most fruitful to pursue. Complexities arise in defining the metric (what counts as income? what is wealth?); judgements in relation to poverty are more settled but there is an emerging body of scholarship on wealth. Several of the existing approaches to setting a poverty threshold are relevant to methods for determining an extreme wealth line. Finally, reflecting on the value of a poverty gap statistic to augment the information contained in a poverty headcount leads to the suggestion that a total or average ‘excess wealth’ statistic could be developed as well as a count of the number of people above an extreme wealth line. The paper concludes that while there is much work to be done to develop the conceptualisation, definition and measurement of extreme wealth, the challenges are not of a different kind to those that researchers have encountered and overcome in relation to poverty. Poverty measurement provides a useful roadmap for the development of a social indicator of extreme wealth.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Line drawing: can poverty measurement inform the methodology for a social indicator of extreme wealth?

papers.abstract: Using a statistically robust decomposition framework, we assess group-level contributions to overall economic inequality. Applying this approach to comprehensive microdata spanning from 1962 to 2019, we find that the recent surge in U.S. inequality is primarily driven by rising within-group income dispersion among the top decile of earners, rather than by between-group inequality (mean differences) relative to the rest of the population. Specifically, our results indicate that over 87% of post-2000 U.S. pre-tax income inequality can be attributed to income variation within the top 10%, with the top 1% alone accounting for more than 70%. Our post-tax income analysis reveals a similar, though slightly weaker, pattern. A further decomposition by income source underscores the growing importance of within-group labor income dispersion among top earners in driving U.S. economic inequality.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: The Deepening Divide Within the Rich as a Key Driver of U.S. Economic Inequality

papers.abstract: This paper examines how asset tests in minimum income programs affect low-income households' savings, exploiting the introduction of Spanish minimum income scheme (Ingreso Mínimo Vital, IMV). Using administrative panel data and the Callaway–Sant’Anna difference-in-differences design, we compare income-eligible beneficiaries to households rejected solely due to the asset threshold. We find that IMV receipt increases liquid savings substantially: after two years, beneficiaries' current account balances are approximately 60% higher than those of (potentially) rejected households by the asset test. Effects are strong for liquid assets but muted for real estate. The results demonstrate that a guaranteed income floor can foster precautionary savings, challenging the view that the poor cannot save. These findings highlight a key trade-off in means-tested program design between accurate targeting and household financial security.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Asset Tests and Household Dissaving: Evidence from Spanish Minimum Income Scheme; Regional wealth inequality in Spain: evidence from the Spain Wealth Atlas

papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: The Global Justice Platform: Distributional Pathways, the Global Justice Fund and the New Democratic International Order, 2026-2100

papers.abstract:
The wage gap between Black and white Americans narrowed in the 1960s-1970s
but stagnated after 1980. This study argues that routine-biased technological
change (RBTC) contributed to this stagnation by affecting races differently
across the wage distribution. Using new empirical evidence on occupational
patterns and wage determinants by race, I rationalize these patterns with
a novel theoretical framework incorporating RBTC and statistical discrimination.
Contrary to expectations, Black workers’ employment in routineintensive
occupations increased, while white workers experienced a significant
decline. Applying the Oaxaca-RIF decomposition, I show that occupational
sorting amplifies wage disparities, particularly at the lower end of the wage
distribution. These findings, interpreted through the novel theoretical framework,
offer new insights into the mechanisms driving racial wage disparities at
the close of the 20th century.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Technological Change and Racial Disparities

papers.abstract:
This paper establishes a link between the measurement of inequality and the
optimal transport theory. We introduce a new class of inequality indices that are
characterized as solutions to the optimal transport problem of transforming the
observed income distribution into a perfectly equal distribution. Indices within
this class differ in terms of the underlying transportation cost function. The
Gini coefficient is a member of this class and corresponds to the solution of the
optimal transport problem with the Euclidean distance as the cost function. We
show that this new class of inequality indices ranks some intersecting Lorenz
