curves unanimously. Thus, optimal transport theory can be used to refine the
Lorenz order to rank intersecting Lorenz curves.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Optimal Transport and the Measurement of Inequality

papers.abstract: This paper studies the use and relevance of trusts in the UK, to fill a gap in the literature on using administrative data to measure top income and wealth. Although trusts hold assets for the benefits of individuals, research that uses administrative data to measure income and wealth at the top usually misses this wealth from their estimations. We address this issue by allocating income and wealth held in trusts to the individuals that benefit from the trusts, and show how this impacts their position in the income and wealth distribution. For this purpose, we use administrative data to estimate the total income and wealth held in UK trusts. First, we show the directly observable income and wealth held in trusts. We find that trust income is highly concentrated and that trusts are mainly used for income and wealth accumulation as only a small share of trust income is distributed to beneficiaries. Second, to address limitations of the administrative data, we apply an imputation and income capitalisation methods to estimate the total income and wealth held in trusts. We show that [key findings on missing income and wealth under clearance and will be available at the time of the conference]. Lastly, we allocate the estimated total income and wealth held in trusts to the individuals benefitting from it and show how it affects their position in the income and wealth distribution. On average [key findings on allocating income/wealth under clearance and will be available at the time of the conference].
papers.subtheme: Taxation and Evasion - General
papers.title: Using trusts in the UK: income, wealth and beneficiaries

papers.abstract: This paper builds a new historical and comparative database on global wealth accumulation covering all world regions . For recent decades (1980 - 2025), we provide decompositions of wealth accumulation into volume effects (savings) and price effects (capital gains), as well as global series on capital shares and rates of return. W e also present estimates for na tional wealth, domestic capital and foreign wealth, private and public wealth throughout the 1800 - 2025 period . Over this long horizon, we find large variations in wealth - income and capital - output ratios, ownership patterns and capital shares, which challenge the well - known “Kaldor facts”. Since the 1980s, global wealth - income ratios have experienced an unprecedented increase while capital shares have risen in most world regions, primarily due to growing within - country corporate profitability. As capital sha res have risen less than wealth - income ratios, domestic rates of return have declined only moderately relative to the collapse in foreign returns worldwide
papers.title: Global Wealth Accumulation and Ownership Patterns, 1800-2025

papers.abstract: Economists often define the middle class based on income distribution, yet selecting which segment constitutes the `middle' is essentially arbitrary. This paper proposes a definition of the middle class based solely on the properties of income distribution and inequality. It argues that for a collection of unequal societies, the poor and rich extremes of the distribution unambiguously worsen or improve their respective income shares with inequality. In contrast, such an effect is moderated at the center. I define the middle class as the segment of the income distribution whose income shares are insensitive to changes in inequality. This unresponsiveness property allows one to single out, endogenously and with minimal arbitrariness, the location of the middle class. The paper first provides a theoretical argument for the existence of such a group. It then uses detailed percentile data from the World Income Database (WID) to empirically characterize the world middle class: a group skewed toward the upper part of the distribution—comprising much of the affluent population below the very rich—with stable borders over time and across countries. The definition aligns with the prevailing view in political economy of the middle class as as a moderating actor, given their null incentives to engage in distributive conflict.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: A Political Economy Definition of the Middle Class

papers.abstract: We study racial inequality in 21st century France. Using parents' nationality at birth, we overcome the lack of ethno-racial statistics stemming from the country's "color-blind'' approach. We document substantial earnings penalties for racial minorities along the income distribution. Penalties are larger at the median than the top and for Middle-Eastern and North African (MENA) and Sub-Saharan African origin (Black) individuals. We compare racial inequality in France vs. the U.S. by simulating where French minorities would fall in the U.S. distribution. Black and Non-White individuals in France benefit from the country's lower overall inequality, but experience comparable, occasionally larger, rank gaps.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Racial Inequality in France

papers.abstract: Top income shares are easier to compute and interpret than competing inequality measures, yet they violate the Pigou-Dalton transfer principle and are not connected to any social welfare function. We show that there is only one top income share that minimizes Pigou-Dalton violations while leading to a reasonable social welfare function: the income share of those earning more than the average income minus their population share. We compute the joint evolution of inequality and social welfare globally based on WID data. We document three sets of new empirical facts. First, the fraction of people earning more than the average income is often decreasing since 1980, which mechanically increases inequality. Second, inequality has increased slower than with conventional thresholds in some countries, such as the US, but faster in others, such as Luxembourg. Third, looking at the corresponding notion of social welfare gives us a new perspective, with American and French social welfare, for instance, being almost identical in trends and levels today, despite opposite dynamics in growth and inequality.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Top x%, Income Inequality and Social Welfare

papers.abstract: The paper delivers new evidence on patterns of intergenerational social mobility across countries by exploiting the OECD Survey of Adult Skills, a product of the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC). The paper examines the link between parent’s education and their offspring’s economic outcomes, across multiple dimensions including: 1) individual earnings; 2) women’s labour market participation; and 3) individual educational attainment. In almost all countries covered, the paper finds a positive earnings premium associated with having high-educated parents, and a corresponding earnings penalty for individuals with low-educated parents (Figure 1). Women’s labour market participation is significantly lower when parents, especially mothers, have lower levels of education.  In many countries, the effects of parental background have faded away once an individual’s own education is accounted for, suggesting that education and skills development are key mechanisms for intergenerational social mobility. Yet, the paper also finds that in several countries bringing children from lower socio-economic background to higher education is not a sufficient condition, as even when individuals study at similar levels and fields of education, parental background continues to exert a significant influence on offspring’ economic outcomes. Finally, the paper finds substantial intergenerational persistence in educational outcomes. The results also reveal considerable cross-country heterogeneity across the different dimensions, underscoring the complexity and multi-faceted nature of intergenerational social mobility.
papers.subtheme: Income/Education mobility
papers.title: Does the apple fall far from the tree? New evidence on intergenerational social mobility across OECD countries

papers.abstract: This paper studies regional disparities in the cost of job loss between West and East Germany. Based on German administrative data, I document that, relative to their pre-displacement level, earnings losses of displaced workers are on average lower in East Germany than in West Germany. A shift–share decomposition shows that roughly one-third of this West–East gap is due to differences in the industry mix of job destruction: after the early de-industrialization of the East, job losses there were less concentrated in manufacturing and more in construction than in the West. The remaining two-thirds reflects smaller earnings losses in the East within industries, which are linked to lower firm wage premia among East German employers. Structural effects - the earnings losses associated with the same job lost across different regions - allow identifying an earnings penalty for displaced workers in the East that is more in line with the weaker labor market performance of the East. Although regional mobility to the West offsets earnings losses among movers, the vast majority of East Germans do not relocate to the West after job loss.
papers.subtheme: Political Inequalities - General
papers.title: Left Behind? West-East German Disparities in the Cost of Job Loss

papers.abstract:
Agricultural land inequality affects rural development and constrains economic growth and poverty reduction, yet comprehensive global datasets to monitor it have been lacking. This study introduces the LINEQ (Global Database of Land Distribution and Inequality) dataset, which integrates agricultural census and survey data with Earth Observation-based proxies for land quality to provide a more nuanced and cross-country comparable measurement of land inequality. Expanding on traditional indicators like the land operated Gini coefficient, we incorporate measures that account for tenure rights, potential productivity differences, and landless populations.
 
Situating land distribution within broader patterns of structural transformation, we examine correlations between land inequality and key macroeconomic indicators: the share of employment in agriculture and the agricultural value added as a share of GDP. The analysis reveals systematic variation. The most troubling cases are those with high inequality and high shares of employment in agriculture/high agricultural value added, as these indicate a combination of heavy reliance on agriculture with concentrated access to land, raising risks of exclusion and persistent rural poverty, and the likelihood that future growth will be captured by a narrow set of landholders, limiting broad-based development gains.
 
Inequality decomposition using the Theil index shows that the Americas contribute the largest share to global agricultural land inequality, followed by Europe, while Africa and Asia contribute relatively little to the global total, despite their demographic weight and prevalence of smallholders. Within regions, Latin America and the Caribbean (excluding Brazil) account for more than half of their region’s contribution, Brazil itself remains a major driver, and in Europe Russia dominates the picture. In Asia, Central and Western Asia together with China are key contributors, while Oceania’s inequality is driven almost entirely by Australia and New Zealand. 
 
Country-level trajectories highlight marked heterogeneity in recent changes. Overall, the results indicate that global land inequality is markedly higher than previously estimated, and that its developmental significance depends on both the structure of national economies and the regional concentration of large, unequal landholding systems.

Finally, a deeper examination of survey data allows us to explore additional dimensions of inequality, including the distribution of land tenure and land quality. Restricting the analysis to land with secure tenure rights markedly increases measured inequality, suggesting that secure rights are concentrated among larger and better capitalised farms, while many smallholders operate land under informal or insecure arrangements. Standardising landholdings for land quality also tends to raise inequality, indicating that larger farms control not only more land but also land of systematically higher potential productivity. The inclusion of landless rural populations has a mixed effect on inequality measurement across regions: the impact is relatively modest in Africa, where widespread engagement in on-farm activities means that landlessness is less sharply delineated, but it is more pronounced in Asia and Latin America, where landless households represent a substantial share of the rural population and their inclusion materially stretches the lower tail of the land distribution. Taken together, these results underscore that conventional land area indicators likely understate the true extent of inequality in access to secure, high-quality and productive land.
papers.subtheme: Agricultural Productivity, Smallholders and Rural Inequality
papers.title: Divide in the fields: A study of global agricultural land inequality

papers.abstract:
In this paper, we employ a gravity model to explore the effect of weather shocks on bilateral manufacturing trade flows from 41 Sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries by controlling for intermediary roles of key measures of economic freedom and quality of institutions. For robustness purposes, we use detailed disaggregated measures from the five broad categories of economic freedom, which are published by the Fraser Institute. We provide sufficient evidence to show how weather shocks, especially temperature shocks, disrupt manufacturing exports. Our results indicate that, while variations in temperature directly impact manufacturing exports, countries with relatively stronger economic freedom and high-quality institutions are able to mitigate some of the adverse effects of weather shocks on bilateral manufacturing
exports. These results are not only robust across several disaggregated subcomponents of economic freedom measures but are also consistent with measures of institutional quality published by the World Bank- World Governance Indicators. In addition, the impact of these economic freedom measures in moderating the adverse effects of weather shocks on trade flows increases for African countries in the upper-level percentile distribution of economic freedom measures. These results have implications for any global policy effort intended to counter the negative effects of weather shocks on the economic activity of low-income developing countries with inadequate economic freedom and poor institutions.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Weather Shocks and Manufactured Exports from Sub-Saharan Africa: How Economic Freedom and Institutional Quality Shape Resilience

papers.abstract: Public goods are meant to be universal, but they are inherently place-based. This paper systematically measures spatial access to public goods and quantifies the implications of distance to public facilities for income inequality. First, we map all schools and hospitals across Belgium. We compute the distance to facilities for each of the 20,000 neighborhoods and document large spatial inequalities in access to public facilities. Second, we find that this unequal distribution favors high-income neighborhoods: allocating public goods spending proportionally to our access index increases income inequality compared to measures based solely on disposable income. Third, we show that the positive relationship between income and access can be rationalized by a simple model of public goods allocation with an inequality-neutral social planner. Finally, we provide evidence that access is strongly correlated with educational and health outcomes, emphasizing the need to consider the place-based nature of public goods when measuring inequality.
papers.subtheme: Public goods
papers.title: Do Public Goods Actually Reduce Inequality?

papers.abstract: This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of absolute intergenerational mobility (AIM) in Hong Kong, using census data spanning four decades. Employing the "copula and marginals" method, we document a sharp decline in AIM, from 85% for the 1976 birth cohort to 49% for the 2001 cohort, driven largely by diminished labor income mobility. This erosion stems primarily from slower economic growth rather than rising inequality; under constant economic growth, AIM would stabilize at approximately  67%, accounting for nearly all of the decline, with minimal residual from inequality or copula changes. Findings are robust across specifications. Our innovative Mincer equation-based decomposition highlights education's critical role in mitigating declines, offering general insights into how tertiary expansion shapes mobility in transitioning economies.
papers.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
papers.title: From Lion Rock to Locked Gates: The Decline of Upward Mobility in Hong Kong

papers.abstract:
South Korea presents a decisive empirical challenge to the Routine-Biased Technological Change (RBTC) framework. Although Korea is the world’s most robot-intensive economy—arguably the strongest “most-likely case” for job polarization—it exhibits two patterns that contradict core RBTC predictions. First, occupational changes during 2009–2019 display an almost inverted U-shape: middle-skill employment remains stable, low-wage service jobs contract, and employment losses are concentrated in upper-middle nonroutine occupations. Second, rather than widening inequality, Korea experienced significant wage compression, including a decline in the P50/P10 ratio and a stable P90/P10 ratio during peak robot adoption. These dual anomalies reveal theoretical limits in the task-based logic of RBTC, which presumes flexible wage-setting and weak institutional segmentation.
We argue that automation in Korea operates through hierarchical labor-market stratification rather than task routineness. Korea’s labor market is structured by firm size, contract type, and subcontracting status, generating institutionalized insider–outsider boundaries that filter technological shocks. To capture these boundaries, we develop a Labor Market Stratification Index (LMSI) and show that robot exposure complements protected insiders while increasing precarity and labor-force exit among peripheral workers. Aggregate non-polarization emerges as an artifact of mixing these heterogeneous groups within standard occupational categories, while the most vulnerable workers disproportionately disappear from observable wage distributions.
Empirically, the paper proceeds in three steps: (1) replicating RBTC methods on Korean data to show the anomaly is not a measurement artifact; (2) assessing whether minimum wage increases and unions alone can account for wage compression; and (3) estimating a stratification-mediated automation model demonstrating that the effects of robot exposure are conditional on institutional position. Korea thus exemplifies how technological change unfolds in “segmented coordinated economies,” where institutional boundaries—rather than task content—shape the distributional consequences of automation.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: From Polarization to Dualization : How Stratification Filters Automation Shocks in Korea

papers.abstract:
Land is generally the most important endowment in developing countries with large agricultural
populations. We describe the patterns of agricultural land distribution in rural India
using village-level data for 270,000 villages. We show that agricultural, trade, and historical
factors explain 18% of the existing land inequality; with agricultural factors explaining 38%
of this variation, trade 19%, historical factors 43%. Historical landlord land tenure systems,
Schedule Caste (SC) population share, and close proximity to urban areas and roads are all
strongly positively associated with inequality. We also find that agricultural productivity is
positively associated with inequality, but that this relationship is weakened in close proximity
to urban areas. Finally, we find a generally positive and concave relationship between
inequality and the availability of public goods.
papers.subtheme: Agricultural Productivity, Smallholders and Rural Inequality
papers.title: Land Inequality in India

papers.abstract: Temperatures in Europe are rising at twice the rate observed in other continents, posing unprecedented challenges to ecosystems, livelihoods and economies. These changes reveal a pronounced North–South divide, with wealthier northern regions exposed to fewer extreme climate events than those in southern Europe. However, critical gaps persist in understanding how income groups within European countries are differently exposed to extreme climate events. By integrating high-resolution disposable income data with climate and hydrological models, we provide the first quantification of present and future income-based inequalities in exposure to extreme climate events across combinations of socioeconomic and warming scenarios. Our analysis reveals systematic inequalities within European countries: high-income groups reside in areas with significantly lower exposure to extreme heatwaves, cold spells, wildfires, riverine flooding, and coastal flooding, while low-income populations are relatively more exposed. We found that these inequalities will persist throughout the 21st century, though the total population exposed varies substantially depending on climate scenarios. Our findings underscore the urgent need for tailored adaptation strategies that explicitly address exposure inequalities, alongside ambitious mitigation policies to curb escalating climate impacts.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Persistent inequalities in exposure to extreme climate events over the 21st century in Europe

papers.abstract: Public in-kind provision of education, healthcare, or cultural amenities accounts for a large share of government spending, even though redistribution can be achieved with cash transfers and externalities addressed with subsidies. We propose a new theory of in-kind provision, grounded in two features: (i) these goods are luxuries, with consumption rising more than proportionally with income; and (ii) they generate externalities that depend not only on the total level of consumption but also on its distribution across households. In a tractable heterogeneous-agent model, we show that these features make direct in-kind provision welfare-improving, even when cash transfers and subsidies are available. Using household- and country-level data, we document that most publicly provided goods exhibit both features. We then apply the framework to the design of fiscal consolidation, showing in a calibrated model that optimal consolidation should reduce provision of goods without private counterparts more strongly, and that income-targeted in-kind benefits can generate substantial fiscal savings. Finally, we develop a welfare-based imputation method for in-kind benefits, to provide a more accurate assessment of the distributional impact of government spending.
papers.subtheme: Data Fusion, Harmonization and Measurement Error
papers.title: Luxury for All: A Theory of Public Provision and Inequality

papers.abstract: How do childhood environments contribute to intergenerational economic mobility? This paper explores the relative roles of family background (parents’ wages, income, and wealth during the early years), and neighbourhoods (including access to services during childhood), in determining intergenerational economic mobility in Egypt. The research leverages 25 years of panel data, across five waves, spanning 1998–2023. Relative and absolute changes within wage, income, and wealth distributions are examined, along with tests of origin independence. The findings demonstrate that, while there is substantial intergenerational mobility in both wages and income, there is, in contrast, strong intergenerational persistence in wealth. Family background plays a larger role than neighbourhood effects, with access to services having particularly little impact, suggesting that more robust public policies, beyond providing access to public services, are needed to address intergenerational inequality.
papers.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
papers.title: How do childhood environments contribute to intergenerational economic mobility? Evidence from 25 years of panel data in Egypt

papers.abstract: In the economic context of high and sustained growth, ASEAN’s national accounts exhibit favourable macroeconomic figures, indicating that GDP per capita, which measures average income per inhabitant, is increasing, suggesting a general improvement in the material conditions of the people in ASEAN nations. However, the individual rewards of economic growth aren't evenly distributed within ASEAN countries, and improvements in living conditions are far from benefiting the lower strata of society nor the workers as a whole. As one of the most classical questions in economics, asking how national income is divided between wages, profits, and rent, in Southeast Asia, and the ASEAN vibrant economy, the share of wages and profits is rarely regarded as an interesting problem; however, it has to be considered as a key issue. In a recent set of consistent policies, Malaysia is currently addressing this feature, with large macroeconomic ambition, precise administrative tools, but also with limitations.
papers.subtheme: Labour shares
papers.title: Addressing labour share in Southeast Asia: Malaysian Anomaly and Current Reform

papers.abstract:
The Middle East is among the most unequal regions in the world today, yet little is known
about the long-term dynamics of inequality in the region. This paper presents detailed
and newly digitized estimates of land inequality in Egypt from 1896 to 2020, drawing on
comprehensive records of private agricultural land ownership. This unique dataset enables a
systematic analysis of the evolution of land distribution over more than a century and sheds
light on the historical forces and redistributive policies that shaped it. To the best of my
knowledge, no similarly long-run and granular series on land inequality exists for any other
country or land reform context. The results reveal an extreme concentration of land in the
early 20th century, with the top 1% of landowners controlling over 42% of privately owned
agricultural land on the eve of Egypt’s 1952 agrarian reform. Subsequent redistribution
efforts reduced this figure to 27% by 1980. During the same period, the share held by the
next 9% of landowners increased modestly, from 32% to 35%. The most notable gains were
achieved by middle landowners (owners of 1 to 5 feddans), whose share increased from 20%
to 30%. In contrast, the reform had limited impact on the landless and smallest landowners:
the bottom 50% saw only a marginal increase in their land share, from 6% to 8%.
papers.subtheme: Land inequality
papers.title: Long-term Land Inequality and Post-Colonial Land Reform in Egypt (1896-2020)

papers.abstract: This paper examines the within-country impacts of climate change on firms’ labour decisions, the resulting wage distribution, and wage inequality. Focusing on employer–employee relationships, we study how heterogeneous firm-level exposure to weather shocks is transmitted to workers’ wages. In the presence of assortative matching, when weather sensitivity is correlated with firm productivity, weather shocks are likely to correlate with workers’ productivity and, consequently, their wages. By analysing the heterogeneity of firm-level damages and their implications for hiring, firing, and wage-setting, we provide novel evidence on how climate-related shocks shape both firm and income inequality. We quantify these mechanisms using French employer–employee matched data, combining methods from climate econometrics with a structural Diamond–Mortensen–Pissarides–type search-and-matching model to assess both distributional and aggregate economic effects of climate change.
papers.subtheme: Environmental Inequalities - General
papers.title: Climate Change, Labour Markets, and Wage Inequality

papers.abstract: Welfare policies aim to reduce poverty and inequality to foster inclusive economic growth, but their effectiveness is often inconsistent. This is particularly true in federal systems like India, where states have discretion over policy design, leading to varied outcomes. Existing research typically focuses on individual case studies, failing to capture the aggregate impact of these policies. This study addresses this gap by analysing the aggregate influence of welfare spending on inclusive growth in India from 1983 to 2012, using a unique state-level panel dataset. We define inclusive growth using advanced "pro-poor growth" indices instead of simple poverty measures. Crucially, we investigate whether the impact of these policies is linear or non-linear, especially concerning education levels. Our findings reveal that aggregate redistributive policies significantly enhance the pro-poorness of growth and reduce poverty. This positive effect holds even after accounting for different state-level economic conditions. However, the impact on overall inequality remains inconclusive. Most importantly, our analysis identifies a critical non-linearity: welfare policies are more effective in states with higher levels of tertiary education. Primary and secondary schooling show no significant relationship with policy effectiveness. This suggests that higher education acts as a complementary policy tool, amplifying the benefits of welfare programs and making growth more inclusive. This highlights the importance of education for maximizing the return on welfare investments.
papers.subtheme: Public spending, education
papers.title: Welfare Policy, Education and Inclusive Growth: Evidence from India

papers.abstract:
We provide new stylized facts on the dynamics of the inter-generational wealth correlation
(IWC) in the long run in France, for cohorts born between 1778 and 1982. Using a special
feature of the French wealth survey, we propose an original use of the Two-Sample Two-
Stage Least Squares approach to study the IWC over the second half of the 20th century.
This method is simple to use and aims at overcoming the major data limitations in most
countries. We complement this analysis with data from the 19th century. We show that
the IWC follows a U-shaped pattern. It fell from 0.37 to 0.17 between the cohorts born
before 1875 and those born in the 1940s. The IWC then rose steadily and was back to
its 19th century level by the end of the 1960s and has since plateaued. We also examine
the mechanisms driving this increase. We show that children of wealthy parents (i) are
more and more educated and white collars over time, (ii) have increasingly received gifts
over time, (iii) are more and more likely to buy their main residence before the age of 35,
(iv) hold more frequently high-yielding assets and invest more of their wealth in these
assets, and (v) do not save more than children of less affluent parents. We additionally
find evidence for the persistence of the effect of parental wealth over the life cycle
papers.subtheme: Wealth mobility (FR)
papers.title: Intergenerational Wealth Mobility over Two Centuries: Evolution and Determinants

papers.abstract: This paper investigates the effects of automation on employment dynamics and within-firm wage inequality in South Africa’s formal manufacturing sector. Leveraging matched employer-employee administrative records linked to firm-level import transactions, we find that firms adopting automation are typically on a strong growth trajectory prior to adoption and continue to expand thereafter—particularly smaller establishments. However, when accounting for selection by comparing early and late adopters, automation is associated with a relative deceleration in employment growth. Average wages exhibit a modest post-treatment decline, though estimates are not always statistically significant. In contrast, effects on within-firm inequality are more heterogeneous: while overall changes are limited, inequality increases more clearly among firms with above-median automation investments and among larger firms. These findings suggest that automation may contribute to rising wage dispersion within firms, especially in contexts of more substantial technological upgrading.
papers.subtheme: Automation
papers.title: Automation and Inequality Within Firms: Evidence from South Africa

papers.abstract:
We examine how land ownership shapes educational mobility in rural India. Using full-count
rural census microdata, we document a robust step-function pattern across the land distribution: educational mobility rises sharply from the landless to marginal landholders and then plateaus. Exploiting historical variation in British-era land-tenure regimes, we demonstrate a causal link between landlessness and lower educational mobility. To unpack mechanisms, we develop a model where parents allocate children’s time between school and work under a subsistence constraint. With little or no land, the constraint binds, increasing child labour and suppressing schooling; a small rise in land relaxes it, producing a sharp drop in child labour and a jump in schooling and upward mobility. The framework endogenously generates the step-function, matches the core facts, rationalizes heterogeneities, and yields testable predictions that we validate.
papers.subtheme: Mobility Traps, Segregation and Stratification
papers.title: Land for Opportunity? Deprivation and Immobility in Rural India

papers.abstract: Prior studies, relying on aggregate income data and focusing on residents, typically find that low-income households are more exposed to flooding. Yet this approach overlooks half of the exposed housing stock–those owned by non-residents. Using dwelling-level data covering the entire French housing market, I show that the picture changes markedly when distinguishing by ownership status. Once non-resident ownership is accounted for, flood risk appears to disproportionately affect second homes, while subsidence primarily impacts owner-occupied dwellings. These patterns carry important policy implications. First, untargeted flood insurance subsidies disproportionately benefit second homes, whereas subsidence coverage mainly supports owner-occupied dwellings. Second, using a new approach to estimate risk discounts, I show that natural disaster risks are not priced into rental, second, and vacant properties, contributing to at least 15% of the total overvaluation in flood-prone areas. Finally, place-based adaptation policies, such as building resilient defenses, may fail to target the most critical areas if ownership structures are ignored. These findings underscore the importance of examining inequalities by ownership status and covering the entire housing market, rather than focusing solely on residents’ incomes.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Real estate wealth inequality and exposure to natural disasters

papers.abstract: This paper analyses the distributional impact of health in-kind benefits across EU Member States. Specifically, we evaluate the impact of health Social Transfers in-Kind (STiKs) on different measures of inequality and poverty. For this purpose, we integrate non-monetary income components of health STiKs into households’ income, using confidential data from the Ageing Working Group of the European Commission, and also developing a novel approach to valuate health STiKs that combines the so-called ‘actual’ and ‘insurance’ approaches. We find that health STiKs considerably reduce inequality and at-risk of poverty rates in all countries of the EU. To put this effect into perspective: in about half of the Member States, more income inequality reduction is achieved through health STiKs than with social transfers in cash (excluding pensions).
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Health In-Kind Benefits are Pro-Poor: Measuring their Distributional Impact in the EU

papers.abstract: This study investigates inequality of opportunity in labor markets across Egypt, Jordan, and Sudan using recent waves of the Labor Market Panel Surveys: Egypt (2012, 2018, 2023), Jordan (2010, 2016), and Sudan (2022). It applies the Human Opportunity Index, including its multidimensional extension (MHOI), by combining several employment-related opportunities to reflect different levels of jobrelated well-being. This allows for measuring unequal access not only to employment but also to better job opportunities - specifically formal, stable, and satisfying positions. The study employs Shapley decomposition to assess the contribution of predetermined circumstances such as gender, parental background, and geographic origin. The results indicate that a considerable share of disparities in employment outcomes and labor income is driven by these exogenous factors. Cross-country differences are substantial: Egypt shows relatively broader employment access, Jordan exhibits more equitable outcomes, while Sudan faces both restricted access and higher inequality. The findings highlight the importance of inclusive labor market policies aimed at reducing structural disadvantages and ensuring equal chances for all individuals.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Inequality of Opportunity in Labor Markets: A Comparative Analysis of Employment and Wage Disparities in Egypt, Jordan, and Sudan

papers.abstract:
This paper presents a family of spatial polarization indices that integrates distri-
butional and spatial dimensions to measure economic polarization. Traditional
polarization metrics either focus solely on distributional aspects or rely on
exogenously defined regional partitions, limiting their applicability to dynamic
spatial economies. Building on economic polarization theory and spatial inequal-
ity decomposition, the proposed indices incorporate spatial adjacency relations
and dynamically evolving regional configurations. By constructing intersection
graphs that capture both attribute similarity (e.g., income levels) and geographic
associations, this framework identifies spatially coherent clusters, and multiscalar
measures of spatial polarization across global, meso, and local scales. The indices
extend beyond bipolarization to multipolarization, allowing for richer insights
into complex spatial-economic patterns. As an illustrative case study, the paper
analyzes the evolution of spatial income polarization across Mexican states from
1940 to 2000. Findings highlight persistent north-south disparities, spatially cohe-
sive low-income clusters, and fragmented high-income regions, underscoring the
importance of dynamic spatial frameworks for understanding and addressing
regional inequality. This approach provides policymakers and researchers with
a flexible tool to examine the spatial dynamics of economic polarization and
identify endogenous regional formations over time.
papers.subtheme: Distributional Decomposition and Counterfactual Methods
papers.title: Mind the gap and the map: Measuring distributional and spatial income polarization

papers.abstract: This article investigates how inequality perceptions shape redistribution preferences and inclination to populist narratives in four European countries: France, Italy, Austria, and Czechia. Building on psychological and economic theories, we conduct a survey experiment that combines inequality information with a priming manipulation based on sources of wealth that respondents had previously identified as (un)deserved, such as privatization and inheritance. We find that respondents exposed to higher-than-expected inequality express stronger support for redistribution and are more likely to endorse populist views portraying politics as a conflict between virtuous people and corrupt elites. These effects are amplified when combined with a deservingness-based framing.
papers.subtheme: Information, Narratives and Belief Formation
papers.title: Perceptions of Undeserved Inequality Make Europeans More Vulnerable to Populist Narratives

papers.abstract: We link French households' tax records to the corporations they control, and build a payout-policy-neutral income measure, with corresponding tax burdens including those of "billionaires": the top 0.0002%. Defined as such, income is more concentrated than taxable income, it better predicts rich-list membership, and persists more among billionaires. Personal taxes remain progressive until the top 0.1%, but eventually decline to 2% of income. Corporate taxes are an imperfect progressive backstop, as total tax rates fall from 45% at the 0.1% threshold to 25% for billionaires. Among these, the tax burden is global and tax-efficient pyramidal control over businesses ubiquitous.
papers.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
papers.title: Do Billionaires Pay Taxes?

papers.abstract:
We study the effects of trade liberalization on the full wage distribution, exploiting Spain’s 1993 entry into the European Single Market. Using employer-employee data, we identify the causal effects of trade across the entire wage distribution, using a novel shift-share instrument embedded in an unconditional quantile regression. We find that the liberalization reduced wage inequality, leading to wage compression through earnings gains at the bottom of the distribution and wage losses at the top. We trace this compression to two asymmetric channels: import competition disproportionately harmed high earners, while export opportunities benefited low earners. The key mechanism is an import-driven “skill-downgrading.” A multi-region multisector
model shows that the key insight for understanding these empirical results is that trade’s distributional effects depend on the skill intensity of a country’s tradable sector, and Spain’s was relatively low-skill intensive.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: When Trade Compresses: The Impact of Liberalization on Wage Inequality

papers.abstract: Current global consumption patterns significantly exceed planetary boundaries, yet the responsibility for this environmental burden is unequally distributed. While previous research has largely focused on carbon footprints using input-output models, this study introduces a novel, high-resolution methodology to assess multidimensional footprint inequality across the European Union. By integrating harmonized microdata from the European Household Budget Survey with process-based Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), we analyze household consumption across 16 environmental impact categories, including climate change, particulate matter, and resource depletion. Our results reveal a stark disparity in environmental impact: the top income quintile creates a footprint nearly double that of the bottom quintile (a ratio of 1.77). We identify that this inequality is driven not only by a "size effect" (higher consumption volume) but also by a "selection effect," where wealthier households substitute towards more environmentally intensive goods, particularly regarding meat consumption and private transport. Furthermore, we monetize these externalities, estimating that the highest earners generate approximately €15,725 in annual environmental costs per household, compared to €8,415 for the lowest earners. Crucially, while both income groups transgress planetary boundaries for climate change and particulate matter, only high-income households exceed safe operating spaces for freshwater eutrophication and mineral resource depletion. These findings underscore the necessity for differentiated policy interventions that target specific "inequality hotspots"—such as food and mobility—to ensure environmental sustainability does not come at the cost of social fairness.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Drivers of Environmental Consumption Footprint Inequality in Europe

papers.abstract: Inequality of opportunity has great normative importance. This has led to a literature on measuring the part of overall inequality that is due to circumstances outside of a person’s control. We contribute to such studies by evaluating the implications of uncertainty about circumstance variables and linear versus nonlinear transmission of circumstances on inequality of opportunity estimates. Applying linear Bayesian model averaging methods and three ensemble tree-based machine learning approaches to data from 31 European Union countries, we find that ignoring model uncertainty can lead to substantial overstatement of levels of inequality of opportunity.
papers.subtheme: Historical Measurement - General
papers.title: Model Uncertainty and Measures of Inequality of Opportunity

papers.abstract: We analyze income inequality between and within German regions from 1957 to 2021 using a newly collected panel. We confirm previous evidence on convergence between regions during the decades after World War II, but do not find pronounced regional divergence since the 1990s -- in contrast to some earlier studies. Instead, the national income inequality trends are closely tracked by the near unanimous rise in income concentration among the top decile within regions. Regression analysis suggests that regional growth switched from equality-enhancing to inequality-increasing in the 1990s.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Spatial income inequality in Germany, 1957-2021

papers.abstract: Global economic governance is under increasing strain from unequal local development. While previous research has shown that the backlash against globalization is stronger in communities that experienced long-term economic and social decline, the evidence is inconclusive about what is the causal mechanism through which local inequality affects public trust in global economic governance. We argue that people trust global economic governance less not only when they perceive economic hardship in their specific geographical area, but more so when they think the area they live in loses more compared to other areas in the same country. Low levels of trust in global economic governance reflects a concern for local inequality, without requiring accurate perceptions of local inequality, processes of decline, and political responsibility. Our argument yields testable hypotheses, which this registered report proposes investigating in a novel survey experiment based on a nationally representative sample in the United States (US) and on representative samples for high- and low-growth US counties. In the experiment, respondents will be treated with vignettes explaining local economic development and relative inequality in local development within their own country, before being asked to report their levels of trust in international organizations and multilateral treaties, which constitute the key pillars of rules-based global economic governance. By combining an experimental with a causal mediation analysis, we will test the role of concern for local inequality as a causal mechanism. The results will broaden the understanding of the role of geographic inequality in global economic governance and the backlash in public opinion toward global economic governance.
papers.subtheme: Polarization, Media and Democratic Trust
papers.title: Local Inequality and the Backlash Against Global Economic Governance

papers.abstract: We estimate income and taxes for the wealthiest group of US households by matching Forbes 400 data to the individual, business, estate, and gift tax returns of the corresponding group in 20102020. In our benchmark estimate, the total effective tax rate—all taxes paid relative to economic income—of the top 0.0002% (approximately the “top 400”) averaged 24% in 2018–2020 compared with 30% for the full population and 45% for top labor income earners. This lower total effective tax rate on the wealthiest is substantially driven by low taxable individual income relative to economic income. First, the C-corporations owned by the wealthiest distributed relatively little in dividends, limiting their individual income tax unless they sell their stocks. Second, top-owned passthrough businesses reported negative taxable income on average in spite of positive book income, further limiting their individual income tax. The top-400 effective tax rate fell from 30% in 2010–2017 to 24% in 2018–2020, explained both by a smaller share of business income being taxed and by that income being subject to lower tax rates. Estate and gift taxes contributed relatively little to their effective tax rate. Top-400 decedents paid 0.8% of their wealth in estate tax when married and 7% when single. Annual charitable contributions equalled 0.6% of wealth and 11% of economic income in 2018–20.
papers.subtheme: Taxation and Evasion - General
papers.title: How Much Tax Do US Billionaires Pay? Evidence from Administrative Data

papers.abstract: We study the outsourcing of low-skilled service tasks (cleaning, catering and security) with French matched employer-employee data from the period 2001-2019. In line with the literature, we find a substantial penalty in the earnings of the outsourced employees, that persists 7 years after treatment. In contrast to the literature, we find that it is entirely explained by a fall in hours. Interviews with various stakeholders in these industries indicate that cutting the hours on a given site is a common way to compete on prices for subcontractor firms, and that the decline in hours results in both work intensification and a decrease in quality.
papers.subtheme: Outsourcing
papers.title: Cutting hours through outsourcing

papers.subtheme: Income Distribution Drivers
papers.title: Prosperity Within Limits? Planetary Habitability, Global Convergence and Structural Transformation, 2026-2100

papers.abstract: Extending the inequality of opportunity conceptual framework to a dynamic setting, this paper proposes the metric of circumstance elasticity of income as a measure of the degree of persistence over time in the income effects of circumstances. These elasticities are readily computable over time and for each “type” identified by their particular combination of circumstances. An application to longitudinal data for Australia and South Korea over a fifteen-year period finds that an overwhelming majority of circumstance elasticities of income across circumstance types and years are not significantly different to unity, which provides strong evidence of highly persistent effects of circumstances on economic outcomes in both countries.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Circumstance Elasticity of Income

papers.abstract: The rise of economic inequalities in advanced economies has been often linked with the growth of spatial inequalities within countries, yet there is limited comparative research that studies the relationship between national and subnational economic inequality. This paper presents the first systematic attempt to create internationally comparable evidence showing how different countries perform in terms of geographic wage inequalities. We create cross-country comparable measures of spatial wage disparities between and within similarly-defined local labour market areas (LLMAs) for Canada, France, (West) Germany, the UK and the US since the 1970s, and assess their contribution to national inequality. By the end of the 2010s, spatial inequalities in LLMA mean wages are similar in Canada, France, Germany and the UK; the US exhibits the highest degree of spatial inequality. Over the study period, spatial inequalities have nearly doubled in all countries, except for France where spatial inequalities have fallen back to 1970s levels. Due to a concomitant increase in within-place inequality, the contribution of places in explaining national wage inequality has remained fairly constant over the 40-year study period, except in the UK where we document a significant increase. Whilst common global social, economic and technological shocks are important drivers of spatial inequality, this variation in levels and trends of spatial inequality opens the way to comparative research exploring the role of national institutions in mediating how global shocks translate into economic disparities between places.
papers.subtheme: Regional and Global Comparison of Inequality Trajectories
papers.title: Spatial wage inequality in North America and Western Europe: changes between and within local labour markets 1975-2019

papers.abstract: This paper investigates how participation in a citizens’ assembly affects individuals’ redistributive preferences and (perceived) role in democracy. We implement a pre-registered field experiment embedded in a real-world citizens’ assembly on wealth inequality in Austria. Using a three-group-design comparing assembly participants, non-selected volunteers, and a population sample, we isolate the causal effects of taking part in a citizens’ assembly from self-selection into participation. We find that while participating in the citizens’ assembly substantially improves factual knowledge about the wealth distribution and promotes convergence around specific tax policy proposals, notably a EUR 1 million allowance, it has no measurable effect on political efficacy or broader civic engagement. We also document significant political self-selection: individuals willing to participate in the citizens’ assembly were already more engaged and supportive of redistribution than the general population. These findings suggest that while deliberative formats can foster informed convergence on policy proposals, their ability to mobilize broader publics is limited.
papers.subtheme: Political Economy of Redistribution
papers.title: The Good Council: Deliberating Inequality in a Field Experiment

papers.abstract:
This paper uses rich administrative data to study income inequality before and after re-
distribution in the Netherlands. We use a corporate ownership registry to link profits to
shareholders and evaluate alternative methods of doing so. This allows us to provide the
first exact estimate of the overall tax rate of the super rich internationally. At the very top,
the effective individual income tax rate is nearly zero and the only significant tax paid is
the corporate tax. We use exceptionally precise data on cash and in-kind transfers to study
their redistributive impact and to assess the validity of methods typically used to assign
in-kind spending to individuals. Finally, we investigate inequality and redistribution across
age, gender and geography.
papers.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
papers.title: Inequality and Redistribution in the Netherlands

papers.abstract: Labor market mobility is often viewed as an individual phenomenon, driven by a worker’s essential productivity—an outcome of innate talent and accumulated human capital prior to entering the labor market. In the classical framework, the exit option reveals a worker’s market value and, by extension, their individual productivity. But what if mobility is not only individual, but also collective? This occurs when a firm hires an already-formed team from another firm. In such cases, the output of the group exceeds the sum of its members’ individual human capital. Team moves, therefore, challenge the classical individualistic and essentialist view of labor markets. Previous research has shown that team moves play a key role in high-end professions such as law and finance. Drawing on qualitative fieldwork and interviews in these sectors, I document how team moves facilitate the transfer of business activity—especially clients—from one firm to another. To test whether workers are compensated for this transfer, I analyze the French administrative wage dataset (BTS) for managers and professionals in the Paris region. I identify team moves as instances where three to fifteen individuals simultaneously move between firms within the same industry. Using staggered difference-in-differences methods, I find that team moves lead to substantial wage gains. Two years post-move, team movers earn 9% more than stayers and 4% more than solo movers. In finance, the premium is even higher: 20% over stayers and 14% over solo movers. More broadly, team moves are more lucrative than solo moves in occupations and sectors where clients are the primary resources, as opposed to those where knowledge and expertise dominate. This suggests that team mobility is an effective mechanism for transferring clients between firms. Ultimately, team moves contribute to the reconfiguration of capitalism by enabling groups of highly skilled workers to leverage their collective power, challenge firm boundaries, and reallocate key resources—especially clients—in pursuit of their own interests.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Return on team moves

papers.abstract:
The decarbonization of residential heating and transport requires widespread
adoption of climate-friendly technologies such as heat pumps and electric vehicles.
As efforts to price emissions from these sectors ramp up, differences in
the propensity and speed with which households switch to green substitutes
will have immense distributional consequences. In this article, I argue that
inequality in the ‘capacity to switch’ is central to the fairness of climate policy
in consumer-focussed sectors. Importantly, households’ ‘capacity to switch’
is often constrained by factors outside their control, including market failures
such as under-provision of transport infrastructure or split incentives in
rented housing. I argue that fairness principles should be sensitive to these
non-responsible factors. This would require abandoning fairness conceptions
predicated on ‘equality of outcome’, such as vertical and horizontal equity,
in favour of ‘equality of opportunity’ in reacting to carbon pricing. Building
on luck-egalitarian theories of justice, I outline how such an approach can be
operationalised and tested empirically. The article concludes by showing how
this perspective can inform the design of equitable climate policies.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Ready to switch? Fairness implications from heterogeneous access to climate-friendly substitutes

papers.abstract: This paper examines how climate shocks, credit access, and local poverty interact across rural India using a newly assembled subdistrict-level dataset. Rural households remain heavily exposed to climatic volatility and often face acute credit stress, with limited access to affordable formal lending and a continued dependence on costly informal credit. To study these pressures, we combine small-area poverty estimates from DHS 2015–16, long-run temperature and rainfall anomalies from ERA5, and a rare credit bureau dataset from TransUnion CIBIL containing over 600 million loan records from 2014–2024. This integrated framework makes it possible to assess whether areas facing more severe climatic disruptions also experience deeper poverty, and whether the structure of local credit markets—particularly the growing presence of FinTech lenders—shapes this relationship in environments where traditional credit systems may be strained or insufficient. The current draft focuses on data construction and empirical design, laying the foundation for analyses that will leverage the rich temporal depth of these datasets to explore dynamic responses, credit-market vulnerabilities, and potential causal mechanisms linking environmental stress, financial access, and welfare.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Credit Redistribution in the Age of Fintech:  Climate Shocks and Inequality in Rural India

papers.abstract: This paper documents perceptions of intergenerational mobility in 18 Latin American countries using data on self-reported economic status of survey respondents and that of their parents. Perceived mobility closely tracks standard income-based mobility measures. Results show that perceptions in the region are both low and highly heterogeneous: a clear hierarchy emerges, with Central American countries showing the lowest perceived mobility. For most countries, mobility perceptions have remained broadly stable over time, with the notable exceptions of Chile and Peru, where they have declined sharply. A complementary cohort analysis corroborates this trend, as younger cohorts tend to report lower perceived mobility.
papers.subtheme: Perceived mobility
papers.title: Perceived Intergenerational Mobility in Latin America

papers.abstract:
The use of personal holding companies has long been understood as a key challenge for
progressive income taxation. We exploit twenty years of administrative micro-data linking
firms to owners in Sweden and Norway to analyze the use of holdings across the income
distribution. About half of the income of the top 0.1% is paid to personal holding com-
panies, defined as firms with five owners or less and for which more than 60% of income
is investment income. Event-study results show that the creation of a holding leads to
a collapse in individual income tax payments and a negligible increase in corporate tax
payments, because most income paid to holdings is not subject to the corporate tax. As a
result, eﬀective tax rates fall from about 50% (all taxes included) at the bottom and in the
middle of the income distribution to about 15%–20% at the top. The use of holding com-
panies rose after the implementation of rules extending the tax exemption of intra-group
dividends in Sweden and increasing personal dividend taxation in Norway. Accounting for
income paid to personal holding companies erases half of the diﬀerence in the 1980–2020
rise of the top 1% fiscal income share between Scandinavian countries and the United
States, wheres rules penalizing the use of holdings have been in place since the 1930s.
papers.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
papers.title: Personal Holding Companies, Tax Progressivity, and Inequality

papers.abstract: Most European labor markets are structured by industry-wide wage bargaining. We study the relationship between this labor market institution and wage inequality by differentiating between wage coordination -- inequality in wage floors -- and wage centralization -- inequality in deviations from wage floors. We introduce a novel data set of over 30,000 major German sectoral bargaining agreements between 1950 and 2025 which lets us reconstruct wage coordination for the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. We find that inequality in bargained wage floors declined substantially between 1960 and 2025. This is driven by white collar contracts and the service industry. There is also less gender discrimination and less regional differentiation in contracts. These findings contrast with rising wage inequality during our later study period and show that wage inequality in Germany has not been driven by bargaining fragmentation, but by decentralization.
papers.subtheme: Sectoral bargaining
papers.title: Sectoral Bargaining and the Wage Structure

papers.abstract:
The relationship between income inequality and carbon emissions remains am-
biguous in both theory and evidence. A declining–marginal–propensity-to-emit
(MPE) framework predicts a short-term trade-off between reducing inequality and
limiting emissions, whereas political-economy perspectives suggest that higher struc-
tural inequality increases carbon output. Empirical studies often report negative
associations, but these frequently conflate within-country dynamics with cross-
country differences. We argue that distinguishing these levels can reconcile the ev-
idence: the MPE mechanism primarily operates within countries over time, while
political-economy channels shape structural, cross-country variation. Using data
from the World Inequality Database, we conduct two complementary analyses.
First, simulations on a global sample of 162 countries from 2019 test whether shifts
in national income distributions alter carbon emissions at constant GDP, isolat-
ing the within-country MPE effect. Second, cross-sectional panel analyses examine
whether households at equivalent income levels generate more emissions in more
unequal societies. Our results show a modest within-country trade-off — most pro-
nounced in low- and middle-income countries and when the income share of the
middle class rises — alongside a cross-country pattern in which higher inequality
is systematically associated with higher emissions across the income distribution.
These findings highlight the coexistence of opposing dynamics and underscore that
climate policy should balance short-term trade-offs against the structural benefits
of reducing inequality.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: The Climate Cost of Inequality: Trade-offs and Structural Effects

papers.abstract:
Literature in World-systems theory has argued that economies in the periphery and semi-periphery (the global South) are dependent on the core (the global North), to an extent that maintains them in a position of subordination and vulnerability to exploitation through
unequal exchange. Here we assess this dynamic empirically using ICIO (Inter Country Input Output) tables from the OECD (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) which provides detailed information on linkages across international trade networks for the period 1995 to 2020. Specifically, we develop a framework of metrics to assess how Southern production and consumption is dependent on outputs from the North by analyzing direct and indirect trade. We
also assess how this relationship has evolved over time. We find that even as individual global South countries have grown more reliant on foreign production, their dependence on Northern production has been declining in relative terms. We then focus on specific sectors and zoom in on three: Nutrition, Energy and Manufacturing. We find that the overall pattern of declining proportional dependence on Northern production holds across these sectors. However, Northern
dependency remains a substantial feature of Southern economies in the Manufacturing sector. We then apply our framework to study China’s economic development and its effect on Northern dependence for the rest of the global South. We conclude with a discussion of strategic policy proposals that can further reduce dependence.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Global South dependence on production in the core: an empirical assessment of trends from 1995-2020

papers.abstract: This research investigates the effects of natural resources rents on gender (in)equality in education in a panel of 52 African countries over the period 2000-2022. We test the gendered Dutch Disease theory which points to natural resources wealth as a potential explanation for the slow progress towards gender equality. We use Two-stage least square (2SLS) and instrumental variables quantile regressions (IVQR). We find four main results. First, natural resources exploitation reduces gender equality in education at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels. Second, the reductive effect of equality by natural resources increases with the level of education. Third, this reductive effect is higher in countries with low levels of educational equality. Fourth, government education expenditure moderates the negative effects of natural resources on gender equality in education. Therefore, natural resources are a curse in the educational sector. However, this curse can be exorcised by raising public spending on education to at least 10.85 percent of GDP. African governments should use revenues from the natural resources sector to invest in education and improve gender equality.
papers.subtheme: Gender Inequality - General
papers.title: Natural resources and gender (in)equality in education in Africa

papers.abstract: Gender role expectations shape how investors assess entrepreneurs, privileging men in commercial ventures and women in social ventures. Entrepreneurs defying these roles face early-stage funding challenges. We examine whether female angel investors mitigate these inequalities. Using a unique dataset of 7,336 investment decisions made by 111 angel investors across 14 countries, we find that male investors systematically rely on gender role expectations: they are 1.47 times more likely to invest in male-led commercial ventures and 1.43 times more likely to invest in female-led social ventures. Female investors, by contrast, show little evidence of using such heuristics and are more likely than male investors to support gender role-defying founders. We further find that gender role-defying founders funded by female angel investors achieve subsequent funding and exit outcomes comparable to gender role-conforming founders. Our findings highlight the role of female investors in reducing gender inequalities without compromising performance.
papers.subtheme: Gender Inequality - General
papers.title: Female Angel Investors Challenge the Gender Roles: An Analysis of Gender Dynamics Between Investors and Founders

papers.abstract:
This paper reconstructs global inheritance-flow series from 1995 to 2024 using the economic flow method, which offers a comparable framework where fiscal administrative data are unavailable or inconsistent. Drawing on mortality statistics, household surveys, and wealth aggregates from multiple international sources, we estimate inheritance flows for all world regions. We find a clear rise in the global inheritance-to-national-income ratio over the period, with inheritance flows growing especially quickly in the United States and Asia, and stabilizing in the EU27 after 2008. We provide the first global decomposition of inheritances into financial wealth, non-financial wealth, liabilities, and gifts, showing that worldwide inheritances consist of about 40\% financial assets, 33\% non-financial assets, and 30\% gifts. 
We also construct the first global series of effective inheritance tax rates, which fell from 3.5\% in 1995 to 1.3\% in 2023. A simple revenue exercise suggests that applying a 6\% minimum effective rate—equal to the long-run French average—would have generated between \$210 billion and \$590 billion globally over the period.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: The Return of Inheritance

papers.abstract: In the absence of a wealth register, Belgian wealth inequality needs to be estimated. Here I apply the mortality multiplier approach to Belgian inheritance tax tabulations and administrative microdata, collectively covering 1935 to 2022. Belgian wealth inequality has strongly declined during the 20th century and seems relatively stable in recent years. I triangulate my estimates with national accounts aggregates and previous work on Belgian wealth inequality. The evolution of Belgian wealth inequality is in line with other European countries for which long-run estimates are available.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Belgian wealth inequality, 1935-2022

papers.abstract: We study the portfolios and characteristics of cryptocurrency owners, including their position in the wealth distribution. We first use Norwegian tax returns to investigate portfolios and find that 0.85 percent of the adult population declares owning cryptocurrency. We then use a battery of novel data sources and statistics to understand the extent of non-compliance, finding that the actual population of cryptocurrency owners was approximately 5 percent of the full population. We also find that cryptocurrency owners are notably younger than the typical owners of traditional types of assets, and that cryptocurrency has become a considerable wealth object among younger generations.
papers.subtheme: Tax Compliance, Administration and Enforcement
papers.title: Who Owns Cryptocurrency?

papers.abstract: This paper constructs a new database on global trade flows and the world balance of payments (including goods, services, income and transfers) covering 57 core territories (48 main countries + 9 residual regions) over the 1800-2025 period. This allows us to analyze patterns of global imbalances, current account surplus/deficit and net foreign wealth accumulation over more than two centuries. We quantify the role of colonial transfers and low commodity prices (due to forced labor and other factors) in the build-up of Europe’s foreign wealth during the 1800-1914 period. We compare this experience to the global imbalances which developed during the 1970-2025 period. We stress the persistent role of unequal bargaining power and terms of exchange and the need for collective rules. We also provide counterfactual simulations on foreign wealth accumulation under alternative trade & monetary regimes.
papers.subtheme: Balance of payments
papers.title: Unequal Exchange and North-South Relations: Evidence from Global Trade Flows and the World Balance of Payments 1800-2025

papers.abstract:
Terrestrial water storage (TWS) is the total amount of water in all continental storage compartments and is an essential resource for food and energy production, manufacturing and ecosystem health. Even though absolute TWS is unknown, satellite gravimetry-based methods enable global estimations of spatial and temporal TWS changes, revealing significant alterations over the past two decades due to natural variability, direct human influence, and climate change. Here we show that %climate-induced
declines in TWS reduce economic growth. Combining GRACE TWS anomaly measurements from 2004 to 2018 with data on economic growth from more than 1600 subnational regions worldwide, we isolate the impact of climate by means of three complementary empirical strategies. Using a long-difference approach and fixed-effects panel regressions with either a control for human water consumption or an instrumental variable approach, we find consistent evidence for negative impacts of TWS declines on economic production. Among the regions with the largest TWS-induced growth rate reductions are the Caspian Sea Region and India, whereas others such as in Tanzania or the US Mid-West benefitted, pointing to pronounced regional heterogeneity even within countries. To further investigate this heterogeneity in response to TWS change, we combine a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis with tree-based classification techniques and a feature importance analysis. The results imply that regions with a high share of agricultural area or low income per capita experience higher growth reductions under declining TWS, implying a reinforcement of global inequality. Our findings contribute to the discourse on sustainable water management and its implications for economic prosperity.
papers.subtheme: Macroeconomic Drivers: Inflation, Growth and Cycles
papers.title: The impact of freshwater changes on economic production worldwide

papers.abstract: Gender gaps across the wage distribution are well-studied phenomena. However, focusing onlyon labor income, most studies miss out on substantial sources of income such as business, capitaland self-employment – which amount to almost a quarter of national income. As these becomeincreasingly more important at the top of the income distribution, the inclusion of non-laborincome yields higher but also more accurate estimates of (gender) inequality at the top. The aimof this paper is to contribute to a comprehensive picture of gender income inequality in Germany.How unequally ranked are men and women across the distribution, when considering all forms ofincome? What are the drivers of gender gaps in business and capital incomes? How do they addto the existing gender gaps in labor incomes – especially at the top of the distribution?
papers.subtheme: Gender Wage Gaps and Labor Income Inequality
papers.title: The double glass ceiling: Female top incomes and the role of capital

papers.abstract:
We use unexpected deaths during the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic to estimate
the extent of inheritance tax planning in the United Kingdom. As tax-planning
strategies require time and foresight, the pandemic provides an exogenous shock to the
opportunity to plan before death. Using administrative inheritance-tax returns linked
to demographic mortality data, we compare estates of decedents exposed to the mortality
shock with those in preceding years. Estates associated with unexpected deaths
are significantly larger and face higher tax liabilities, implying that prior planning substantially
reduces reported wealth at death. Notably, our findings are indicative of
inter-vivos transfer as more prevalent in planning compared to restructuring of estates
to minimize tax liabilities. We also find that inheritance tax planning lowers effective
liabilities by around 50% percent, corresponding to £3–4.5 billion in forgone annual
revenue. The results highlight the role of anticipatory wealth transfers in shaping
inheritance-tax outcomes and inform the design of future wealth-tax policy.
papers.subtheme: Wealth Taxation and Capital Income Tax Design
papers.title: Death and Taxes: Inheritance Tax Planning and Unexpected Mortality

papers.abstract:
Theories that connect growth and inequality typically posit an inverted U-shape, a Kuznets-type relationship. This paper reassesses this relationship with respect to wealth inequality both empirically and theoretically. In a first step, using subnational data, we provide causal evidence on the positive effect of industrialization on the top percentile's wealth share and find that this effect operated trough the fattening of the wealth distribution's tail. Individual-level return data link this fattening to heterogeneity in capital returns across industry and agriculture.
In a second step, we introduce a dynamic two-sector structure into an overlapping generations model. It allows us to disentangle the mechanisms that produce the observed wealth concentration and tail fattening: dynastic type and scale dependence of capital returns. Moreover, it shows that, in the absence of factors outside the model such as World Wars and institutional change, nothing suggests that  wealth inequality would have fallen in the 20th century.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: The Kuznets Curve with No Return: The Industrial Revolution and Wealth Inequality

papers.abstract: The Value-Added Tax incentivizes taxpayers to self-enforce compliance within a supply chain.
