Combining administrative tax data and a randomized experiment in New Delhi nudging on-time payment, we show that the same incentives that create positive compliance spillovers can constrain enforcement when suppliers are delinquent, because influencing supplier behavior is costly. While nudges increase compliance by 8 percent on average, only taxpayers with high compliance in their supplier network respond. Taxpayers file on time, yet lower net tax payments and continue buying from delinquent suppliers. Our findings highlight how the effectiveness and distributional burden of enforcement depends on production networks.
papers.subtheme: Tax Compliance, Administration and Enforcement
papers.title: Limits to VAT Self-Enforcement: Role of Network Frictions in Compliance

papers.abstract:
We document a robust positive relationship between income inequality and current
account balances. In advanced economies, a one percentage point increase in the share
of disposable income held by the top 1 percent is associated with a 0.8 percentage point
increase in the current account balance. This relation is driven by inequality in the permanent component of income and operates primarily through higher private saving rather
than changes in investment. We rationalize these findings using a tractable two-country
heterogeneous agent model with non-homothetic preferences, where saving rates increase
with permanent income. The model predicts capital flows from unequal to equal countries
and helps explain the observed co-movement between inequality and global imbalances
since the 1980s.
papers.subtheme: Savings, Capital Accumulation and Wealth Mobility
papers.title: Domestic Inequality and Global Imbalances

papers.abstract: Large increases in material wellbeing over the last 50 years were achieved at the cost of both rising intra-country economic inequality and unprecedented levels of environmental degradation. We combine detailed data on biodiversity with village-level socio-economic information to investigate the causal impact of wealth inequality on biodiversity in Cambodia's Keo Seima Wildlife Sanctuary (KSWS) between 2012 and 2022. Instrumenting economic inequality with agricultural production risk, measured by seasonal variability in the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), we show that increased inequality significantly reduces biodiversity, with a one standard deviation rise in inequality resulting in a 0.270 decrease in our measure of biodiversity. Our analysis also shows land use changes during this period are unlikely to be the primary pathway through which inequality impacts biodiversity.
papers.subtheme: Environmental Inequalities - General
papers.title: Economic Inequality and Biodiversity Loss. An empirical analysis of Keo Seima Wildlife Sanctuary, 2012-2022

papers.abstract:
Despite 74% of employers in the garment manufacturing industry in Punjab, Pakistan
believing women are as capable as men at on-site production jobs, few hire women on
factory floors. While much research has been conducted into the constraints women
face in obtaining out-of-home employment, this paper instead investigates: What deters
firms from hiring women? We use unique firm and worker survey data, complemented
by behavioral experiments to measure willingness to comply with gender norms and
estimate the impact of economic costs on hiring decisions. We find that top managers
exhibit low willingness to comply with segregation norms and do not expect resistance
from male workers. However, economic costs, particularly the cost of providing safe
transportation, significantly constrain female hiring, reducing the likelihood by 15%.
These findings indicate that reducing economic burdens, such as transportation costs,
could effectively increase female employment, highlighting the need for targeted policy
interventions.
papers.subtheme: Gender Wage Gaps and Labor Income Inequality
papers.title: Willing but Unable: Social Norms and Costs of Female Hiring in Pakistan

papers.abstract: This paper demonstrates that intergenerational transfers of housing assets generate spatial misallocation of talent, reducing aggregate productivity. Specifically, wealthy but less productive individuals concentrate in high-productivity cities through inherited real estate, crowding out more talented but liquidity-constrained workers.  Using a newly constructed micro-dataset covering all housing transactions--including sales, inheritances, and inter vivos gifts--in France from 2011 to 2022, we establish three findings. First, approximately one-third of housing transactions occur within families. Second, these transfers exhibit extreme concentration: the top 1% of heirs received over 55% of bequested housing assets during this period. Third, preferential tax treatment for family transfers induces households to retain properties within families, lengthening ownership durations and reducing turnover, particularly in high-productivity cities. This pattern is not unique to France and is generalizable to other tax systems (e.g., ``step-up in basis'' at death in the U.S. or California's Proposition 13). We exploit a distinctive feature of the French tax system, known as property-right splitting (``démembrement''), which introduces clear notches, to measure how homeowners value ownership duration. We then develop a spatial model to quantify the aggregate productivity costs associated with reduced housing turnover. In this model, misallocation arises because heirs inherit location advantages without commensurate ability, crowding out high-talent migrants from poorer family backgrounds. Leveraging a 2012 French tax reform (exemption reduction from €159k to €100k) in a shift-share design, we causally link local housing wealth inequality to talent misallocation. Our results underscore the importance of capital ownership turnover and show that higher inheritance taxation can generate meaningful productivity gains by promoting turnover and improving the allocation of resources.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Housing Inheritances and the Spatial Misallocation of Talent: A Geography of Missed Opportunities

papers.abstract:
This paper introduces a framework for estimating long-run series of measures of overall inequality and top wealth shares when data consist of a combination of historical tabulations
and modern administrative registers of taxable wealth. The proposed framework is applicable when historical wealth tabulations as a minimum provide information on bracket boundaries and the proportion of tax units for each of the wealth brackets.
The framework has been used to produce evidence on wealth inequality in Norway from 1912 to 2019. The empirical results show that wealth inequality as measured by the Gini coefficient was very high at the beginning of the twentieth century, fell during the post-war period and has increased substantially since the 1980s. The rise in wealth inequality over the recent four decades is driven by a rise in the wealth share of the top 1 per cent, while equalization among the bottom 99 per cent accounted for 70 percent of the reduction in wealth inequality from the early 1950s to the late 1960s.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Measuring long-run wealth inequality: Empirical results for Norway 1912-2019

papers.abstract: Cryptocurrencies pose substantial challenges to tax enforcement due to their anonymous and decentralized properties, undermining conventional regulatory practices. We study the impact of an ambitious new enforcement initiative aimed at addressing these challenges: domestic third-party reporting of crypto income. We estimate tax compliance and behavioral responses to this new policy by combining unique Danish microdata from domestic crypto platforms, administrative tax records, and cross-border bank transfers. Despite the introduction of domestic third-party reporting, over 90% of crypto investors do not declare crypto income. Moreover, we identify a significant and persistent evasion response to the policy as investors shift trading activity from domestic platforms, subject to third-party reporting, to foreign platforms outside regulatory reach. Our findings underscore the limits of domestic enforcement strategies in addressing tax evasion for decentralized, borderless assets like cryptocurrencies, highlighting the need for international coordination.
papers.subtheme: Tax Compliance, Administration and Enforcement
papers.title: Enforcing Taxes on Cryptocurrencies

papers.abstract:
Abstract
Hyper-globalisation (Piketty 2014; UNCTAD 2018; UNRISD 2022), or unfettered capitalism, causes multiple, interlinked economic, social, environmental and climate inequities, harming norms of social justice and at times even ignoring human rights outright. One of many avenues to help redress these impacts could come from a multilateral treaty on business and human rights. Such treaty can be understood as a global value chain due diligence law, which in addition includes provisions  for access to remedy in the case of rights abuse or violations. This is needed to stop altogether – and overcome the impunity of – outcomes of business activities when they are harmful. 

If a binding treaty materialised, it could support a move towards socially and economically just, environmentally sound, gender-equitable societies across the globe – negotiated via a new eco-social contract. 

The paper begins with a portrait of hyper-globalisation and the evolution of TNCs, international  investment and global value chains (GVCs) and the unequal hierarchy of power between large TNCs and major home countries vis-à-vis small suppliers and low-income countries. The paper presents selected examples of major “accidents” and harmful outcomes in the textiles, electronics, and minerals sectors. It argues that while such negative actions are not deliberate, they are nevertheless systemic in that they stem from the logic of a profit-driven system, and are driven by and reinforce economic and political power inequities.

The paper  then reviews  the history of regulations addressing the socioeconomic impacts of trade, investment and GVCs. Discussions, advisory work and negotiations ping-ponged between the UN Secretariat and the Human Rights Council, with a parallel process at the tripartite ILO. Starting from efforts to create an International Trade Organisation in 1947, with the mandate to ensure fair labour standards, through a Centre on TNCs active from 1975 to 1992, followed by voluntary guidelines from the UN and the ILO during the early 2000s, up to the creation, in 2014,  of an intergovernmental working group on transnational corporations and other business enterprises with respect to human rights whose mandate shall be to elaborate an international legally binding instrument to regulate, in international human rights law, the activities of transnational corporations and other business enterprises. The paper describes the positions of powerful government and TNC actors, and of civil society. In closing, it speculates on conceivable constellations for an outcome in light of interests and hierarchy of power among different actors. And the outlook remains open: can such multilateral negotiations contribute to redressing systemic inequities?

The underlying objective of this review is to offer support to progressive coalitions to move forward the process towards a comprehensive binding agreement on business and human rights, as a node in multilateral eco-social contract negotiations –underpinning action with research.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Redressing hyper-globalisation and the inequities systemically generated in GVCs: Multilateral efforts at the UN

papers.abstract: This paper examines the distributional consequences of land take - the conversion of natural and agricultural land to developed uses - in France between 2018 and 2022. Drawing on comprehensive administrative data linking land registry parcels to owner socioeconomic characteristics, we document stark inequalities in who benefits from land conversion and analyse the associated ecological costs. Our analysis reveals several key findings. First, land take predominantly benefits wealthy, multiple-property owners rather than first-time homebuyers. Post-development landowners have incomes 40% higher than pre-development owners and own an average of 1.8 dwellings, indicating that artificialization concentrates wealth among those already asset-rich. Second, we demonstrate that artificialization disproportionately affects ecologically valuable grasslands, particularly in mountain regions developed for tourist accommodation. This spatial analysis reveals that simple land area metrics obscure significant variation in ecological impact across habitat types and geographic contexts. These findings have important policy implications. Current land use and taxation policies fail to prevent wealth concentration through land conversion or to account for the ecological value destroyed in the process. We argue that achieving France's "no net land take" target by 2050 requires reforms that internalize ecological costs and redistribute the substantial rents generated by land conversion. Our results contribute to literatures on environmental inequality, property rights, and the political economy of land use regulation, while highlighting the need for spatially differentiated protection measures based on habitat vulnerability rather than simple area constraints.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Who benefits from land take? Inequality, property ownership and the ecological debt of artificialization in France

papers.abstract: In 2022, the IMF launched the Strategy Toward Mainstreaming Gender while continuing to push for fiscal consolidation and market liberalization. While the strategy acknowledges the gendered impacts of IMF-supported policies, it offers only limited mitigation measures, raising the question of whether gender clauses have any real impact. The case of Argentina can help clarify this. Between 2018 and 2022, Argentina signed two agreements with the IMF, both including gender clauses. However, these clauses lacked effective diagnostics, binding commitments, and monitoring. At the same time, IMF-backed policies deepened gender inequalities in labor markets, incomes, and pensions, while poverty levels rose. Since 2023, President Javier Milei has eliminated all gender-equality policies, including those in the 2022 gender clause, without consequences in IMF negotiations. Argentina’s case highlights that, as long as “macro-stability” takes priority and macroeconomic policies ignore their inmediate and medium-term gender effects, gender clauses remain ineffective in protecting women from the impacts of fiscal consolidation.
papers.subtheme: Polarization, Media and Democratic Trust
papers.title: The last IMF loan to Argentina: Were gender clauses effective in protecting women?

papers.abstract: Women rely on intra- and inter-generational transfers for wealth accumulation more than men, yet the role of inheritance in closing gender wealth gaps remains poorly understood. Using Swedish registry inheritance data from 2002-2004 combined with panel data on individual wealth portfolios and labour income from 1999-2007, we examine how wealth and income evolve upon inheriting. Inheritance does not lead to long-term convergence in wealth between genders. Differences in portfolio composition as well as gendered inheritance of productive assets may play a role. We find evidence indicative of structural barriers to financial resource accumulation over the lifecycle rather than inherent gender differences in investment preferences. The disparity in wealth accumulation post-inheritance is reinforced by gendered labour supply responses. Daughters reduce their paid labour supply more than sons, seemingly to provide unpaid eldercare. Given these findings, inheritance alone should not be viewed as an effective mechanism for reducing gender wealth inequality.
papers.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
papers.title: Shaping women's fortunes: inheritance and gender disparities

papers.abstract: The history of inequality over the English Industrial Revolution is still poorly understood. Here we present a set of steps to deduce the level of wealth inequality. We first estimate the will-making rate, by county, and by year, from 1400 to 1858. Next we use a large sample of ~30,000 wills to examine the distribution of wealth amongst wealth holders. By combing these two moments we are then able to derive wealth share estimates for the male population. We find that wealth inequality is stable before exploding during the Industrial Revolution. These new results suggest a far more dramatic rise in inequality than previously understood.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Wealth Inequality in England 1258-1858: Evidence from Wills

papers.abstract: We use matched employer-employee data on the universe of French firms to study the role of multinational enterprises' (MNEs) presence in tax havens in determining within-firm wage inequalities. We implement a difference-in-differences and a panel event-study design to analyze the effect of firm entry in tax havens on firms' wage variance. We find that the average firm wage variance experiences a drop by 4.7\% over the immediate years following the establishment in a tax haven. We argue that wage inequality within MNEs with presence in tax havens is underestimated, due to the "salary split" for the highest wages of the firm. Indeed, we find that top 1\% wages of the firm decline on average by 3.1\% after the tax haven entry. On top of this, when we decompose the effects on the top 1\%, we find a stronger wage decline due to the tax haven entry for the top salaries, as follows: a 4.4\% decline for the top 0.5\% and 4.8\% for the 0.1\% of top wages. The drop in wage variance is explained by a decline in wages at the top of the distribution and not by an effect on the rest of wages, on which there is no statistically significant effect. We show that these developments are exclusively related to tax haven foreign investment and not to other foreign investments. Finally, we introduce a methodology to estimate the macro-level effect of firm-level use of tax havens and we find that it represents around 2\% of the observed change in the aggregate variance of wages.
papers.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
papers.title: Offshoring wage inequality in tax havens

papers.abstract:
International climate negotiations continue to be hampered by disagreement over how burdens should be shared across countries. The pledge-and-review architecture institutionalized by the Paris Agreement heavily relies on perceived fairness: countries draft and justify their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) using competing fairness principles, and reputational incentives are expected to shape both ambition and compliance. Yet existing analyses only partially explain how heterogeneous fairness norms influence collective outcomes.

This paper develops a new theoretical framework—in which discrete and continuous choices coexist—to explain how fairness heterogeneity interacts with reputational incentives to shape mitigation pledges and their subsequent implementation. The model departs from standard public-good formulations by explicitly linking pledge formation to later compliance decisions and by allowing countries to interpret fairness in self-serving yet heterogeneous ways. This structure yields provides a partial explanation for key stylized features of the Paris system: inflated pledges, gaps between pledges and implementation, and mitigation efforts that persist above business-as-usual despite the absence of binding enforcement.

By clarifying the strategic role of fairness pluralism, the framework highlights how inequality and fairness perceptions can either enable or obstruct collective climate action. It also yields concrete policy implications, hinting at reforms in institutional design choices that could strengthen cooperation and reduce policy-driven climate inequalities.

Overall, the analysis offers new insights into the dynamics and limitations of pledge-and-review systems and provides an analytically grounded perspective on the interplay between fairness, inequality, and global climate cooperation.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Argue, Pledge and Implement: Investigating the Role of Fairness in International Climate Policy

papers.abstract: From a long-term perspective little is known about income inequality in Venezuela. This is regrettable as the country offers a unique opportunity to study distributional dynamics in an economy dominated by oil richness since the 1920s amid an accelerated process of structural change, demographic and institutional transformations. The main reason for this lacuna is scarcity of data. The paper benefits from a set of Ginis based on dynamic social tables with four occupational groups defined by their skill level, and National Accounts data. Income inequality has been primarily oil driven, first, by a steady rise in oil production and fiscal revenues; and, since 1973, by the timing of oil-price shocks. Altogether, overall inequality widened during the 1970s and 2000s booms, but also during the slump of the 1980s and 1990s. Prosperity favoured most those in the top group; adversity impacted worst those in the bottom group.
papers.subtheme: Natural ressources
papers.title: Has oil richness been a force for income equality in Venezuela over the long term?

papers.abstract: We study gender disparities in intergenerational wealth transfers in Germany over more than four decades, focusing on inheritances and inter vivos gifts. Using individual-level data from the Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP), we document persistent gaps: while women are in some cases more likely to report receiving an inheritance, men are more likely to receive gifts and obtain larger overall transfer amounts. These differences are not uniform. In West Germany, younger women face particularly large disadvantages in gifts, whereas no systematic gaps are observed in East Germany. We also show that transfers, particularly gifts, contribute to the gender wealth gap. Oaxaca–Blinder decompositions indicate that gifts account for a measurable share of the mean gap in 2019, and RIF decompositions reveal that transfer amounts contribute to both explained and unexplained components across the wealth distribution. Despite gender-neutral inheritance law, our findings suggest that testamentary freedom and persistent social norms continue to generate unequal outcomes. Addressing these disparities is essential to prevent wealth transfers from reinforcing intergenerational and gender-based economic inequality.
papers.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
papers.title: Dissecting the gender gap in intergenerational transfers: the case of Germany

papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT

Wealth inequality has gained importance in the international debate following the publication of Capital in the 21st Century, by Thomas Piketty, which contains systematic data on the size and evolution of the phenomenon in advanced economies over the last few centuries. In particular, Piketty's research reveals an important decrease in wealth concentration throughout the 20th century, a decrease that has not been sustained in the first decades of the 21st century. What can be said about the levels and historical trajectory of wealth inequality in Brazil, one of the world’s most unequal countries? We investigated all available estimates since the 17th century. The work is organized based on the different sources and approaches used to construct the estimates, which cannot be directly obtained from national household surveys or censuses. Two conclusions stand out: a) wealth concentration presents extreme levels and notable stability over time, despite profound transformations in the composition of assets; and b) all available estimates have significant limitations. The availability of adequate public data, along with improvements in the procedures employed so far, is essential for the development of a literature on wealth inequality in the country – the first step towards effective public engagement with the issue.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: What do we know about wealth inequality in Brazil?

papers.abstract: We examine the determinants of taxing-rights allocation in Bilateral Tax Treaties (BTTs) signed between developed and developing countries. Our analysis covers 848 treaties concluded between 23 OECD economies and developing partners over 1950-2021. We draw on a new dataset from the International Centre for Tax and Development, which constructs indices capturing the balance of source and residence based taxing rights embedded in each treaty. We further extend these data by coding the presence of tax sparing provisions, which protect the effectiveness of tax incentives offered by developing countries. Our preliminary results yields three main insights. First, developed countries do not appear systematically more accommodating toward poorer treaty partners: the level of economic development of developing countries is essentially unrelated to the taxing rights they obtain, and this null relationship has remained stable in recent decades. Second, developed countries do display selective generosity, granting more source-based taxing rights in treaties that also include tax sparing clauses. Third, bargaining power matters. Developing countries with larger populations secure more taxing rights, whereas those more economically dependent on their developed partner obtain fewer. Finally, geopolitical distance significantly increases the share of taxing rights allocated to developing countries, consistent with the view that BTTs are used as instruments to stabilize relationships with geopolitically distant partners.
papers.subtheme: Taxation and Evasion - General
papers.title: Inequality in BTT Bargaining? Allocation of Taxing Rights between Developed and Developing Countries

papers.abstract: This paper studies the intergenerational transmission of wealth among the top wealthiest US individuals between 1875-1950. We combine historical rich-lists with crowd-sourced genealogies to link top wealthy individuals with both their vertical and extended kinship across cross-sections of rich-lists. For 18% of individual in these lists we can find a vertical descendent in a rich list twenty-five years later. This declines to 14% when considering seventy-five year periods. Persistence is much higher when we consider extended families, we find that over 40% of wealthy individuals are linked to a wealthy individual twenty-five years later when we consider extended kinship. We provide evidence supporting that these extended kinship connections are strategic and improve the likelihood of wealth persistence at the very top. We document that, among the hyperwealthy, the offspring of wealthier individuals have a social connectivity advantage, meaning that they serve as bridges between wealth dynasties through extended family relations. This connectivity is valuable, IV estimates exploiting within-dynasty higher-order connectivity shocks show that one standard deviation increase in children connectivity increases the likelihood of wealth persistence by 29% and total observed wealth in the next cohort by 44%. Finally, children connectivity increases the likelihood of wealthy elites branching out into another elite: US Congress dynasties.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Stayin’ Elite: Wealth, Multigenerational Persistence, and Political Power Among the US Hyperwealthy, 1875-1950

papers.abstract:
Recent evidence for Germany indicates that income inequality after accounting for
housing expenses has risen almost twice as rapidly as inequality before housing costs,
driven by the disproportionately faster growth of housing expenditures among lower-
income households (Dustmann et al., 2021). This paper extends that analysis to other
four major economies —France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and the United
States— and expands the Germany series, using harmonized microdata from national
income and expenditure surveys since the early 1980s. We construct comparable mea-
sures of disposable income before and after-housing expenditures, and examine how
housing markets contribute to overall inequality. The results show that post-housing
income inequality has widened substantially in all countries, even more than income,
driven by rising rents and stagnant real incomes for renters. These findings underscore
the growing role of housing affordability in shaping income distribution and living
standards in the developed world.
papers.subtheme: Macroeconomic Drivers: Inflation, Growth and Cycles
papers.title: Housing costs and the distribution of income.

papers.abstract:
This paper uses the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) to analyze inter- and intra-generational wealth mobility in the United States over the period 1969-2021. I produce several novel contributions and findings. First, for the inter-generational (family-level) analysis, I develop a machine learning model to approximate wealth ranks back to 1969. This proxy outperforms the housing-based proxies commonly used in the literature. I find that wealth rank resemblance between (grand)parents and their (grand)children increases with age,
that inter-generational wealth mobility has declined over time, and that the U.S. mobility is lower compared to other countries. Second, intra-generational (individual-level) wealth mobility is concentrated between ages 30 and 39, has declined at the top of the distribution, and is lower than in the Nordic countries. Diverging wealth rank trajectories relate to variation in inter-generational transfer receipts, business ownership, labor income, health, and non-mortgage indebtedness. Third, bridging the inter- and intra-generational perspectives, I find positive interdependence between the wealth rank trajectories of individuals and those of their parents over the same historical time period.
papers.subtheme: Wealth Mobility
papers.title: Wealth Mobility in the United States: Empirical Evidence from the PSID

papers.abstract: This paper presents the first reconstruction of income inequality in Italy during the so-called ‘Golden Age’, by building Dynamic Social Tables (DSTs) from 1951 to 1973, consistent with existing series for 1901-50. We reveal increasing income inequality between 1951 and 1961 (the ‘proper’ Economic Miracle). The first strikes in the metalmaking sector and a sudden recession then led to a stagnation in inequality. While within-labour inequality steadily declined after 1966, overall inequality reached a peak in 1969, to decline towards the levels recorded by household surveys by early-1970s. While showing a ‘Kuznetsian’ trend in the period of most sustained structural change of Italian history, we highlight socio-political developments, in line with the literature which links both the end of Italy’s ‘Golden Age’, and the post-1968 reduction in inequality to the explosion of social conflicts. Somehow at odds with prevailing narratives, we also find an increase from 1951 in the share of income accrued by Italian working women.
papers.subtheme: Long run income inequality in Europe
papers.title: A Golden Age for All?  Income Inequality and Social Classes in Italy, 1951-1973

papers.abstract: Residual income progression, defined as the elasticity of after-tax income with respect to before-tax income, is one of the most widely used metrics of effective tax progressivity. Using a novel methodology, this paper provides new estimates of residual progression for the years 1913 to 2021 in the United States, advancing the historical study of this metric by more than half a century. Contrary to the traditional linear regression framework which necessitates comprehensive microdata, our methodology only requires tabulated before- and after-tax income shares. We validate our methodology by comparing it with the OLS and PPML estimators of residual progression, demonstrating its suitability, particularly for the study of progressivity among top earners. Our historical series reveal that progression for top earners follows an inverted-U shape over time and is highly correlated with the statutory top marginal tax rate. Additionally, progression for the entire income distribution shows a consistent upward trend.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Residual Income Progression in the Twentieth and Twenty-First Centuries

papers.abstract: Persistent inequalities in incomes, energy uses and living standards between world regions remain a major challenge for climate change mitigation. While current scenarios increasingly promote sufficiency in high-income countries, few consider post-growth transitions that simultaneously enable development in the Global South. Here, we use a hybrid integrated assessment model to explore four global mitigation scenarios that combine regionally differentiated carbon pricing, sufficiency policies, and post-growth strategies. We show that only a scenario featuring post-growth transitions in high-income countries and rapid convergence in productivity across regions reduces multidimensional inequalities to unprecedented low levels — while remaining within a 2°C carbon budget. When taken individually, regional differentiation of carbon prices or sufficiency policies are insufficient to meet social thresholds for all regions. Our findings highlight the potential of post-growth frameworks to drive structural economic change and support multidimensional inequality reduction, underscoring the need for scenario modeling that integrates macroeconomic and distributive dynamics.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Post-growth mitigation scenarios to reduce multidimensional inequalities between world regions

papers.abstract:
How do radical changes in property rights regimes affect long-run wealth inequality? We address this question by reconstructing the distribution of wealth in Georgia before, during, and after the Soviet experiment. By linking historical property records from the Georgian National Archives with contemporary real estate ownership data, we test whether the Soviet objective of leveling class structure succeeded in permanently breaking intergenerational transmission of advantage. Methodologically, we utilize surname affinity analysis to overcome the lack of longitudinal panel data, proxying wealth through land and private property ownership.

The data reveal a "U-shaped" trajectory of inequality but a linear trajectory of elite survival. We document that while the initial years of Soviet rule successfully stripped the pre-Soviet elite of physical assets, these families did not disappear; rather, they adapted by securing positions within the professional and technical intelligentsia. However, the re-introduction of private property post-1991 did not restore these families to their former economic dominance. Instead, our findings indicate that the primary beneficiaries of the market transition were the heirs of the Soviet political elite. This suggests that modern Georgian inequality is a legacy of Soviet institutional access rather than pre-Soviet dynastic wealth.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: From Aristocratic Estates to Bureaucratic Fortunes: Intergenerational Wealth in Georgia (1900–2020)

papers.abstract: Estimating the market value of private businesses is essential for understanding both aggregate firm dynamics and top wealth inequality, yet these values are inherently unobservable. This paper introduces an econometric approach that treats the gap between true market values and initial estimates as measurement error. I employ time-series restrictions on these errors as moment conditions within a GMM framework, and use the fitted values from these estimations as error-free estimates of private business wealth and capital stocks. Applying this method to Dutch administrative data linking the universe of firms to their owners, I find that aggregate private business wealth increases by 30% of GDP initially, and is more stable than the unadjusted series. Top 1% and 0.1% wealth shares increase by 3–5 percentage points, peaking at 38% and 20%, respectively. Adjusted returns to firm wealth exhibit a steeper gradient across the wealth distribution than unadjusted returns, consistent with models of return heterogeneity.
papers.subtheme: Data Fusion, Harmonization and Measurement Error
papers.title: Robust Estimation of Private Business Wealth

papers.abstract:
This paper analyzes the dynamics of poverty and income in Argentina over the 2003–2023 period by integrating data from one-year rotating panels, and cross-sectional household surveys through synthetic panel estimation techniques. The study has two main objectives: first, to trace the evolution and structural patterns of welfare dynamics over two decades characterized by alternating periods of rapid economic expansion and severe macroeconomic downturns; and second, to evaluate the performance and validity of recent synthetic panel methodologies in this volatile context, as tools for approximating longer-term welfare dynamics in data-scarce
environments.
papers.subtheme: Advanced Panel and Time-Series Methods
papers.title: Poverty and Mobility in the Time of Synthetic Panels: Evidence from Argentina (2003–2023)

papers.abstract:
The deregulation of Britain's financial sector has long been praised for its success in times of high inflation and stagnating economic growth. However, increasing attention has been given to the
Larger implications of financialisation on welfare. This study examines the effects of Britain's 1986 Big Bang on inequality and economic welfare. Using the synthetic controls method, I find that the
Big Bang caused a 5.3 percentage point increase in living standards inequality in the UK, relative to a scenario of gradual financial deregulation. Incquality gains rose rapidly until the early 19905 and have since stabilised around 6 percentage points. These results are statistically significant and robust to specification changes, demonstrating strong internal validity. Consequently, the Big Bang elevated the UK's relative inequality ranking by 10 places among peer countries. By 2000, Britain was the second-most unequal high-income economy globally, behind the United States; without the Big Bang, it would have ranked twelfth. Furthermore, this analysis finds that the economic benefits from the Big Bang disproportionately favoured the highest percentiles of the wealth distribution and were unevenly distributed regionally. The regions that benefited most from the Big Bang have become the most unequal and are now slower-growing than other less-unequal regions.
papers.subtheme: Global Wealth Convergence and Divergence
papers.title: Britain's 1986 Big Bang: how state-led financial deregulation durably boosted inequality and hampered long-term economic welfare in the UK

papers.abstract: This paper examines employer-side payroll tax incidence for older workers, a population whose proximity to retirement, accumulated firm-specific capital, and strong employment protections create distinct adjustment frictions compared to prime-age employees. I exploit a reform in Spain that introduced, and later repealed, an employer-side payroll tax reduction for workers aged 60 to 64 on open-ended contracts with certain firm tenure. Using administrative Social Security data and matched employer-employee records, I apply dynamic difference-in-differences models at both individual and firm levels. Individual-level analysis reveals no significant impact of tax changes on treated workers' earnings, suggesting short-run incidence falls on firms. However, firm-level analysis of the incentive's repeal reveals partial to full pass-through to workers collectively two years after the tax increase, alongside gradual employment adjustments. These findings demonstrate that even for a workforce segment with high adjustment costs and strong protections, payroll tax incidence ultimately falls at least partially on employees through firm-level spillovers. Heterogeneous effects of the policy are also explored by gender, age, education and skill level. The results highlight how worker age and contract characteristics shape the dynamics and distribution of tax incidence, with important implications for evaluating employment policies targeting older populations in ageing economies. (There is a lot of work in progress that I hope to complete in the next months, I can submit an updated version of the paper in January/February)
papers.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
papers.title: Who benefits from payroll tax subsidies for older workers? Incidence at the individual and firm level

papers.abstract:
This paper examines global inequality in the international mobility of persons and compares it to inequality in mobility rights and economic welfare. Using the Global Transnational Mobility Dataset 2.0, we compute outward mobility rates for 186 countries from 1995 to 2022 and derive global mobility Gini coefficients. Our findings reveal that inequality in actual cross-border movements (de facto mobility) is substantially higher than inequality in visa-free travel rights (de jure mobility) and GDP per capita (economic welfare), making international mobility one of the globally most unequal capabilities. While mobility Ginis declined slightly over the two decades preceding the COVID-19 pandemic, the crisis caused a sharp reversal, pushing inequality above 1995 levels. Post-pandemic recovery has been uneven, and mobility inequality remains close to its historical highs. De facto mobility rankings of countries and world regions have changed little over time, pointing to deep-rooted structural factors shaping mobility opportunities. Regression analyses show that economic welfare and legal mobility rights both matter for explaining cross-country variation in levels of mobility rates, but economic welfare is the stronger predictor. Mobility returns to economic welfare are highest among low-mobility countries, suggesting that it contributes to convergence rather than additional divergence. Within-country income inequality can dampen the mobility-boosting effect of economic welfare. Our findings highlight that, despite globalization, opportunities for cross-border movement remain deeply tied to individuals’ home country, reinforcing territorial disparities in life chances.

We upload the abstract and the authors' list. As discussed with Lucas Chancel, a full paper will be submitted in the coming weeks
papers.subtheme: Polarization, Media and Democratic Trust
papers.title: Global Mobility Ginis: The Inequality of International Mobility between 186 Countries (1995-2022)

papers.abstract: Wealth concentration has risen globally over the past three decades, yet we know little about who constitutes the economic elite or how elite composition varies across institutional contexts. Drawing on a new dataset tracking 5,366 billionaires across 84 countries from 1996 to 2025, I document three patterns.  First, billionaires' share of global household wealth has more than doubled from 1.2 percent to 3.0 percent, with increases occurring across diverse institutional regimes.  Second, elite composition varies systematically by country: heirs dominate in European Coordinated Market Economies and Mixed Market Economies while Liberal Market Economies show mixed composition with substantial representation of financiers.  Third, concentration levels and elite composition are not associated.  Countries with compositionally distinct elites exhibit similar trajectories.  These findings challenge theories linking institutional regimes to distributional outcomes and suggest that wealth concentration operates through mechanisms distinct from those shaping income or broader wealth inequality.  By classifying economic elites according to wealth source and tracking individuals over time, I demonstrate how elite analysis can reveal dynamics obscured by aggregate inequality measures.
papers.subtheme: Global Wealth Convergence and Divergence
papers.title: Economic Elites and Wealth Concentration Cross-Nationally, 1996-2025

papers.abstract: This paper studies the distribution of housing expenditure and its relationship to income in Spain from 1994 to 2024. Using a consumption-cost approach that deducts housing expenses from disposable income, it constructs measures of income inequality before and after housing costs and traces their evolution across the income distribution, age groups, and tenure types. Spain provides a particularly relevant setting over this period: homeownership rates are high overall but have declined sharply among younger cohorts, and housing markets have undergone a pronounced boom–bust cycle.
papers.subtheme: Historical Measurement - General
papers.title: Housing Expenses and the Evolution of Income Inequality in Spain

papers.abstract: Work-from-home (WFH) technology, which has become a lasting feature of the post-pandemic economy, remains disproportionately available to high-income and college-educated workers. This paper studies how this unequal access affects intergenerational mobility through two novel mechanisms: a parental time channel and a residential sorting channel. Using U.S. microdata, I document that WFH parents devote about 23 percentage point more time, equivalent to roughly 0.15 additional hours per week, to their children's educational activities than comparable non-WFH parents. I also show that WFH families are 3.3 percentage points more likely to move to neighborhoods with higher-quality public schools, as measured by standardized test scores. To quantify the implications of these mechanisms, I develop and calibrate a spatial overlapping-generations model with endogenous neighborhood spillovers and parental time allocation between market work, home-based work, and child education. The model calibrated to U.S. data reveals a persistent intergenerational advantage: even among adults who do not themselves work from home, those with a WFH parent are 1.05 percentage points more likely to reach the top income decile, corresponding to a 12% relative increase compared to their peers. Counterfactual experiments show that more than 95% of this intergenerational advantage arises from the parental time channel rather than residential sorting. These findings suggest that WFH transmits advantage primarily through how parents use their time at home rather than through where they live.
papers.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
papers.title: Work-From-Home and Intergenerational Mobility

papers.abstract:
We reconstruct national income and household wealth by income & asset category in France on a yearly basis throughout the Second World War from a national accounts perspective.

First, we find that over the war years, nominal labour & mixed incomes rose while capital incomes stagnated or even declined, pushing the capital share down. We argue that the decline in the capital share is primarily the byproduct of “government regulation” rather than physical capital destruction or tax evasion. Second, despite physical capital destruction, nominal wealth increased due to soaring asset prices across asset categories. Nominal wealth however did not keep pace with nominal income growth towards the end of the war, hence the fall in the household wealth–to–national income ratio.

Together with the lack of new assets put on to markets & severe restrictions on transactions on existing assets – with the notable exception of State bonds for the politique du circuit – we argue that these findings could explain why income inequality declined in France while the impact on the decrease in wealth inequality was very mild over the period. We believe that these results bear relevance for other countries over the same period, whether belligerent or not.
papers.subtheme: Distributional National Accounts and Data Infrastructure
papers.title: Income & Wealth in WW2-France: A Macroeconomic & Fiscal Overview

papers.abstract: We study the effects of a progressive tax reform on tax compliance, using a research design that distinguishes between two channels. First, using a quasi-experimental design, we estimate the direct effects of the reform—namely, how changes in a household’s own tax rate affect its own compliance. Second, leveraging a large-scale natural field experiment, we estimate the indirect effects: holding a household’s own tax rate constant, we examine how its compliance is influenced by changes in the tax rates of other, poorer or richer, households. We find substantial direct effects: lowering taxes for poor households increases their compliance, while raising taxes for rich households reduces theirs. We also find sizable indirect effects: when poor households learn about the tax hikes on the rich, their stated perceptions of tax fairness and their actual compliance both increase. Among rich households, learning about tax cuts for the poor also improves perceived fairness, but, if anything, reduces compliance. Using an additional reform and follow-up field experiment conducted a year later, we replicate both the quasi-experimental and experimental results. Together, our findings show that tax compliance responds not only to a household’s own tax burden but also to its perception of fairness of the broader tax system. Our results also underscore the potential disconnect between stated and revealed preferences for redistribution. Finally, we present a counterfactual analysis that illustrates the implications of the direct and indirect effects for designing progressive tax reforms.
papers.subtheme: Wealth Taxation and Capital Income Tax Design
papers.title: From Flat to Fair? The Effects of a Progressive Tax Reform

papers.abstract: Migration remains a key driver of development, offering pathways to improved economic conditions and diversified livelihoods. This study evaluates whether migration enhances household welfare in India, proxied by the share of food expenditure in total household expenditure (excluding rent and conveyance costs) in line with Engel’s law. Using data from the 64th round (2007-08) of the Employment and Unemployment Survey, we estimate the causal impact of migration on food share using parametric and non-parametric methods, including Double Machine Learning. Migration reduces the household food expenditure share by about 0.5 percentage points at the All-India level. We also examine the impact of migration on dietary diversification using a Theil entropy index and find a small decline in food diversity. However, analysis of food subgroup-wise expenditure shares reveals a dietary shift away from staples toward higher-value and nutrient-rich foods, indicating qualitative dietary improvements despite lower diversity. Welfare gains are heterogeneous across migration streams, with rural–urban migrants experiencing the largest benefits. Remittances sent to families by migrants emerge as a potential mechanism for improving welfare, strengthening migration’s contribution to enhancing welfare in India, whereas welfare effects for non-remittance-receiving migrants are noticeably muted.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: From Roots to Returns: Does Migration Improve Economic Welfare? Evidence from India

papers.abstract:
We present new evidence that privately held firms are used to transfer income to underage 
children. This exacerbates wealth and income inequality among children and persists at least 
into early adulthood. Underage children at the top 1% of the parental income distribution are 
20 times more likely to be owners of a privately held firm compared to children in the bottom 
90%. The average age of these underage firm owners is 12 years, with ownership occurring 
across all ages from 0 to 17. Tracking data across generations shows that nearly half of 
these underage children come from non-entrepreneurial family backgrounds suggesting that 
childhood ownership is not entirely explained by anticipated family succession. We further 
study the intergenerational persistence in incomes and find that, conditional on observable 
parental characteristics, childhood owners with a parent from the top 1% are 15 percentage 
points more likely to be in the top of their cohort’s gross income distribution as young adults 
than a non-childhood owner with similarly affluent parents. Childhood ownership of firms is 
strongly associated with having a larger share of total income as capital income in the age 
of 30. We also discuss potential tax savings obtained by managing family wealth within a 
privately held firm, and find support for tax motivated income shifting within the family. 
(JEL: D3, H2, H3, M1)
papers.subtheme: Mobility, inheritance
papers.title: Income Inequality Early in Life: Underage Children as Owners of Privately Held Firms

papers.abstract: Abstract We examine the special features of the upper tail of income and wealth distributions. We explain why naive use of the raw data may lead to misleading conclusions and consider the way in which a modelling approach may be effectively designed. Focusing on the type of functional forms introduced by Pareto, we analyse the shortcomings standard methods of tail modelling.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Towards Narratives of Inequality

papers.abstract:
This paper examines the role of sibling gender composition as a potential explana-
tion of the transmission of parental advantages to the next generation. The presence
of a brother affects the family environment and parents’ decisions, influencing the sib-
lings’ labor market outcomes in the long term. The results show a negative effect of
approximately 2% on the permanent income of women for the presence of a younger
brother. This effect does not modify the intergenerational persistence of income. Re-
garding mechanisms, we find evidence that the effect is amplified when households face
tighter budget constraints. Moreover, it is more pronounced in households with tradi-
tional gender norms, shaping permanent income, educational choices, and motherhood
decisions. These findings underscore the importance of sociocultural mechanisms in
accounting for the persistence of inequality
papers.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
papers.title: Gender and intergenerational mobility: unequal economic outcomes between siblings

papers.abstract:
Economic historians have substantially expanded the evidence on personal income and wealth levels in the USA during the pre–World War II era, documenting that inequality typically peaked at the beginning of the 20th century and remained high throughout much of the interwar period (Piketty and Saez 2003; Bengtsson and Waldenström 2018; Geloso et al. 2022). Some scholars (Milanovic 2019; 2023) have characterized this period as the archetypal era of classical capitalism, during which income inequality was primarily driven by factor incomes—capital incomes were concentrated among capitalists, while wages and salaries constituted nearly all income for workers. Subsequent shifts in the shares of factor income, a wage compression and the gradual diffusion of asset and property incomes eventually contributed to a reduction in inequality.
This paper argues that the standard explanations for the rapid shift from classical to welfare capitalism produce an overly simplified narrative. By contrast, our perspective highlights that when one examines a clearly defined metric—specifically, the overlap between top labor and top capital earners (Atkinson and Lakner 2021)—a different picture emerges. This overlap grew because a substantial minority of top capital earners who had not been working in the pre-WWII era gradually entered the labor force in the 1940s and 1950s. It also increased with the rising prominence of self-employed workers, who inherently combine labor and capital income and were more likely to receive returns from other assets. Finally, it was reinforced by sociodemographic change, particularly the growing labor force participation of married women, which further strengthened the correlation between labor and capital incomes.
The paper uses for the first time two exceptionally detailed set of sources. One is derived from the federal income tax for the year 1936 (U.S. Treasury Department, Division of Tax Research 1940) and covers approximately the top 5% of the US population. The second dataset leverages from census microdata from IPUMS ((Ruggles et al. 2024), which typically up to the top 1% of the population and provide an invaluable insight into the sociodemographic of top earners. With these inputs we create quasi-micro datasets that illustrate the distribution of wages, mixed incomes, and property incomes (including dividends, interest, rents, and others) and thus offer a unique opportunity to study the correlation between capital and income in the pre- and post-WW2 scenarios.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Did Classical Capitalism Ever Exist? New Evidence from Income Tax and Census Microdata from the USA (1936-1980)

papers.abstract: Using confidential administrative data on the universe of UK taxpayers, we study the efficiency and equity implications of taxing capital gains at lower rates than income. We first provide evidence that a large portion of taxable capital gains appear to be repackaged income that is taken as gains due to their favourable tax treatment. We then identify clear instances of income shifting by analysing company liquidations in response to a 2016 anti-avoidance reform. Next, we consider a 2011 reform that allowed some successful entrepreneurs to pay less Capital Gains Tax than expected on the sale of their business, with beneficiaries receiving an average windfall of £120,000. We find no evidence that this stimulated further investment; instead the reform accelerated retirement. Finally, we show that the exclusion of capital gains from official inequality figures biases the picture of inequality in the UK: the pre-tax (post-tax) share of income plus gains going to the top 0.01% is 60% (100%) higher than for income only, and this gap has been steadily rising. Taken together, our findings cast doubt on common efficiency justifications for lower taxes on capital gains while highlighting their equity concerns.
papers.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
papers.title: Should capital gains be tax privileged?

papers.abstract: The labour market in developing countries is characterised by a dual nature comprising formal and informal sectors. In this context, this study examines the earnings differentials between migrants and non-migrants in regular and casual labour markets of India using data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey 2020–21. We employed unconditional quantile decomposition in conjunction with the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to analyse the wage gap and the factors contributing in wage disparities between migrants and non-migrants. Findings indicate that within the regular salaried, non-migrants earn more than migrants at the lower quantiles of the wage distribution. Migrants surpass non-migrants in earnings beyond the 50th quantile of the wage distribution. In contrast, the casual labour market exhibits a persistent wage disadvantage for migrants across the distribution, with a marginal advantage observed only at the 90th quantile. The decomposition results further reveal that the wage gap in the regular salaried sector is primarily driven by the unexplained component. While in the casual labour market, it is primarily attributed to the explained component. Furthermore, the wage differentials in both labour markets are determined by the individual characteristics, mainly gender, experience, and area of residence. The findings underscore the policy suggestion to reduce the wage gap between migrants and non-migrants through prioritising the enforcement of labour regulations, ensuring access to minimum wages, and expanding social security coverage, primarily within the casual labour market.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Earning disparities between migrant and non-migrant workers: A quantile decomposition analysis of the Indian Labour Market

papers.abstract: What is the welfare effect of colonial agriculture on the colonized population? There could be a growth effect spurred by modernization, or a redistribution of production factors in favor of colonists, which could worsen native well-being. We investigate these two channels in French Morocco (1912-1956), a settlement colony. We use a novel individual dataset of Moroccan soldiers born around the onset of colonization with granular information on place of birth, intra- and inter-generational migrational choices. We estimate the effect of being born near a colonial farm on adult height-per-age, a proxy for early-life conditions. A difference-in-difference strategy indicates that cohorts exposed to colonial farms grew up to be shorter by 10 percent of a standard deviation of height-for-age. To address spatial sorting, we exploit the staggered attribution of colonial land via a public auction program, using never-attributed plots as counterfactuals. We find evidence of a redistributive channel, whereby the height loss is driven by a diversion of agricultural inputs, namely land and water, resulting in reduced local productivity. Suggestively, in the long run, the height effect is not persistent among post-independence cohorts. However, we find delayed industrialisation and increased insecurity in agricultural land ownership. These results shed new light on the colonial determinants of structural change in developing countries.
papers.subtheme: Agricultural Productivity, Smallholders and Rural Inequality
papers.title: The Negative Impact of Colonization on the Local Population: Evidence from Morocco

papers.abstract: This study investigates how extreme inequality influences economic growth through demand composition and sectoral differences in production. Drawing on household and firm level data, we document pronounced segmentation in consumption: poorer households devote substantially larger shares of their budgets to informal, relatively low quality mass produced goods, while richer households allocate more to formal and labor intensive high quality goods. These findings build the foundation of a simplistic model featuring non-homothetic preference and dual production structures, aimed to replicate the stylized facts from data, to examine how redistribution will shift economic growth. This paper contributes an integrated theoretical empirical account of the inequality growth dynamics in demand constrained, structurally heterogeneous economies.
papers.subtheme: Historical Measurement - General
papers.title: Extreme Inequality and Economic Growth

papers.abstract:
The paper presents the results of two research projects that investigate the long-term relationship between economic inequality and the inclusiveness of municipal political institutions across various environmental and socio-economic contexts in north-central Italy between 1500 and 1800.
Both projects are based on the idea that, during the early modern period—and, in some respects, even today—local institutions managed a substantial share of public finances and influenced the effective fiscal burden. They determined how to respond to the fiscal and military demands of the State, whether through the imposition of direct taxes or through the leasing and/or sale of municipal assets such as forests, pastures, buildings, and rights to collect duties, among others. The strategies adopted in managing local finances could have a significant impact on economic inequality. For instance, direct taxation—often regressive in relation to the way in which it was distributed—tended to increase inequality, whereas leasing communal assets might have reduced the need for taxation. However, leasing the commons could also deprive the lower and middle classes of a source of income, potentially creating further opportunities for local elites to profit. Hence, the extent to which different social groups could participate in local economic policy decisions becomes crucial. It can generally be assumed that less inclusive institutions—characterized by low turnover and limited representativeness—were more likely to pursue policies that exacerbated inequality. Conversely, greater participation of the lower and middle classes in the management of local finances could promote a more equitable distribution of wealth or at least mitigate the growth of economic disparities.
Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that the relationship between institutional inclusiveness and economic inequality is far from straightforward. Instead, it depends on a variety of contextual factors that are specific to each case examined.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Political inclusion and economic inequality in the long run: Central-Northern Italy, 1500-1800

papers.abstract: This research addresses the moderating role of meritocratic beliefs in the association of inequality with subjective well-being (SWB) across subjective social classes. The literature suggests that inequality is positively associated with the SWB of those in the upper class and negatively with that of the lower class. Additionally, it posits that meritocratic beliefs serve as a palliative for the negative relationship in the lower class by giving them hope for social mobility, presenting as system-justifying beliefs. To empirically assess these propositions, multilevel linear regression models were estimated, introducing a three-factor interaction and using a measure of inequality different from the GINI. The results indicate that, contrary to the literature, as inequality increases SWB decreases for those with high meritocratic beliefs who perceive themselves as lower class. Meaning that, considering a sample covering different regions and countries with varying income levels, the palliative effect attributed to these beliefs does not hold.
papers.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
papers.title: Unfulfilled Prophecy: The Moderating Role of Meritocratic Beliefs in the Relationship Between Inequality and Subjective Well-Being

papers.abstract:
Access to higher education is a key driver of socio-economic mobility, yet financing remains a central barrier for disadvantaged groups in India. This study investigates whether caste-based discrimination affects the approval of education loans using an experimental design that combines elements of an audit study and a lab-in-the-field experiment. Loan officers evaluated fictitious but realistic student loan applications that were identical in financial and academic characteristics but varied only by caste. Each application received two ratings: (1) the likelihood of approval and (2) the likelihood of successful repayment.
The results show that applicants from Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe backgrounds receive significantly lower approval scores than their Upper Caste counterparts, despite no differences in expected repayment ability. This pattern aligns with taste-based discrimination rather than risk-based statistical discrimination. We also find no significant approval penalty for Other Backward Caste applicants relative to Upper Caste applicants, indicating that bias is concentrated against the most marginalised caste groups rather than following a linear caste hierarchy. These findings suggest that caste prejudice influences loan approval decisions and restricts access to higher education for historically disadvantaged communities.
papers.subtheme: Discrimination (caste)
papers.title: Does Discrimination Exist in the Market for Educational loans? Experimental Evidence from India’s Caste System

papers.abstract: In the last two centuries many countries underwent substantial demographic changes that appear to have had substantial consequences for each country's economy. Both mortality and fertility declined. We examine the impact of these changes in theory, using an overlapping-generations model, and in application to a highly important case, China. We demonstrate the importance of demographic change by studying the effects of increased life expectancy (ILE) and the One Child Policy (OCP), introduced in 1980 and abolished in 2016.  We find that the effect of ILE is modest, but that OCP has dramatic consequences.
papers.subtheme: Demographic change
papers.title: Demographic Change and Intergenerational Transmission.  With an application to China

papers.abstract:
We construct a detailed dynamic social table to trace the evolution of income distribution in Poland between 1924 and 1938 at both national and regional levels. By incorporating the ethnic composition of occupational groups, we extend the analysis to income differentials across Poles, Jews, Germans, Ukrainians, and Belarusians. We then combine these estimates with data on wartime losses to calculate “survival rates” across the income distribution and to assess the impact of World War II and the Holocaust on both income distribution and aggregate wealth.
Our results show that interwar Poland was a high-inequality economy, more comparable to Latin America than to European peers. Growth in this period was pro-poor, but compression occurred largely at the expense of the urban middle class. The survival rate across the income distribution followed an inverse U-shaped pattern; thus, wartime human losses significantly reduced inequality. While the assets of the annexed German territories could offset either war destruction in Central Poland or assets lost in the Soviet Union, they could not cover both. Yet, once the transfer of Jewish and German property into Polish hands is considered, Poles, on average, were richer in 1945 than in 1938.
papers.subtheme: Historical Measurement - General
papers.title: Income distribution in Poland, 1924–1945: pro-poor growth, ethnic inequality, and the consequences of World War II and the Holocaust

papers.abstract: This article examines inequalities underlying the employment of domestic workers, combining data from cross-national and national surveys. Across a large sample of countries we find a positive correlation between the level of economic inequality and the share of domestic workers in the workforce. We zoom in on eight countries with comparable data - Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Mexico and Russia – to reveal who employs these workers, and how this links with households’ unpaid social reproduction labour. The highest-inequality country, Mexico, displays the expected pattern: high levels of domestic work confined to high-income employers. But we find two very different models in low-inequality countries. Eastern Europe sees barely any employment of domestic workers, whereas in Belgium, and to a lesser extent France, many households pay for domestic work, but in small quantities. Though still more common among richer households, paid domestic work is used across the income distribution. This subsidized and more fragmented model may alter the domination and social inequality typically associated with domestic work.
papers.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
papers.title: The rich, the poor and the cleaners A multinational comparison of domestic service and inequality

papers.abstract: I collect and harmonize income surveys, new tax data, national accounts, and wealth rankings to correct survey-based inequality estimates that understate top incomes; estimate wealth distributions in the absence of direct data; and distribute non-fiscal components of national income across income groups to make distribution figures consistent with macroeconomic aggregates in Turkey. The study’s main methodological contribution lies in leveraging top taxpayer lists where detailed tax tabulations are unavailable. I find that the historical evolution of fiscal income inequality follows a U-shaped pattern: a sharp decline in top-income concentration from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, followed by a sustained rise through the 1980s and 1990s, and a renewed acceleration in the 2010s, most no- tably after 2018. Under conservative assumptions, the national income share of the top 10 percent increased from 42.1 percent to 50.5 percent between 2005 and 2022, while the middle 40 percent’s share fell from 39 percent to 32.8 percent. Wealth inequality was more pronounced, with the top 10% holding 75.6% of gross wealth in 2022. The most cautious lower-bound estimates, accounting for the uncertainty arising from multiple limitations, imply a significant upward revision of official inequality statistics.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Six Decades of Unequal Growth: Income and Wealth Inequality in Turkey, 1968–2022

papers.abstract: Economic inequality has become an important element of political debates, capturing significant attention in media coverage, public discourse, as well as academic research. In a survey experiment on a representative sample of the Dutch population (N = 4501), we examine how individuals explain economic inequality. We employ responses from an open-ended survey question about sources of inequality and link them on an individual level to administrative data on respondents’ income and wealth. We find that respondents predominantly attribute inequality to structural factors rather than personal responsibility or luck. Explanations are somewhat insensitive to information about inequality in the Netherlands, or about one’s standing in the income or wealth distributions. We observe significant differences in the content of the explanations based on respondents’ characteristics, such as wealth or political affiliation, and inequality-related attitudes. In a subsequent data collection, we aim to estimate the causal impact of explanations of inequality on redistributive preferences.
papers.subtheme: Experimental and Survey Evidence on Inequality Attitudes
papers.title: Societal Explanations of Economic Inequality

papers.abstract:
This paper examines the impact of integration policies within India’s Affirmative Action
framework in public engineering institutes. Exploiting random assignment of students
to hostel rooms, I study how exposure to peers from different caste groups influences
academic performance, job market outcomes, mental health, and socio-political attitudes.
I find that lower-caste students assigned to mixed-caste rooms perform better academically
and secure better internships after first year. However, they report poorer mental
health, measured by PHQ-4 scores and self-reported anxiety about academics and
discrimination, and fewer close friendships. Among upper-caste students, mixed-room
assignment reduces academic performance but does not significantly improve attitudes
toward social justice or the perceived meritocracy of affirmative action. I also find both
upper and lower caste students assigned to mixed rooms are more likely to live in mixed
rooms at the end of first year, suggesting integration despite cultural frictions.
Using additional variation in room composition comparing fully mixed versus partially
mixed three-sharing rooms, I explore whether having one same-caste roommate moderates
these effects. I find that partial mixing mitigates mental health effects and friendship
effects. Secondary outcomes on interactions and mutual support further corroborate the
role of caste and ability of the roommate, level diversity in the room.
papers.subtheme: Political Inequalities - General
papers.title: Backlash or Bonding? Effect of Integration Policies in a Context of Affirmative Action

papers.abstract:
We estimate the effects of exposure to income and wealth inequality during adolescence on long-term educational and labor market outcomes. Using detailed Swedish register data covering all students completing compulsory education between 1989 and 2013, we construct measures of inequality among students’ schoolcohort peers and exploit variation between cohorts within schools to identify plausibly causal effects. We find no evidence that exposure to inequality affects GPA, high school graduation, university enrollment, university completion, or income up to age 35. These null results are precisely estimated and robust across alternative
measures of inequality, sample definitions, and specifications. Moreover, we find no evidence of systematic heterogeneity by socioeconomic background. These findings provide reassurance that school integration policies mixing students from different socioeconomic backgrounds do not carry hidden long-run costs from inequality exposure. More broadly, they challenge the view that exposure to peer inequality during adolescence is a causal driver of human capital accumulation or later-life mobility.
papers.subtheme: Environmental Inequalities - General
papers.title: Exposure to Inequality, Human Capital Investment, and Labor Market Outcomes

papers.abstract: This paper digitizes archival tax records, integrates newly available survey data, and finds that (a) World War II service explains postwar wage compression, productivity growth, and economic mobility; and that (b) the relative gains of the New Deal era were both more pronounced and more durable for the upper middle class than for the poorest. After linking the full-count US Census of 1950 to that of 1940 and both of these to a survey of WWII enlistees, I exploit an exogenous discontinuity in the probability of being drafted to show the causal impact of service on wages. This impact was strongest for the working class.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: National Service and the Great Leveling: New evidence on midcentury American inequality

papers.abstract: This article reinterprets modern growth through a Schumpeterian lens, linking innovation dynamics to today’s surge in wealth and market concentration. We document the dramatic rise of billionaire wealth since the mid-1990s and show how individual fortunes are anchored in a small set of highly profitable corporate groups, especially in technology and pharmaceuticals. Using the Amazon case, we trace the shift from creative destruction to “creative appropriation,” where platform control, data advantages, and expansive intellectual property enable incumbents to internalize disruption, preserve rents, and convert global revenues into lightly taxed domestic profits. We then connect firm-level rents to macro outcomes, misallocation, slower diffusion, and a widening pipeline from corporate profits to private power -- with risks for productivity and democratic accountability.
