The policy section sets out three levers to reverse these trends: rebuild effective corporate tax capacity; modernize competition policy (mergers, interoperability, data access, and self-preferencing limits); and narrow over-broad IP and open essential interfaces. Together, these reforms can redirect innovation toward diffusion, curb extreme accumulation, and restore the complementarity between growth, equality, and democratic resilience.
papers.subtheme: Top wealth, productivity
papers.title: From Creative Destruction to Creative Appropriation – Rethinking Growth in Intellectual Monopoly Capitalism

papers.abstract:
Using Danish administrative data from 1980–2021, we document substantial lifetime income
inequality and its evolution across cohorts. Lifetime inequality increases steadily with
age and is highest among individuals with lower education and lowest for individuals with vocational education. Variance decompositions shows that differences in employment attachment— non-employment spells and part-time work— account for 30–50% of lifetime earnings dispersion, and is particularly important among the low educated. Across cohorts, lifetime inequality has risen for low- and medium-educated workers. A part of this increase can be linked to increasing dispersion in employment attachment. Redistribution through taxes and transfers
reduces inequality, but transfers play a larger role than taxes, and the equalizing effect has
weakened over time. Income mobility declines with age and across cohorts, making early-career
differences increasingly persistent. These findings underscore that rising lifetime inequality
reflects both labor market dynamics and limited re-distributive offset.
papers.subtheme: Historical Measurement - General
papers.title: Life-time Income Inequality in Denmark

papers.subtheme: Polarization, Media and Democratic Trust
papers.title: Online media and polarization: Theory and cross-country evidence

papers.abstract: Reparations have been proposed to remedy enduring inequalities between racial or ethnic groups, but little is known about the social and political consequences of such policies. We study caste-based reparations by evaluating a program that provides a one-time group-targeted wealth transfer of 1 million rupees ($12,000) to Dalit households in Telangana, India. We test competing theoretical expectations of advancement, persistence, and retrenchment using a natural experiment and original survey of 3,184 households. The program improved Dalit asset ownership and narrowed the gap with non-Dalits. It increased Dalits’ confidence in engaging dominant castes and reduced caste conflict, against the expectation of social backlash. However, segregation norms persisted, and dominant castes expressed reduced support for a
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Caste Reparations: Economic Advancement, Social Concord, and Policy Backlash

papers.subtheme: Education, Skills and Human Capital Channels
papers.title: Human Capital, Unequal Opportunities and Productivity Convergence: A Global Historical Perspective, 1800-2100

papers.abstract: In poor countries, about 50% of national income is tied to subsistence and therefore cannot feasibly flow to the top 1%. Most studies ignore this hard constraint on income concentration. Extending Milanovic et al. (2011), I set a subsistence floor and derive the maximum feasible top 1% share, distinguishing extractable from non-extractable income. I then adjust for how this inequality frontier rises with growth: income above the subsistence floor expands and so does the scope for extraction by elites. This enables meaningful top 1% comparisons across countries and history. Using long-run data, I document three findings. First, colonial slave economies —theoretically the most extractive—cluster near the predicted inequality frontier (maximum feasible top 1%). Second, today, in poor countries, despite similar top 1% income shares to rich countries (16-17%), the top 1% holds 42% of feasibly extractable income —they sit 2.5 times closer to the frontier. Third, while the world’s top 1% income share rose from 17% in 1820 to 18% today, their share of feasibly extractable income fell from 48% in 1820, 38% in 1920, to 21% today. Modern economic growth has radically liberated income from subsistence, yet elites have captured a declining share of this rising surplus. This decline occurred between 1880-1980, as labour rights and democracy in the Global North first, and decolonisation in the Global South later, constrained elite extraction. The secular rise of top incomes masks a fundamental transformation: from a world where most live at subsistence and elites held nearly all of society’s surplus as in colonial systems, to one where economic freedom —the ability to meet needs beyond mere subsistence, emphasised by Sen— has been greatly equalised.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: How Much Can Elites Extract? Subsistence Constraints and the Long-Run Evolution of Top Incomes, 1700-2022

papers.abstract: In this paper we provide a comprehensive analysis of the quality of life among the elderly in the U.S. over the last decade. We use a novel approach to measure a multidimensional well-being index and compile data on four well-being indicators, namely, income, housing costs, disabilities and internet connectivity from three rounds of the American Community Survey. We find that multidimensional well-being among elderly Americans increased by 36 percent between 2014 and 2023. We also find a rise in inequality in well-being overtime. Well-being levels varied significantly among elderly people belonging to different racial and ethnic groups. American Indian elderly had the least well-being and highest inequality level.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Multidimensional Inequality among the Elderly in the United States

papers.abstract:
Recent work in the Piketty–Atkinson tradition has documented the long-run evolution of
income and wealth inequality using tax data and distributional national accounts, with
Sweden as a key case of dramatic 20th-century equalization. Building on this literature, we
link changes in the structure of jobs to changes in the distribution of incomes in Sweden
from 1870 to 1950. We thus connect the contemporary labour-economics literature on job
polarization and upgrading (e.g. Goos and Manning 2007; Autor and Dorn 2013) to the
literature on the historical drivers of inequality.

We use decadal population censuses to measure the occupational structure of employ-
ment, and a newly assembled 1% sample of income taxpayers every tenth year to recover
occupational income levels. We complement the tax data with our own income estimates
for non-filers (farmers and low-income workers). These extensive microdata (N = 232,000)
allow us to construct fine-grained, occupation-specific income distributions for the period
when Sweden moved from a predominantly agrarian economy towards an industrial welfare
state.

Our analysis proceeds in four steps. First, we document the evolution of the job struc-
ture when occupations are ranked by their position in the income distribution. From 1870
to 1900, employment growth was concentrated in low-pay jobs. Between 1900 and 1920,
employment in the bottom two quintiles contracted while the middle of the distribution
(quintiles 3–4) expanded, indicating upgrading. From 1920 to 1950 this upgrading inten-
sified: the employment share of the bottom quintile of the 1920 pay distribution fell by
about 10 percentage points, while the top quintile rose by a similar amount. Second, we
relate these patterns to structural change, focusing on the downsizing and increasing capital
intensity of agriculture and the expansion of manufacturing and services. Third, we decom-
pose changes in the overall income distribution into a “quantity effect” driven by changing
employment shares across occupations and a “price effect” driven by changing relative occu-
pational pay. From 1900 to 1920, an upgrading job structure coincided with rising relative
pay at the top, producing little overall equalization. By contrast, 1920–1950 combined up-
grading with falling pay differentials and hence substantial equalization, while 1870–1900
featured a downgrading job structure but narrowing differentials.

Fourth, given the strong gender segregation of the labour market, we analyse the gen-
der dimension of these changes. Average female incomes rose from about 25% of average
male incomes in 1920 to around 50% by 1950, a larger catch-up than observed for women
in the United States. We show that this was closely related to the reconfiguration of the
job structure, notably the decline of low-pay female-dominated groups such as family as-
sistants in agriculture and agricultural workers. Our findings contribute to the literature
by highlighting the role of structural change in shaping income concentration and earnings
gaps.
papers.subtheme: Gender Wage Gaps and Labor Income Inequality
papers.title: Job Composition, Gender and Income Inequality in the Long Run: Sweden, 1870–1950

papers.abstract: This paper examines how confirmation bias and media fragmentation jointly contribute to political polarization. As media environments become increasingly fragmented, individuals are exposed to distinct sets of information, reinforcing ideological divides and reducing shared understanding. We argue that confirmation bias not only drives selective exposure but also amplifies political polarization as fragmented information environments create self-reinforcing narratives. Using inflation perceptions in Germany as a case study, we provide empirical evidence that preferences on media consumption reinforce extreme political views and support for radical parties, more concretely towards the right. Additionally, we document a backfire effect, where exposure to contradictory information deepens ideological entrenchment. Our findings highlight the critical role of fragmented media landscapes and biased news consumption in shaping political attitudes and electoral behavior.
papers.subtheme: Information, Narratives and Belief Formation
papers.title: Biased Information, Biased Preferences: How Fragmented Media Environments Undermine Support for Redistribution

papers.abstract: This paper examines the impact of financial inclusion in reducing caste-based social exclusion using a quasi-experimental setup involving a 2005 branch expansion policy of RBI and employing a regression discontinuity framework. Our findings reveal a significant increase in consumption and a reduction in poverty among marginalized castes compared to non-marginalized castes. Three channels, informal credit, business finance, and the labor market, have been found to contribute to the welfare gains of marginalized castes. We also find reductions in taste-based discriminatory practices. This study underscores the role of formal banking sector in mitigating deep-rooted social norms such as caste-based discrimination.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: Does Financial Inclusion Mitigate Social Exclusion?

papers.abstract: This paper studies how organized crime presence transforms local communities and human capital formation. Identifying these effects is challenging, as crime is endogenous to local conditions. We address this by leveraging the recent case of Ecuador, where criminal organizations from neighboring countries have rapidly established a new cocaine export route. This externally driven shock generated sharp increases in violent crime, allowing us to estimate causal effects using a difference-in-differences design based on proximity to areas prone to cocaine smuggling. Crime-affected areas experienced higher dropout rates among children at grades characterized by weak school attachment, the end of primary education and the first years of secondary school. While we do not find evidence of increased dropout among older students aged 15-18, individuals in this age group already out of education at the time of the crime surge exhibited a marked rise in risky behaviors, reflected in higher homicide victimization and earlier pregnancies. We also document severe economic disruption: household income fell by nearly 30%, driven mainly by a decline in informal employment. Declining earnings are a key mechanism linking crime exposure to school dropout. These findings show that the externalities of organized crime impose persistent social costs, deepening inequality and undermining human capital development.
papers.subtheme: Crime
papers.title: When Organized Crime Moves In: Economic and Human Capital Disruption

papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of child multidimensional deprivation on school enrollment and subsequent learning outcomes in undivided Andhra Pradesh, India. Using longitudinal data from the Younger Cohort of the Young Lives study across three survey rounds (2002, 2006, and 2009–10), we construct a continuous multidimensional deprivation index along the dimensions of health, education, and standard of living, following the Alkire–Foster framework adapted to child-specific conditions. We employ rare-event logit models to examine the effect of deprivation on school enrollment and apply Instrumental Variable (IV) and Control Function (CF) approaches to identify causal impacts on learning outcomes. We find that children deprived across multiple dimensions—whether measured strictly or flexibly—are systematically less likely to attend formal schooling. We find that multi- dimensional deprivation significantly reduces school attendance across all social groups, with particularly strong effects among Muslims and backward castes, while intersectional analysis shows that Muslim girls experience the steepest attendance penalty. We find that multidimensional deprivation exerts large and statistically significant negative effects on children’s learning outcomes. The effects are strongest for language and numeracy domains and remain robust under both strict and flexible deprivation definitions. Heterogeneity analysis further reveals that girls, Muslim children, and Scheduled Tribes experience the steepest learning penalties.
papers.subtheme: Education, Skills and Human Capital Channels
papers.title: Child Deprivation and Early Educational Outcomes: Evidence from Young Lives, India

papers.abstract:
This study investigates gender-based attribution bias, the tendency to attribute men’s success to ability and women’s failure to a lack of ability—using a controlled principal- agent online experiment. We test for this bias across male- and female-typed tasks. In male-typed tasks, we
find evidence of attribution bias after task success: principals are more likely to attribute success to ability when the agent is male. We do not observe such bias following failure. In contrast, in female-typed tasks, we find bias against men following task failure, pointing to the importance of
task domain in shaping attribution patterns. Our design allows us to rule out taste-based and statistical discrimination. Attribution bias is stronger among individuals with more regressive gender attitudes but only for male-typed task, suggesting an attitudinal basis for attribution patterns.
papers.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
papers.title: Attribution Bias by Gender

papers.abstract: Measuring political equality has always been fraught with challenges. Taking roads distribution as a reflection of local political dynamics, I propose a novel way to measure political equality using satellite data of local roads and other infrastructure while accounting for contextual factors like population density, topography and initial development levels. Against expectations, I find that development aid generates more economic growth when provided to regions with less, not more, political equality. This counterintuitive result can be explained by the idea of growth potential. Since aid agencies generally target areas that consistently lag in development, more politically equal areas were likely to have already reached their growth limits while aid provided to less equal areas helps unlock suppressed potential.
papers.subtheme: Political Inequalities - General
papers.title: Measuring Political Inequality: Roads Distribution and Developement Aid Effectiveness in Indonesia

papers.abstract: This article investigates how national income convergence, redistribution, and climate change will shape the world distribution of income until 2050, using a novel source of data on global inequality before and after taxes. Despite ongoing convergence in national income, the global bottom 50% post-tax income share only marginally rises from 10% to 12% under "business-as-usual", while the top 1% share remains constant. Yet, if countries were to adopt the most effective redistribution policies implemented by the best performer in their respective region, the global bottom 50% income share could increase to over 19%. Redistribution of pre-tax incomes account for 62% of this increase, with the remainder due to post-tax redistribution. Climate change is set to exacerbate inequalities, potentially offsetting all the increase in the global bottom 50% share since 1980.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: Global Inequality by 2050: The Role of Redistribution and Climate Change

papers.abstract: This paper studies how economic inequality shapes the risk of violent conflict. We construct a new measure of local agricultural income and inequality by combining time-invariant agro-ecological suitability from FAO/GAEZ with year-to-year variation in global crop prices. This approach yields plausibly exogenous, spatially disaggregated predictions of rural income that vary across ethnic territories, administrative units, and neighboring communities. Using data for sub-Saharan Africa from 1997--2023 and a fine $0.5^{\circ}$ hexagonal grid with cell and country--year fixed effects, we find that price-induced increases in agricultural income inequality, particularly within and between ethnic territories, significantly raise the likelihood of conflict onset. By contrast, mean agricultural income has a limited and often negative association with conflict. Interaction estimates show that conflict take place in locations characterized by high inequality and poverty. Our findings underscore the central role of distributional tensions, rather than average income shocks, in explaining the origins of political violence.
papers.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
papers.title: Inequality and Insurgency

papers.abstract:
Using the novel GC Wealth Project Data warehouse, this paper shows that most countries have experienced rising wealth inequality since the 1990s, with gains concentrated
among the top 10% and declines among the bottom 50%. We reveal substantial variation
of estimates across data sources and units of analysis which complicates international comparison of wealth inequality. Yet, core trends at the country level are generally robust.
Individual-based series generally report higher inequality than household-based ones. Regional patterns reveal sharp increases in inequality in Latin America, North America, India,
and China, while Europe and Asia-Pacific exhibit more stable trends. Incorporating Forbes
billionaire data extends coverage to low-income countries and Africa—where, notably, billionaire wealth relative to GDP has remained stable, marking a distinct exception to global
patterns.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Wealth Inequality Trends Around the World: a first view from the GC Wealth Project data

papers.abstract:
Do unequal gender norms limit women’s productivity? We study this question using three decades of World Bank project and HR data. Women are less likely than men to lead aid projects in countries with high gender inequality, despite no evidence of llower ability. Using a difference-in-differences design, we show that female-led projects suffer a performance penalty relative to men’s in such settings, consistent with cultural constraints. These effects remain after controlling for project leader and country fixed effects and instrumenting female leadership with the gender composition of the pool of potential
leaders.
papers.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
papers.title: Cultural Constraints on Women’s Productivity: Evidence from World Bank Lending

papers.abstract: I revisit the empirical relationship between wealth and returns on wealth of U.S. households over the past 70 years. While recent studies suggest that returns on wealth increase with wealth and that the richest households earn the highest returns, I show that this pattern is specific to post-1980. Before 1980, returns declined at the top 10 percent of the wealth distribution, and the bottom 90 percent had higher returns than the top 10 percent. I attribute this reversal to differences in households’ exposure to interest rate risk. Because wealthier households tend to hold longer-duration assets, such as stocks and private businesses, changes in real interest rates affect their portfolios more strongly. When real rates rose, as they did before 1980, the top 10 percent households experienced lower returns, whereas falling real rates after 1980 boosted their returns. To explain why wealthier households hold longer-duration assets, I develop a model in which households select portfolio duration to hedge their income risk. Since richer households’ income correlates more with short-term interest rates, they optimally choose a longer-duration (countercyclical) to hedge this exposure.
papers.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
papers.title: Scale-dependent returns and the interest rate

papers.abstract: High schools have lasting academic and economic consequences for their students. I use de- tailed Chilean administrative data to show that interactions among primary school peers shape how students sort into high schools. I exploit the random assignment of students into oversub- scribed primary schools, together with repeated data on graduates’ applications, to identify the causal effect of primary school peers on students’ choice of high school. I find that studying with a particular peer significantly increases the probability that a student applies to and at- tends the same high school. Peer effects interact nonlinearly with the spatial distribution of high school quality, shaping educational inequality. Embedding peer effects into a model of school choice, I show that when high school quality is unevenly distributed across space, interactions among peers can reduce applications to high-quality schools from students in disadvantaged areas, amplifying inequality. Empirically, I find that peer effects account for one-sixth of the gap in the probability that low- and high-income students attend a high-quality high school. To address these gaps, I show that policies that expand students’ access to high-quality high schools can benefit from increasing returns to scale through spillovers within peer networks, without generating negative externalities for untargeted students.
papers.subtheme: Education,  Peer Effects
papers.title: Go Your Own Way? Peer Effects, School Choice, and Educational Inequality

papers.abstract:
We investigate whether traditional poverty alleviation policies, typically designed for immediate poverty reduction, also enhance households’ resilience to future unexpected shocks. We revisit a randomized control trial in Bangladesh which undertook a two year intervention across two rural regions of Bangladesh. Using an improved resilience metric and machine learning methods, we present new findings of the impact of the different poverty alleviation strategies, both at the endline and four years post intervention. Our study reveals that poverty alleviation interventions, such as unconditional cash transfers, and cash or food transfers combined with intensive group-based behavior change communication (BCC), significantly improve resilience compared to pure in-kind transfers. However, these policies are primarily effective in strengthening resilience to extreme poverty. Four years after the intervention, we find some evidence of cash transfers enhancing resilience to extreme poverty. We explain our findings through both short-term
coping strategies and long-term adaptive mechanisms
papers.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
papers.title: Do Poverty Alleviation Policies Enhance Household Resilience to Poverty? Evidence from Bangladesh

papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel application of the Kaya identity to assess the roles of technological change and consumption behaviour in shaping global greenhouse gas emissions. Drawing on numerical insights from counterfactual emission-reduction scenarios, we quantify the adjustments in technology and consumption required to remain within the carbon budget by 2050 and explore their distributional implications. Building on this analysis, we develop a simple analytical model that formalizes the resulting carbon budget trilemma: under binding ecological constraints, rising consumption, gradual technological progress, and widening inequality cannot sustainably coexist. We place these transformations in historical perspective by examining a set of precedents—from wars and epidemics to economic collapses and episodes of rapid technical upgrading—that provide comparative magnitudes for the scale of change implied by a binding carbon budget. Our conclusions unveil a race between technological innovation and consumption sobriety to reach planetary sustainability, in which global inequality acts as a boundary constraint. Given past technological progress, and current levels of global inequality, it is unlikely that sustained reductions in average consumption can be avoided if we are to respect ecological constraints.
papers.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
papers.title: The Race Between Technology and Sobriety: Distributional Pathways to Planetary Sustainability

papers.abstract: In many countries, both charitable and political donations benefit from generous – and often similar – tax incentives. While a large literature has studied the tax-price elasticity of charitable giving, little is known on political donations. Using a large-scale survey experiment (N = 12, 600), we investigate the relative efficiency of different tax schemes, and document that repealing the existing non refundable income-tax credit decreases charitable donations but not political donations, pointing toward more fiscal incentives behind charitable giving. We next show that, conditional on giving, matching increases both political and charitable giving, but that it decreases the probability to give to charities at the extensive margin. Finally, relying on PCA and on general machine learning, we document important dimensions of heterogeneity, and discuss the policy implications of our findings.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Should Charitable and Political Donations Benefit from Similar Tax Treatments? Evidence from a Survey Experiment

papers.abstract: We develop a comprehensive framework that modifies the Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) to recover the wealth distribution over both families and individuals by carefully parsing wealth within coupled households. All of our estimates agree that wealth has become more equally held within couples over time changes because of changes in pension holdings, but is still imply a substantial gender gap. By ignoring unequal wealth holdings within families, we show that existing estimates understate inequality across individuals. That said, both ours and other leading estimates of wealth concentration all point to increasing concentration at the top of the wealth distribution since 1989.
papers.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
papers.title: Has Experience Made Me Rich? Analysis of the U.S. Gender Wealth Gap

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce novel estimates of wealth inequality, integrating the standard household wealth concept with newly assessed individual human capital. Using microdata and national accounts from numerous countries since 1979, we explore the distribution across age, gender, education, and occupation. Our analysis reveals two key findings: human capital is more evenly distributed than financial capital, and total wealth, the sum of human and financial capital, is significantly more equal than financial wealth alone. This study offers a groundbreaking perspective on global wealth dynamics, emphasizing the critical, yet often overlooked, role of human capital in wealth distribution.
papers.subtheme: Human capital as wealth
papers.title: The Global Distribution of Human and Nonhuman Wealth

papers.abstract:
This paper studies how political instability, spatial informality, and household context interact to shape human capital investment and long-run gender disparities in post-revolution Egypt. In the wake of the 2011 political uprising, Egypt experienced a multi-dimensional shock: political uncertainty, institutional breakdown, and a rapid, unregulated expansion of informal settlements. This period provides a rare opportunity to disentangle how families respond to both political and spatial risks when making high-stakes decisions about adolescent education.

In the first part of the paper, I use nationally representative survey data to examine how exposure to political instability affected university enrollment. I find that current macroeconomic shocks and worsening expectations about the future (proxied by changes in saving behavior) do not appear to significantly affect educational decisions. In contrast, political violence and instability during 2011–2013 had a sizable and gendered impact. Female enrollment dropped sharply, while male enrollment was largely unaffected. The gender gap is concentrated among adolescents who were at a critical schooling juncture during the political crisis—specifically, girls in their final year of high school at the onset of the revolution.

Importantly, this effect is not uniform across socioeconomic groups. The decline in enrollment is most pronounced among girls from wealthier households, suggesting that better-off families may have been more reactive to the instability. This may reflect a combination of perceived physical safety risks, changing marriage market expectations, and shifts in the opportunity cost of schooling.

Preliminary analysis of long-term outcomes suggests that these “unlucky cohorts” of exposed women face worse labor market prospects and no observable compensating gains in the marriage market. This implies a persistent negative impact on women’s economic opportunities, rooted in disrupted human capital formation during adolescence.

In the second part of the paper, currently in progress, I extend the analysis by incorporating the geographic expansion of informal settlements. I am constructing a novel slum expansion dataset by digitizing satellite imagery and urban planning maps to trace informal housing growth between 2011 and 2013. This allows me to identify households exposed to sudden increases in crowding, spatial disadvantage, and degraded service provision — channels likely to amplify the gendered effects of instability. I will exploit natural barriers (e.g., highways, canals, railways) to implement a spatial regression discontinuity design and isolate the effects of slum exposure on education and labor outcomes.

Finally, I will estimate a dynamic structural model of household decision-making under spatial and political risk, where parents choose whether to invest in adolescent education facing both direct costs and uncertain returns. The model incorporates heterogeneity by gender, wealth, and slum exposure, and will be calibrated using reduced-form moments from the data. This structural approach will allow counterfactual simulations of urban and education policies, such as slum upgrading or cash transfer programs targeting adolescent girls.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Political Instability, Urban Informality, and Labor Markets: Evidence from Egypt

papers.abstract: We study the effects of minimum wage (MW) increases on poverty and food hardship in the United States from 1981–2019 using stacked difference-in-differences models and the Supplemental Poverty Measure. A $1 MW increase reduces poverty by 0.3–0.7 percentage points among all working-age adults and 1.2–1.7 percentage points among likely MW workers, while also reducing food insufficiency by 1.5 percentage points for this group. Effects on poverty are partially offset by higher living costs in MW-increasing states. MW increases meaningfully reduce poverty and food hardship for the workers most directly affected but deliver modest improvements for the broader working-age population.
papers.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
papers.title: The Effects of Minimum Wage Increases on Poverty and Food Hardship

papers.abstract: Climate change raises important fairness issues linked to distributional impacts and the unequal resilience of territories, yet within-country inequality and climate change damages are not described in the Shared Socio-economic Pathways baseline database. This study extends the latter data set by integrating the joint distribution of income inequality and economic damages at a fine-grained sub-national level. The results show that global income inequality, which has been falling since the early 2000s, is projected to rise again in all SSP scenarios but the SSP1 Sustainability scenario, partly due large economic damages affecting the poor in a disproportionate manner. Moreover, the Sustainability scenario SSP1 records the strongest rates of economic and welfare growth net of economic damages, despite displaying lower baseline economic growth than the Fossil-fuel scenario SSP5.
papers.subtheme: Climate Justice, Vulnerability and Adaptation
papers.title: The Shared Socio-economic Pathways of global welfare: A sub-national database integrating income inequality and  climate change impacts

papers.abstract:
College education is a key determinant of political attitudes in the United States and
other countries. This paper highlights an important source of variation among college
graduates: studying different academic fields has sizable effects on their political attitudes.
Using surveys of about 300,000 students across 477 U.S. colleges, we find several results.
First, relative to the natural sciences, studying the social sciences and humanities tends
to make students more left-leaning, whereas studying economics and business makes them
more right-leaning. Second, the rightward effects of economics and business come from
shifts on economic policy issues (taxation, healthcare), whereas the leftward effects of the
humanities and social sciences come from shifts on cultural issues (LGBTQ, race). Third,
these effects extend to behavior: the social sciences and humanities increase activism,
while economics and business increase the emphasis on financial success. Fourth, the
effects operate through teaching rather than socialization or earnings expectations. Finally,
the implications are substantial. If all students majored in economics or business, the
college–noncollege ideological gap would shrink by about 30 percent. A uniform-major
scenario, in which everyone studies the same field, would reduce ideological variance and
the gender gap among graduates. Together, the results show that academic fields shape
students’ attitudes and that field specialization contributes to political fragmentation.
papers.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
papers.title: Changing Minds: How Academic Fields Shape Political Attitudes

papers.abstract:
A growing body of research estimates child penalties, the gender gap in the effect of parenthood on earnings, using event studies that normalize treatment effects by counterfactual earnings. I formalize the identification framework underlying this approach and show that it does not identify its target estimand when the parallel trends assumption \emph{in levels} is violated. Insights from human capital theory suggest such violations are likely: higher-ability individuals tend to delay childbirth and have steeper earnings growth, a mechanism that causes conventional estimates to understate child penalties for early-treated parents.
I propose instead to target the effect of parenthood on the gender earnings ratio and show that this parameter is identified without additional assumptions. Using Israeli administrative data, a bias-bounding exercise for the conventional estimator suggests substantial understatement (25–50\%) of child penalties for early-treated parents, while later-treated groups exhibit smaller biases. I also document that estimates of the new parameter are roughly 30\% smaller in absolute value than the conventional estimates for later-treated parents.
papers.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
papers.title: Identification of Child Penalties

papers.abstract:
We estimate the parameters of a macroeconomic model of the dynamics of the distribution of
wealth - as driven by stochastic earnings, differential savings, and capital income risk. We do not
impose any assumption on the stationarity of the process, centering in fact on the transitional
dynamics of the wealth distribution in the U.S. in the period we have SCF data for - from 1962-
63 to 2022. We show that the model, at the estimated parameter values, fits well the dynamics
of the wealth distribution in the U.S., accurately producing the dramatic increase in inequality
observed in this period, which is the focus of most policy debates, e.g., about wealth taxation.
We show how tax reforms - and how agents anticipate them - affect wealth accumulation. We
identify (conditions on) future taxation processes which induce the dynamics to be stationary;
that is, which lead wealth inequality to settle. Furthermore, we study the dynamics of the racial
wealth gap and the relative role of stochastic earnings, differential savings, and capital income
risk in driving it. We identify conditions of tax processes leading the gap to explode vs to be
eliminated. We simulate the effects of reparations - that is, the transfer of a given amount of
wealth to blacks - to assess conditions under which they would eliminate the racial wealth gap.
papers.subtheme: Savings, Capital Accumulation and Wealth Mobility
papers.title: Non-Stationary Wealth Dynamics and Taxation in the U.S. With an Application to the Racial Gap

papers.abstract: This study examines the extent of education-occupation mismatch (EOM) in India and its implications for wage outcomes, using data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2024. The findings indicate that EOM is widespread, with both undereducation and overeducation contributing substantially to the overall mismatch. Workers in either category experience notable wage penalties relative to those whose educational qualifications are appropriately aligned with their jobs. Interestingly, the wage penalty associated with overeducation is less severe for women, suggesting that additional years of schooling continue to improve their positions in the labor market, even when they are not perfectly matched to their jobs. These findings highlight a structural imbalance between the increasing levels of educational attainment and the availability of suitable job opportunities in India, raising important concerns about the efficient use of human capital in the workforce. Moreover, the wage losses resulting from mismatch are most pronounced among lower and middle segments of the wage distribution, where both undereducated and overeducated workers face significant earnings compression. At higher wage levels, these penalties diminish, especially for the undereducated, though overeducated workers continue to experience persistent disadvantages, highlighting the segmented nature of the labor market.
papers.subtheme: Gender Wage Gaps and Labor Income Inequality
papers.title: Does Educational Mismatch Penalize Women Less? Evidence from India’s Labour Market

papers.abstract: This study examines the impact of funding from the Program to Support and Promote Entrepreneurial Initiatives (PAVIE) on the economic performance of beneficiaries in Senegal, as measured by job creation and income growth. Using the Generalized Propensity Score (GPS), it analyzes the marginal and nonlinear effects of the amount of funding, going beyond traditional binary approaches. The results reveal an inequitable allocation of resources: despite their high participation rate (62.83%), women receive on average less than half the amount granted to men, with men, the most educated entrepreneurs, and those active in the manufacturing or service sectors benefiting most. The analysis of dose-response functions highlights critical thresholds of effectiveness. For job creation, the effect is positive from the earliest levels of financing, but accelerates significantly above 1.2 to 1.5 million CFA francs, reflecting increasing marginal returns. For income, a clearly positive effect only emerges above 1,824,000 CFA francs. The gender-differentiated analysis shows that women entrepreneurs, although systematically underfunded, are more sensitive, with an effectiveness threshold for income of only 264,000 CFA francs. In contrast, among men, job creation only becomes significant above 2,268,000 CFA francs. The sectoral analysis shows that in commerce, the effects on employment are immediate, while in services and manufacturing, a threshold of 534,000 CFA francs is required to generate a significant impact on employment. These results call for an overhaul of allocation mechanisms in favor of strategic targeting differentiated by gender and sector, combining amounts calibrated to impact thresholds and enhanced technical support, in order to transform formal inclusion into substantial economic equity.
papers.subtheme: Voting, Participation and Electoral Cleavages
papers.title: Impact of financial support for entrepreneurship on economic performance  in Senegal: The case of PAVIE

papers.abstract:
This paper develops a conceptual framework for assessing long-run global justice pathways in a world of roughly ten billion people living within planetary boundaries. Building on the empirical agenda of the World Inequality Database and the Global Justice Project, I interpret global distributions of income, wealth and environmental use as implicit insurance contracts that allocate exposure to macroeconomic, climate and political risks across countries, social groups and generations. The framework combines a risk-sharing perspective with five minimal justice constraints: (1) achievement of a global social minimum by mid-century; (2) convergence in average incomes between countries by 2100; (3) compression of within-country inequality below specified thresholds; (4) respect for climate and broader planetary boundaries; and (5) political and epistemic arrangements that prevent those who lose in the short run from being systematically excluded from shaping long-run pathways.

Within this structure, I classify distributional pathways to 2100 into regimes such as convergent sustainability, unequal decarbonisation, carbonified stagnation, and green oligarchy, and I map these regimes to a simple policy architecture involving a global justice fund, progressive wealth and carbon taxation, reforms of international monetary and financial arrangements and governance of emerging technologies. The framework is designed as a normative “map” for the design and interpretation of Global Justice Report scenarios, helping to make explicit the ethical content of long-run inequality and climate trajectories and to bridge empirical measurement with debates over feasible and desirable global justice futures.
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Global Justice Pathways for Ten Billion: Inequality, Risk Sharing and Planetary Boundaries to 2100

papers.abstract:
Tax amnesty programs have become a recurring feature of Brazil’s fiscal
policy, often justified as necessary responses to economic crises, but
frequently implemented regardless of macroeconomic conditions. Despite
their budgetary impact, little is known about the political mechanisms
underlying the repeated granting of such tax benefits. This study
investigates whether corporate electoral donations are associated with
subsequent participation in tax amnesty programs, and whether these
donations are strategically timed during critical policy windows—
specifically, the period between the issuance of executive decrees
(Medidas Provisórias) and their conversion into law. Using a novel panel
dataset combining over 130,000 Brazilian firms’ campaign donation
records (2002–2014) with oﬃcial data on Refis participation, we test for
diﬀerences in donation patterns by amnesty status and timing. Results
show that firms participating in Refis donate substantially more than
others, and that donation amounts peak for repeat participants during
critical policy windows. These findings suggest that business interest
groups may strategically deploy campaign contributions to influence the
allocation and design of tax benefits. However, as the analysis relies on
observational data with limited transparency on informal channels of
influence, the results should be interpreted as robust associations rather
than causal eﬀects. The study highlights the need for greater transparency
in both tax expenditure and political finance in emerging markets.
papers.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
papers.title: Quid pro quo? Electoral Donations and Tax Amnesty Programs in Brazil

papers.abstract:
We study whether gender-focused informational campaigns can generate backlash among those excluded from participation. In a randomized evaluation of school-based menstrual awareness sessions in 52 Nepalese schools, we compare the effects of girls-only sessions—common in practice—to mixed-gender sessions and a control group. Excluding boys produces a sizeable backlash: boys become less willing to support girls in confronting menstrual stigma and report less progressive views, while girls' attitudes and behavior remain unchanged. Including boys fully eliminates these negative effects.

Mechanism evidence shows that exclusion shifts boys' beliefs and emotions in ways consistent with reduced empathy and reinforced gender boundaries: they expect less prosocial behavior from peers, view menstruation as ``a women’s problem,'' and react more negatively to menstruation-related situations at school. These results demonstrate that even purely informational interventions can backfire when participation is unequal, highlighting inclusion as a key design feature for awareness-based norm change.
papers.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
papers.title: Why Awareness Needs Inclusion: Evidence from a Menstrual Health Campaigns in Nepal

papers.abstract:
Research on the long-run evolution of inequality heavily relies on reconstructions of top shares, abstracting from what happens to the remainder 90% of the population. Moreover, the dimensions of social stratification that lie behind inequality figures are usually not considered. Relying on grouped data from the Netherlands between 1950 and 1976, this paper studies inequality and social stratification for the total population by creating multivariate synthetic microdata, covering the distribution of income as well as additional socio-demographic information. The paper seeks to answer the question whether the Trente Glorieuses were truly glorious for everyone. To the best of my knowledge, it is the first paper that studies income inequality during this period in such detail. 

(The paper is still work in progress, but a full draft is expected by the start of the conference.)
papers.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
papers.title: Glorious for whom? Income inequality in the Netherlands during les Trente Glorieuses

sessions.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design

talks.abstract:
Across developed nations, economic and political inequalities have crossed the threshold. In their historical trajectory, severity, and resistance to change, twenty-first century inequalities suggest more than an unfortunate confluence of circumstances in markets or geopolitics, more than an ill-fated policy consensus or coalition of political movements, and more, even, than a pernicious ideological or technological paradigm. Involving but transcending such factors, the inequality crisis engulfing the developed world suggests the emergence of oligarchy. 

This article offers a new procedural account of democracy that tracks and conceptualises the emergence of oligarchy. This new procedural account specifies developed nations' primary and secondary means of political production, which oligarchy captures through private financial control. The means of political production function as mechanisms for participation, representation, leadership, accountability and moderation of state power, but never in a neutral sense. Whether those mechanisms are equal or unequal, democratic or oligarchic, depends on a great body of fundamental law, the law that constitutes governments, governs law and policy making, and determines the relationship between private financial power and political power.

Part I analyzes the minimal procedural definition of democracy that spread around the world at the end of the twentieth century. Part II examines the extreme inequalities, democratic backsliding and unmitigated climate change produced in conjunction with this limited form of democracy. Part III analyzes a neglected body of evidence that exposes what the components and mechanisms of oligarchy that emerged within the limited procedural definition of democracy. Part IV arranges these components and mechanisms in a systematic fashion to provide revised procedural accounts of democracy and oligarchy.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: The Fundamental Law of Oligarchy: on the Transnational Constitutional Foundations of the Inequality Crisis

talks.abstract: This study uses Costa Rica to examine how income shocks and inequality affect declining voter turnout and the rise of multi-party systems. Since 1998, Costa Rica has experienced a significant decrease in electoral participation, providing a unique perspective to investigate socio-economic factors influencing voter behaviour. By combining electoral registries with social security employer-employee records at the individual level, this research delivers novel insights from a developing democracy with a robust electoral tradition. The findings indicate a positive relationship between income and voter turnout, significantly moderated by inequality. High inequality increases electoral mobilisation among voters at income extremes, while lower inequality enhances participation among middle-income groups. Individuals experiencing downward income mobility exhibit higher electoral engagement, suggesting economic hardship motivates voter turnout in the short term. These conclusions are validated through three identification strategies: random assignment of voters to polling stations within polling centres, income loss from unexpected mass layoffs, and income variations linked to changes in international agricultural prices. Income shocks have also notably reshaped electoral dynamics, especially affecting the historical PLN party, which shifted its support from middle-income voters to the poorest and wealthiest segments.
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Income Shocks, Economic Inequality, and Political Realignment: Voter Turnout and the Shift to a Multi-Party System in Costa Rica

talks.abstract: Inequality in the Global North has skyrocketed over the past few decades, and yet voters have not demanded redistribution at the ballot box. This curious phenomenon has recently revitalised the study of political cleavages and political inequality. Why are redistributive parties not electorally successful and why are poor voters not supporting them en masse? In this paper, I argue that the 2010s saw the emergence of a new type of redistributive party, that was both electorally successful and supported by working class voters. I call these parties anti-austerity parties, because they emerged in European countries that implemented severe austerity after the Global Financial Crisis. I assemble a dataset that includes the history of political cleavages in the so-called European periphery (Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Ireland, Portugal, Spain). To that end, I also include an original discussion of the history of political cleavages in Greece (1981-2023) and Cyprus (2001-2021), adding both countries to the World Political Cleavages and Inequality Database (WPID). This allows me to analyse the distinct demand-side characteristics that anti-austerity parties display. My main finding is that unlike other left-wing parties, anti-austerity parties continue to enjoy strong working-class support.
talks.subtheme: Voting, Participation and Electoral Cleavages
talks.title: The Anti-Austerity Party: A Neglected Party of the Working Class

talks.abstract: Western democracies seem to be approaching the tipping point of a long and profound transformation in the structures of their political conflict. This paper studies the Portuguese exception, a unique case where traditional left-right divides remain stable relative to other Western countries. Exploring newly assembled granular local-level data, I uncover a remarkable persistence of income, ownership, education, and professional political cleavages, even after the recent emergence of the nationalist right. Contrary to other countries, traditional left-wing parties continue to find strong support from the least educated and lower income working-class communities, while the traditional right attracts more educated and higher income voters. I argue that the Portuguese left's success in demonstrating effective predistributive education and labor policies has preserved its historic working-class voter base, while the traditional right has retained the support from upper middle-class voters with `meritocratic' preferences. The nationalist right was exceptionally successful in the richest but relatively less educated communities. Its rise could be seen as a backlash from historically privileged groups who have seen the catching-up of an increasingly educated upper middle class, and an increasingly well-off working-class, erode their previously unchallenged social status. Overall, these findings indicate that political parties' ability to carry out policies and reforms that effectively address long-term inequality can be a key factor in maintaining resilient voter bases.
talks.subtheme: Political Inequalities - General
talks.title: The Western Exception: Declining Inequality and Persistent Political Cleavages in Portugal

sessions.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity

talks.abstract: Does capital or labor income drive overall relative income mobility? This article examines the dynamics of capital and labor intra-generational income mobility, utilizing individual-level income registers from Norway covering almost 300,000 individuals observed over 26 years. It introduces a novel methodological framework to decompose total income mobility into the contributions of its components across the life cycle. We present three key findings on the subject. First, different capital and labor income mobility measures along the respective uni-dimensional distributions do not convey clear income-factor mobility orderings. Second, upward total income mobility is mainly driven by upward labor income mobility and by the joint upward mobility of capital and labor. Third, downward total income mobility is mainly driven by downward capital income mobility and by the joint downward mobility of capital and labor.  These results are robust to considering only high upward or downward jumps and are discussed in light of recent theoretical and empirical findings on the dynamics of compositional inequality and homoploutia in capital and labor, both within countries and globally.
talks.subtheme: Income Mobility Over the Life Cycle
talks.title: Capital and Labor Income Mobility

talks.abstract: We examine how intergenerational educational mobility has evolved in South Africa - one of the most unequal countries in the world, where inequality is historically rooted in a single key inherited circumstance: race. Using nationally representative panel data, we estimate both absolute and relative mobility trends across birth cohorts spanning five decades covering both the Apartheid and post-Apartheid periods, and formally decompose mobility into within- and between-race components. We show that mobility has risen dramatically, with South Africa now ranking among the most mobile countries in the world with respect to educational attainment. These gains are heterogeneous. Mothers exert stronger influence than fathers; daughters, who began with lower mobility, have converged to sons; and mobility has improved most for African Black and Coloured adults. Most importantly, we show that the structure of persistence has shifted fundamentally from being historically overwhelmingly explained by between-race differences to now being determined by within‐race variation. These findings indicate that race no longer primarily determines intergenerational mobility, reflecting real progress in dismantling the legacy of Apartheid in the country, but should not be interpreted as evidence that broader economic inequality has eased.
talks.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
talks.title: Progress and Persistence: Race and Intergenerational Educational Mobility in South Africa

talks.abstract:
The effects of regional mobility during childhood on educational attainment and its transmission across generations remain underexplored in Europe. Using micro-level data on three linked generations from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), we track moves across European regions linked to historical GDP per capita at the regional level. For the parents’ generation (G2), born between 1920–1950, moving to a better region before age 18 is associated with gains of up to 0.85 years of schooling. Conversely, for the children’s generation (G3), born between 1960–1980, it is associated with a reduction of roughly 0.6 years of education, except when parents have tertiary education, in which case moving becomes beneficial. To achieve causality, we also adopt a sibling comparison strategy exploiting variation
in the age of move and length of exposure which nets out all unobserved parental
characteristics. We find that an additional year in a better region raises educational
attainment by about 0.03 years. Overall we find evidence of a generational reversal
indicating growing stratification by family background.
talks.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
talks.title: Born Here, Raised There: Regional Mobility And Intergenerational Transmission of Education in Europe

talks.abstract: Widely regarded as a barometer for equality of opportunity, intergenerational mobility has attracted renewed attention amid concerns that it has declined in the wake of rising economic inequality since the 1970s. Although earlier research documents stability, or even modest increases, in mobility among cohorts who entered the labor market before this period, evidence for more recent cohorts is limited and inconsistent. In this study, we analyze contemporary trends in class mobility using a new approach based on the "synthetic dynasties" represented in Markov chains. This approach yields several novel measures of movement and memory, which respectively capture how class positions differ from one generation to the next and how the influence of class origins dissipates across generations. Applying these methods to data from the U.S., we find that overall levels of movement and memory have remained largely stable across cohorts born between 1945 and 1990. This stability, however, masks offsetting class-specific trends. Among those from the upper and lower classes, movement has declined and memory has increased. In contrast, among the middle classes, movement has risen and memory has weakened.
talks.subtheme: Class mobility (U.S.)
talks.title: Class Mobility in the Era of Rising Inequality: A Synthetic Dynasty Analysis

sessions.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects

talks.abstract:
Demographic ageing in Europe is expected to increase age-related public expenditures while placing pressure on future tax bases, raising concerns about the long-term sustainability of public finances. At the same time, the ageing of large wealth-holding cohorts will substantially increase the volume of intergenerational wealth transfers. Since 50–60 percent of wealth in Europe is inherited rather than self-accumulated, the design of inheritance taxation is central to debates on wealth concentration, intergenerational equity, and fiscal sustainability.

This paper applies the Inheritance Tax Simulation Model (INTAXMOD) to 13 EU Member States, combining HFCS microdata with a top-tail Pareto correction using rich-list information and harmonized demographic projections. It presents the first cross-national microsimulation of a harmonized inheritance tax framework in the EU. Three policy scenarios are analyzed: a French-style progressive schedule, a main-residence exemption scheme, and a top-1% inheritance tax. The results show that inheritances are highly concentrated, with roughly two thirds accruing to the top decile, and that all scenarios can generate substantial revenue—around 0.5% of GDP—despite high exemption thresholds. Projected inheritance volumes are expected to double by 2050, underscoring the growing relevance of inheritance taxation for addressing wealth inequality and ensuring fiscal sustainability.
talks.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
talks.title: The Distribution and Taxation of Inheritances: Microsimulation Evidence for a Common European Inheritance Tax

talks.abstract:
This paper introduces a novel global database on estate, inheritance, and gift (EIG) taxation,
which covers more than 160 countries — some with data going back to the 18th century — and
represents over 90% of the world’s population and GDP. Using this comprehensive and harmonised dataset, we document long-term global trends in EIG taxation, which are marked by
declining numbers of countries levying such taxes, reductions in top marginal rates, and diminished progressivity since the 1980s. However, substantial cross-country heterogeneity persists in tax design, rates, and exemption thresholds. Leveraging both global and U.S. state-level data, we estimate the elasticity of EIG tax revenues with respect to top marginal rates, finding that a one percentage point increase in the top rate raises revenues by approximately 7%, with larger effects in recent decades.We also show that the erosion of EIG taxes is associated with long-term increases in wealth concentration: five years after a one percentage point decrease in the top rate, the Gini coefficient increases by 0.14, on average. Our conclusions offer new insights into the pivotal role of EIG tax policies in shaping fiscal resources and wealth distribution.
talks.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
talks.title: Inheritance Tax Around the Globe Over Two Centuries: Revenue and Distributional Implications

talks.abstract: Wealth inequality is increasing around the world, sparking political and academic debate about whether and how to address it; hence, a wealth tax is back in the discussion. Evidence about the distribution of wealth in Latin America is relatively scarce but is growing, pointing at an extreme concentration of wealth. Could a wealth tax help reduce this inequality? How much revenue could it actually raise? We combine wealth surveys, lists of billionaires, and net wealth macro-aggregates to simulate the distributional effects of different designs for a wealth tax in Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Uruguay. We also account for administrative costs and behavioural responses, based on the literature, to assess the tax's capacity to raise revenue and illustrate some of the trade-offs to be considered. The estimates of the distributional effects of such taxation are modest in the short run, but a simple dynamic exercise shows that the cumulative effect is substantial. In addition, our benchmark revenue estimate, which takes into account behavioural responses, indicates that a 1% tax on the top 1% of the wealthiest households would raise on average 0.9% of the GDP in revenue. Different designs of this tax (both in terms of rates and tax base) and assumptions regarding behavioural responses change the projected revenue, but the orders of magnitude involved suggest that wealth taxes could indeed help raise much-needed revenue in the region.
talks.subtheme: Wealth Taxation and Capital Income Tax Design
talks.title: Taxing the Rich in Latin America: Effects of a Wealth Tax on Revenue and Distribution

talks.abstract: Transaction taxes on housing are widely used but often viewed as inefficient and poorly targeted. We study the United Kingdom's 2020-21 Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) holiday, which unexpectedly raised the tax-free threshold on residential purchases from £125,000 to £500,000 and temporarily eliminated tax liability for most transactions. Using universe-level administrative data on property transfers and SDLT receipts, combined with local-authority-level measures of exposure based on pre-reform price distributions, we implement a high-frequency continuous difference-in-differences event-study design. The holiday increased transactions by about 18 percent and raised prices by roughly 1 percent, with around 37 percent of the tax cut capitalized into higher prices. We estimate a fiscal cost of £1.6 billion - about one-quarter of residential SDLT revenue during the relief period - with no persistent stimulus once the policy expired. Distributional effects were markedly regressive: upper-middle-income households (income deciles 7-9) captured net gains of around 10 percent of annual income, while first-time and lower-income buyers benefited only marginally, and the Gini coefficient of transaction values increased slightly. Linking transactions to buyer wealth proxies, we show that SDLT operates as a de facto wealth tax that falls disproportionately on younger, middle-wealth cohorts rather than on the wealthiest households. The episode highlights a central policy trade-off: temporary cuts to transaction taxes can spur short-run market activity, but at the cost of eroding fiscal capacity and exacerbating wealth inequality.
talks.subtheme: Wealth Taxation and Capital Income Tax Design
talks.title: Transaction Taxes and Housing Inequality: Evidence from the UK Stamp Duty Holiday

sessions.subtheme: Preferences for redistribution

talks.abstract: Using an original survey of 12,000 respondents representative of eleven high-income countries (the United States, Japan, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and seven European countries), I examine public support for international redistribution and climate policies, as well as its sensitivity to key policy features such as the size of transfers and country coverage. Although global inequality is not a salient concern, it is perceived as a significant injustice. There is majority acceptance in every country for nearly all global policies tested, including those that would redistribute 5 percent of global income or entail personal costs for respondents. An information treatment shows that support for global policies causally increases among respondents who perceive them as likely; an effect opposite to warm glow. Support for international policies decreases only slightly as country coverage shrinks. Overall, the results reinforce previous findings and suggest that a broad coalition of countries could feasibly advance sustainable development.
talks.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
talks.title: Public Acceptance of International Redistribution in High-Income Countries

talks.abstract: This paper compares the "mental maps'' of redistribution among politicians and citizens across seven parliaments, using original in-person surveys of sitting MPs and nationally representative citizen samples. Fairness beliefs and ideology are the strongest correlates of support for redistribution in both groups, while misperceptions of wealth concentration matter for citizens but much less for politicians. A central finding is that politicians hold markedly more polarized views on redistribution than citizens, including within the same party families. We also find systematic elite-voter gaps: left MPs are more supportive than their voters (notably on inheritance taxation), whereas right/liberal MPs are less supportive than theirs. These patterns point to a representation concern and a bargaining space among elites that is narrower than in the electorate.
talks.subtheme: Preferences for redistribution
talks.title: Preferences for redistribution policies among politicians and citizens

talks.abstract:
Using a combination of individual-level, bioclimatic, ethnographic, and archaeological data, we investigate the ancient origins of cross-country differences in preferences for redistribution. Our hypothesis is that contemporary attitudes toward redistribution originate from ancestral levels of inequality, which are the result of adaptive responses of pre-Neolithic hunter-gatherer societies to seasonal food shortage determined by the seasonality of the wild progenitors of domesticated crops. 
Employing contemporary survey data and an epidemiological approach, we first show that migrants originating from countries with higher ancestral inequality exhibit lower support for redistribution, and we establish that this relationship is driven by the level of crop seasonality in the migrants' origin countries. 
Next, using data from premodern societies, we show that crop seasonality induces food storage practices, which in turn lead to inequality through population growth and social complexity. The positive effect of food storage on inequality is corroborated by data from archaeological sites. 
Finally, using data from preindustrial polities, we uncover that the mechanism linking food storage to redistributive preferences is represented by the positive influence of the former on tolerance for inequality.
talks.subtheme: Preferences for redistribution
talks.title: Ancestral Inequality and Preferences for Redistribution

talks.abstract: Recent G20 and UN discussions have considered an unprecedented globally coordinated annual minimum tax of 2% on the wealth of dollar billionaires. We present results from two original studies of 92,696 respondents across 40 countries, examining public and institutional support for the globally coordinated billionaire tax. The policy is supported by 72% of respondents and opposed by only 9%. It has majority support in every surveyed country and among voters in 167 of 168 represented political parties. Supporters often engage in pro-tax political activities (e.g., donations, petitions), while opponents to a lesser extent engage in anti-tax activities. Fairness is the value most strongly associated with support, while concerns about efficiency or national autonomy are limited. The billionaire tax is more popular than broad domestic redistribution in the West, driven by high support among high-income and right-leaning voters. Respondents in all countries underestimate the extent of global support and overwhelmingly doubt implementation. Correcting misperceptions about support substantially increases the share who believe the tax will be implemented, indicating that respondents see global support as influencing policymakers. At the same time, governments remain divided and often non-committal, leaving the policy’s future uncertain. Whichever direction global policy ultimately takes, our results show clear and widespread support for addressing rising top-end wealth inequality.
talks.subtheme: Perceptions of Fairness and Social Mobility
talks.title: Majority in 40 Countries Support Unprecedented Coordinated Billionaire Tax Discussed by G20

sessions.subtheme: Gender Inequality - General

talks.abstract: Newly matched data on IVF treatments are used to estimate the long run impact of children on labor market earnings, also known as child penalties. We compare the earnings of first-time treated women and men up to 25 years after their first IVF treatment. For women, not  men, we find a large penalty shortly after the birth of the first child, but in the long run, the penalty fades out, vanishes after 10 years, and even turns into a positive but insignificant premium after 15 years. These findings challenge the notion that children are the primary drivers behind the persistent gender gap in earnings.
talks.subtheme: Gender Inequality - General
talks.title: Is There Really a Child Penalty in the  Long Run? New Evidence from IVF Treatments

talks.abstract: Since intra-household resource distribution is unobserved, it is difficult to compare how women and children fare across countries. To address this, we analyze 45 household expenditure surveys from predominantly low- and middle-income countries, i.e. an international sample of around 2.4 million individuals. Using harmonized estimations of intra-household resource sharing, we construct globally comparable measures of gender inequality and child poverty in consumption. Our findings reveal a widespread imbalance: women receive about one-fifth less than men, leading to a 60% higher poverty rate. Children appear to fare even worse, though this is partly explained by differences in needs and sibling economies of scale. Intra-household inequalities are more pronounced in poorer countries and among low-income households within countries. Cross-checks with nutritional proxies tend to validate our results, linking household poverty and intra-household disparities to child undernutrition. Finally, we decompose global individual consumption inequality and find that 13%-32% (across measures) stems from inequality within households.
talks.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
talks.title: Global Evidence on Gender Gaps and Child Poverty in Consumption

talks.abstract: This paper examines how the use of formal childcare services affects parental allocation of paid and unpaid work time in Austria. Using microdata from the Austrian Time Use Survey 2021/22, we analyse a sample of 671 different-sex couple households with children who use some form of formal childcare. We distinguish between paid work, unpaid housework, and unpaid carework, and estimate the effects of increasing children’s hours spent in formal childcare on (1) parents’ combined working hours, (2) mothers’ and fathers’ individual work time, and (3) gender time gaps within households. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression models are employed to estimate the associations, controlling for relevant socio-demographic characteristics. The results show that increased use of formal childcare is associated with a significant increase in couples’ combined working hours on the labour market and an even bigger and significant reduction in unpaid working time, particularly in childcare duties, which results in an overall reduction in total working hours for parents. The results on parents’ individual work time patterns, however, reveal that these shifts are primarily driven by mothers, who reduce their unpaid care and housework hours while increasing their participation in the labour market. Fathers’ time allocation, in contrast, remains largely unaffected: their paid working hours show no significant change, and their unpaid work decreases only marginally. These findings demonstrate that the expansion of formal childcare services has substantial potential to alleviate mothers’ double burden of balancing paid and unpaid work, and to narrow gender time gaps within households. However, the persistence of traditional gender norms in Austria limits the extent of this progress. The observed convergence in parental working hours arises predominantly through mothers’ adaptation, rather than a corresponding increase in fathers’ engagement in unpaid work. From a policy perspective, the results imply that the provision of high-quality, affordable, and full-day childcare is a critical lever for promoting gender equality in both the labour market and the household and complementary social and family policies, such as non-transferable parental leave quotas for fathers, flexible working arrangements, and initiatives promoting men’s participation in carework are essential to foster more equitable work-family dynamics.
talks.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
talks.title: Closing the gender time gap: how formal childcare affects parental work and care dynamics

talks.abstract: This paper examines the long-run effects of a large-scale income shock on gender gaps in labor and education, leveraging agriculture productivity gains generated by the construction of India’s national irrigation canal network. Using a regression discontinuity design based on village elevation relative to canals, we identify the causal impact of canal access on labor force participation and educational attainment more than 30 years after construction. We find that canals raised agricultural productivity and household consumption but widened gender gaps: female labor force participation fell by 5\%, driven by women’s exit from paid agricultural work into unpaid domestic labor, while male participation declined only slightly, with some reallocation into services and education. Although education improved for both genders, men’s gains were nearly twice as large, further increasing the education gap. These effects are most pronounced among landowning households, who captured the largest income gains. To understand the role of cultural institutions in shaping these outcomes, we constructed a novel dataset linking over 140 million individuals to their caste group’s traditional gender practices.  Our findings suggest that localized development can generate persistent, unequal gains—highlighting a potential tension between income growth and gender equality.
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Income shocks and gender gaps: long-run evidence from India

sessions.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects

talks.abstract:
Although economists widely advocate carbon pricing as an effective
solution to reduce carbon emissions, this mechanism has had so far limited
effects. This paper proposes a new type of tax to help finance (and accelerate)
the green transition. The A Carbon Wealth Tax (CWT) is proposed
to be levied on carbon-intensive (brown) wealth rather than primarily on
