carbon-intensive goods. We consider tax implementation issues such as tax
base, incidence, and efficiency. Moreover, we analyze the impacts of such
a tax scheme by setting up a model of asset pricing and dynamic portfolio
decisions. Green and carbon-intensive returns used in the model are
calibrated with low-frequency returns on stock prices between 2010 and
2021. We find that such a tax and subsidy scheme is a feasible and effective
instrument in speeding up the transition to a greener economy, particularly
in protracted periods of economic contraction. Our approach also brings a
new perspective to the wealth inequality discussions.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: A Carbon Wealth Tax: Modelling, Empirics, and Policy

talks.abstract: Evidence increasingly highlights large disparities in emissions both between and within countries. However, detailed individual-level data on emission-intensive activities remain scarce. In this paper, we analyze the asset and sectoral composition of the wealth of the top 501 billionaires and construct a dataset linking assets to emissions. Our estimates reveal extreme concentration of wealth and emissions even within this small sample, with publicly traded equity in Basic Materials, Industrials, and Utilities playing a disproportionate role as sources of emissions. We propose a carbon wealth tax that achieves a triple objective: effectively taxing billionaires to curb inequality, targeting the most polluting activities, and raising substantial resources to finance a sustainable and equitable transition.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: Billionaires’ emissions and climate finance: the case for a carbon wealth tax

talks.abstract: This paper studies the distributional impacts of carbon pricing policies using a multi-sector general equilibrium (GE) model with input-output linkages, heterogeneous agents, and segmented labor markets. Households differ in their consumption patterns, labor types, and ownership of equity and capital. Pricing the carbon content of products affects households’ real income through an expenditure channel, according to the emissions intensity of their consumption baskets, and an earnings channel, as GE responses shift the relative demand for labor types and returns on profits and rents. Calibrating the model with matched microdata for the Brazilian economy, we find regressive effects stemming from both channels. Ignoring the production networks and the gross complementarity between fuels, inputs, and factors leads to a substantial underestimation of both aggregate and distributional effects. The incidence of the policy depends on how the revenue is recycled: expanding targeted social transfers fully offsets the regressive impact, whereas using the revenue to reduce preexisting consumption taxes improves efficiency but does not eliminate regressivity.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: The Network Origins of Carbon Pricing Regressivity

talks.abstract: Climate policies may impact inequalities through their effects on structural change via the source of income channel, and on household expenditures via the use of income channel. We compare the impact of carbon pricing on within-country inequalities when revenues are recycled through lump-sum transfers or labor tax cuts. We account for the impact of the labor share on inequalities, and compare results across regions with contrasted levels of economic development, using four macroeconmic models. We find that the progressivity of policies depends on the volume of tax revenues, and decreases as the carbon tax base depletes. We show that lump-sum transfers are progressive in all countries, while labor tax cuts are sometimes regressive in high-income countries and progressive in low-income countries. Overall, our results show that strong climate policy combined with carbon tax recycling over the coming decades is compatible with reducing inequality and increasing consumption among the poorest households in most regions, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Accounting for the impact of the source of income on inequalities reduces the performance gap between recycling schemes: it mitigates the regressivity of labor tax cuts, while reducing the progressivity of lump-sum transfers. These results highlight the central role of labor income in shaping the distributional consequences of climate policy beyond consumption-side price effects. They also suggest that sustaining the labor share in the economy can strengthen the progressivity of climate policies.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: The equity and efficiency of carbon taxation: a multi-model, multi-country analysis

sessions.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design

talks.abstract:
In India, elections decide both political power and access to economic resources. Agricultural credit, vital for rural livelihoods, is particularly vulnerable to partisan influence. This study investigates whether political alignment with the ruling coalition systematically affects the allocation of agricultural credit and uncovers the mechanisms through which alignment shapes credit delivery. In doing so, it connects the literature on distributive politics, agricultural institutions, and causal inference using close elections.
The study employs a fuzzy regression discontinuity design (RDD), exploiting quasi-random variation from closely contested state assembly elections in India from 2010 and 2024. Electoral data from the Election Commission of India are merged with district-level agricultural credit data from the Reserve Bank of India. Political alignment is defined as the share of constituencies in a district represented by members of the ruling coalition. In this two-stage least squares (2SLS) framework, the instrumental variable is the fraction of constituencies narrowly won (≤2% margin) by the ruling coalition, following established close-election approaches. Robustness checks, including alternative bandwidths, election-year fixed effects, and covariate continuity tests, confirm the validity of the design.
The analysis shows that political alignment exerts no significant impact on aggregate credit flows across all banks. However, disaggregated results highlight important institutional variation. Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) exhibit statistically significant increase of 6.02 percent in direct agricultural credit to aligned districts. Given their hybrid governance structure (jointly owned by the Centre, the State, and sponsoring banks) and deep rural penetration, RRBs emerge as the primary conduit of politically motivated credit allocation. Private and Small Finance Banks display positive but less robust responses, suggesting indirect sensitivity to political cycles through integration with public schemes. The effects are concentrated in direct agricultural lending (e.g., crop loans, input financing), which is electorally salient and immediately visible to rural voters, rather than in indirect credit for long-term investments.
This study contributes to political economy debates by showing that partisan alignment influences not only intergovernmental transfers, but also sector-specific credit delivery. It highlights the institutional channels, particularly RRBs, through which distributive politics operate in rural economies and demonstrates the utility of fuzzy RDD and electoral discontinuities for causal inference in complex political-financial contexts. The findings underscore that, while aggregate agricultural credit flows remain stable, political alignment systematically shapes their distribution through local institutions. This raises concerns about allocative efficiency, moral hazard, and regional inequality in rural credit markets, offering new insights into the intersection of politics, finance, and rural development.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Political Influence on Agricultural Credit Allocation: Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design in India

talks.abstract: This paper investigates how global governance structures shape the provision and distribution of global public goods (GPGs). We compile a novel historical database on the finances and governance of multilateral institutions since their inception after World War I, covering annual balance sheets and decision-making rules of the League of Nations, the Bretton Woods institutions (IBRD, IDA, IMF), the United Nations and its key agencies (ILO, WTO, UNESCO, WHO), as well as regional and multilateral development banks. We find that less democratic institutions—those governed by wealth-weighted voting systems such as the World Bank and the IMF—generate two systematic distortions: (a) unequal burden sharing and (b) geopolitical appropriation of resources. First, richer countries with greater voting power contribute less as a share of GDP, contradicting Olson’s (1965) hypothesis of the “exploitation of the great by the small” and revealing instead an “exploitation of the small by the great.” Second, around 90% of IBRD and 60% of IMF disbursements are directed toward G7 military and commercial allies. To address potential endogeneity, we exploit the network structure of partnerships to construct leave-own-out instrumental variables based on third parties military alliances and free trade agreements. Importantly, more democratic institutions such as the United Nations display progressive contribution schemes and show no evidence of GPG appropriation. Finally, we develop a simple theoretical model of GPG provision under weighted-voting systems that rationalizes these empirical patterns. The findings have implications for the design of a more democratic and equitable architecture of global governance.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: The Global Democratic Deficit: Institutional Asymetries and the Provision of Global Public Goods

talks.abstract: Turnout gaps may arise from informal barriers that influence beliefs about voting rights, limiting the effective scope of universal suffrage. This study examines the role of gender norms and social pressure in shaping the gender gap in voter turnout in Switzerland. A triple-difference design exploits three sources of variation: results of the 1971 referendum on female suffrage to measure (male) local norms about whether women should vote, gender differences in turnout, and the staggered introduction of postal voting between 1978 and 2005, which reduced the observability of voting. Before postal voting, women in municipalities with more regressive norms voted significantly less, resulting in a wider gender turnout gap. This gap decreases by approximately 80% when voting becomes less observable, mainly due to higher turnout among women in regressive areas. These findings show that turnout gaps are not only due to preferences, but they are also influenced by social norms, and that reducing observability through institutional reforms can weaken social pressure, enhance representation, and strengthen universal suffrage.
talks.subtheme: Voting, Participation and Electoral Cleavages
talks.title: Gender Norms, Social Pressure, and the Gender Gap in Turnout: Evidence from Swiss Elections

talks.abstract: The welfare state is first and foremost discussed as a redistributive institution; however, as this paper illustrates, its policies also relate to patterns of inequality in political participation. This paper examines how welfare-state institutions are associated with political participation gaps between labour-market insiders and outsiders in Western Europe. Building on the resource model of political participation and policy-feedback theory, it shows that labour market dualization, both as a status-based divide between permanent and temporary contracts and as a risk-based continuum of exposure to unemployment and atypical work, is linked to systematic inequalities in political participation that vary across institutional contexts. The extent of dualization in income differs between countries and reflects distinct path-dependent responses of welfare states to heightened global competition and rising unemployment since the 1990s. Institutional configurations concerning Employment Protection Legislation and Social Investment Policies are not only relevant for labour-market structures, shaping income patterns, collective bargaining systems, and job security, but are also closely associated with the extent of political inequality between insiders and outsiders.  Using data from the European Social Survey (2012–2018), combined with OECD, ILO, and EU-SILC macro-indicators, the study estimates logistic regression models, linear models, and KHB decompositions to assess both conventional participation (voting) and unconventional participation (protest, petitions, boycotts, and organizational engagement). The findings show that outsiders participate less in elections than insiders across both measures of dualization. By contrast, temporary workers do not withdraw from non-electoral forms of civic engagement to the same extent, suggesting a form of silent protest through abstention from the ballot box rather than a wholesale retreat from political life. The welfare-state context appears closely connected to these patterns. Stricter Employment Protection Legislation is associated with larger insider advantages in electoral participation and with lower unconventional engagement among temporary workers. Welfare regimes also coincide with different participation gaps: Nordic welfare states show comparatively limited outsider demobilization, whereas continental and liberal regimes display markedly stronger withdrawal among groups facing higher labour-market risks. Overall, these results point to the political relevance of segmented labour markets and indicate that welfare-state design remains an important factor in sustaining democratic inclusiveness in post-industrial societies.
talks.subtheme: Voting, Participation and Electoral Cleavages
talks.title: The Democratic Welfare State: How does the Welfare State moderate Political Participation Gaps between Labor Market Insiders and Outsiders?

sessions.subtheme: Distributional Decomposition and Counterfactual Methods

talks.abstract:
Introduction. Standard indicators such as the Gini coefficient summarize inequality but hide where inequality is most intense along the distribution. This limitation is especially visible for wealth, where negative asset positions inflate generalized Gini values and complicate cross-national comparisons. This paper introduces isogini measures, based on the isograph representation of medianized income and wealth over logit ranks, to distinguish inequality at the bottom, middle, and top of the distribution. This approach clarifies why countries with similar Ginis may have structurally different distributions.
Methods. Using aggregated data from the World Inequality Database (WID) for the years 2010 and 2020, the analysis considers income (tdiinc) and wealth (thweal) thresholds and their associated inequality indicators. Isoginis (iso10, iso50, iso90) are computed as percentile-specific Gini-equivalent measures derived from medianized distributions. Their behaviour is compared with traditional and generalized Gini coefficients, and their asymptotes are related to inverse Pareto coefficients to describe top-tail concentration.
Results. Income distributions across countries tend to be flatter and close to log-logit (Fisk) forms. Wealth distributions show steeper slopes, stronger deviations from Fisk regularity, and substantial concentration. The method identifies distinct shapes: countries such as the Netherlands display moderate wealth inequality at all levels; the United States and South Africa show extreme concentration both at the bottom and at the top; Sweden appears as a paradox in generalized Gini terms because it combines very low or negative median wealth with only moderately high top-tail concentration. Isogini asymptotes correlate strongly with inverse Pareto coefficients, while iso50 captures the structural weakness of middle-class wealth holdings.
Discussion. The results show that Gini coefficients alone can misrepresent inequality, especially for wealth. Isogini measures clarify whether high Gini values stem from top-end concentration, bottom-end deprivation, or both. This decomposition provides a clearer basis for cross-national comparisons and for interpreting the structural sources of income and wealth inequality.
JEL codes: D31, C16, C46. 
Keywords: inequality, income, wealth, distributions, isograph, logitrank
talks.subtheme: Distributional Decomposition and Counterfactual Methods
talks.title: Understanding distortions in Gini coefficient comparisons:   Isogini measures of income and wealth distributions with WID 2010-2020

talks.abstract: Inference about inequality indices based on conventional asymptotic and bootstrap methods is unreliable. We provide the first systematic application to real-world income data of three methods for improved inference – the semiparametric bootstrap and semiparametric asymptotic approaches proposed by Davidson and Flachaire (Journal of Econometrics, 2007) and Cowell and Flachaire (Journal of Econometrics, 2007), and the ‘Student-t’ approach of Ibragimov et al. (Econometric Reviews, 2025), while also modifying them to deal with survey weights and a large portfolio of inequality indices. The paper shows how these different approaches affect inference about inequality differences in comparison to the conventional asymptotic approach.
talks.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
talks.title: Assessing the statistical significance of inequality differences: the problem of heavy tails

talks.abstract: This paper revisits the longstanding question of how to decompose inequality indices into contributions of factor components, such as labor income and capital income. We start from the axiomatic framework of Shorrocks (1982) and discuss why one of his core axioms, two factor symmetry (Axiom 6), is not suitable for rank-dependent inequality indices such as the Gini coefficient and top income shares. We propose an alternative axiom, monotonicity, to replace two factor symmetry and show that the so-called natural decomposition is the unique source decomposition that satisfies the axioms for any rank-dependent inequality index. Furthermore, we show that the marginal decomposition by Lerman and Yitzhaki (1985) can be uniquely derived from a similar framework where two of the axioms are adjusted.
talks.subtheme: Distributional Decomposition and Counterfactual Methods
talks.title: Source Decomposition of Inequality Revisited

talks.abstract:
Latin America remains one of the most unequal regions in the world, yet most empirical work still focuses on income distributions alone. This paper advances the emerging agenda on multidimensional inequality by applying the Foster and Lokshin (2024) methodology to harmonised household survey data from twelve Latin American countries, using the BADEHOG database compiled by ECLAC. We construct a household-level wellbeing index that combines three core dimensions – income, education and housing – with explicit normative weights and then measure inequality in this composite using a standard Gini index. The Foster–Lokshin framework allows us to decompose multidimensional inequality into a “specific” component, reflecting disparities within each dimension, and an “overlap” component that captures the extent to which disadvantages accumulate on the same households through the joint distribution of achievements. We also introduce a dynamic normalisation strategy that keeps normative weights constant while accommodating structural changes over time in each dimension. Together, these features provide a transparent and policy-relevant summary of multidimensional inequality that is comparable across countries and periods. The paper lays the conceptual, methodological and data foundations for a regional diagnostic of multidimensional inequality in Latin America. 

The results reveal substantial variation across the region and meaningful changes over the past two decades. Multidimensional inequality declines in most cases between 2003 and 2023, although several trajectories are non-linear, with increases during the 2000s followed by reductions in the subsequent decade. The structure of inequality also evolves unevenly: the overlap component varies widely and shifts in ways that indicate either increasing concentration of disadvantages within the same households or a more dispersed pattern of deprivations across dimensions. Under the dynamic normalisation, inequality falls more sharply—reflecting improvements in average education and housing—while the overlap component rises, suggesting a reconfiguration of deprivation patterns rather than simple convergence.

The paper lays the conceptual, methodological, and empirical foundations for a regional diagnostic of multidimensional inequality in Latin America.
talks.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
talks.title: Multidimensional Inequality in Latin America

sessions.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects

talks.abstract:
Pricing greenhouse gas emissions is a crucial tool in environmental policy, following the Pigouvian principle. However, carbon pricing can have significant distributional consequences. To address these concerns, we examine household-level inequality in greenhouse gas emissions across the entire EU. We develop an improved cross-sectional dataset of household carbon footprints in all 27 EU countries by merging data from EXIOBASE, a multi-regional, environmentally extended supply-use dataset, with the European Household Budget Survey.
Our findings reveal substantial inequality in greenhouse gas emissions both between and within countries, with the major variation occurring within countries. Interestingly, net income is a weak predictor of households carbon footprints. A decomposition suggests that carbon emissions at the household level are due to the consumption-income relationship, the structure of the consumption baskets and differences in the emission intensity of different items of the consumption basket. To interpret these patterns and evaluate policy implications, we develop a heterogeneous-agent model with a non-homothetic CES aggregator that is able to replicate the empirical relationship between income, consumption, and emissions. After calibrating it to 26 EU countries, the model provides a framework for analysing the distributional and welfare consequences of carbon pricing.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: Carbon Inequality in the EU

talks.abstract: Achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement will require significant investment to replace the current capital stock with less carbon-intensive alternatives. The success of this transition depends largely on the actions of capital owners who control the production process and can direct investments towards cleaner technologies. However, such investments and the production process often require feasible third-party financing. In this context, we propose a new approach that distributes the responsibility for the environmental impacts of economic sectors between equity capital holders and creditors based on the sectors’ equity and financial debt ratios. The environmental accounting framework proposed prevents double-counting of emissions and can be used with any environmental responsibility allocation criteria (e.g. the production-based and the consumption-based accounting criteria). Additionally, by explicitly integrating the equity and financial debt ratios into an environmentally extended multi-regional input-output model, we can track the equity-financed and debt-financed environmental reasonability for emissions over the global value chains. Finally, we also assess the Spanish sectors’ exposure to climate-related transition risks using equity-financed/debt-financed emission intensities.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: Capital- and finance-based environmental accounting framework

talks.abstract:
This proposal examines the link between global environmental inequality and the structural position of Latin America and the Caribbean within the world economic metabolism, in line with the objectives of the 3rd World Inequality Conference (WIC 2026). The analysis focuses on three dimensions that allow for the study of international environmental asymmetries: per capita CO₂ emissions, per capita domestic material consumption, and per capita material footprint. It draws on international databases and original calculations based on UNEP IRP (2025) and The World Bank (2025). Global per-capita Gini values show limited variation: in material consumption, the Gini declines from 0.50 in 1970 to 0.47 in 2024; in material footprint—calculated using the equation Material footprint = DE + RMEIM − RMEEX—it decreases from 0.53 in 1970 to 0.50 in 2024; in CO₂ emissions it drops from 0.76 in 1970 to 0.59 in 2023. These reductions express moderate convergence without significant structural changes in countries of the Global South that sustain the extraction and supply of resources to the rest of the world.
For Latin America and the Caribbean, these global values do not adequately reflect the region’s historical position or its material contribution to international trade. Regional per-capita material consumption (15.9 tons) is close to the world average (13 tons), with increases associated with GDP growth and population size. CO₂ emissions remain relatively low (2.7 tons compared to 9.9 tons in high-income economies in 2023), concentrated in industrial and urban sectors, which places the region far from the core group of countries responsible for global emissions concentration. A fundamental paradox emerges in the material footprint: countries with moderate domestic consumption contribute intensely to global material pressure through resource-based exports with high material burdens, revealing a structural inequality not captured by global coefficients and associated with ecological conflicts and socio-environmental costs that disproportionately fall on the region (Martínez Alier, 2023).
The analytical separation of emissions, material consumption, and material footprint allows for a more precise definition of the region’s position with respect to potential transitions toward dematerialization. Material consumption reflects the internal productive structure; emissions reflect the energy matrix and level of industrialization; the material footprint reveals the distributive effects of international trade and the externalization of impacts. The relationship between economic growth, material intensity, and export specialization determines whether countries in the region approach relative dematerialization—lower material use per unit of output—or remain far from absolute dematerialization, which would imply a real reduction in resource use. Economic growth may reduce material intensity without reducing total material use, making explicit the need to clarify the assumptions guiding the research.
The general objective is to interpret how global variations in the Gini coefficients of CO₂ emissions, material consumption, and material footprint between 1970 and 2024 help explain the position of Latin America and the Caribbean in transitions toward dematerialization. The specific objectives aim to interpret the trajectories of global Gini values and their translation for the region, to explain how productive structures and primary specialization define the absolute and relative use of materials and energy, and to determine whether the region, its subregions, and representative cases tend toward relative or absolute dematerialization, considering the role played by international trade in this interpretation.
The hypotheses suggest that the moderate reduction in global per-capita environmental Gini coefficients stems mainly from the rise in consumption in middle-income economies, without significant structural changes in countries of the Global South that sustain resource extraction. This pattern improves Latin America’s comparative position without altering its role as a supplier of materials to the world economy. The proposal further argues that the region exhibits weak relative dematerialization—with only small reductions in material intensity—while experiencing an absolute increase in extraction and total material use. Economic growth marked by strong extractive activities prevents advances toward absolute dematerialization and reproduces environmental inequalities both within and between countries.
The methodology consists of building global and regional historical series on material flows, emissions, and intensities based on UNEP IRP (2025) and The World Bank (2025), and interpreting the results within analytical frameworks from ecological economics and social metabolism. The expected contribution of the paper is to offer a rigorous interpretation of how the structural position of Latin America in the world economy conditions its dematerialization trajectories and reproduces environmental inequalities, in line with the thematic lines of the World Inequality Conference 2026 on environmental inequalities and methods for their comparative measurement.
References
Martínez-Alier, J. (2023). Land, water, air and freedom: The making of world movements for environmental justice. Edward Elgar Publishing.
The World Bank (2025). World Bank Open Data.
United Nations Environment Programme, International Resource Panel, Global Material Flows Database (2025). Global Material Flows Database.
talks.subtheme: Energy Transition, Fossil Lock-in and Decarbonization
talks.title: Transitions toward Dematerialization and Environmental Inequalities in Latin America: CO₂ Emissions, Material Consumption and Material Footprint in the Framework of the World Inequality Conference 2026 (1970–2024)

talks.abstract:
Food consumption is a significant contributor to households’ carbon footprints. However, consumer heterogeneity in food-related carbon footprints remains underexplored, primarily due to limited data linking real-world consumption choices to environmental impacts. I address this gap by matching detailed purchase data with environmental impact estimates at the transaction level for a representative sample of 7,540 French households between 2017 and 2019. Using this unique dataset, I provide a comprehensive overview of the distribution of food carbon footprints and employ a structural demand
model to estimate how price and expenditure changes influence food basket composition and carbon emissions. The analysis reveals three key insights. 1) There is heterogeneity in the distribution of food carbon footprints, with 20% of households accounting for 40% of total food emissions. 2) Households with higher carbon footprints are more price-sensitive, particularly regarding high-emission products like red meat. 3) Simulations indicate that a 44.60€/tCO2e food carbon tax would reduce food-related emissions (8.5%), especially among high-emission households. While modest carbon tax levels appear effective at reducing emissions, they may also lead to a trade-off between lowering emissions and preserving diet quality.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: Households' food carbon footprints

sessions.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives

talks.abstract: This paper uses labor force surveys from 160 countries to build a new microdatabase on hours worked covering 97% of the world population in cross section. We also construct time series spanning over 20 years in 86 countries. Hours worked per adult are slightly bell-shaped with GDP per capita but weakly correlated with development overall. Hours worked by the young (aged 15-19) and elderly (aged 60+) decline with development, driven by growing school attendance and public pension coverage. Hours worked among prime-age adults (aged 20-59) are mildly bell-shaped with development for men while they are increasing for women. The fall in male hours in middle-to-higher income countries is driven by reduced hours per worker and is offset by increases in female labor force participation. These two forces have exactly compensated each other in many countries, leading to a remarkable long-run stability of prime-age hours worked. Labor taxes are strongly negatively correlated with prime-age hours worked both in international comparisons and overtime within countries. Controlling for government transfers only partly reduces the link between labor taxes and prime-age hours, ruling out substitution and income effects on labor supply as the only driver. Controlling for working hours regulations and the size of the formal sector eliminates this link, suggesting that regulations also play a large role in reducing intensive hours in higher-income countries.
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Global Working Hours

talks.abstract: We study the labour market impact of the “Veblen effect” by estimating the relation between inequality and average work hours in society, and how the effect varies between the poor and the non-poor households. Using data on actual hours worked by members of a household from India’s Periodic Labour Force Survey, we report three main findings. First, members belonging to absolutely and relatively poor households work for fewer hours than those in non-poor households. After controlling for a rich set of household-level characteristics and regional supply and demand side conditions, we observe that absolutely poor (relatively poor) households work, on average, 49 (25) minutes less per day than non-poor households. Second, we find that a one standard deviation increase in the regional 90/50 percentile ratio of the consumption expenditure distribution is associated with a 1.96 percent increase in the average work hours of non-poor and relatively poor households. However, the impact on the work hours of absolutely poor households is smaller at 0.81 percent. By isolating the impact of the rise in the 90th percentile’s consumption, we further demonstrate the cascading of the Veblen effect on the poor households. These findings are robust to alternate measures of inequality. We also demonstrate the robustness of these results to endogeneity concerns by instrumenting regional inequality with an indicator for conspicuous consumption, in addition to other approaches. Third, we find evidence that poor households are no less likely to be available to work for additional hours than non-poor households.
talks.subtheme: Experimental and Survey Evidence on Inequality Attitudes
talks.title: Poverty, Inequality, and Working Hours: Evidence on Veblen Effects from Labour Markets in India

talks.subtheme: Firm Dynamics, Market Power and Productivity
talks.title: Global Labour Hours in Paid and Unpaid Work: Productivity and Structural Transformation, 1800-2100

talks.abstract: How efficiently do societies convert collective time into the fulfillment of basic needs, and what are the implications for wellbeing and development? Traditional poverty and wellbeing metrics, such as the International Poverty Line and Multidimensional Poverty Index, largely ignore time as a critical resource. This article addresses this gap and proposes the “time conversion factor,” a metric that quantifies how effectively countries transform societal time inputs into outputs that satisfy essential needs. Empirical data from time-use surveys reveal stark cross-country differences in time spent on food provisioning, highlighting structural inequalities that limit discretionary time and economic growth. We demonstrate that time-inefficient provisioning systems trap societies in a cycle of deprivation and delay development. Prioritizing the measurement and improvement of time conversion in provisioning systems is therefore essential to advancing sustainable wellbeing and breaking persistent cycles of inequality.
talks.subtheme: Macroeconomic Drivers: Inflation, Growth and Cycles
talks.title: Time for Development

sessions.session_title: III/LSE Session: Inequality of opportunity around the world
sessions.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research

talks.abstract: We analyze how the country of origin, alongside other uncontrollable factors like parental education and occupation, predicts income in adulthood in Europe. Using this definition of inequality of opportunity and employing advanced data-driven methods, we measure inequality of opportunity in household disposable incomes, treating Europe as a single entity. To ensure representativeness, we gather data from EUROSTAT and three different household surveys to construct a sample that exactly represents the population of Europe, accounting for country-of-birth population shares within countries. We estimate a level of overall inequality in Europe (2019) of 39 Gini points, with inequality predicted by ascriptive characteristics rising to 23 Gini points. The country of origin accounts for 64% of this inequality, emerging as the most significant predictor compared to other factors such as parental occupation (26%) and parental education (9%). Our findings demonstrate that, while European countries generally exhibit substantially lower levels of inequality of opportunity at the national level, accounting for country of origin as a circumstance and analyzing at the continental level reveal that equality of opportunity is still far from being realized. The level of inequality of opportunity observed is comparable to that in China and India and significantly higher than estimates for the United States.

talks.title: Playing the birth lottery in Europe
