talks.abstract:
The super-rich contribute substantial sums to charity, with many publicly pledging
 to donate at least half of their wealth in the coming years. Western governments often
 offer favorable tax treatment for these charitable donations. Despite the considerable
 impact of such philanthropy, our understanding of its broader implications remains
 limited. This paper explores the implications of philanthropy for the politics of
 inequality through two studies conducted in the U.S. It argues that philanthropy
 can reduce individuals’ support for taxing the super-rich by enhancing perceptions
 of their benevolence and contributions to social welfare. The findings from Study 1
 indicate that respondents exposed to higher levels of philanthropy hold more positive
 views of these two aspects of the super-rich than those exposed to lower levels. The
 results from Study 2 replicate the association between levels of philanthropy and
 perceptions of the super-rich and, additionally, find that higher levels of philanthropy
 reduce individuals’ willingness to tax the super-rich. This reduction, however, is
 modest, suggesting that the charitable donations of the super-rich are seen only as
 partial substitutes for the taxes they must pay. Moreover, the results also show that
 supporting lower fiscal duties for the super-rich who make charitable donations does
 not imply reduced support for general public redistribution
talks.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
talks.title: Better Call Bill? Philanthropy and Preferences for  Taxing the Super-rich.

talks.abstract:
This paper draws on the quantitative part of my book project to examine how does social hierarchy has shaped redistributive politics in Independent India. While mainstream theories of welfare are premised on the material interests of social classes, I argue that in societies like India with long histories of ascriptive discrimination, distributive politics in shaped by status inequality. High-status groups are more likely to oppose redistribution to maintain their ascriptive privilege, while low-status groups aim at reducing social hierarchy by prioritizing descriptive representation, which I refer as the politics of dignity. I test this theory by drawing on several sources of original data on major Indian states from 1960 to 2012. This includes data on the caste-identity of all legislators – high-status or upper-caste groups, and various low-status or lower-caste groups, including ex-untouchable castes called Scheduled Castes (SC), indigenous groups called Scheduled Tribes (ST), and intermediate castes called Other Backward Classes (OBCs). For the outcome variable – redistribution or proportion of developmental spending in social sectors, I digitized more than fifty years of public expenditures records from the Reserve Bank of India. I generate a new dataset on caste quotas from the colonial period. And finally, I develop an original measure of status inequality through data on endogamy.

Four main findings emerge. First, I find that states with higher status inequality, which reflects upper-caste dominance, are less likely to be redistributive. Status inequality is, in fact, a stronger predictor of redistribution than income inequality. Second, upper-caste political representation is consistently associated with negative redistributive spending, which aligns with our understanding of the economic elite (Acemoglu and Robinson 2006; Rueschemeyer, Huber, and Stephens 1992; Esping-Andersen 1990). These results hold after accounting for a range of relevant economic, political, and structural factors and remain robust to alternative measurement and estimation strategies. Third, unlike working-class coalitions, lower-caste political representation does not present a clear association with redistribution. I find that elites from politically mobilized groups have instead consistently prioritized representational policies – OBC representation in government is a strong predictor of OBC quotas. Finally, though such measures have traditionally been viewed as patronage or symbolic politics, this research demonstrates that places with higher OBC representation in both the legislature and bureaucracy (i.e., interaction effects) are associated with higher redistributive spending. To examine potential mechanisms, I rely on qualitative fieldwork in the state of Bihar that suggests that a representative bureaucracy can generate conditions for redistributive politics by reducing discrimination in policy design and implementation and weakening elite patronage networks. 

This research advances two agendas of the World Inequality Lab – Political inequalities, and Methodological advances in the measurement of inequalities. 

Political Inequality:

The findings of this study are closely aligned with the research on World Political Cleavages and Inequality Database. The India chapter of the book and related article (Gethin, Martínez-Toledano, and Piketty 2021b; Banerjee, Gethin, and Piketty 2019), in fact, drew on a previous version of this research (my job market paper) (Chakrabarti 2019). Banerjee, Gethin, and Piketty (2019) find strong evidence for political cleavages based on caste and religion in India, but show that these cleavages do not seem to shape redistributive spending. This seem to be in line with global trends wherein sectarian interests and cultural priorities have taken precedence over economic issues in recent years (Gethin, Martínez-Toledano, and Piketty 2021b; Norris and Inglehart 2019). In Western democracies, the rise of green and anti-immigration movements has resulted in a shift in the social base of the social democratic parties towards the educated elite while the right continued to attract the business elite, what the authors refers as the “Brahmin Left versus the Merchant Right” (Gethin, Martínez-Toledano, and Piketty 2021a). Banerjee, Gethin, and Piketty (2019) interpret their findings in India to suggest that the country’s poor record in social development stems from the salience of identity politics. However, they qualify their argument with an important caveat: “the big political fights seem to be about caste and religious identity in its many forms and the caste quotas in educational institutions and government jobs, the one place where the identity and economic dimensions intersect.” (Banerjee, Gethin, and Piketty 2019, 43 emphasis mine). This research speaks to this important gap in the literature. The question of quotas distinguishes India from its Western counterparts. Unlike other aspects of identity, caste quotas are not just symbolic or cultural. As the longest-standing identity-based affirmative action programs in the world (Jensenius 2017), the Indian case offers a unique opportunity to examine how status mediates the complex relationship between the identity of the political elite and the nature of distributional politics. The findings challenge influential works that have been pessimistic about the redistributive potential of caste politics (Jaffrelot 2003; Weiner 2001; Kohli 2012).

Normatively, the findings speak to the limitations of mainstream theories of social justice that is premised on equality of opportunity across social classes. The history of ascriptive discrimination in societies like India presents distinct challenges to social opportunity that mere investment in public goods cannot capture (Sen 1999). An identity-based idea of justice faces the additional burden of dismantling status biases – both psychological and institutional, thus involving concerns of recognition and systemic discrimination in addition to redistribution (Fraser 1995; Mills 2022). Lower-caste mobilization in India draws on a long tradition of anti-caste thinkers, including Phule, Periyar, Ambedkar, and Lohia, that is rooted in a broader notion of social justice that seeks equalization of status across social groups (Omvedt 2008; Teltumbde 2018; Ambedkar 2014; O’Hanlon 2002). It is hence not surprising that in contrast to the conventional left-right paradigm, ideological differences in Indian politics are based on the role of the state in regulating groups-rights and affirmative action (Chhibber and Verma 2018). The single most important finding in Piketty’s (2020, 7) thousand-page global history of inequality is that “inequality is neither economic nor technological; it is ideological and political.” From a policy perspective, it calls for the need to examine the role of discrimination in policy design and implementation. Further, by suggesting that the inclusion of low-status groups in the bureaucracy can influence development outcomes, this research pushes the boundaries of existing debates on affirmative action that have largely revolved around questions of meritocracy and efficiency (Bhavnani and Lee 2021; Deshpande and Weisskopf 2014).

Measurement of Inequalities:

Second, the research speaks to the research agenda on conceptualization and measurement of inequality (Piketty 2000). Most existing research, including the World Inequality Reports, have focused on income/wealth or socioeconomic inequality. This research focused on the undertheorized and understudied concept of status (Ridgeway 2019). This research contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded, contextually relevant, and generalizable measure of status inequality.

The idea of status goes back to Weber’s conceptualization of inequality, which he argued is based on three interrelated but distinct sources: resources, power, and status (Weber 1978). Status broadly refers to the ranking or position in a social hierarchy in terms of prestige, respect, and worth (Ridgeway 2019). The rise in right-wing populism in recent years has reignited interest in status politics (Parker 2021; Berman 2021; Norris and Inglehart 2019). Support for Trump, for example, was driven by status anxiety rather than economic hardship (Mutz 2018). Poor-high-status individuals, like the white-working-class in the United States and Europe (Baccini and Weymouth 2021; Gidron and Hall 2020) and poor-Brahmins in India (Suryanarayan 2019) have been shown to vote against their material interests to preserve their ascriptive privilege. At the same time, mobilizations for the “struggle for recognition” under the banners of nationality, ethnicity, and race have become the paradigmatic form of social movements since the end of the twentieth century (Fraser 1995). Concerns of status are at the heart of ethnic mobilizations across the ideological spectrum, but much like the literature on inequality, research on ethnic politics has also largely focused on economic inequality between groups (Baldwin and Huber 2010; Alesina, Michalopoulos, and Papaioannou 2016; Houle, Kenny, and Park 2019).

This research addresses this gap by drawing on theories of justice to distinguish between different forms of ethnic inequality – i) economic, ii) social, and iii) status. Consistent with the existing literature, I conceptualize economic inequality as disparity in economic outcomes, like income or wealth, while social inequality captures the idea in equality of opportunity, as reflected in disparity in access to public goods across groups (Sen 1999; Roemer 2009). In contrast to unequal access to material resources, status inequality, rooted in the idea of recognition, is manifested through segregationist norms in inter-group relations (Taylor 1994; Horowitz 1985). While difference in income and literacy between castes can be used to measure economic and social inequality respectively, this study develops an original measure of status inequality through data on endogamy. Endogamy captures the idea of segregation, which is the mechanism that has been shown to maintain and reproduce inequality between ethnic groups across different contexts.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Status Inequality and Ideology: How Social Hierarchy shaped Redistribution in India

talks.abstract: Corporate philanthropy has been increasing inWestern democracies in recent decades, a rise often explained by the development of tax policies offering substantial incentives to donate to charities. Yet, corporate philanthropy is also increasingly perceived as a means to influence politics. In this paper, we estimate the tax price elasticity of corporate donations, and investigate how it differs depending on the recipients’ purposes and the donors’ characteristics. To do so, we use an exhaustive administrative panel dataset on firms’ tax returns in France from 2013 to 2022, including the identity of the charities that benefit from the donations, from which we recover their purpose using state-of-the-art NLP methods. Exploiting two reforms that affect the price of donations for firms, we document significant bunching around major regulatory thresholds. We then show that the tax-price elasticityvaries significantly depending on the type of beneficiaries.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Tax Incentives or Political Motivations? Evidence from Corporate Contributions

talks.abstract:
This paper examines causal mechanisms linking corruption awareness to inequal-
ity perceptions in post-socialist Europe. Using pre-registered vignette experiments
across Lithuania, Hungary, and Moldova (n=3,500), I demonstrate that factual cor-
ruption information increases inequality perceptions by approximately 5 percent-
age points yet produces no effect on redistribution preferences. This effect remains
consistent across countries despite substantial variation in institutional quality, EU
membership status, and corruption levels. Drawing on governance theory, system
justification theory, and social identity perspectives, I develop an integrated frame-
work identifying disruption of legitimizing narratives about economic fairness as
the primary mechanism. Effects prove particularly pronounced among right-wing
voters, older citizens, the economically insecure, and incumbent supporters, who
exhibit the largest perceptual shifts when confronted with corruption information.
These findings establish the first experimental evidence of causality between corrup-
tion information and inequality perceptions at the individual level, while revealing
a paradox: corruption information neutralizes partisan differences in inequality
perceptions but fails to generate policy demands.
talks.subtheme: Perceptions of Fairness and Social Mobility
talks.title: Corruption Information and Inequality Perceptions: Causal Evidence from Central and Eastern European Democracies

sessions.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research

talks.abstract:
This paper presents the first systematic analysis of regional wealth inequality in Spain. We
do so by combining administrative fiscal data with household surveys and national
accounts between 2016 and 2022. We document substantial regional disparities in both
average household wealth and its concentration. Madrid stands out as the region with the
highest average wealth and top 1% wealth share. Our findings are relevant in the Spanish
institutional context, where autonomous communities exercise considerable control over
wealth taxation and public expenditure.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: Regional wealth inequality in Spain: Evidence from the Spain wealth Atlas

talks.abstract:
This paper extends our earlier work with the World Inequality Lab on measuring inflation inequality in India. While the previous analysis focused on national patterns, this study turns to the state level to show how inflation is experienced very differently across regions and across income groups within those regions.  This paper is the first attempt to track the inflation rates of the distribution of households based on consumption weights of different fractiles of households from 2012 to 2024 at the state-level. This paper constructs the consumption basket of households in different consumption brackets based on the 68^{th} round of the NSS Household Consumption Expenditure Survey and also provides a comparison with the recent rounds of HCES survey in 2023--24. We compute the consumption expenditure shares  of different fractiles of households, from the poorest to the richest, and compute the inflation faced by them in all major states of India.


The data point to large fluctuations in state-level inflation, driven by varying levels of food dependence, storage capacity, market integration, and exposure to climate shocks. These differences translate into unequal welfare losses for households: in some states, the poorest groups face far sharper price volatility than the rich, affecting their nutrition, savings, and ability to plan for the future. Yet policy continues to rely on a single national inflation rate and a uniform monetary stance, even though inflation dynamics diverge widely across states and within the population strata for any given state.
talks.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
talks.title: Measuring Inflation Inequality in India: A State-level Analysis

talks.abstract: People’s ability to access essential services is key to their labour market and social inclusion. An important dimension of accessibility is physical accessibility, but little cross-country evidence exists on how close people live to the services facilities they need. This paper helps to address this gap, focusing on three types of essential services: Public Employment Services, primary schools and Early Childhood Education and Care. It collects and maps data on the location of these services for a selection of OECD countries and links them with data on population and transport infrastructure. This allows to compute travel times to the nearest service facility and to quantify disparities in accessibility at the regional level. The results highlight substantial inequalities in accessibility of essential services across and within countries. Although large parts of the population can easily reach these services in most countries, some people are relatively underserved. This is particularly the case in non-metropolitan and low-income regions. At the same time, accessibility seems to be associated with the potential demand for these services once accounting for other regional economic and demographic characteristics.
talks.subtheme: Spatial inequality, accessibility
talks.title: Geographic inequalities in accessibility of essential services

talks.abstract:
Income inequality across and within nations is trending in opposite directions: the former is declining, while the latter is increasing. This scissor-like trend of increasing GDP growth divergence within countries is also well documented in regional analyses across the OECD (OECD, 2024). Unlike cross-country comparisons, which can rely on robust purchasing power parity programmes for meaningful real-term assessments, harmonised data on spatial price variation are rarely accessible, constraining the ability to evaluate changes in wealth or disposable income in real terms and to draw fully informed conclusions about within-country disparities.
The lack of comparable subnational price data constrains and may significantly bias regional economic analysis. In the absence of subnational price indices, regional wealth/income indicators are often deflated using national-level indices, thereby not only masking the impact of regional price differences but also potentially inflating disposable income and wealth in many regions. National PPPs for OECD countries are primarily collected in the capital city-region, with some adjustments for the rest of the country done every six years. As a result, assessments of real wealth and living standards are less precise, limiting the effectiveness of policy design, targeting, and monitoring at the regional level.
To address this information gap, the OECD has launched an initiative to develop a harmonised framework for measuring subnational Purchasing Power Parities (sPPPs). The first phase of this initiative focuses on establishing a processing pipeline and an open-source R package, OECDsPPPs, that provides a fully documented framework for the methodological steps required to estimate subnational price indexes harmonised across and within countries.
OECDsPPPs builds on the existing methodological literature and follows the international standards of the International Comparison Programme (ICP) and the Eurostat-OECD PPP Programme. It leverages official data produced by national statistical offices (NSOs), often for consumer price index (CPI) programmes, as well as alternative data sources and regional household expenditure weights. The development of OECDsPPPs has been guided by expert input and extensive stakeholder consultations, including senior officials from national statistical offices in OECD member and accession countries. The platform has been co-developed with stakeholders to support ongoing methodological refinement and accommodate flexible extensions. It features robust data validation tools and options for non-linear estimation methods used in index construction. 
In the current phase of the project, microdata for Czechia, Germany, the Slovak Republic and the United Kingdom will be incorporated, with further European economies planned for inclusion in 2026. The present draft of the paper draws only on preliminary data and analysis for the United Kingdom and underscores the importance of adjusting regional wealth and income indicators for spatial variations in price levels. The emerging evidence suggests that price levels vary more widely for services than for goods, although even goods with relatively low variability display common patterns, most notably the capital city price premium. Price movements differ across categories and generally behave as expected, such as in food and communications, but some notable patterns also appear, including rising spatial variability in relatively homogeneous categories, particularly food. Consistent with cross-country meta analyses, variations in prices across regions, as well as the way these variations change over time, are strongly correlated with gross disposable household income in UK TL2 regions.
talks.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
talks.title: Mapping subnational price differences across countries: Evidence from OECD regions

sessions.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation

talks.abstract:
This paper identifies a novel mechanism in the wealth-health causal relationship: wealth
 improves survival not through traditional health capital investment, but by enabling relocation
 to areas with superior health infrastructure. I leverage lottery and prize winnings as exogenous
 wealth shocks within a unique administrative dataset linking income and wealth tax records
 to population-wide health examinations, healthcare claims, and cause-specific mortality for a
 5% random sample of South Koreans aged 40–49 (2007–2018). Using a stacked difference-in
differences design, I find precisely estimated null effects of wealth on traditional health capital measures: all-cause mortality, non-external mortality, cardiovascular mortality, biomarkers
 (blood pressure, glucose, BMI, cholesterol), medication use, and most health behaviors are un
affected. However, mortality from external causes—accidents, homicides, drug overdoses, and
 natural disasters—declines by 35% within 1–2 years of winning. This reduction is driven by
 residential sorting: winners systematically relocate to cities with better health infrastructure.
 Critically, only substantial amount of windfalls that enable this migration produce these effects;
 smaller windfalls have no impact. These findings suggest that for prime-age adults, the “health
wealth gradient” operates primarily as a “health-location gradient,” with important implications
 for policies aimed at reducing health inequality.
talks.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
talks.title: Wealthier and Healthier? Place-Based Mechanisms in the  Wealth-Health Relationship

talks.abstract:
Views on adult literacy programs are mixed. While there have been a few studies analyzing
maternal literacy and child health outcomes, there is scant literature examining the impact
of adult literacy on child educational outcomes showing null or at best modest impacts on
academic skills of children. In this paper, we explore the impact of such an adult literacy
program named ‘Saakshar Bharat’ implemented in 2009 in selected rural backward districts
in India for adults aged 15 or above, on a host of scholastic indicators such as private school
enrollment, probability of dropping out and reading scores of 5 to 16 year old children using
ASER data in a difference-in-difference framework. Results show that while private school par-
ticipation rises for some, dropout decisions and learning outcomes do not improve in general,
which point out towards a possible quality compromise with increased access in schooling, com-
monly referred to as the ‘quantity-quality tradeoff’ in educational context. There is significant
heterogeneity based on maternal literacy and child age-groups. Mechanisms reveal the role
of ‘aspiration-frustration-dynamic’ playing out in the form of reduced human capital invest-
ment and lesser parental involvement coupled with household labour substitution in these low
income-constrained households due to lack of time and resources.
talks.subtheme: Inequality Perceptions - General
talks.title: ‘Diminishing One Gap, Widening Another’: Unintended Consequences of Adult Literacy on Medium-Term Child Dropouts in India

talks.abstract: This paper examines the effects of exposure to hard-security counterinsurgency operations during school-age years on human capital formation. We exploit the 1989 introduction of the Greyhounds—a specialized commando force created to combat Naxalite insurgents—in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, as a natural experiment. Among all states affected by Naxalite violence, only Andhra Pradesh established such a force during that period. Difference-in-differences estimates suggest that exposure to the policy during school-age years led to increased educational attainment. We provide suggestive evidence that a plausible mechanism underlying these effects is increased household investment in education due to reduced uncertainty stemming from improved security. Our findings highlight the economic returns to peace and stability in conflict-affected regions.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Guns and Gains: Human Capital Effects of Exposure to Counterinsurgency Operations

talks.abstract: While the literature on technology and education is growing in India, specifically after the COVID-19 pandemic, yet there is a lack of evidence to date on understanding the inequalities in access to smartphones and internet and how it determines students learning outcomes. In this paper, using a recent nationwide rural household education survey, we examine socioeconomic inequalities in access to smartphones and internet and how they matter for children’s learning level in reading, math and language skills. We find significant socioeconomic variations in access to smartphones and internet among rural households in India - internet use is higher among rich and educated households than poor and less educated counterparts. We also find some evidence suggesting that access to smartphones and internet in the household produces learning gains in reading, math and language skills for children, with considerable variations across households’ socioeconomic positions. In a context where technology is increasingly integrated in educational transactions, our results have important policy implications for India and other developing countries. The study contributes novel insights to a nascent body of research in India on the impact of technology on student learning outcomes, as well as to a wider literature concerning technology and educational inequalities.
talks.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
talks.title: Does inequalities in access smartphone and internet lead to poor learning outcomes? Evidence from rural India

sessions.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power

talks.abstract: What drives lifetime income inequality? We estimate a continuous-time lifecycle model incorporating human capital accumulation, innate ability, search frictions, job wage premia, and non-wage amenities. Workers make consumption-savings decisions, and their asset position affects job acceptance. We estimate the model on Danish matched employer-employee data for 2008–2023. Counterfactuals show that innate ability is the dominant source of lifetime earnings inequality, accounting for over 90 percent of the variance. Search frictions and amenities matter for welfare rather than earnings: removing frictions reduces lifetime utility inequality by nearly 80 percent while leaving earnings inequality unchanged. Finally, several mechanisms have opposite effects on cross-sectional versus lifetime inequality, showing that the two measures provide different information.
talks.subtheme: Lifetime cycles
talks.title: Drivers of Lifetime Earnings and Wealth: Skills, Frictions and Choices

talks.abstract:
This paper unveils a novel externality of product market regulation in the labour market. It
shows theoretically and empirically that higher barriers to entry in product markets translate into higher employers’ labour market power, measured by the wage markdown—–the ratio between the marginal product of labour and the wage. Using quasi-exogenous variation in investment restrictions across 389 manufacturing product markets in Indonesia, the analysis finds that wage markdowns would have been almost 10% lower without restrictions and workers would have earned a larger fraction of their marginal product. The analysis supports the model’s prediction that lower entry is the main driver of the positive relationship between investment restrictions and wage mark-downs, and that restrictions increase markdowns more in commuting zones where employers have already substantial labour market power. The restrictions do not affect employment, consistently with recent models based on search frictions and wage bargaining, but not with classical monopsony models.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: Product Market Monopolies and Labor Market Monopsonies

talks.abstract: This paper studies the role of changes in workforce composition in monopsony power, a significant driver of income inequality. We develop a monopsony model in which a firm’s wage markdown—the wedge between MRPL and wage—is a weighted average of markdowns for heterogeneous workers. We empirically test the theory using India’s National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA), which generates non-manufacturing jobs in rural villages. Consistent with the model predictions, at manufacturing firms, we find that the program increases average markdowns by crowding out mobile workers and effectively increasing the share of immobile workers with low labor supply elasticity.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: Public Works Program, Labor Supply, and Monopsony

talks.abstract: Do cooperative firms foster local economic development? This paper examines Mexico, assembling a new georeferenced panel dataset at the 10 × 10 km grid-cell level for 2015–2023. Across multiple research designs, we consistently find that cooperative presence boosts local development, measured by nightlight intensity. An event-study design shows persistent extensive margin gains of 6–8% within four years of entry. To address selection concerns, we implement a shift–share IV strategy based on endogenous lagged-cooperative presence and plausibly exogenous sectoral growth shocks; the results imply that one additional cooperative increases nightlight density by about 2.7%. Complementary census evidence links cooperatives to higher schooling, home asset ownership, and decrease migration pressures. We also document stronger effects in Indigenous communities, where cooperatives have longer survival spells. Aggregate patterns suggest that cooperatives increase agricultural specialization but with clear productivity gains, while redistributive effects raise local disposable income and decrease poverty. These findings provide novel causal evidence that cooperatives can function as engines of inclusive local development.
talks.subtheme: Firm Dynamics, Market Power and Productivity
talks.title: Lifting Each Other Up: How Cooperative Firms Foster Local Development

talks.abstract: How do labor market institutions shape the propagation of inflation shocks? We address this question by studying Brazil’s annually indexed minimum wage in a highinflation context. Conventional wisdom suggests that inflation can “grease” labor market adjustments, but institutional wage-setting may alter this mechanism. Using administrative data, we show that indexation creates upward nominal wage rigidity: workers exposed to the policy experience fewer month-to-month wage increases before indexation events, and firms anticipate the policy by rigidifying wages of workers who will be newly bound. We evaluate the macroeconomic implications by introducing a cost-push shock to a New Keynesian model with heterogeneous labor and an indexed minimum wage. While staggered indexation amplifies the inflation as grease mechanism by introducing nominal rigidities, anticipation dampens it via intertemporal substitution. Overall, amplification matters more since cost-push shocks have a weaker effect compared to a setting where the minimum wage indexes every period. Our findings demonstrate that even in high-inflation environments, the institutional structure of wage-setting fundamentally shapes how shocks propagate through the economy.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: Do Institutions Remove Inflation’s Grease? Evidence from Brazil’s Indexed Minimum Wage

sessions.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation

talks.abstract:
Wealth distribution, and in particular the gap between the richest and the poorest, remains a highly relevant topic in the public discourse and an increasingly important concern for policymakers. While distributional results are available from micro-statistics, work in macro-statistics is relatively less developed. To address this gap, the Expert Group on Distributional Household Wealth (EG DHW) was launched in 2023 to help provide systematic, robust and comparable distributional information aligned to national accounts. The EG DHW is part of the G20 Data Gaps Initiative, with the main goal of producing annual wealth deciles by the end of 2026. 

The paper first presents the methodology that aligns micro data to the national accounts. This approach enables distributional information to be comparable with macroeconomic aggregates such as GDP, final household consumption, and net wealth. It also enhances the timeliness, international comparability, and coverage of such information. Second, the paper discusses inequality results from an experimental data collection conducted in 2025. Moreover, it examines the effects of employment-related pensions on the wealth distribution and the wealth share of the top 1% in the United States. The paper concludes with a discussion on the work’s future direction.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: Distribution of household wealth in line with national accounts: Methodology and results from the 2025 experimental data collection

talks.abstract:
This detailed draft presents an analysis of personal income and wealth distribution in Brazil for 2023 by innovatively combining data from the Individual Income Tax Return (DIRPF) and the Continuous Annual National Household Sample Survey (HS). This combined methodology, based on the work of Blanchet, Flores, and Morgan (2022), addresses the traditional limitations of household surveys in capturing high incomes and tax data’s lack of coverage at the bottom of the distribution. The integration of these sources allows for a more accurate evaluation of inequality, particularly across gender and race/color dimensions. Notably, the effective PIT rate exhibited regressivity at the very top, falling from a peak of 12.0% (93rd percentile) to 4.6% for the richest 0.01%.

Examining the full adult population, women are underrepresented in high-income strata and face a significantly lower average annual income compared to men. The largest income disparities were observed across the race/color dimension: white people constitute 78.6% of the richest 1%, while black women form the largest portion of the poorest 10%. These findings underscore that both gender and race/color are critical social conditioning factors that exacerbate income inequality in Brazil.
talks.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
talks.title: Personal Distribution of Income and Wealth of the Brazilian Population

talks.abstract: We combine detailed administrative and survey data with national accounts to estimate the distribution of national income in Finland. In addition to being the first to construct distributional national accounts (DINA) for a Nordic welfare state, we make several methodological contributions. Most notably, we analyze how the treatment of retained earnings affects estimates of income inequality. We are currently working on allocating education and health care services using individual-level registry data, and on extending the DINA framework from annual income to income over the life cycle. On the distribution of income in Finland, the DINA series show higher levels of income inequality than the narrower fiscal income series, but trends are very similar across the two approaches.
talks.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
talks.title: Income Inequality in a Nordic Welfare State: Finnish Distributional National Accounts

talks.abstract: The literature on inequality and top-income concentration in developing countries lacks studies covering longer time frames. This study introduces Ecuador’s first comprehensive Distributional National Account (DINA) series, covering the period from 1990 to 2022, and provides detailed pretax and posttax income indicators. An innovative integration method that merges extensive household and tax microdata allows for a nuanced analysis of income inequality across three decades characterized by economic booms and crises. The results indicate that Ecuador’s extreme income concentration at the top persists into the present. In 2022, the top 1% captured 25% of pretax income, and Ecuador stands out among Latin American countries for having the highest income share held by the top 0.1%. Although not designed for causal inference, this study offers insights into the political economy of inequality in a primary goods exporting country during exogenous economic shocks. Economic institutions in Ecuador have probably passed from an extractive equilibrium before the banking crisis and subsequent dollarization in 2000 to a weak inclusive equilibrium during the commodity price boom until 2014. This inclusive equilibrium has been endangered in recent years, as economic power concentration could not be further reduced and the redistributional capacity built up during the commodity price boom has been undermined after the COVID-pandemic.
talks.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
talks.title: Extreme Income Inequality in Ecuador - Dollarization, Commodity Price Boom, and Citizen Revolution

talks.abstract:
We use population-wide administrative micro-data to provide new estimates of income
inequality and effective tax rates by income groups in Brazil, capturing all income and all tax
payments. Our data allow us to link businesses to their owners and thus to allocate business
income and associated taxes to the corresponding individual firm owners. We provide sharp
upward revisions to official inequality estimates: the top 1% earns 27.4% of total income in
2019, one of the highest level recorded in the world. The tax system, which relies heavily
on consumption taxes, is regressive: while the average tax rate in the economy is 42.5%, this
rate falls to 20.6% for million-dollar earners (roughly the top 0.01% of the distribution), due to
the non-taxation of dividends and provisions that reduce corporate tax liabilities. We provide
evidence suggesting that inequality in developing countries may be systematically underestimated, as even in Brazil—where dividends are untaxed, and hence incentives to retain income within companies are limited—attributing profits to business owners substantially raises in_x0002_come inequality.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: Tax Progressivity and Inequality in Brazil: Evidence from Integrated Administrative Data

sessions.subtheme: Asset Prices, Returns and Portfolio Dynamics

talks.abstract: Using historical income and wealth data, we show that war reduces inequality: the top-1% income share falls by 20\% and the top-1\% wealth share by 10%. We measure three key drivers of inequality---capital destruction, taxation, and inflation---in the data and quantify their role with a Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian (HANK) model. Destruction depresses profits and thus top incomes. Taxation primarily influences wealth dynamics, while inflation has little effect on top shares, but reduces indebtedness among poorer households. We validate our findings using new data on inequality across German towns in World War 2 and cross-country data on profits.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: The Great Leveler According to HANK

talks.abstract: In recent decades, the United States has experienced a notable rise in markups, a slowdown in productivity growth, and an increase in wealth inequality. We present a framework that unifies these trends into a common driving force. In particular, increased barriers to entry raises markups and boost corporate profits. Rising profits elevates firm valuations, fuels the demand for capital, and drives up asset returns. At the same time, the reduction in competition stifles overall economic growth. Wealth inequality is shaped by the return gap, r − g, which represents the difference between asset returns and the economy’s growth rate. The rise in capital demand together with a reduction in growth leads to a widening of the return gap, which amplifies inequality by affecting the saving patterns of households in different ways across the wealth distribution, deepening the divide between the rich and the poor. These trends result in substantial welfare losses for the majority of households, while only the top 1%, and especially the top 0.1%, experience gains.
talks.subtheme: Asset Prices, Returns and Portfolio Dynamics
talks.title: Market power, growth and wealth inequality

talks.abstract: This paper examines the role of wealth inequality as a predictor of financial crises, analyzing data from 18 countries between 1870 and 2020. Unlike previous research focused on the effects of financial crises on inequality, we explore whether increases in wealth concentration—specifically in the top 1%—elevate crisis risk. Our findings indicate that, even after accounting for key crisis predictors, a one standard deviation rise in the growth of the top 1% wealth share is associated with a 3 to 8 percentage points increase in crisis probability, with results robust across various crisis lists and empirical approaches. Temporal dynamics reveal that while a credit boom can jeopardize the financial system as early as the following year, it takes several years for an increase in private wealth accumulation and wealth concentration at the top to significantly heighten the risk of a systemic bank run, serving as early signals of potential instability. Furthermore, we find evidence that asset price bubbles can serve as transmission channels, although these relationships vary by asset class and “bubble” definition. Our findings suggest that addressing wealth concentration could reduce inequality while acting as a stabilizing force for financial systems, highlighting the importance of incorporating broader inequality metrics in crisis prediction models and exploring policy mechanisms to mitigate systemic risks.
talks.subtheme: Asset Prices, Returns and Portfolio Dynamics
talks.title: Wealth Inequality, Asset Price Bubbles and Financial Crises

talks.abstract:
Achieving global climate and biodiversity goals requires unprecedented levels of green investment, yet the financing conditions facing public and private actors remain deeply unequal. This paper develops a heuristic, dynamic framework to explain how financing conditions for green assets and actions emerge, evolve, and interact with macroeconomic structures. Combining insights from ecological macroeconomics, neo-Schumpeterian theory, and balance-sheet approaches, we conceptualise the green finance gap not as a static shortfall, but as a dynamic misalignment between needed actions, the agents capable of implementing them, and the funding sources they can effectively access. We demonstrate how heterogeneous costs, risks, expected returns, and context-specific constraints shape a path-dependent selection
of green investments, thereby influencing their distributive and economic effects.
Our approach clarifies how different green-finance mechanisms — including costreducing instruments, resource-enabling tools, and risk-mitigation schemes — can
reshape the investment environment and alter agents’ financing conditions to reach
ecological targets. These insights provide a foundation for more context-specific policy design and call for future empirical work linking project-level dynamics, institutional arrangements, and macro-financial vulnerabilities across diverse national settings.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: Who Owns the Green Transition? Unequal Access to Finance in a Dynamic Framework

talks.abstract: This paper uses extended series on income and wealth inequality from the World Inequality Database (WID) covering all world regions over the 1800-2025 period, together with new series on hourly productivity and human capital expenditure, to revisit the relationship between equality and development, with a much broader comparative and historical perspective than previous studies. Over the long-run, we find a strong positive association between equality and productivity. Our proposed interpretation is that the rise of inclusive “social-democratic” institutions (including extended access to human capital, public services and democratic participation) led both to more equality and higher productivity, particularly in Western and Nordic Europe. We discuss the implications for future sustainable development strategies.
talks.primary_theme: Measurement of historical income and wealth inequality dynamics
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Equality and Development: A Comparative & Historical Perspective 1800-2025

sessions.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion

talks.abstract: How do wealthy individuals use offshore financial structures like shell companies to protect personal assets?  And how is such offshore wealth structuring itself variably organized? This article supplies the first systematic image of two key layers employed in offshore structures by analyzing expensive residential properties in the UK held via overseas entities. We use these data to make three contributions to debates around offshore. First, we identify a specific regional offshore circuit in flows and magnitude by isolating two key layers. These we term the entry layer, which is used to connect into the UK property market, and the action layer, which is used for the actual or projected appearance of managing the offshore structure. We next pinpoint three patterns of offshore formations between these layers, which we term global funnel, selective gateway, and self-stacker, and we discuss their implications. Finally, we offer indirect evidence of which jurisdictions people are more likely to choose for “brass plate” incorporation and which they employ for more complicated structuring, either in actuality or in appearance, which has implications for policymaking. Our findings supply a pioneering analysis of the scope, scale, and key formations of offshore structures for holding property that probes systematically beyond the first layer.
talks.subtheme: Asset Prices, Returns and Portfolio Dynamics
talks.title: Gateways, Funnels, and Stackers:  How People Hide Property Ownership through Offshore Structures

talks.abstract: This paper studies VAT avoidance in private jet ownership using administrative aircraft registry data from 41 European countries linked to high-frequency ADS-B flight tracking for 1,902 business jets. I document that 35% of European private jets are registered in tax havens, yet virtually none operate in their country of registration: only 7 of 664 tax-haven-registered jets are primarily grounded locally. Exploiting cross-country VAT differentials, I estimate that a 1-percentage-point increase in the VAT rate raises the probability of tax-haven registration by 3.8 percentage points, implying an avoidance elasticity of 0.22. Combining aircraft price data with statutory VAT rates, I estimate at least 1.05 billion in VAT avoidance over the past 15 years. The findings provide new evidence on the mobility of high-value assets and highlight structural weaknesses in VAT enforcement for cross-border luxury goods.
talks.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
talks.title: Turbulence in Taxation: A Study on Tax Avoidance with Private Jets

talks.abstract: Using exhaustive microdata on the worldwide activity of multinational firms from Country-by-Country Reports linked to employer-employee data, we study how profit shifting affects workers' earnings. We overcome two challenges: we build a credible counterfactual profit allocation and relate profit-sharing to profit shifting using the mandatory profit-sharing policy in France. We estimate that large French multinationals shift 19% of their foreign profits annually to low-tax jurisdictions, resulting in €10.3 billion shifted out of France and €3.7 billion in lost tax revenues. We show that profit shifting then reduces annual employees' earnings by 2.6%. Low-income workers are disproportionately affected, the bottom 10% losing 3.2% of wages compared to 2.3% for top 10% earners. Changing the profit-sharing formula to account for global profitability, rather than subsidiary-level profitability, would increase wages by 4.1% for workers in profit-shifting subsidiaries.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: Shift or Share? Profit Shifting and Implications for Workers Profit-Sharing

talks.abstract: Over the past decade, more than 100 jurisdictions have signed automatic exchange of financial information agreements (AEoI) in an effort to fight cross-border tax evasion. This paper studies the effectiveness and coverage of these agreements using account data leaked from an Isle of Man bank with a large customer base in countries participating to AEoI. We establish three sets of results. First, we find that the design of the governing AEoI agreement absolved the bank from reviewing and reporting a very large share (81%) of all the wealth owned by tax residents of AEoI participating countries, and instead the responsibility passed to smaller entities with weaker incentives to comply. Second, out of the wealth that fell under the bank's reporting responsibility, foreign tax authorities only received reports covering  50% of what their tax residents held at the bank. We estimate that a further 32% went unreported due to loopholes in rule design. The rest of the accounts did not appear to have been reported, although through the information available in the leak we classified them as reportable. Third, we find evidence that bank clients who were more at risk of being reported on preemptively closed their accounts, potentially circumventing the AEoI reporting process. This paper provides new evidence on the potential limits of these agreements and how sophisticated individuals can ultimately avoid the AEoI transparency shock.
talks.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
talks.title: When Bankers Become Informants: Behavioral Effects of Automatic Exchange of Information

talks.abstract: This study presents preliminary evidence that the European Emission Trading Scheme (EU ETS) is exploited by multinational companies to artificially shift profits between European countries.  Specifically, using the EU transaction log and Orbis ownership data, I highlight abnormally high levels of internal trade in emission allowances at year-end—despite the April surrender deadline – within firms under the same Global Ultimate Owner (GUO). This activity is especially marked in transactions involving firms without actual emission certificate needs. Towards the year-end, allowances are moved from subsidiaries in strict accounting jurisdictions to those in lenient ones, indicating regulatory arbitrage. These patterns hint to a potential misuse of the EU ETS for financial manipulation rather than emission reduction. I hope to add further analysis, in particular related to the market price of allowances, to contribute to ensuring the EU ETS remains an effective tool for environmental objectives without facilitating unintended financial exploitation.
talks.subtheme: Corporate Taxation, Profit Shifting and Evasion
talks.title: Profit Shifting via Carbon Emission Trading: First Indications

sessions.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives

talks.abstract: This paper provides a new long-run database of group-specific rates of return to wealth for major advanced economies. We combine historical series on the asset composition of different wealth groups with asset-specific pre-tax returns and apply group-specific average tax rates to obtain post-tax returns to wealth. The resulting series cover more than a century and allow us to document how returns differed across the wealth distribution, how these differences evolved over time, and how they relate to changing portfolio structures and tax regimes. The database provides the first harmonised long-run evidence on heterogeneous returns across wealth groups and offers a new empirical foundation for analysing the long-run evolution of wealth inequality.
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Returns to wealth for everyone: Long-run evolution of group-specific rates of return along the wealth distribution

talks.abstract:
This paper leverages household-level data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID)
to investigate saving rate heterogeneity across the wealth distribution in the United States.
I estimate saving rates across wealth deciles using two complementary approaches: the
cross-sectional method and the aggregate method. Four empirical facts emerge. First, saving
rates out of labor income and new resources rise with wealth ranks (flow-based saving
rates), whereas saving rates out of wealth and composite resources are roughly stable
or only modestly increasing (stock-based saving rates). Second, wealth (rank) mobility
contributes substantially to saving rate heterogeneity. However, the direction of its effect
differs between cross-sectional and aggregate methods due to their distinct treatment
of wealth (rank) mobility. Third, the synthetic method (commonly used in the absence
of panel data) overestimates saving rates below the 80th percentile, and underestimates
them for the top 20%. Fourth, saving increasingly consists of saving out of capital gains
as households are richer: wealthier households save for the most part by holding appreciating
assets. The paper provides several empirical moments that are of interest to the
heterogeneous agent macro literature.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: Saving Rate Heterogeneity across the Wealth (Rank) Distribution in the United States

talks.abstract:
This paper constructs the first harmonized long-run series of Chinese national wealth from
1911 to 2020 by combining newly assembled archival data with historical national accounts.
The resulting evidence reveals a distinctive J-shaped trajectory of wealth-to-income ratios that
stands in sharp contrast to the U-shaped pattern documented forWestern economies. China’s
net national wealth-to-income ratio remained broadly stagnant around 300–400 percent for
most of the twentieth century—reflecting the combined legacies of political fragmentation,
wars, state intervention, and price distortions—and fell to a wartime nadir of around 200
percent amid the destruction of World War II, before rising steeply and persistently from
the mid-1980s to nearly 900 percent in 2020. This delayed yet dramatic surge suggests that
large-scale wealth accumulation in developing economies tends to emerge only when political
centralization coincides with institutional and market transformations, including property
rights reforms and the liberalization of asset prices. The long-run evolution of Chinese
national wealth also reveals profound compositional shifts driven by ideological change. The
public share of national wealth followed an inverted-U pattern—rising from negative shares
during the Republican era to nearly 90 percent under Maoist socialism, before falling back to
about 30 percent in the 2010s under a mixed-ownership regime—reflecting the century-long
redefinition of the boundary between state and private property. Within the private sector,
the asset composition shifted from farmland to residential housing and financial savings,
while public wealth became increasingly concentrated in corporate assets. Finally, we observe
a near-zero correlation between national saving and wealth growth, indicating that long-term
changes in Chinese national wealth were primarily driven by capital gains and losses shaped
by the interaction of market forces, state policies, and ideological transformations across
successive political regimes.
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Ideological Shifts and Wealth Dynamics: Unraveling the Century-Long Accumulation of Chinese National Wealth, 1911-2020

talks.abstract: There has been a seismic shift in age-wealth profiles in the U.S. over years 1983 to 2022. The most notable is the sharp rise in the relative household wealth of age group 75 and over. Correspondingly, the relative wealth holdings of all other age groups dropped over these years. Using the Survey of Consumer Finances, the paper focuses on the youngest age group, 35 and under, and the oldest age group, 75 and over, and analyzes the factors behind these relative shifts in wealth. I find that the three principal factors are the homeownership rate, total stocks directly and indirectly owned, and home mortgage debt. The homeownership rate is the same in the two years for the youngest group but falls relative to the overall rate, whereas it shoots up for the oldest group both in actual level and relative to the overall average. The value of stock holdings rises for both age groups but vastly more for the oldest households compared to the youngest ones and accounts for a substantial portion of the elderly’s relative wealth gains. Mortgage debt rises in dollar terms for both groups but considerably more in relative terms for the youngest group.
talks.subtheme: Generational wealth dynamics
talks.title: The Extraordinary Rise in the Wealth of Older American Households

talks.abstract: We show that high-income buyers earn higher financial returns to housing using detailed transaction data from Denmark. The gap in housing returns is explained by location, with little role for market timing, property type, buyer characteristics, or risk-taking. Higher-income households purchase in areas with persistently higher house price growth but comparable risk, liquidity, and downside exposure to those chosen by lower-income households. Credit constraints and consumption needs limit the feasible choice set of lower-income households, limiting access to high-return locations. Our results highlight how spatial sorting amplifies differences in wealth accumulation: returns on the largest household asset are shaped less by risk or investment skill than by consumption needs, housing supply, and financial constraints.
talks.subtheme: Macroeconomic Drivers: Inflation, Growth and Cycles
talks.title: Housing Returns across the Income Distribution

sessions.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration

talks.abstract:
We investigate long-term labour market risks and pension contribution dynamics among Italian workers enrolled in the Notional Defined Contribution (NDC) pension system, which applies to all individuals entering the labour market from 1996 onwards. Using a large administrative sample of individual contribution histories (covering about 15% of all workers, including the self-employed), we analyse career trajectories from labour market entry to 2021 for cohorts entering between 1996 and 2011.

We focus on two key dimensions of career fragility: (i) the share of weeks with actual or credited pension contributions—expressed also in full-time-equivalent terms—relative to potential weeks, and (ii) the accumulated pension wealth compared with that of a representative continuously employed worker earning either the median annual wage or the median full-time annual wage as benchmark. For each cohort, we document average trajectories, the incidence of “poor careers” (defined as contributing for less than 60% of potential time and/or accumulating less than 60% of the representative benchmark), and the degree of inequality in both labour supply and pension accumulation. Results are presented by gender, contractual status, and age at entry.

We complement the descriptive evidence with counterfactual simulations that vary GDP growth (the return on contributions), introduce wage floors, and reduce part-time and unemployment risks, thereby assessing the relative contribution of these factors to low pension accumulation.

Across the 1996–2011 entry cohorts, we find persistent and sizeable career instability, particularly among women. The share of individuals with low work intensity and insufficient contribution accumulation is high and increasing in more recent cohorts, even when observed at the same distance from entry. For example, in the 2001 cohort, after twenty years, around 30% of men and 40% of women have contributed for no more than 60% of potential time, and a similar share has accumulated less than 60% of the benchmark pension wealth—suggesting substantial risks of receiving very low pensions if career conditions do not improve.
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: From fragile careers to inadequate pensions: a cohort comparison of career dynamics in Italy

talks.abstract: This paper examines the levels and dynamics of wealth inequality in Chile between 2007 and 2021, focusing on two major macroeconomic events: the sharp increase in housing prices following the introduction of a value-added tax (VAT) on new dwellings in 2016 and the large-scale liquidation of pension assets through early withdrawals during the COVID-19 pandemic. To do so, we construct a micro–macro consistent wealth distribution by extending existing methodologies to integrate administrative pension fund balances into household wealth surveys using machine learning techniques. Our results reveal pronounced wealth concentration: the top 1\% hold roughly one-third of total private wealth—levels comparable to those observed in the United States—driven by their disproportionate ownership of financial assets. In contrast, the bottom 50\% hold 7–9\%, primarily in housing and pension assets—shares that exceed those observed in most European countries. Nevertheless, we document a modest decline in wealth inequality over the period, particularly after 2016, reflecting the combined influence of two opposing forces: housing appreciation, which mostly benefited the bottom 90\% of households, and pension withdrawals, which broadly reduced wealth across the distribution while relatively increasing inequality. Our findings on levels, trends, and counterfactuals are robust across alternative specifications and methodological approaches.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: From Housing Gains to Pension Losses: Micro-Macro Integration to Reveal Wealth Inequality Dynamics in Chile

talks.abstract: Although the nature of private wealth depends considerably on institutional contexts, studies have yet to elucidate how welfare states shape the patterns of wealth inequality. In this study we investigate wealth inequality and redistribution through pension systems by translating pension entitlements into wealth values. Using cross-nationally harmonized wealth surveys merged with remaining life expectancy data constructed from population projections, we estimate inequalities in ‘augmented wealth’ – a concept that counts pension entitlements as wealth – among older households across 17 high-income countries. Results show that augmented wealth inequality is considerably lower than marketable wealth inequality in all countries, with a substantial cross-national variation in the degree of redistribution through pension wealth. Moreover, the cross-national patterning of augmented wealth inequality resembles that of income inequality when pension entitlements are treated as a household wealth component. Our decomposition of inequality combined with regression analysis also shows that the relative size of pension wealth matters more than the system’s progressivity in achieving redistribution. Finally, it is the public-private mix rather than the sole capacity of public systems that limits the influence of marketable wealth. Overall, our study contributes to multiple bodies of the literature, including studies on wealth inequality, redistributive policies and institutions, and the public-private governance of the welfare state.
talks.subtheme: Global Wealth Dynamics - General
talks.title: Wealth Inequality and Welfare States: Pension systems, the Public-Private Mix, and Augmented Wealth in Old Age

talks.abstract: Housing wealth plays a central but complex role as a factor shaping wealth inequality in advanced economies. Recent comparative research identifies housing equity as the central determinant of cross-national variation in wealth inequality, demonstrating that real estate is not only the largest component of household portfolios but also the most equally distributed relative to financial assets, nonhousing real assets, and consumer debts. Yet this literature treats real estate as a monolithic category, obscuring the dual nature of property as both a consumption good and an investment vehicle. We extend this framework by disaggregating housing wealth into Household Main Residence (HMR) and Other Real Estate (ORE) to examine how each contributes distinctly to national wealth inequality levels. Using harmonized microdata from the Household Finance and Consumption Survey (EU, 2021) and the Survey of Consumer Finances (US, 2022), we demonstrate that HMR and ORE operate as opposing forces: while primary residences equalize wealth distributions, secondary properties concentrate them. Using Gini decomposition methods, we show that ORE is the most unequally distributed wealth component in every country examined, exceeding even the concentration of financial assets. Thus, the equalizing role of housing, emphasized in prior work, holds only for primary residences while Other Real Estate, though largely overlooked, emerges as a potent driver of wealth concentration in advanced economies.
talks.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
talks.title: The Wealth Inequality of Real Estate: Other Real Estate and Its Role in Wealth Concentration

talks.abstract: We study whether higher taxes on housing relative to financial assets for wealthy households can improve housing affordability for the rest of the population. We exploit the 2017 French wealth tax reform, which transformed the comprehensive wealth tax into a real-estate tax and sharply deteriorated the after-tax return to housing relative to financial assets at the top. Using cadastral data, we construct a measure of local exposure to the reform and show that wealthy owners increased housing sales significantly more in highly exposed areas, while non-wealthy owners did not respond. We then examine local redistribution effects and find that, in the most exposed areas, post-reform transactions increasingly involve buyers who are less wealthy than the sellers, alongside a rise in first-time buyers. Finally, portfolio responses occur only for properties benefiting from capital gains tax rebates, suggesting an interaction with capital gains taxation. Our findings indicate that fiscal policies affecting portfolio incentives at the top can influence local housing market dynamics.
talks.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
talks.title: Portfolio Allocation and Housing Markets

sessions.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration

talks.abstract: We provide new estimates of top fiscal income shares and top national income shares in Japan, using most recent tax statistics and other data in 2008-2023. We find that both top fiscal income shares and top national income shares increased only modestly during the period of economic recovery since 2012. When capital gains are included, however, the top 0.01% fiscal income share increased sharply in the recent decade, approaching the level reached at the peak of the bubble economy. When compared with major Western and East Asian countries, the degree of income concentration in Japan is at the lowest level in recent years. We also discuss data limitations and plan to address potential bias that may rise with those limitations.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: Recent Trends in Income Concentration in Japan, 2008-2023:  New Estimates of Top Fiscal Income Shares and Top National Income Shares

talks.abstract: This paper provides the first estimates of top income shares in twentieth-century Mexico based on personal income tax tabulations. Using newly digitised schedular tax data for 1927, 1930, and 1943, together with global-income tabulations for 1970, I reconstruct gross taxable income at the top of the distribution and relate it to control income and population series consistent with national accounts. The benchmark estimates indicate very high concentration at the top of the distribution: the top 1% received about 15.5% of national income in 1927 and 18.4% in 1970, with no sign in the available tax data of the large mid-twentieth-century decline in top shares observed in many advanced economies. Evidence for the merchant elite-roughly the top 0.08\% of the population-shows that this group accounted for between 3% and 10% of total income across the four benchmark years. While the sparse nature of the historical tax record does not allow a full annual series, the new estimates close a major gap in the historical evidence on Mexican top incomes and, within the limits of the available benchmark years, are consistent with the view that Mexico did not experience the "Great Egalitarian Leveling" in top income shares that took place in many advanced economies during the mid-twentieth century.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: Top Incomes in Twentieth-Century Mexico: New Evidence from Tax Records

talks.abstract: Using a statistically robust decomposition framework, we assess group-level contributions to overall economic inequality. Applying this approach to comprehensive microdata spanning from 1962 to 2019, we find that the recent surge in U.S. inequality is primarily driven by rising within-group income dispersion among the top decile of earners, rather than by between-group inequality (mean differences) relative to the rest of the population. Specifically, our results indicate that over 87% of post-2000 U.S. pre-tax income inequality can be attributed to income variation within the top 10%, with the top 1% alone accounting for more than 70%. Our post-tax income analysis reveals a similar, though slightly weaker, pattern. A further decomposition by income source underscores the growing importance of within-group labor income dispersion among top earners in driving U.S. economic inequality.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: The Deepening Divide Within the Rich as a Key Driver of U.S. Economic Inequality

talks.abstract: This paper studies the use and relevance of trusts in the UK, to fill a gap in the literature on using administrative data to measure top income and wealth. Although trusts hold assets for the benefits of individuals, research that uses administrative data to measure income and wealth at the top usually misses this wealth from their estimations. We address this issue by allocating income and wealth held in trusts to the individuals that benefit from the trusts, and show how this impacts their position in the income and wealth distribution. For this purpose, we use administrative data to estimate the total income and wealth held in UK trusts. First, we show the directly observable income and wealth held in trusts. We find that trust income is highly concentrated and that trusts are mainly used for income and wealth accumulation as only a small share of trust income is distributed to beneficiaries. Second, to address limitations of the administrative data, we apply an imputation and income capitalisation methods to estimate the total income and wealth held in trusts. We show that [key findings on missing income and wealth under clearance and will be available at the time of the conference]. Lastly, we allocate the estimated total income and wealth held in trusts to the individuals benefitting from it and show how it affects their position in the income and wealth distribution. On average [key findings on allocating income/wealth under clearance and will be available at the time of the conference].
talks.subtheme: Taxation and Evasion - General
talks.title: Using trusts in the UK: income, wealth and beneficiaries

sessions.subtheme: Savings, Capital Accumulation and Wealth Mobility

talks.abstract:
Can the rise in the wealth-to-output ratio observed in advanced economies over recent decades be explained by an increase in top income inequality? Recent contributions that advance this interpretation struggle to account for the fact that the increase in wealth was driven by asset prices, rather than capital accumulation. This paper shows that these stylized facts can be reconciled in the presence of insatiable preference for wealth. Such preferences induce a cap on optimal consumption—which is more likely to become binding when income inequality is large. When it does, top-income agents accumulate diverging wealth over time while keeping their consumption bounded. This consumption-saving behavior then supports the existence of a  uniquely determined rational bubble, which grows at a rate that exceeds that of the economy.
The bubble crowds out investment, while its diverging price sustains a permanent rise in wealth
inequality. In this environment, wealth and capital income taxes are not equivalent, but both can shift the equilibrium from bubbly to non-bubbly—thus being potentially redistributive and growth-enhancing. A quantitative exercise suggests that a 1.5 percent wealth tax in the U.S. would raise capital by 4.5 percent over 30 years.
talks.subtheme: Savings, Capital Accumulation and Wealth Mobility
talks.title: A Scrooge McDuck Theory of Wealth Dynamics

talks.abstract:
Aguiar, Moll, and Scheuer (2024) show that whenever asset-price changes are driven by
changes in discount rates, the optimal tax base for capital gains taxes must target realized
trades. This result stands in contrast to recent proposals for the taxation of ultra-high-net-
worth individuals which generally feature accrual-based capital gains taxes (Zucman, 2024).
In this paper, I take the theoretical propositions in Aguiar et al. (2024) to an empirical
analysis focusing on U.S. billionaires and the publicly traded firms of which they are major
shareholders. Using data from Forbes, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and
Compustat, I show that (i) capital gains realizations of U.S. billionaires in 2024 amounted
to approximately 1.35% of their wealth and that (ii) between 1998 and today around 75%
of the increase in market valuation of the billionaire-owned publicly traded firms can be
attributed to the rise in their past and future expected profits while around 25% are due
to changes in discount rates. These results show that the theoretical propositions in Aguiar
et al. (2024) do not necessarily weaken the case for accrual-based capital gains taxes on
ultra-high-net-worth individuals.

NOTE to Conference Organizers: This work is a continuation of my master thesis at PSE and receives continuous guidance from my supervisor Gabriel Zucman. Part of the results in this work have been already leveraged and cited in "How Much Tax Do US Billionaires Pay? Evidence from Administrative Data" (Balkir et al., 2025). In my current position as Predoc in the Wealth Team at the EU Tax Observatory, I continue working on this project and plan to have a revised and extensively improved version to be presented at the World Inequality Conference. Among other extensions, we plan to retrospectively simulate the effects of different capital gains tax systems on the ownership shares of US Billionaires in the listed firms they own. The updated and improved version will hopefully be ready for circulation as a working paper around Summer 2026.
talks.subtheme: Historical Measurement - General
talks.title: Are US Billionaires' Unrealized Capital Gains "Paper Gains"?

talks.abstract: This paper examines how asset tests in minimum income programs affect low-income households' savings, exploiting the introduction of Spanish minimum income scheme (Ingreso Mínimo Vital, IMV). Using administrative panel data and the Callaway–Sant’Anna difference-in-differences design, we compare income-eligible beneficiaries to households rejected solely due to the asset threshold. We find that IMV receipt increases liquid savings substantially: after two years, beneficiaries' current account balances are approximately 60% higher than those of (potentially) rejected households by the asset test. Effects are strong for liquid assets but muted for real estate. The results demonstrate that a guaranteed income floor can foster precautionary savings, challenging the view that the poor cannot save. These findings highlight a key trade-off in means-tested program design between accurate targeting and household financial security.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Asset Tests and Household Dissaving: Evidence from Spanish Minimum Income Scheme; Regional wealth inequality in Spain: evidence from the Spain Wealth Atlas
