Across a large sample of countries we find a positive correlation between the level of economic inequality and the share of domestic workers in the workforce. We zoom in on eight countries with comparable data - Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Mexico and Russia – to reveal who employs these workers, and how this links with households’ unpaid social reproduction labour. The highest-inequality country, Mexico, displays the expected pattern: high levels of domestic work confined to high-income employers. But we find two very different models in low-inequality countries. Eastern Europe sees barely any employment of domestic workers, whereas in Belgium, and to a lesser extent France, many households pay for domestic work, but in small quantities. Though still more common among richer households, paid domestic work is used across the income distribution. This subsidized and more fragmented model may alter the domination and social inequality typically associated with domestic work.
talks.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
talks.title: The rich, the poor and the cleaners A multinational comparison of domestic service and inequality

talks.abstract: This article reinterprets modern growth through a Schumpeterian lens, linking innovation dynamics to today’s surge in wealth and market concentration. We document the dramatic rise of billionaire wealth since the mid-1990s and show how individual fortunes are anchored in a small set of highly profitable corporate groups, especially in technology and pharmaceuticals. Using the Amazon case, we trace the shift from creative destruction to “creative appropriation,” where platform control, data advantages, and expansive intellectual property enable incumbents to internalize disruption, preserve rents, and convert global revenues into lightly taxed domestic profits. We then connect firm-level rents to macro outcomes, misallocation, slower diffusion, and a widening pipeline from corporate profits to private power -- with risks for productivity and democratic accountability. The policy section sets out three levers to reverse these trends: rebuild effective corporate tax capacity; modernize competition policy (mergers, interoperability, data access, and self-preferencing limits); and narrow over-broad IP and open essential interfaces. Together, these reforms can redirect innovation toward diffusion, curb extreme accumulation, and restore the complementarity between growth, equality, and democratic resilience.
talks.subtheme: Top wealth, productivity
talks.title: From Creative Destruction to Creative Appropriation – Rethinking Growth in Intellectual Monopoly Capitalism

talks.abstract: In this paper we provide a comprehensive analysis of the quality of life among the elderly in the U.S. over the last decade. We use a novel approach to measure a multidimensional well-being index and compile data on four well-being indicators, namely, income, housing costs, disabilities and internet connectivity from three rounds of the American Community Survey. We find that multidimensional well-being among elderly Americans increased by 36 percent between 2014 and 2023. We also find a rise in inequality in well-being overtime. Well-being levels varied significantly among elderly people belonging to different racial and ethnic groups. American Indian elderly had the least well-being and highest inequality level.
talks.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
talks.title: Multidimensional Inequality among the Elderly in the United States

sessions.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives

talks.abstract:
The paper presents the results of two research projects that investigate the long-term relationship between economic inequality and the inclusiveness of municipal political institutions across various environmental and socio-economic contexts in north-central Italy between 1500 and 1800.
Both projects are based on the idea that, during the early modern period—and, in some respects, even today—local institutions managed a substantial share of public finances and influenced the effective fiscal burden. They determined how to respond to the fiscal and military demands of the State, whether through the imposition of direct taxes or through the leasing and/or sale of municipal assets such as forests, pastures, buildings, and rights to collect duties, among others. The strategies adopted in managing local finances could have a significant impact on economic inequality. For instance, direct taxation—often regressive in relation to the way in which it was distributed—tended to increase inequality, whereas leasing communal assets might have reduced the need for taxation. However, leasing the commons could also deprive the lower and middle classes of a source of income, potentially creating further opportunities for local elites to profit. Hence, the extent to which different social groups could participate in local economic policy decisions becomes crucial. It can generally be assumed that less inclusive institutions—characterized by low turnover and limited representativeness—were more likely to pursue policies that exacerbated inequality. Conversely, greater participation of the lower and middle classes in the management of local finances could promote a more equitable distribution of wealth or at least mitigate the growth of economic disparities.
Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that the relationship between institutional inclusiveness and economic inequality is far from straightforward. Instead, it depends on a variety of contextual factors that are specific to each case examined.
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Political inclusion and economic inequality in the long run: Central-Northern Italy, 1500-1800

talks.abstract: I collect and harmonize income surveys, new tax data, national accounts, and wealth rankings to correct survey-based inequality estimates that understate top incomes; estimate wealth distributions in the absence of direct data; and distribute non-fiscal components of national income across income groups to make distribution figures consistent with macroeconomic aggregates in Turkey. The study’s main methodological contribution lies in leveraging top taxpayer lists where detailed tax tabulations are unavailable. I find that the historical evolution of fiscal income inequality follows a U-shaped pattern: a sharp decline in top-income concentration from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, followed by a sustained rise through the 1980s and 1990s, and a renewed acceleration in the 2010s, most no- tably after 2018. Under conservative assumptions, the national income share of the top 10 percent increased from 42.1 percent to 50.5 percent between 2005 and 2022, while the middle 40 percent’s share fell from 39 percent to 32.8 percent. Wealth inequality was more pronounced, with the top 10% holding 75.6% of gross wealth in 2022. The most cautious lower-bound estimates, accounting for the uncertainty arising from multiple limitations, imply a significant upward revision of official inequality statistics.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: Six Decades of Unequal Growth: Income and Wealth Inequality in Turkey, 1968–2022

talks.abstract:
Using Danish administrative data from 1980–2021, we document substantial lifetime income
inequality and its evolution across cohorts. Lifetime inequality increases steadily with
age and is highest among individuals with lower education and lowest for individuals with vocational education. Variance decompositions shows that differences in employment attachment— non-employment spells and part-time work— account for 30–50% of lifetime earnings dispersion, and is particularly important among the low educated. Across cohorts, lifetime inequality has risen for low- and medium-educated workers. A part of this increase can be linked to increasing dispersion in employment attachment. Redistribution through taxes and transfers
reduces inequality, but transfers play a larger role than taxes, and the equalizing effect has
weakened over time. Income mobility declines with age and across cohorts, making early-career
differences increasingly persistent. These findings underscore that rising lifetime inequality
reflects both labor market dynamics and limited re-distributive offset.
talks.subtheme: Historical Measurement - General
talks.title: Life-time Income Inequality in Denmark

talks.abstract:
Recent work in the Piketty–Atkinson tradition has documented the long-run evolution of
income and wealth inequality using tax data and distributional national accounts, with
Sweden as a key case of dramatic 20th-century equalization. Building on this literature, we
link changes in the structure of jobs to changes in the distribution of incomes in Sweden
from 1870 to 1950. We thus connect the contemporary labour-economics literature on job
polarization and upgrading (e.g. Goos and Manning 2007; Autor and Dorn 2013) to the
literature on the historical drivers of inequality.

We use decadal population censuses to measure the occupational structure of employ-
ment, and a newly assembled 1% sample of income taxpayers every tenth year to recover
occupational income levels. We complement the tax data with our own income estimates
for non-filers (farmers and low-income workers). These extensive microdata (N = 232,000)
allow us to construct fine-grained, occupation-specific income distributions for the period
when Sweden moved from a predominantly agrarian economy towards an industrial welfare
state.

Our analysis proceeds in four steps. First, we document the evolution of the job struc-
ture when occupations are ranked by their position in the income distribution. From 1870
to 1900, employment growth was concentrated in low-pay jobs. Between 1900 and 1920,
employment in the bottom two quintiles contracted while the middle of the distribution
(quintiles 3–4) expanded, indicating upgrading. From 1920 to 1950 this upgrading inten-
sified: the employment share of the bottom quintile of the 1920 pay distribution fell by
about 10 percentage points, while the top quintile rose by a similar amount. Second, we
relate these patterns to structural change, focusing on the downsizing and increasing capital
intensity of agriculture and the expansion of manufacturing and services. Third, we decom-
pose changes in the overall income distribution into a “quantity effect” driven by changing
employment shares across occupations and a “price effect” driven by changing relative occu-
pational pay. From 1900 to 1920, an upgrading job structure coincided with rising relative
pay at the top, producing little overall equalization. By contrast, 1920–1950 combined up-
grading with falling pay differentials and hence substantial equalization, while 1870–1900
featured a downgrading job structure but narrowing differentials.

Fourth, given the strong gender segregation of the labour market, we analyse the gen-
der dimension of these changes. Average female incomes rose from about 25% of average
male incomes in 1920 to around 50% by 1950, a larger catch-up than observed for women
in the United States. We show that this was closely related to the reconfiguration of the
job structure, notably the decline of low-pay female-dominated groups such as family as-
sistants in agriculture and agricultural workers. Our findings contribute to the literature
by highlighting the role of structural change in shaping income concentration and earnings
gaps.
talks.subtheme: Gender Wage Gaps and Labor Income Inequality
talks.title: Job Composition, Gender and Income Inequality in the Long Run: Sweden, 1870–1950

sessions.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity

talks.abstract: This research addresses the moderating role of meritocratic beliefs in the association of inequality with subjective well-being (SWB) across subjective social classes. The literature suggests that inequality is positively associated with the SWB of those in the upper class and negatively with that of the lower class. Additionally, it posits that meritocratic beliefs serve as a palliative for the negative relationship in the lower class by giving them hope for social mobility, presenting as system-justifying beliefs. To empirically assess these propositions, multilevel linear regression models were estimated, introducing a three-factor interaction and using a measure of inequality different from the GINI. The results indicate that, contrary to the literature, as inequality increases SWB decreases for those with high meritocratic beliefs who perceive themselves as lower class. Meaning that, considering a sample covering different regions and countries with varying income levels, the palliative effect attributed to these beliefs does not hold.
talks.subtheme: Intergenerational Mobility and Equality of Opportunity
talks.title: Unfulfilled Prophecy: The Moderating Role of Meritocratic Beliefs in the Relationship Between Inequality and Subjective Well-Being

talks.abstract: Economic inequality has become an important element of political debates, capturing significant attention in media coverage, public discourse, as well as academic research. In a survey experiment on a representative sample of the Dutch population (N = 4501), we examine how individuals explain economic inequality. We employ responses from an open-ended survey question about sources of inequality and link them on an individual level to administrative data on respondents’ income and wealth. We find that respondents predominantly attribute inequality to structural factors rather than personal responsibility or luck. Explanations are somewhat insensitive to information about inequality in the Netherlands, or about one’s standing in the income or wealth distributions. We observe significant differences in the content of the explanations based on respondents’ characteristics, such as wealth or political affiliation, and inequality-related attitudes. In a subsequent data collection, we aim to estimate the causal impact of explanations of inequality on redistributive preferences.
talks.subtheme: Experimental and Survey Evidence on Inequality Attitudes
talks.title: Societal Explanations of Economic Inequality

talks.subtheme: Polarization, Media and Democratic Trust
talks.title: Online media and polarization: Theory and cross-country evidence

talks.abstract: This paper examines how confirmation bias and media fragmentation jointly contribute to political polarization. As media environments become increasingly fragmented, individuals are exposed to distinct sets of information, reinforcing ideological divides and reducing shared understanding. We argue that confirmation bias not only drives selective exposure but also amplifies political polarization as fragmented information environments create self-reinforcing narratives. Using inflation perceptions in Germany as a case study, we provide empirical evidence that preferences on media consumption reinforce extreme political views and support for radical parties, more concretely towards the right. Additionally, we document a backfire effect, where exposure to contradictory information deepens ideological entrenchment. Our findings highlight the critical role of fragmented media landscapes and biased news consumption in shaping political attitudes and electoral behavior.
talks.subtheme: Information, Narratives and Belief Formation
talks.title: Biased Information, Biased Preferences: How Fragmented Media Environments Undermine Support for Redistribution

sessions.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power

talks.abstract:
Access to higher education is a key driver of socio-economic mobility, yet financing remains a central barrier for disadvantaged groups in India. This study investigates whether caste-based discrimination affects the approval of education loans using an experimental design that combines elements of an audit study and a lab-in-the-field experiment. Loan officers evaluated fictitious but realistic student loan applications that were identical in financial and academic characteristics but varied only by caste. Each application received two ratings: (1) the likelihood of approval and (2) the likelihood of successful repayment.
The results show that applicants from Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe backgrounds receive significantly lower approval scores than their Upper Caste counterparts, despite no differences in expected repayment ability. This pattern aligns with taste-based discrimination rather than risk-based statistical discrimination. We also find no significant approval penalty for Other Backward Caste applicants relative to Upper Caste applicants, indicating that bias is concentrated against the most marginalised caste groups rather than following a linear caste hierarchy. These findings suggest that caste prejudice influences loan approval decisions and restricts access to higher education for historically disadvantaged communities.
talks.subtheme: Discrimination (caste)
talks.title: Does Discrimination Exist in the Market for Educational loans? Experimental Evidence from India’s Caste System

talks.abstract:
This paper examines the impact of integration policies within India’s Affirmative Action
framework in public engineering institutes. Exploiting random assignment of students
to hostel rooms, I study how exposure to peers from different caste groups influences
academic performance, job market outcomes, mental health, and socio-political attitudes.
I find that lower-caste students assigned to mixed-caste rooms perform better academically
and secure better internships after first year. However, they report poorer mental
health, measured by PHQ-4 scores and self-reported anxiety about academics and
discrimination, and fewer close friendships. Among upper-caste students, mixed-room
assignment reduces academic performance but does not significantly improve attitudes
toward social justice or the perceived meritocracy of affirmative action. I also find both
upper and lower caste students assigned to mixed rooms are more likely to live in mixed
rooms at the end of first year, suggesting integration despite cultural frictions.
Using additional variation in room composition comparing fully mixed versus partially
mixed three-sharing rooms, I explore whether having one same-caste roommate moderates
these effects. I find that partial mixing mitigates mental health effects and friendship
effects. Secondary outcomes on interactions and mutual support further corroborate the
role of caste and ability of the roommate, level diversity in the room.
talks.subtheme: Political Inequalities - General
talks.title: Backlash or Bonding? Effect of Integration Policies in a Context of Affirmative Action

talks.abstract: Reparations have been proposed to remedy enduring inequalities between racial or ethnic groups, but little is known about the social and political consequences of such policies. We study caste-based reparations by evaluating a program that provides a one-time group-targeted wealth transfer of 1 million rupees ($12,000) to Dalit households in Telangana, India. We test competing theoretical expectations of advancement, persistence, and retrenchment using a natural experiment and original survey of 3,184 households. The program improved Dalit asset ownership and narrowed the gap with non-Dalits. It increased Dalits’ confidence in engaging dominant castes and reduced caste conflict, against the expectation of social backlash. However, segregation norms persisted, and dominant castes expressed reduced support for a
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Caste Reparations: Economic Advancement, Social Concord, and Policy Backlash

talks.abstract: This paper examines the impact of financial inclusion in reducing caste-based social exclusion using a quasi-experimental setup involving a 2005 branch expansion policy of RBI and employing a regression discontinuity framework. Our findings reveal a significant increase in consumption and a reduction in poverty among marginalized castes compared to non-marginalized castes. Three channels, informal credit, business finance, and the labor market, have been found to contribute to the welfare gains of marginalized castes. We also find reductions in taste-based discriminatory practices. This study underscores the role of formal banking sector in mitigating deep-rooted social norms such as caste-based discrimination.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: Does Financial Inclusion Mitigate Social Exclusion?

sessions.subtheme: Demographic change

talks.abstract: In the last two centuries many countries underwent substantial demographic changes that appear to have had substantial consequences for each country's economy. Both mortality and fertility declined. We examine the impact of these changes in theory, using an overlapping-generations model, and in application to a highly important case, China. We demonstrate the importance of demographic change by studying the effects of increased life expectancy (ILE) and the One Child Policy (OCP), introduced in 1980 and abolished in 2016.  We find that the effect of ILE is modest, but that OCP has dramatic consequences.
talks.subtheme: Demographic change
talks.title: Demographic Change and Intergenerational Transmission.  With an application to China

talks.abstract:
We estimate the effects of exposure to income and wealth inequality during adolescence on long-term educational and labor market outcomes. Using detailed Swedish register data covering all students completing compulsory education between 1989 and 2013, we construct measures of inequality among students’ schoolcohort peers and exploit variation between cohorts within schools to identify plausibly causal effects. We find no evidence that exposure to inequality affects GPA, high school graduation, university enrollment, university completion, or income up to age 35. These null results are precisely estimated and robust across alternative
measures of inequality, sample definitions, and specifications. Moreover, we find no evidence of systematic heterogeneity by socioeconomic background. These findings provide reassurance that school integration policies mixing students from different socioeconomic backgrounds do not carry hidden long-run costs from inequality exposure. More broadly, they challenge the view that exposure to peer inequality during adolescence is a causal driver of human capital accumulation or later-life mobility.
talks.subtheme: Environmental Inequalities - General
talks.title: Exposure to Inequality, Human Capital Investment, and Labor Market Outcomes

talks.subtheme: Education, Skills and Human Capital Channels
talks.title: Human Capital, Unequal Opportunities and Productivity Convergence: A Global Historical Perspective, 1800-2100

talks.abstract: This paper studies how organized crime presence transforms local communities and human capital formation. Identifying these effects is challenging, as crime is endogenous to local conditions. We address this by leveraging the recent case of Ecuador, where criminal organizations from neighboring countries have rapidly established a new cocaine export route. This externally driven shock generated sharp increases in violent crime, allowing us to estimate causal effects using a difference-in-differences design based on proximity to areas prone to cocaine smuggling. Crime-affected areas experienced higher dropout rates among children at grades characterized by weak school attachment, the end of primary education and the first years of secondary school. While we do not find evidence of increased dropout among older students aged 15-18, individuals in this age group already out of education at the time of the crime surge exhibited a marked rise in risky behaviors, reflected in higher homicide victimization and earlier pregnancies. We also document severe economic disruption: household income fell by nearly 30%, driven mainly by a decline in informal employment. Declining earnings are a key mechanism linking crime exposure to school dropout. These findings show that the externalities of organized crime impose persistent social costs, deepening inequality and undermining human capital development.
talks.subtheme: Crime
talks.title: When Organized Crime Moves In: Economic and Human Capital Disruption

sessions.subtheme: Education, Skills and Human Capital Channels

talks.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of child multidimensional deprivation on school enrollment and subsequent learning outcomes in undivided Andhra Pradesh, India. Using longitudinal data from the Younger Cohort of the Young Lives study across three survey rounds (2002, 2006, and 2009–10), we construct a continuous multidimensional deprivation index along the dimensions of health, education, and standard of living, following the Alkire–Foster framework adapted to child-specific conditions. We employ rare-event logit models to examine the effect of deprivation on school enrollment and apply Instrumental Variable (IV) and Control Function (CF) approaches to identify causal impacts on learning outcomes. We find that children deprived across multiple dimensions—whether measured strictly or flexibly—are systematically less likely to attend formal schooling. We find that multi- dimensional deprivation significantly reduces school attendance across all social groups, with particularly strong effects among Muslims and backward castes, while intersectional analysis shows that Muslim girls experience the steepest attendance penalty. We find that multidimensional deprivation exerts large and statistically significant negative effects on children’s learning outcomes. The effects are strongest for language and numeracy domains and remain robust under both strict and flexible deprivation definitions. Heterogeneity analysis further reveals that girls, Muslim children, and Scheduled Tribes experience the steepest learning penalties.
talks.subtheme: Education, Skills and Human Capital Channels
talks.title: Child Deprivation and Early Educational Outcomes: Evidence from Young Lives, India

talks.abstract: High schools have lasting academic and economic consequences for their students. I use de- tailed Chilean administrative data to show that interactions among primary school peers shape how students sort into high schools. I exploit the random assignment of students into oversub- scribed primary schools, together with repeated data on graduates’ applications, to identify the causal effect of primary school peers on students’ choice of high school. I find that studying with a particular peer significantly increases the probability that a student applies to and at- tends the same high school. Peer effects interact nonlinearly with the spatial distribution of high school quality, shaping educational inequality. Embedding peer effects into a model of school choice, I show that when high school quality is unevenly distributed across space, interactions among peers can reduce applications to high-quality schools from students in disadvantaged areas, amplifying inequality. Empirically, I find that peer effects account for one-sixth of the gap in the probability that low- and high-income students attend a high-quality high school. To address these gaps, I show that policies that expand students’ access to high-quality high schools can benefit from increasing returns to scale through spillovers within peer networks, without generating negative externalities for untargeted students.
talks.subtheme: Education,  Peer Effects
talks.title: Go Your Own Way? Peer Effects, School Choice, and Educational Inequality

talks.abstract:
This paper studies how political instability, spatial informality, and household context interact to shape human capital investment and long-run gender disparities in post-revolution Egypt. In the wake of the 2011 political uprising, Egypt experienced a multi-dimensional shock: political uncertainty, institutional breakdown, and a rapid, unregulated expansion of informal settlements. This period provides a rare opportunity to disentangle how families respond to both political and spatial risks when making high-stakes decisions about adolescent education.

In the first part of the paper, I use nationally representative survey data to examine how exposure to political instability affected university enrollment. I find that current macroeconomic shocks and worsening expectations about the future (proxied by changes in saving behavior) do not appear to significantly affect educational decisions. In contrast, political violence and instability during 2011–2013 had a sizable and gendered impact. Female enrollment dropped sharply, while male enrollment was largely unaffected. The gender gap is concentrated among adolescents who were at a critical schooling juncture during the political crisis—specifically, girls in their final year of high school at the onset of the revolution.

Importantly, this effect is not uniform across socioeconomic groups. The decline in enrollment is most pronounced among girls from wealthier households, suggesting that better-off families may have been more reactive to the instability. This may reflect a combination of perceived physical safety risks, changing marriage market expectations, and shifts in the opportunity cost of schooling.

Preliminary analysis of long-term outcomes suggests that these “unlucky cohorts” of exposed women face worse labor market prospects and no observable compensating gains in the marriage market. This implies a persistent negative impact on women’s economic opportunities, rooted in disrupted human capital formation during adolescence.

In the second part of the paper, currently in progress, I extend the analysis by incorporating the geographic expansion of informal settlements. I am constructing a novel slum expansion dataset by digitizing satellite imagery and urban planning maps to trace informal housing growth between 2011 and 2013. This allows me to identify households exposed to sudden increases in crowding, spatial disadvantage, and degraded service provision — channels likely to amplify the gendered effects of instability. I will exploit natural barriers (e.g., highways, canals, railways) to implement a spatial regression discontinuity design and isolate the effects of slum exposure on education and labor outcomes.

Finally, I will estimate a dynamic structural model of household decision-making under spatial and political risk, where parents choose whether to invest in adolescent education facing both direct costs and uncertain returns. The model incorporates heterogeneity by gender, wealth, and slum exposure, and will be calibrated using reduced-form moments from the data. This structural approach will allow counterfactual simulations of urban and education policies, such as slum upgrading or cash transfer programs targeting adolescent girls.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Political Instability, Urban Informality, and Labor Markets: Evidence from Egypt

talks.abstract: This study examines the extent of education-occupation mismatch (EOM) in India and its implications for wage outcomes, using data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2024. The findings indicate that EOM is widespread, with both undereducation and overeducation contributing substantially to the overall mismatch. Workers in either category experience notable wage penalties relative to those whose educational qualifications are appropriately aligned with their jobs. Interestingly, the wage penalty associated with overeducation is less severe for women, suggesting that additional years of schooling continue to improve their positions in the labor market, even when they are not perfectly matched to their jobs. These findings highlight a structural imbalance between the increasing levels of educational attainment and the availability of suitable job opportunities in India, raising important concerns about the efficient use of human capital in the workforce. Moreover, the wage losses resulting from mismatch are most pronounced among lower and middle segments of the wage distribution, where both undereducated and overeducated workers face significant earnings compression. At higher wage levels, these penalties diminish, especially for the undereducated, though overeducated workers continue to experience persistent disadvantages, highlighting the segmented nature of the labor market.
talks.subtheme: Gender Wage Gaps and Labor Income Inequality
talks.title: Does Educational Mismatch Penalize Women Less? Evidence from India’s Labour Market

sessions.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion

talks.abstract:
This study investigates gender-based attribution bias, the tendency to attribute men’s success to ability and women’s failure to a lack of ability—using a controlled principal- agent online experiment. We test for this bias across male- and female-typed tasks. In male-typed tasks, we
find evidence of attribution bias after task success: principals are more likely to attribute success to ability when the agent is male. We do not observe such bias following failure. In contrast, in female-typed tasks, we find bias against men following task failure, pointing to the importance of
task domain in shaping attribution patterns. Our design allows us to rule out taste-based and statistical discrimination. Attribution bias is stronger among individuals with more regressive gender attitudes but only for male-typed task, suggesting an attitudinal basis for attribution patterns.
talks.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
talks.title: Attribution Bias by Gender

talks.abstract:
Do unequal gender norms limit women’s productivity? We study this question using three decades of World Bank project and HR data. Women are less likely than men to lead aid projects in countries with high gender inequality, despite no evidence of llower ability. Using a difference-in-differences design, we show that female-led projects suffer a performance penalty relative to men’s in such settings, consistent with cultural constraints. These effects remain after controlling for project leader and country fixed effects and instrumenting female leadership with the gender composition of the pool of potential
leaders.
talks.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
talks.title: Cultural Constraints on Women’s Productivity: Evidence from World Bank Lending

talks.abstract: We develop a comprehensive framework that modifies the Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) to recover the wealth distribution over both families and individuals by carefully parsing wealth within coupled households. All of our estimates agree that wealth has become more equally held within couples over time changes because of changes in pension holdings, but is still imply a substantial gender gap. By ignoring unequal wealth holdings within families, we show that existing estimates understate inequality across individuals. That said, both ours and other leading estimates of wealth concentration all point to increasing concentration at the top of the wealth distribution since 1989.
talks.subtheme: Care Work, Household Dynamics and Time Use
talks.title: Has Experience Made Me Rich? Analysis of the U.S. Gender Wealth Gap

talks.abstract:
A growing body of research estimates child penalties, the gender gap in the effect of parenthood on earnings, using event studies that normalize treatment effects by counterfactual earnings. I formalize the identification framework underlying this approach and show that it does not identify its target estimand when the parallel trends assumption \emph{in levels} is violated. Insights from human capital theory suggest such violations are likely: higher-ability individuals tend to delay childbirth and have steeper earnings growth, a mechanism that causes conventional estimates to understate child penalties for early-treated parents.
I propose instead to target the effect of parenthood on the gender earnings ratio and show that this parameter is identified without additional assumptions. Using Israeli administrative data, a bias-bounding exercise for the conventional estimator suggests substantial understatement (25–50\%) of child penalties for early-treated parents, while later-treated groups exhibit smaller biases. I also document that estimates of the new parameter are roughly 30\% smaller in absolute value than the conventional estimates for later-treated parents.
talks.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
talks.title: Identification of Child Penalties

talks.abstract:
We study whether gender-focused informational campaigns can generate backlash among those excluded from participation. In a randomized evaluation of school-based menstrual awareness sessions in 52 Nepalese schools, we compare the effects of girls-only sessions—common in practice—to mixed-gender sessions and a control group. Excluding boys produces a sizeable backlash: boys become less willing to support girls in confronting menstrual stigma and report less progressive views, while girls' attitudes and behavior remain unchanged. Including boys fully eliminates these negative effects.

Mechanism evidence shows that exclusion shifts boys' beliefs and emotions in ways consistent with reduced empathy and reinforced gender boundaries: they expect less prosocial behavior from peers, view menstruation as ``a women’s problem,'' and react more negatively to menstruation-related situations at school. These results demonstrate that even purely informational interventions can backfire when participation is unequal, highlighting inclusion as a key design feature for awareness-based norm change.
talks.subtheme: Gendered Institutions, Norms and Social Exclusion
talks.title: Why Awareness Needs Inclusion: Evidence from a Menstrual Health Campaigns in Nepal

sessions.subtheme: Political Inequalities - General

talks.abstract: Measuring political equality has always been fraught with challenges. Taking roads distribution as a reflection of local political dynamics, I propose a novel way to measure political equality using satellite data of local roads and other infrastructure while accounting for contextual factors like population density, topography and initial development levels. Against expectations, I find that development aid generates more economic growth when provided to regions with less, not more, political equality. This counterintuitive result can be explained by the idea of growth potential. Since aid agencies generally target areas that consistently lag in development, more politically equal areas were likely to have already reached their growth limits while aid provided to less equal areas helps unlock suppressed potential.
talks.subtheme: Political Inequalities - General
talks.title: Measuring Political Inequality: Roads Distribution and Developement Aid Effectiveness in Indonesia

talks.abstract:
We investigate whether traditional poverty alleviation policies, typically designed for immediate poverty reduction, also enhance households’ resilience to future unexpected shocks. We revisit a randomized control trial in Bangladesh which undertook a two year intervention across two rural regions of Bangladesh. Using an improved resilience metric and machine learning methods, we present new findings of the impact of the different poverty alleviation strategies, both at the endline and four years post intervention. Our study reveals that poverty alleviation interventions, such as unconditional cash transfers, and cash or food transfers combined with intensive group-based behavior change communication (BCC), significantly improve resilience compared to pure in-kind transfers. However, these policies are primarily effective in strengthening resilience to extreme poverty. Four years after the intervention, we find some evidence of cash transfers enhancing resilience to extreme poverty. We explain our findings through both short-term
coping strategies and long-term adaptive mechanisms
talks.subtheme: Technology, Automation and Digital Transformation
talks.title: Do Poverty Alleviation Policies Enhance Household Resilience to Poverty? Evidence from Bangladesh

talks.abstract: We study the effects of minimum wage (MW) increases on poverty and food hardship in the United States from 1981–2019 using stacked difference-in-differences models and the Supplemental Poverty Measure. A $1 MW increase reduces poverty by 0.3–0.7 percentage points among all working-age adults and 1.2–1.7 percentage points among likely MW workers, while also reducing food insufficiency by 1.5 percentage points for this group. Effects on poverty are partially offset by higher living costs in MW-increasing states. MW increases meaningfully reduce poverty and food hardship for the workers most directly affected but deliver modest improvements for the broader working-age population.
talks.subtheme: Labor Markets, Wages and Bargaining Power
talks.title: The Effects of Minimum Wage Increases on Poverty and Food Hardship

talks.abstract: This study examines the impact of funding from the Program to Support and Promote Entrepreneurial Initiatives (PAVIE) on the economic performance of beneficiaries in Senegal, as measured by job creation and income growth. Using the Generalized Propensity Score (GPS), it analyzes the marginal and nonlinear effects of the amount of funding, going beyond traditional binary approaches. The results reveal an inequitable allocation of resources: despite their high participation rate (62.83%), women receive on average less than half the amount granted to men, with men, the most educated entrepreneurs, and those active in the manufacturing or service sectors benefiting most. The analysis of dose-response functions highlights critical thresholds of effectiveness. For job creation, the effect is positive from the earliest levels of financing, but accelerates significantly above 1.2 to 1.5 million CFA francs, reflecting increasing marginal returns. For income, a clearly positive effect only emerges above 1,824,000 CFA francs. The gender-differentiated analysis shows that women entrepreneurs, although systematically underfunded, are more sensitive, with an effectiveness threshold for income of only 264,000 CFA francs. In contrast, among men, job creation only becomes significant above 2,268,000 CFA francs. The sectoral analysis shows that in commerce, the effects on employment are immediate, while in services and manufacturing, a threshold of 534,000 CFA francs is required to generate a significant impact on employment. These results call for an overhaul of allocation mechanisms in favor of strategic targeting differentiated by gender and sector, combining amounts calibrated to impact thresholds and enhanced technical support, in order to transform formal inclusion into substantial economic equity.
talks.subtheme: Voting, Participation and Electoral Cleavages
talks.title: Impact of financial support for entrepreneurship on economic performance  in Senegal: The case of PAVIE

sessions.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects

talks.abstract: This article investigates how national income convergence, redistribution, and climate change will shape the world distribution of income until 2050, using a novel source of data on global inequality before and after taxes. Despite ongoing convergence in national income, the global bottom 50% post-tax income share only marginally rises from 10% to 12% under "business-as-usual", while the top 1% share remains constant. Yet, if countries were to adopt the most effective redistribution policies implemented by the best performer in their respective region, the global bottom 50% income share could increase to over 19%. Redistribution of pre-tax incomes account for 62% of this increase, with the remainder due to post-tax redistribution. Climate change is set to exacerbate inequalities, potentially offsetting all the increase in the global bottom 50% share since 1980.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: Global Inequality by 2050: The Role of Redistribution and Climate Change

talks.abstract: This paper introduces a novel application of the Kaya identity to assess the roles of technological change and consumption behaviour in shaping global greenhouse gas emissions. Drawing on numerical insights from counterfactual emission-reduction scenarios, we quantify the adjustments in technology and consumption required to remain within the carbon budget by 2050 and explore their distributional implications. Building on this analysis, we develop a simple analytical model that formalizes the resulting carbon budget trilemma: under binding ecological constraints, rising consumption, gradual technological progress, and widening inequality cannot sustainably coexist. We place these transformations in historical perspective by examining a set of precedents—from wars and epidemics to economic collapses and episodes of rapid technical upgrading—that provide comparative magnitudes for the scale of change implied by a binding carbon budget. Our conclusions unveil a race between technological innovation and consumption sobriety to reach planetary sustainability, in which global inequality acts as a boundary constraint. Given past technological progress, and current levels of global inequality, it is unlikely that sustained reductions in average consumption can be avoided if we are to respect ecological constraints.
talks.subtheme: Carbon Pricing and Climate Policy Distributional Effects
talks.title: The Race Between Technology and Sobriety: Distributional Pathways to Planetary Sustainability

talks.abstract: Climate change raises important fairness issues linked to distributional impacts and the unequal resilience of territories, yet within-country inequality and climate change damages are not described in the Shared Socio-economic Pathways baseline database. This study extends the latter data set by integrating the joint distribution of income inequality and economic damages at a fine-grained sub-national level. The results show that global income inequality, which has been falling since the early 2000s, is projected to rise again in all SSP scenarios but the SSP1 Sustainability scenario, partly due large economic damages affecting the poor in a disproportionate manner. Moreover, the Sustainability scenario SSP1 records the strongest rates of economic and welfare growth net of economic damages, despite displaying lower baseline economic growth than the Fossil-fuel scenario SSP5.
talks.subtheme: Climate Justice, Vulnerability and Adaptation
talks.title: The Shared Socio-economic Pathways of global welfare: A sub-national database integrating income inequality and  climate change impacts

talks.abstract:
This paper develops a conceptual framework for assessing long-run global justice pathways in a world of roughly ten billion people living within planetary boundaries. Building on the empirical agenda of the World Inequality Database and the Global Justice Project, I interpret global distributions of income, wealth and environmental use as implicit insurance contracts that allocate exposure to macroeconomic, climate and political risks across countries, social groups and generations. The framework combines a risk-sharing perspective with five minimal justice constraints: (1) achievement of a global social minimum by mid-century; (2) convergence in average incomes between countries by 2100; (3) compression of within-country inequality below specified thresholds; (4) respect for climate and broader planetary boundaries; and (5) political and epistemic arrangements that prevent those who lose in the short run from being systematically excluded from shaping long-run pathways.

Within this structure, I classify distributional pathways to 2100 into regimes such as convergent sustainability, unequal decarbonisation, carbonified stagnation, and green oligarchy, and I map these regimes to a simple policy architecture involving a global justice fund, progressive wealth and carbon taxation, reforms of international monetary and financial arrangements and governance of emerging technologies. The framework is designed as a normative “map” for the design and interpretation of Global Justice Report scenarios, helping to make explicit the ethical content of long-run inequality and climate trajectories and to bridge empirical measurement with debates over feasible and desirable global justice futures.
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Global Justice Pathways for Ten Billion: Inequality, Risk Sharing and Planetary Boundaries to 2100

sessions.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design

talks.abstract: This paper studies how economic inequality shapes the risk of violent conflict. We construct a new measure of local agricultural income and inequality by combining time-invariant agro-ecological suitability from FAO/GAEZ with year-to-year variation in global crop prices. This approach yields plausibly exogenous, spatially disaggregated predictions of rural income that vary across ethnic territories, administrative units, and neighboring communities. Using data for sub-Saharan Africa from 1997--2023 and a fine $0.5^{\circ}$ hexagonal grid with cell and country--year fixed effects, we find that price-induced increases in agricultural income inequality, particularly within and between ethnic territories, significantly raise the likelihood of conflict onset. By contrast, mean agricultural income has a limited and often negative association with conflict. Interaction estimates show that conflict take place in locations characterized by high inequality and poverty. Our findings underscore the central role of distributional tensions, rather than average income shocks, in explaining the origins of political violence.
talks.subtheme: Methodological Innovations in Inequality Research
talks.title: Inequality and Insurgency

talks.abstract: In many countries, both charitable and political donations benefit from generous – and often similar – tax incentives. While a large literature has studied the tax-price elasticity of charitable giving, little is known on political donations. Using a large-scale survey experiment (N = 12, 600), we investigate the relative efficiency of different tax schemes, and document that repealing the existing non refundable income-tax credit decreases charitable donations but not political donations, pointing toward more fiscal incentives behind charitable giving. We next show that, conditional on giving, matching increases both political and charitable giving, but that it decreases the probability to give to charities at the extensive margin. Finally, relying on PCA and on general machine learning, we document important dimensions of heterogeneity, and discuss the policy implications of our findings.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Should Charitable and Political Donations Benefit from Similar Tax Treatments? Evidence from a Survey Experiment

talks.abstract:
College education is a key determinant of political attitudes in the United States and
other countries. This paper highlights an important source of variation among college
graduates: studying different academic fields has sizable effects on their political attitudes.
Using surveys of about 300,000 students across 477 U.S. colleges, we find several results.
First, relative to the natural sciences, studying the social sciences and humanities tends
to make students more left-leaning, whereas studying economics and business makes them
more right-leaning. Second, the rightward effects of economics and business come from
shifts on economic policy issues (taxation, healthcare), whereas the leftward effects of the
humanities and social sciences come from shifts on cultural issues (LGBTQ, race). Third,
these effects extend to behavior: the social sciences and humanities increase activism,
while economics and business increase the emphasis on financial success. Fourth, the
effects operate through teaching rather than socialization or earnings expectations. Finally,
the implications are substantial. If all students majored in economics or business, the
college–noncollege ideological gap would shrink by about 30 percent. A uniform-major
scenario, in which everyone studies the same field, would reduce ideological variance and
the gender gap among graduates. Together, the results show that academic fields shape
students’ attitudes and that field specialization contributes to political fragmentation.
talks.subtheme: State Capacity, Institutions and Policy Design
talks.title: Changing Minds: How Academic Fields Shape Political Attitudes

talks.abstract:
Tax amnesty programs have become a recurring feature of Brazil’s fiscal
policy, often justified as necessary responses to economic crises, but
frequently implemented regardless of macroeconomic conditions. Despite
their budgetary impact, little is known about the political mechanisms
underlying the repeated granting of such tax benefits. This study
investigates whether corporate electoral donations are associated with
subsequent participation in tax amnesty programs, and whether these
donations are strategically timed during critical policy windows—
specifically, the period between the issuance of executive decrees
(Medidas Provisórias) and their conversion into law. Using a novel panel
dataset combining over 130,000 Brazilian firms’ campaign donation
records (2002–2014) with oﬃcial data on Refis participation, we test for
diﬀerences in donation patterns by amnesty status and timing. Results
show that firms participating in Refis donate substantially more than
others, and that donation amounts peak for repeat participants during
critical policy windows. These findings suggest that business interest
groups may strategically deploy campaign contributions to influence the
allocation and design of tax benefits. However, as the analysis relies on
observational data with limited transparency on informal channels of
influence, the results should be interpreted as robust associations rather
than causal eﬀects. The study highlights the need for greater transparency
in both tax expenditure and political finance in emerging markets.
talks.subtheme: Tax Incidence, Redistribution and Welfare Effects
talks.title: Quid pro quo? Electoral Donations and Tax Amnesty Programs in Brazil

sessions.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration

talks.abstract:
Using the novel GC Wealth Project Data warehouse, this paper shows that most countries have experienced rising wealth inequality since the 1990s, with gains concentrated
among the top 10% and declines among the bottom 50%. We reveal substantial variation
of estimates across data sources and units of analysis which complicates international comparison of wealth inequality. Yet, core trends at the country level are generally robust.
Individual-based series generally report higher inequality than household-based ones. Regional patterns reveal sharp increases in inequality in Latin America, North America, India,
and China, while Europe and Asia-Pacific exhibit more stable trends. Incorporating Forbes
billionaire data extends coverage to low-income countries and Africa—where, notably, billionaire wealth relative to GDP has remained stable, marking a distinct exception to global
patterns.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: Wealth Inequality Trends Around the World: a first view from the GC Wealth Project data

talks.abstract: I revisit the empirical relationship between wealth and returns on wealth of U.S. households over the past 70 years. While recent studies suggest that returns on wealth increase with wealth and that the richest households earn the highest returns, I show that this pattern is specific to post-1980. Before 1980, returns declined at the top 10 percent of the wealth distribution, and the bottom 90 percent had higher returns than the top 10 percent. I attribute this reversal to differences in households’ exposure to interest rate risk. Because wealthier households tend to hold longer-duration assets, such as stocks and private businesses, changes in real interest rates affect their portfolios more strongly. When real rates rose, as they did before 1980, the top 10 percent households experienced lower returns, whereas falling real rates after 1980 boosted their returns. To explain why wealthier households hold longer-duration assets, I develop a model in which households select portfolio duration to hedge their income risk. Since richer households’ income correlates more with short-term interest rates, they optimally choose a longer-duration (countercyclical) to hedge this exposure.
talks.subtheme: Top Incomes, Wealth Shares and Concentration
talks.title: Scale-dependent returns and the interest rate

talks.abstract: In this paper, we introduce novel estimates of wealth inequality, integrating the standard household wealth concept with newly assessed individual human capital. Using microdata and national accounts from numerous countries since 1979, we explore the distribution across age, gender, education, and occupation. Our analysis reveals two key findings: human capital is more evenly distributed than financial capital, and total wealth, the sum of human and financial capital, is significantly more equal than financial wealth alone. This study offers a groundbreaking perspective on global wealth dynamics, emphasizing the critical, yet often overlooked, role of human capital in wealth distribution.
talks.subtheme: Human capital as wealth
talks.title: The Global Distribution of Human and Nonhuman Wealth

talks.abstract:
We estimate the parameters of a macroeconomic model of the dynamics of the distribution of
wealth - as driven by stochastic earnings, differential savings, and capital income risk. We do not
impose any assumption on the stationarity of the process, centering in fact on the transitional
dynamics of the wealth distribution in the U.S. in the period we have SCF data for - from 1962-
63 to 2022. We show that the model, at the estimated parameter values, fits well the dynamics
of the wealth distribution in the U.S., accurately producing the dramatic increase in inequality
observed in this period, which is the focus of most policy debates, e.g., about wealth taxation.
We show how tax reforms - and how agents anticipate them - affect wealth accumulation. We
identify (conditions on) future taxation processes which induce the dynamics to be stationary;
that is, which lead wealth inequality to settle. Furthermore, we study the dynamics of the racial
wealth gap and the relative role of stochastic earnings, differential savings, and capital income
risk in driving it. We identify conditions of tax processes leading the gap to explode vs to be
eliminated. We simulate the effects of reparations - that is, the transfer of a given amount of
wealth to blacks - to assess conditions under which they would eliminate the racial wealth gap.
talks.subtheme: Savings, Capital Accumulation and Wealth Mobility
talks.title: Non-Stationary Wealth Dynamics and Taxation in the U.S. With an Application to the Racial Gap

talks.abstract:
Research on the long-run evolution of inequality heavily relies on reconstructions of top shares, abstracting from what happens to the remainder 90% of the population. Moreover, the dimensions of social stratification that lie behind inequality figures are usually not considered. Relying on grouped data from the Netherlands between 1950 and 1976, this paper studies inequality and social stratification for the total population by creating multivariate synthetic microdata, covering the distribution of income as well as additional socio-demographic information. The paper seeks to answer the question whether the Trente Glorieuses were truly glorious for everyone. To the best of my knowledge, it is the first paper that studies income inequality during this period in such detail. 

(The paper is still work in progress, but a full draft is expected by the start of the conference.)
talks.subtheme: Historical Series and Archives
talks.title: Glorious for whom? Income inequality in the Netherlands during les Trente Glorieuses
